Oh Supergiant Games, how wonderful you are.
Another gem from this developer, filled with beautiful art from Jen Zee!
In comparison to their past two titles, you will see these differences:
- The game is much more text intensive (there's an option to skim through if you're not too keen on reading).
- Relies heavily on choices.
I love playing games; in fact, I own over a thousand of them; but the games I cherish most are ones I can feel involved in; ones that the story lingers with you when you stop playing and you contemplate your next moves even when you're away from the game; heck, you even dream about them during your sleep.
This game gives you the option to define who you are in the world and how your companions fare and how the story progresses.
While in reality your ending world state outcome is restricted to 2 choices, it's how you weave the world that matters. Think of it this way, we as the human race, all die in the end; it's the marks we make and the bonds we form that matter above all else.
Your choices not only define your outcome, but those of your companions and your adversaries.
Will you let your adversaries win out of mercy? Or will you go for glory? This becomes much more of a challenge on higher difficulties as winning battles will be much harder.
In the end, apart from a world state, you will see how everyone fared after your choices, ranging from your companions and neutral characters, to your adversaries, and with there being so many possible battle outcomes, there's a lot of different outcomes that you can experience for your characters.
You lead a group of exiles towards freedom. During your quest, your band of merry folk form bonds: friendships within the group and rivalry with your adversaries.
Your choice for who goes free (be it your adversary or your fellow exiles), impacts those bonds. Do you want two lovers to be reunited? adversaries who might fall in love to be kept together? friends to stay with one another?
There's also the matter of choosing who you are as a person in the game. You can be cocky, smart or humble; you can show mercy to your enemies or you can crush their spirits over time.
This game is something that you will look at and remember fondly, just as every other Supergiant Game title.

I purchased Hook on a whim at full price. I wasn't expecting much out of it, to be completely honest. It looked like a simple, quick puzzle game that I could work through during small spirts of free time.
Each puzzle is a series of locks and lines. In order to complete each level, the lines must be cleared out. In order to do that, you have to click connecting circles in a certain order. Some circles activate and eliminate lines. Others connect activation circles to different lines so lines can be eliminated in order.
Pros:
- The controls are really straight forward: you're clicking on circles with your mouse.
- The puzzles get gradually more complex as the game goes on.
- There's enough challenge to be worth the money, but not so much that you think the game is impossible during the later levels.
- It's minimal and easy to look at.
- The entire game experience is pretty relaxing.
Cons:
- There's only 50 levels.
- There's no replayability once you beat the game.
- Once you make a certain number of mistakes, you have to start the level over. If you're in a level that has a large number of steps, this can be incredibly frustrating.
For $0.99, it's a pretty good buy for people who like puzzle games. Don't expect to get more an a couple of hours out of it though.

is a simplistic puzzle game. The goal is to clear each level by removing all the lines. The lines intertwine and are hooked into each other. You need to look for lines that are clear to be removed, and then determine the right way to use the game's mechanics in order to pull those lines away from the rest. Each time you 'pull', you have to make sure you don't pull at a line that's stuck and can't be removed yet, because that means you have to restart the level. In the game's later levels, you get three strikes before you're out, so you're allowed to make up to three mistakes before you need to restart the level.
The game has 50 levels. The problem with
is that at least half of those levels are 'tutorial', teaching the player the different mechanics they need to know to solve the later, more difficult levels. So
has a very, very mild learning curve and I'm sure that will test some players' patience.
Even though they offer no challenge whatsoever, clicking through the first 25 to 35 levels  does pay off in the end, when you're finally offered challenging levels where you need to put everything you learned into practice. You'll know when 'the real game begins' when you see three dots appear on the screen, representing the mistakes you're allowed to make before the level resets.
Considering you only get 15 or 20 'real' puzzles after a very slow build-up,
is still worth playing because those last few puzzles are fun to solve and the full price of the game is only 99 cents, so you can often buy it for even less.

Excellent tactical fleet battle game not just for Galactica fans, but for anyone who likes tactical "strategy" games where battles are solved with tactics more than the speed of your index finger like in RTS games. If you like the WeGo system (think Combat Mission) or pausable real-time (think Total War), the odds are you'll appreciate the need for considered tactics in BSG Deadlock as well.
The pros:
- Hey, it's Battlestar Galactica!
- Seriously the BSG world, even if you're not a fan of the series, gives the game and its ships and ship classes more background and character than you would have if this were a generic scifi game.
- It's not just about massing firing on a target until its HP drops to zero. Maneuvering under fire and while maneuvering matters, as does controlling damage to your ships and timing your missile volleys, flak screens and broadsides.
- Almost all ship classes are well balanced and remain relevant throughout the game and in multiplayer.
- No resource gathering or tech trees involved except on the campaign map on a very rudimentary level.
- It's visually appealing but runs on older PCs as well.
The cons:
- The campaign has limited replay value and lacks both narrative and gameplay depth.
- Some of the effects feel like they are 10 years out of place with the rest of the game engine.
- The AI fleet size is capped to the same as the player's, which makes it difficult to get challenge out of the AI in skirmish mode after you've mastered the game.

I am not a Gothic fan; I have not played previous games in the series.  I came to Arcania without expectations colored by the previous games.  I chose 'recommended' only because Arcania is not a terribly bad game.  It's a fairly mediocre RPG.  There are better games out there, no question.  But if you're in an RPG dry spell and you can get Arcania on sale, it's not a bad 40 or so hours.  It's also pretty stable, the only crash I had was after minimizing several times.
The graphics are fine for 2010.  The game lacks AA but the jaggies didn't really bother me here.  I did have problems with the horizon between the sky and sea blinking constantly, but I don't know if that's an original flaw in the game or it just isn't aging well with newer graphics cards and drivers.  For the most part the game looks pretty good.  The big exception is the human characters.  In dialogs the hair is frequently translucent and faces can look horrible.
For me, the strength of Arcania lies in its combat (melee at least, I didn't use bow and arrow much at all).  I chose to focus on melee and go sword & board.  The combat relies on flurries and power swings.  The flurry system is very similar to combat in The Witcher.  Combine that with dodge rolling to escape getting hit and you have a fairly engaging melee combat system.  I thought melee combat in Arcania was more engaging than in any Elder Scrolls game I've played  (even though, yes, every Elder Scroll game I've played is overall much, much better than Arcania).
The magic system is very simplistic - 3 types of magic (fire, frost, electric) with added features gained on leveling up the appropriate skill.  The magic system enhances the melee combat nicely: you can paralyze opponents with the electricity spell or slow them with the frost spell, before attacking them.  But it's nothing like the complexity in Two Worlds 2.
Crafting is a bit of a let down.  It's all done in a menu, no need to be at a bench or specific location.  I found weapon and armor crafting to be almost useless (except for the one quest specific crafting of a weapon).  Alchemy and cooking was more robust with a decent selection of potions and recipes to buff/heal your character in various ways.
The story is fairly standard - an unknown man (you cannot play as a female) saves the world.  The story starts off as a revenge tale, which would have been just fine, but by the end it morphs into a save the world cliché.  The game is pretty straight forward.  There is the main quest and various side quests.  There are no factions to join or advance in like in Elder Scroll games or Two Worlds (1 and 2).  Arcania is not open world like Oblivion or Skyrim.  Various sections of the world open up as you advance the main quest, similar to Two Worlds 2 or The Witcher.
I've played worse RPGs.  Arcania is stripped down and bare bones compared to something like Oblivion or The Witcher.  I had fun with it considering its limitations.  If I had to do it all over again, I would have waited to get Arcania on sale if I had a fantasy RPG itch that couldn't be scratched in any other way.  It definitely wasn't worth the $50 I paid back in 2010.  But given that I bought it, I don't think it was a total waste of my money.

This game is worth the money and worth your time. It strikes a balance on many fronts that make it a great experience:
1. It's turn based and tactical, but just realtime enough that you can't easily 'solve' for the perfect action. Movements are planned on a turn-by-turn basis, and directional armor makes positioning important, but the simultaneous turns still allow for surprises.
2. It has enough different classes of ships to bring variety, but few enough that each one is distinct from the others. Both factions have: a scout corvette, a light carrier/cruiser, a gunship, a missileboat, a light capital, and a heavy capital.
3. Fleet limits can get to a point where you have a lot to manage per turn, but remain small enough that each individual ship matters. Ship cap is seven (doesn't count the fighters those ships can bring) and maximum point cap is 8000 (where a scout ship is 500, and the biggest battlestar is 2150).
The developer has provided ongoing support, adding multiple quality of life improvements, bugfixes, and new features post-release.
This game really makes you feel like you're tactically commanding a fleet. You can burn through the campaign quickly, or loiter about building up your forces and battling the additional cylon fleets that come to besiege the colonies out from under you. Overall, it offers a focused, quality experience, surprising replay value, and just good fun.

TL;DR: NidHogg 2 is the sequel to Nidhogg, a fencing like game where you must go through stages to get to your opponent's side and win. Your opponent must also do the same and push back through stages. The first person to get to their opponent's side win. This game is a beautiful graphical game with some gore but is fun for singleplayer and multiplayer.
The visuals are an amazing improvement single Nidhogg. In the first game, the colours were dull on the characters and not much detail on the background. There were just simple stickmen in a random area. In this game, the colours are bright and you have fully fleshed, detailed characters which can be customized to wear shirts, glasses and hats. The backgrounds and effects are also amazingly detailed. When looking at pictures, I thought this game's quality would be awful or near enough to Nidhogg but the game blew me away and surprised me with much better detailed visuals. This game is very well optimised and I could not doubt this game for a second. The explosions are pretty detailed and gored to have ribs and guts blowing off the character when stabbed. Animations are also very good in this game and this game could not be done better for the graphic quality and detail.
: The audio is amazing and I am impressed by the stabbing sounds and the background music as well as the OST. It is amazing quality and I find it one of my fav things about the game.
: The main of the game is to get to your opponent's side and win. Your opponent must also do the same and push back through stages. The first person to get to their opponent's side win. You can either play on multiplayer or do campaign. Friend or Bot? The multiplayer servers are really good as my friend from Australia (I live in the EU) can play with me with less than 100 ping while i get the equal amount of ping, which gives no one an advantage or disadvantage.
The multiplayer is top quality for a game like this and is especially fun with friends or family. The campaign singleplayer is very good also as the bots get harder every round, so you cannot sabotage them to get achievements. The first round is near enough a tutorial level where you can test out the gameplay elements and controls. As you go on, it gets tougher and tougher so you need to learn every control and combo before getting into multiplayer. Treat bots like a training and tutorial area and treat multiplayer as a championship with a friend.
:
Very good visual effects
Beautiful graphic detail
Awesome sound quality
Awesome Multiplayer Servers
Singleplayer Campaign included
:
Certain ping lag on multiplayer on maps like volcano due to the fps lag as well as bad ping at times.

I liked the games and I would definitively recommend it, especially if you have played the other Gothic parts. You will feel „home“ immediately. The only thing I can complain about is that it is way too easy on the normal level. In the whole game I died like 3 times – and the boss fights are a piece of cake as well – very unlike the first three parts – so I would recommend to play in in a more difficult level. The character development has changed and now it is more simplistic compared to the other parts, but I wouldn’t say that it has a negative impact on the experience. I finished the game in about 37 hours, completing most of the side quests as well.

Although I have not dabbled much in the campaign, I do know  that this game has a solid multiplayer aspect which I continue to enjoy even now.
If you love turn based games and real time fleet vs. fleet action, this is the perfect game for you. The UI takes a little getting used to, but once you are it's easy enough to use. If you are a fan of BSG, this is an amazing game to have. The publisher Slitherine does a good job getting criticism of the game straight to the devs, who in their own rights do a pretty good job addressing the community's concerns. This game has very nice graphics (at max, I personally haven't dealt with the lower settings), and the sound track fits the game nicely, but if you don't like it you can simply mute it in settings and put on your own music.
Gameplay consists of turns where both players plan out what their ships will do in the next turn, then the action sequences commence (real time battles where ships actually duke it out instead of some cheap knockoff games where they fire shots at each other and make you sit through healthbars counting down to zero). These action sequences enact the plans of both players at the same time. Part of the fun is trying to predict what your opponent will do next and finding ways to counter it. The strategic depth is well... deep. I find myself spending as much time building fleets as I do making them battle it out in a multiplayer match.
Gravitating more towards the multiplayer aspect, I wasn't let down by what I saw.

From October to December I too was very enthusiastic about this game and I actually spent several months defending it from people calling it War Z 2.0 and not giving it an honest chance. (I just recently activated it on Steam) They were wrong at the time, but in the end they were right. The developers slowly stopped listening to the community and started locking threads that aimed to civilly discuss ethical choices made by the developers regarding the introduction of microtransactions in a non-cosmetic fashion. It started with backpacks and tactical grenades. Now things are a lot worse.
Here are the things Nether Gold buys you:
Camo outfits/team outfits: If you don't think blending in with your environment or being instantly identified by team members in close quarters team combat is purely cosmetic, you've been fooled.
Flashlights and flares: Yeah, not really a big deal. But we're playing a survival RPG. The name of the game is loot loot loot. If you can pay for it with real money what's the point?

Nether potions: Are you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by that sniper who killed you? No worries, spawn in as a nether, run 60km/h to his spot, and take him out. Your team mates can now take his shiny military backpack, congrats!
The king daddy of Nether P2W, Golden Keys: I don't think I need to explain this one, but I will. In a game where you literally do two things: Loot and kill things, (the success of killing things heavily depending on how well you loot) you can pay to do one of those things way, way better and easier? They're magical sacks that blind you from a block away, drop stacks upon stacks of MONEY, GUNS, AMMO, and MEDICAL SUPPLIES. Only if you happen to have paid the developers an extra fee of course. Disregard all of the other points. If you don't think Golden Keys -alone- are enough to qualify this game P2W, you're probably a delusional fanboy like I once was when I opened Nether on public beta day 1.
These are just the problems that involve P2W. I could talk for days about how poorly the game has developed and how the developers are now abandoning ship with a last $2.99 cash grab, but that's not the point.

That is a hyperbole, of course.
Yet rarely if ever have I played a game that was such a complete package whilst exceeding in nearly every category and failing in no perceivable aspect.
I have heaped praise upon Supergiant Games' works before, but I fully believe that Pyre stands head and shoulders above Bastion and Transistor.
If you wish for a more measured review, look elsewhere. I have loved the game and urge you with all my heart for you to play it. This review will instead focus more on comparing Pyre to its two predecessors, and see how I feel it measures up.
The reason I took so long to play Pyre is because I truly believed I would dislike its gameplay. It is a sports game - after a fashion - and that isn't something I appreciate. My fears were soon quenched, however, as Pyre's gameplay proved itself a stupidly fast-paced, diverse and engaging experience, all the while containing the action to a single small field, six players and a ball. It is a condensation of everything that made Bastion and Transistor stand out, a microcosm that packs an unbelievable punch.
Every match is different than the last. The terrain, environmental effects, each one of the six players on the field, their skills and items - any alteration in any of those variables can make for an entirely unique experience. If you are intimidated by Pyre's gameplay being like a sports game - fear not. You will be white-knuckled in excitement in no time.
The rest of Pyre's gameplay consists of an Oregon Trail-ish roaming about the magnificent environs, choosing which paths to take, not unlike Banner Saga. Orienting yourself by the stars is a nice touch that melds world-building into decision-making.
I am not knowledgeable about music - at all. So take everything I say here with a grain of salt. Pyre's music is on par with its predecessors - though I do believe it takes a definitive edge by the way in which it is used. The vocals always kick in to throw the dramatic curve over the edge, to outline the stakes of everything you're doing. And, best of all, they subtly alter their lines in accordance to who you're fighting, and the final outcome of the game.
Nothing as iconic or immediatelly quotable as Build that Wall from Bastion - yet still, I feel, more impactful.
As wonderful and engaging as Caelondia or Cloudbank. Perhaps more. I feel the world is much more fleshed out, but that isn't really the point.
Pyre's narrative - is one that you, the player, build yourself, through the Rites you perform, through the characters you choose, and- through both victory and defeat.
Pyre has no apparent explicit or implied fail state, insofar as story progression is concerned. There are no possible Game Overs. Whether you succeed or fail, the story continues, taking that failure into account. Experience is awarded to your character regardless of the outcome of the match. The point of the Rites isn't victory - but Enlightenment.
Every one of those twists and turns can affect the ending, leading to an embarassingly large number of them - for they revolve around the fates of each particular character, and their contributions to the state of things after the game is over.
There is no Best Ending, or True Ending. This is what makes Pyre even more heartwrenching than its predecessors. There are instead a multitude of endings, none of which can satisfy the existential void which sets in. This pain - it is a bittersweet pain.
Pyre -is- its characters. And this is the crucial point.
Supergiant Games excel in most aspects, but I feel like Bastion and Transistor's characters weren't the focus of their respective games. To be sure, there are good characters in those games-
-But they cannot hope to compare to Pyre.
Pyre has a stable of characters with both variety and depth. Companions and rivals. Playable and non-playable. It feels like each character is important in and of itself, as you discover more about them, as you have repeated exchanges with them, friendly or otherwise, growing closer and more familiar.
And it is, of course, reinforced by gameplay. Each playable character plays differently, as does every rival character. And you have a real stake in deciding what happens to each one of them, and how these decisions will organically weave new threads between them and throughout the major story.
And what happens to each and every one of them is both a source of joy and sadness alike, especially because you know you had a hand in their fates. You might even feel tempted to purposefully lose a match or two, in order to ensure a brighter future for one of your favorite rivals. All of this in turn leads back to the sheer variety of endings.
Pyre's greatest strength is the way gameplay, narrative, characters and even music are tightly bound together into a complete, amazing package. What are you doing? Play it already!

The game isn't really about the Rites (a.k.a. Pyreball). They are important part, of course, but if you're looking for 3vs3 basketball in fantasy setting, look somewhere else. Pyre is about the story and your choices. The small ones, like choosing dialog option to get a piece of lore and the big ones, where you decide who from the group of exiles shall gain a chance to be free. And when the game makes you stop thinking "I won't free X, because I'll lose my strongest player" and starts you thinking "I don't think Y would be happy after being free in Commonwealth" or "My opponent deserves freedom more, so I'll lose this Rite", then you have a game that creates the relationship with characters well. Pyre does that.
The story goes on no matter what happens. You may lose a Rite, even a liberation Rite. You may lose all the Rites and still see the ending. It probably won't be the happiest ending, but I don't think there are bad endings. Maybe the main Plan will fail, but life of your characters goes on, not matter if they return to Commonwealth or stay exiled in the Downside. The story definitely has some strong moments, plot twists, well written characters and makes you think what "freedom" really is.
There are also some Supergiant characteristic traits - beautiful visuals and music, great one-voice narration (even though this time each character has it's voice) and "make-our-own-hardmode" system, where you raise XP gained by making the game more difficult.
The Rites themselves... well, for me that part was quite good. I like the idea and in many cases it was quite pleasant. Yet there were moments where the action was a bit chaotic. I didn't like the controls, sometimes they seem unresponsive, jumps weren't precise and switching characters was a bit random. And it may get a bit repetitive. But still, it was a good story-filler.
Summary: don't by the game for the Rites ("main gameplay"). Buy it for the characters participating in Rites, reason they participate in Rites and the results of the Rites. Buy the games for all the parts where you have to read/listen, not where you have to act.

DOOM (later re-released as The Ultimate DOOM in 1995) is a first person shooter developed by id Software and released on December 10th 1993, only a year after the mega-hit success of Wolfenstein 3D. What is there that hasn't already been said about the single most prolific FPS game of the 1990's? Even decent 'Doom clones' like Heretic, successors like Quake, 'Doom killers' like Duke Nukem 3D, and the one and only Half-Life five years down the line couldn't quite fully capture the magic and essence that was DOOM's unmatched and timeless gameplay, perfect balance, highly memorable cast of foes and weaponry, simple yet creative level design, and among the largest modding communities still around to this day.
The development of DOOM began in late 1992, as John Carmack finished creating a new, more versatile 3D engine to power id's next title. While John was busy, the rest of id had closed the chapter of Wolf3D with the release of Spear of Destiny, a prequel to the original game. While Wolf3D enjoyed a large success, being the first FPS game to lay down the groundwork for what would become the most popular video game genre, their new game would be 'Wolfenstein times a million'. The hype was real. Unlike Wolf3D, with its fantasy World War II setting, old castles and fortified bunkers crawling with Nazi denizens, DOOM's main thematic influences would be a crossover between the sci-fi setting of the film Aliens with the demonic occult elements of the film Evil Dead 2, as well as a game of Dungeons & Dragons the developers had been playing prior. Originally, DOOM was in fact going to be an Aliens game, until the license fell through. The title of DOOM was also inspired by cinema, from a scene in The Color of Money, where Tom Cruise shows up at a pool hall with a custom pool cue in a case. When asked what he has in there, he simply replies 'Doom.' with a sadistic grin. This would not only set the tone of the game, but in turn would also spell literal doom for the competition, even in the rapidly evolving games industry.
The backstory of DOOM's events is fairly detailed despite being minimalistic overall, ultimately throwaway once you launch the game. Minus an intermission screen consisting of a wall of text at the end of an episode, all you need to know off the bat is that you're a badass space marine in the future, having been transferred to Mars, which is home of the Union Aerospace Corporation. This multi-planetary conglomerate, with the military as their biggest supplier, has facilities on Mars and its two moons Phobos and Deimos, conducting various secret projects, such as research on inter-dimensional space travel, while you and your squad are on standby in orbit, authorized to only come down if an unruly situation were to arise. Turns out it's your lucky day, as a garbled message is received from Phobos, requesting immediate military support as 'something evil's coming out of the gateways'. The rest was incoherent. Soon after Deimos simply vanishes from the radar, with attempts to contact either moon unsuccessful. You and your buddies arrive on Phobos, while you're ordered to secure the perimeter of the base the rest of the team go inside. Not long after your radio picks up sounds of gunfire, men yelling, flesh ripping and finally silence. Whatever happened in there, it ain't good, and it's all up to you now.
Unlike Wolf3D, DOOM's id Tech 1 technology allows for far more advanced architecture and expansive environments than its predecessor, with varying height levels, non-orthogonal walls, full texture mapping including floors and ceilings, varying light levels, light diminishing to create depth from a distance and enhance the atmosphere, increased interactivity like platforms that move up and down, user operable switches and environmental hazards like dangerous pools of liquid, crushing ceilings and monster closets, animated textures and objects, a stereo sound system with support of up to eight sounds simultaneously (without a source port) and MIDI playback for music. While still not fully 3D, this 2.5D space was way more impressive and immersive than anything that had come before it. The only real downside was that with so much more fidelity the game had to be ran at a capped frame rate of 35 whereas Wolf3D ran at a very silky smooth 70. This isn't an issue nowadays with source ports that allow an uncapped frame rate though.
The gameplay hasn't changed much from Wolf3D. Designer Tom Hall wrote an elaborate design document called the Doom Bible, to which the game would've featured a much more detailed storyline, multiple player characters, a hub level system that predated Hexen, and a number of interactive features far beyond the scope of what would've been possible in 1993. Most of his ideas were discarded during development in favor of more simpler design, advocated by John Carmack and John Romero. Early versions of DOOM had treasure items to collect and a scoring system as well as a lives counter, all of which were dropped by the end, distanting itself from Wolf3D. DOOM is however similarly split into episodes, each containing eight maps and one secret map, with three episodes in total for the original release and an added fourth for The Ultimate DOOM. The goals of play are simple: Kill everything that doesn't look like you, locate valuable munitions and items to aid you in accomplishing this objective, acquire keys to advance further in the levels, ultimately locating the source of the invasion and destroying it, living to tell the tale if possible.
The enemy cast expands upon Wolf3D's five or so types with up to seven common types and two huge bosses. Possessed former marines with rifles and shotguns, the fireball throwing demonic humanoid Imps, shaved gorilla-looking beasts who lack a ranged attack but will charge to bite your face off, including near invisible versions of them, hard to hit flying demonic skulls on fire, the iconic Cacodemon with its sinister one eyed gaze and toothy grin belching powerful projectiles at you, and the rare but mighty Barons of Hell, who are a classic representation of Baphomet. The weapon variety is also greater than Wolf3D. Merely beginning with just your fist and a pistol, you'll soon grab a hold of a trusty shotgun, rapid fire chaingun, powerful rocket launcher and deadly experimental energy weapons like the plasma rifle and series' famous BFG9000. If you go out your way to explore you might even find a chainsaw, perfect for lesser foes who venture too close. Your fist can also become one of the most powerful tools in the game with the aid of a Berserk Pack pickup, allowing you to rip and tear ordinary dolts to pieces. In the absence of treasure, artifacts from the other dimension litter the world, from things like small health and armor bonuses, to full health recoveries above and beyond your normal value, as well as temporary near invisibility or complete invulnerability.
Visually the game aged extremely well, with a lot of care and attention put into detailing the texture and sprite work, this was from a time where devs put as much effort as they could into what little they had to work with and it shows to this day. Sound design contains a lot of stock sound FX but a lot of it is memorable and still effective in bringing things alive. Bobby Prince once again worked on the score and the soundtrack is a combination of high octane metal-esque tunes to get the blood pumping as well as more dreary, atmospheric mixes to reflect the horror side of the game.
My criticisms ultimately boil down to some not so great maps here and there in the later episodes, the lesser variety of monsters compared to its landmark sequel resulting in overall easier fights even when playing on Ultra-Violence, and a lackluster final boss. But other than that? It's a damn near perfect game, and with the amount of source ports, mods and maps on offer to this day, DOOM will never die. Only the players.

If you're coming to Pyre hoping for something like Bastion or Transistor, that's not what you'll get.  What you'll get is something far greater.  Pyre is an outstanding RPG that blew me away in categories I wasn't even expecting.
Obviously, the gameplay is superb.  The controls are tuned perfectly, on keyboard or gamepad.  The basketball-like ceremony of the Rites is amazing.  The triumvirates' moves all feel good to use, and none are too overpowered.
Mechanics themselves are quite innovative, and I've never seen anything like them before.  For time's sake, I'll leave it at this: everything about conducting the Rites works, and it's a remarkably solid foundation for the rest of the game.
The story really is crazy good in Pyre.  I can't go too far because of spoilers, but basiclly you are an exile with the unique gift of reading.  You can interpret the Book of Rites, and can thus lead your new exile friends through the Rites.  Through the them, exiles can be liberated.  Plus, tons of stuff about the Eight Scribes, and more.  The story might even beat out the gameplay in terms of sheer amazingness.  If that's even a word.
Now, in between the Rites is where it can be slightly not fun if you're not into the story.  Between each Rite you navigate through the land, get items, and most of the time speak with your companions.  It's a lot of reading, but if the story hooks you, and it almost certainly will, you'll enjoy it.
This is Pyre's one RPG element: your characters have stats that can be raised and lowered.  That's pretty much it, save a few times where your choices will matter for the rest of the game.  If you're seaching for something that is heavy with RPG elements, still play Pyre, it's amazing, but keep looking for a more RPGey RPG.
To sum everything up, play Pyre if you like innovatively great gameplay, a world ridden with lore, reading, and a single RPG element.  Enjoy Pyre!

Highly recommend this game.
It cannot be stressed enough just how much value you're actually getting in this game.
SHMUPS typically have less replayability than other games. You beat it and then you either never play again or you play it again in case you missed the "True Final Boss".
The Darius Series was probably most well known for its branching paths, which gives it far more replayability than other games. You play a level and you choose between 2 levels, and you choose again, and again, you get the idea.
This one in particular is a bit different because it lets you choose 3 different starting levels, which branch out into different levels. There are 12 levels in Another Chronicle Mode and 12 DIFFERENT levels in Another Chronicle EX for a grand total of 24 levels in the AC Mode.
Sadly each Another Chronicle (and ACEX) Run ends quicker than the previous games because you only play 3/12 stages (G-Darius let you play 5/15 stages and Darius Gaiden let you play 7/28 stages, but you started on the same first level unlike DariusBurst CS), but the levels are excellently designed.
But none of this matters if the game is unfun, right? Well it's a very fun game. It's also difficult to beat if you're not credit-feeding the entire game. The scoring system probably isn't as complex as your average Cave bullet hell (which I think might actually be complex for the sake of complexity) but the scoring system is complex enough to allow for a meaningful leaderboard.
Based on all of this alone, this game is definitely a bit more expensive but it's well worth the asking price.
This doesn't even get into the two extra modes added into this release though.
The two extra modes, Chronicle Mode (It's found in the AC Mode Menu) and Chronicle Saviours Mode (It's the CS Mode right under AC Mode.).
Chronicle Mode is a... different online mode that spans some 3000+ levels. As you and players work to clear these, more levels get unlocked for everyone (provided you're also online). Chances are you won't beat this without seriously investing your time into it regardless of skill.
Chronicle Saviours Mode is the single player campaign (200+ levels too!). They're more like missions where you accomplish certain tasks, sometimes with limitations imposed on you (like no powerup drops). The main draw of this mode is the ability to customize your ship. After each mission you obtain points, and those points go towards ships and upgrades. There are also 3 exclusive ships in this mode that cannot be played with in AC Mode.
Each mission has a "preset" ship, and most customization options will be locked off towards the beginning simply because purchasing a ship chassis is really really expensive.
This game with its some 3224+ levels total is an insane value and by the numbers already justifies the pricing.
Who knows, maybe some of these levels are rehashes or remixes of others? But I think the game is fun enough to warrent playing over and over again.
ALSO On an interesting note, they brought back the whole double monitor setup from the first 2 Darius games (for AC Mode). Shame they couldn't do the same for CS Mode or even provide the option for single or double monitor modes for both modes without any letterboxing.
100% Buy it. The SHMUP industry is dying and show your support for these devs.

The best and most shmup you can buy on Steam.
It's hard to explain how huge this game is. Do you want a lengthy single-player campaign that will take you many hours to complete? CS mode is that. Do you want a classic Darius experience with multiple routes? It has two of those modes: Original and Original EX. Do you want a huge selection of different challenges? Chronicle mode has hundreds and hundreds of challenges with thousands of stages. Even if you aren't the type who plays arcade games repeatedly in order to get higher scores, there's still enough here to occupy you for hundreds of hours.
And how is this gigantic game? In a word: incredible. Dariusburst takes a different tack than many modern bullet hell shooters and instead goes for what I'd call popcorn hell. Huge swarms of tiny enemies and asteroids are everywhere. The bosses are huge, have a large variety of attacks, and are exhilarating to fight. Don't think it's just swarms and bosses, though: there are plenty of bullet-firing medium sized enemies and stage walls to contend with, too. Dariusburst is very much its own thing and doesn't cleanly fit into any of the shmup archetypes.
The scoring system is relatively simple, with a multiplier that ticks up when you destroy waves of enemies and gets reduced when you get hit. Kill an entire enemy wave and the you get a score bonus multiplied by your current multiplier. Kill the final enemy of a wave with your rechargeable laser or bomb and you get that same bonus multiplied by 16. This means the best scoring tactic is to kill everything and try to eliminate the final enemy of each wave with your laser/bomb. This is easier said than done, so there's a lot of depth here in figuring out the ideal movement and timing for killing enemy waves. Bosses fire their own lasers and if you time it right, you can fire your own laser into that laser (like in G-Darius) and counter it for massive damage and large amounts of points if you kill the boss with the resulting counterburst.
The art design is great. It doesn't push a lot of polygons (this is an enhanced port of an arcade game based on a PSP game, after all) but the art more than makes up for it. Backgrounds can be astonishingly beautiful and the boss designs are great. There are also a large number of references to previous Darius games that are cool to pick out. Sound effects are well done. Nothing to write home about (apart from the wonderful boss alert siren), but they get the job done. The music is incredible. The "Freedom" song in the trailer is love-it-or-hate-it (I'm in the latter camp) but it's easily the least good of a long and lengthy soundtrack. The way the soundtrack is perfectly synchronized in the arcade modes is awe-inspiring.
There's only two real flaws with this game. The huge number of modes and missions means that high scores are scattered across a bunch of leaderboards rather than being concentrated and more competitive. Second, there's no practice mode for individual stages and bosses in AC mode. Some of the bosses (looking at YOU, Phantom Castle) have some really mean attacks and it would be nice to be able to practice them in AC mode without going through a series of stages beforehand. CS mode lets you select individual stages, so you can sort of use it for practice, but the aspect ratio is so different that it's not really the same thing as the AC mode boss fights.
All in all, I can't recommend this game enough. The price may be high but it is totally worth it given both the length and quality of Dariusburst: Chronicle Saviours.

using your firearms rather than requiring you to switching back and forth. Even better, the cooldowns on major abilities are reasonable and there's no annoying MP/SP systems.  No "saving it for when I REALLY need it" here.  Go wild and give your enemies a new, bettter reason to fear the dark (if only for the last few seconds of their life).  Hell, you can feasibly go through the whole game without ever using the guns to fight.  I know I certainly had much more fun ripping and slashing and impaling and decapitating everyone in sight with every
in sight than traditional "shoot, run forward, shoot" could have delivered.

Want to rule the world like a James Bond Villain?  Want to laugh maniacally as the world falls at you feet?  Want to show those James Bond wanna bes who's the boss?  Want to spend more time building your evil lair than taking over the world?  Want to spend most of your time waiting for your money to build up?  Want to micromange every little detail when your minions should be doing the job themselves?  Then this game is for you!
Ok in all seriousness even though this game has it's flaws I still think it's a great game.  It just has several big flaws that brings it down.  The waiting for money is my biggest issue.  You would think for a simulation game a fast forward button would be standard, not this one.  That's right you only have play and pause at your fingertips.  Well I hope you have something else to do whilst your waiting for that money to come in because there's little else to do whilst your waiting for the money.
The micromanaging can get very monotanous very quickly.  You see since your evil activities are causing the world to send their "very best" spies to put a stop to your activities you have to keep an eye.  Minions won't automatically attack spies without you tagging them first.  Meaning your going to be randomly searching your base to see if any spies have landed and you really need to keep an eye out otherwise your beautiful base will be ruined in seconds (and trust me that is THE last thing you want unless you enjoy the waiting game).
The basebuilding is the main part of the game.  Really this game should be called Evil Lair Architect.  Not that thats a bad thing the base building is very good.  It's the only simulation game I've played that allows you to plan out a building without it being built first.  This I like alot and other games would benefit from it, Simcity being one.  It's the optimazation of making your minions work hard and keeping spies out that make it a big draw for me however it's the waiting that makes it toturous.
The minions themselves are divided into classes that do certain jobs.  You start of with a basic construction worker that do all the building for you that can then level up.  Scientists can do research for you to get new items (you can decide how they research the items but honestly this system is just luck based).  You have security minions that will beat up the spies.  You then have the social minions that can confuse spies into forgetting their mission (just like mp's).
Taking over the world has little to it.  It's literly just a map.  Thats it.  You sends minions onto the map to complete missions or collect money for you.  Minions of different classes can do certain jobs better but honestly I would have appreciated a playable map similar to XCOM: Enemy Unkown.  Anything that makes the waiting more pleasant.
If your graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ then I'm afraid this game will not satisfy you.  Granted it's an old game but even for it's age it doesn't look good (Rayman 2 was released 4 years before this one and looks just as good).
The only thing that keeps this game up is it's charm and premise.  It's filled with humour (they interogate minions by dancing and putting them in a blender whats not to like?).  The premise itself is also interesting too.  Taking over the world who doesn't want to do that?  Honestly though these are the only things keeping it good for me along with the building mechanics.  If those aren't enough then I'm afraid this game is not for you.  If it is for you then I'd suggest waiting until this game goes on sale first.  Yes it is cheap to begin with at £7 but If your going to be dissappointed (and I wouldn't be surprised if you do) then get it cheap.

I enjoy the combat and the feel of things but after 50 hours the tactics are becoming woefully repetitive.
Another issue that is fustrating is that you have no idea of the size of an enemy fleet prior to engaging so in the mid to late game this renders small fleets with green officers pointless. The only safe way to encounter fleets is by sending your best fleets with best officers.

After approximately 10 hours of gameplay, I got the distinct impression that very little (if any) balancing or play testing went into this game.  I did finish this game before reviewing it, to give a complete impression.  I have never played the original Gothic games, so my I have no input on how close it is to the originals.
I will start with what I felt was wrong.  One, because if your reading this review, that is likely all you care about.  Two, because I believe on closing on a good note.
Cons:
1. The run speed!  Oh my god it is way too slow, and they made the horrible decision of throttling the speed even more when inside.  This made completing the game feel like a Sisyphean task.
2. Invisible walls and impassible gentle slopes.  It is a major pet peeve to have apparently impassible terrain made impassible.
3. Skill tree balancing.  It is not.  Melee is the best, and that’s good because that is what you will mostly find upgrades for.  Archery can be good, but upgrades are sparse.  Magic is a joke.  Even at max level magic is mostly just a support for melee. The skills feel like they are less balanced against each other, and more like they should all compliment each other at max level.  This is technically impossible without cheats however.
4. Inconsistent hit boxes.  This may even be worse than the run speed.  Having a skill that increases damage for head shots on archery, and then only giving some creatures miniscule hit boxes with no head consideration.  The giant lizards are the greatest culprit of this.  It is so difficult to "hit" them with the bow at all, I usually just switched to untrained melee.
5. The voice acting.  The script writing and voice acting for this was bad to the point of being silly.
6. Creepy animations and Graphical errors.  Diego's smile is unnaturally wide.  When in high settings the textures will turn black. When characters talk seeing a black void, and strangely glowing/lit teeth.
7. Inattention to details in a game with collectables that require attention to detail.  A tip too amateur designers, if you aren't going to put the effort to make your walls meet so the sky box won't be seen behind them, then do not include quests for collectibles that will have players looking in every nook and cranny.  This only makes the lack of polish stick out more.
Pros:
1. Putting the voice acting/script writing aside, the overall story was enjoyable.
2. Role play features that can be disabled.  This feature is diminished by it being a single player game.  It allows for interaction with objects of no game importance, but can be interesting for RP.  Looms, forges, and alchemy benches to name a few.
3. The method for alerting the player of intractable/lootable objects.  This system is the least immersion breaking system I have yet seen.  When a world object is intractable it will have flies flying around it or sparkle, they only doe a highlighting glow when the player is able to pick interact (which is unavoidable to a point).  When a corpse can still be looted it will radiate the appearance of a stinky miasma and have tiny flies buzzing around.

This recommendation comes with the biggest  " * " Possible
Lets get one thing straight first: I absolutely adore this game. I think its the most fun melee combat system in a multiplayer game i have ever played by far. It's simple at first, but is suprisingly deep once you get into it. You got your basic fighting game esque concepts like lights, heavys, blocks, parries and so on, that help to create the familiar rock paper scissors dynamic that is more commonly found in games that Street Fighter for example.
There is a weird downside to the combat though. Similar to the Dark Souls games, the combat clearly was desinged with 1v1 in mind and when faced with more than one opponent the combat breaks slightly. Thankfully there is something to compensate that. The revenge mode is a mechanic that activates when a player is faced with multiple opponents. its a power up mode that boosts all your stats for a couple of seconds. It doesn't completely remove the problem, but it helps. Needles to say the game works much better 1v1 and 2v2, wich are my preferred modes.
Another reason i really like the game are the diffrent heroes. Each of the game's 12 heroes play completely different from each other, with their unique weapons, move sets and specials. You have your all-rounders like Warden and Kensei, the fast glass canon rushdowns like Berserker and Peace Keeper  all the way to zoning keepaway characters like Nobushi. There is a high chance you will find a character that fits you and learning said character may not be the easiest thing ever but it sure is satisfying.
BUT, and this is a huge "BUT" the game is not without it's broblems. The netcode ... well its not great. For honor (for some baffling reason) uses peer to peer netcode, you know the one that ♥♥♥♥s the match up for everyone if a single person leaves mid match. It's really infuriating to see the goddamn circle stopping your game, only to Bites the Dust your♥♥♥♥♥back a few seconds and you end up losing a fight for example due to it. Thankfully as of writing this review i have encountered said issue only around 4 times, so i guess i had luck?
I have seen a lot of people mention the balancing issues too. To be completely honest, i haven't noticed too much of a balance issue. The nature of the game is set up that you can relatively easily beat S-tier characters with low tier ones if you learn the match up. It is a thing that most (if not all) mutiplayer games go through, and will improve over time.
Also something needs to be said about the single player.  It's... well... bland. It's still way better than say, Titanfall's single player, but that's not saying much. I can appreciate it being there but don't expect anything amazing out of it.
Besides some rough aspects, I think the game is great. When the combat clicks, it clicks really hard. The feeling you get after a tough match and landing that last heavy attack to execution that wins the game feels absolutely incredible, and you don't want to stop. The game is absoltely not for everyone since some patience is required to learn the combat, but if you have any interest at all i do recommend this. We dont get games like this too often.

If you're thinking of getting this game wait until its on sale. It is hard to recommend this game to people simply because of all the things you have to look past in order to enjoy it. The voice acting is hit or miss (and when it's miss its a HUGE miss), some character models specifically female characters) look really weird and poorly made, and the first couple of hours are just a huge tutorial filled with horribly boring quests, like "kill the molerats invading my farm" and "Bring me some mead" and "collect some iron bolettes".
The strange tradition in RPGs to start the player out doing menial tasks for other people, like the quests referenced above, is super over-done and desperately needs to be retired for something more meaningful and fun in the beginning of a game. This is especially true when the trailer for said game shows a bunch of awesome monsters to fight but only after you go through hours of "go fetch me this" and "kill these rats!" quests. The Witcher 2 did this great by starting out with that badass castle siege pretty early on. Another RPG to have a great opening was Skyrim where once you got to the first village of Riverwood, you had the ability to begin a quest that sends you through a dungeon filled with bandits and draugr, AND ended with you seeing your first wordwall.

A surprisingly enjoyable game for a small studio working with a dead franchise! The WEGO system makes this game stand out from other space strategy games and it dovetails nicely with the XCOM-styled campaign on offer.
That said, this isn't a AAA game and it shows in places, with a few balance tweaks still to be made and the odd technical flaw on display. However, the devs have already released a roadmap and patches are in the works, so they're committed to further support. I've not encountered anything that severely impacted my enjoyment of the game, anyway.
In summary, a must for BSG fans. As a fan of the show, I can say they've chosen a brilliant system to maintain the show's feel while also offering compelling gameplay. The one main caveat I'd suggest is that it's priced a little high, but I made the decision to support the devs in this case - they probably need it more than any AAA studio trying to sponge up my spare change.
So if you're not a Galactica fan, you may want to wait for the price to come down and for a few kinks to be ironed out. But even without the fanboy hook, this game still has something unique to offer in a genre where it's rubbing shoulders with established names like Sins of a Solar Empire, Battlefleet Gothic, Stellaris, and Endless Space 2. So say we all.

I highly recommend this game, especially if you play on Scooby Shack server its very stable and doesn't restart all the time. The game is not finish and from what it sounds like it's boring (eating and drinking to survive) , but it's a lot more thrilling than you think. When you're playing your dino you consistently look around you if someone is stalking you to be their dinner, when you drink you have to be cautious if there's someone waiting in the water or in the treeline. When your an apex and you're hunting you stalk a prey faster than you, and you get into ambush and go for the kill if you're sneaky enough. This game is a lot of fun with friends you get to make a pack or a herd, as a pack you strategize your hunt, and you defend your kill from other predators (unless the other predator is bigger than you). As a herd you defend your herd from carnivores. Progressing to the carnivore you want to be is so satisfying. the game also changes a lot since it's in early access.  The V4 map is amazing more diverse, everyone is spread out through the map and no mega packs.
The downfall of the game is with it's population there's only a few servers that are populated enough to survive such as wynter, scoobshack, pangea and etc... Sometimes you can't even join those server because they're full.  It is also in early access and there's a lot of bugs (but not game breaking enough to make a lot of people want to quit), progressing takes forever, but not with friends (i didn't have any steam friends that played the isle but I made new friends on the Isle of wynter's discord). But this progression is balanced out with the new nesting system which makes the progression shorter.
overall it's a game that is a unique survival game, and probably the best dino game out there. It's both fun and challenging, and most certainly thrilling. If you enjoy dinosaurs and survival games this is for you.

You see most all of what this game has to offer within the first hour of playing and the screenshots (and especially trailer, is that even the game engine??) make it look a lot better than it actually does in motion. It's an interesting game / series, maybe more appealing to a niche market interested in microbiology, and it can be a bit charming in that it's relaxing to swim along as whatever parasite you are. You occassionally have to "save eggs" and such by swimming into or bouncing various abstract objects around, but beyond pointing your head forward and running into things there's not much to the gameplay. There's an upgrade system which seems to initially be explained as way more complex than it actually is, with the option to upgrade your health or make you go faster (along with a third additional stat I don't remember at this time.)
It's a relaxing game but it looks very simplistic and the gameplay of just swimming along pretty bland, repetitive environments gets old very quickly. I got my fill of the game pretty quickly and have no interest in playing any more of it. If you're really into science or microbiology and / or just looking for a simple, relaxed pace game then maybe give it a try but I think there are many other better games to choose from around its pricepoint.

After 235 hours on the game I can honestly say, it's great it's well worth $60, it's the most fun I have had on a game since Total War: Rome 2, with that being said, all of the negative reviews have a very good point. So I want to go the through the pro's and con's of FOR HONOR, that being pro's and con's of a high level *non cheese hero* player with 235 hours on the game.
Let's start with my favorite the PRO'S
Gameplay 10/10 like Skyrim with guns - IGN. No for real, the game play for this game is the smoothest sword to sword to mace to giant death stick you will ever find. They people crying "It's like rock paper scissors ect. ect." for one are full of♥♥♥♥♥♥and for 2 have never played anything but Dom and if they have they don't fully understand the combat system or how to use the hero they are using, if you want to see how well the combat is put together or how deep it actually is, go watch TrueTalent, ISkys or KingRichard on TwitchTV. I 111% guarentee you will not find any better combat on the market right now. Mount and Blade or Chivalry are the only 2 games that even come CLOSE to touching this and they are still just swing with minimal rewarding feeling for killing someone or blocking an attack.
---
Story: Now this is where in my eyes it's split down the middle for even people who love the game, some say it sucks, some say it's amazing, I'm in the middle, it's good, it's definitely EXTREMELY refreshing to see a game like this come out with an actual story mode in it, where as Rainbow Six Siege got nothing even close, and it was made by the same devs. The story tells why the Vikings, Knights and Samurai are fighting, what they're fighting for and who is behind it all, it gives some funny moments and some good story plots, the weakest link as far as that goes was the Vikings, but I actually found myself caring for 3 of the characters in the story and loved the way it set up for either a sequel or DLC story.
---
Heroes customization and hero selection: The game has 12 very different heros and a literal♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of customization, you want to make your Warden look like the Black Knight from either Monty Python or Family Guy? GO AHEAD! You want to make your Orochi straight up Tom Cruise? GO AHEAD! You want to make your Berserker look like Ragnar from Vikings? GO ♥♥♥♥ING AHEAD! The amount that you can change and fiddle with is awesome, now it's still not one of those games where "You never see the samething twice" it's still got a lot too it and still more coming in free DLC. The 12 heroes that you can choose from the Warden, Dumptuck, Memebringer, Orochi, Kensei, Shrek, Berzerker, Borelord, Mr. Legendary, Mrs. I like to move my right stick and poke you real quick, Nobushi, and Valkyrie all have very different play styles, and all are fun too play in some way shape or form, as you can tell I have a very biased opinion on some of them, because some have problems which will be in the cons section, they are all still very diverse and fun to play in some way, and with a Centurion, Ninja and 4 more other heroes coming in DLC the selection and new gear will only expand and get more diverse.
---
Con's
Connection: There isn't much more to say than it's 2017 and we got Peer 2 Peer connection from a blockbuster game, it works half the time, while some of these reviews are a little melodramatic saying it's not worth the money because it never works, is just a straight lie, it works, but in 7-9 hours of playing you'll probably have 50 to 60 players leave without them getting penalty and you'll probably have a total of 10 games disconnect. It works, just half the time. I still stand by my recommendation, because it will be fixed,
Gear and hero imbalancing: The gear is extremely unbalanced if you build for straight revenge on everything you will never die, and as for the heroes, the Warlord, Peacekeeper, and Conqueror make it to the last 3 games of every tournement and the Warlord wins everytime, the game needs some serious balancing and it is getting it, but it is taking a good while.
Basically the game has all of the problems Rainbow Six Siege had on release, all we can hope for is that it is Rainbow Six Siege all over again, with the balancing, new different heroes and game support for 2 years. But even with the con's as bad as they may seem, I can still wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is the least bit interested, just don't buy it thinking you're going to jump in and kick♥♥♥♥♥ it takes time to learn and a hot minute to master, but once you do, you'll become..... LEGENDARY!

OK, first game to make me cry since a long long time. Strangely, not on my first but on my second run.
So, what is the game audience? First of all: to gamers who like new experiences. Pyre doesn't look like anything done before. It's more or less a visual novel with some "sports encounters" between long dialog phases. The Rites (these encounters) are challenging depending of your difficulty lvl, and you can restart (on the 3 basics difficulty levels) the Rite even if you lose it (you have time before the autosave comes up). But if you don't restart, the game will continue. Will this affect the game? It depends on your vision of things. The general story will not be VERY VERY different. It's more about how each character will become after the end of the game that will heavily change depending of your choices.
The game is beautiful, the ost is amazing (but as always with this studio), clearly a great great game. But do not play it if you: don't like long dialog phase; hope a sport game with some story in the background (I don't consider it as a sport game); are insensitive; want an open world; want a nervous and action game :)
Oh, to my fellow french gamer: the english level in this game is pretty high, so you may need some times to decypher some dialogs. But it's a great game, and a french version will come some day (but it has really a lot lot lot of text so I understand the game make some times to be located).

An awesome classic! What can be said about it? The game contained a decent amount of variety regarding environments (from its Tech-based levels, all the way to its Hellish environments), memorable weapons, monsters and levels, and had the massive benefit of being heavily moddable, with so much fan content out there to use.
Although the graphics may be quite dated by today standards, free sourceports like GZDoom can upscale the quality and resolution, also providing greater access to even more complex and amazing fan-made mods, in addition to many options for customisation (including toggling of jumping, mouse aim, amongst other taken for granted features and improvements.
Definitely a must have for anyone who is either curious about early shooters, or anyone looking to have a straight-forward shooter experience, without the constraints of modern shooter tropes or narration. Also, buy Doom II along with this, given it's important similarties and continuation with the original Doom.

Spaceships + Huge Laserz + MECH DOLPHINS? Strange mix, but an amazing one. It's Darius.
There are basically two modes: AC (arcade mode, with dual screen) and CS (the new one, single screen). In AC you can do the classic mode, with multiple difficulty and paths, the EX mode, for japanese pros, and the Chronicle mode. This last one offer thousands of levels, with pre-configured ships and an objective to fulfil (use 1 coin, play in 4 players coop, etc..).
SC mode, instead, offer a proper campaign, with a story that spans about all the Darius Chronology.
If you're a old fan of G-Darius, like myself, you'll probably be disappointed that there are no capture balls anymore, but at least the "counter beams" mechanic is back (although it works a little differently, now you have to time it correctly RIGHT before being hit by the beam).
This is a MUST BUY for every shmup lover, it has an impressive amount of content, even for that price tag at the release (around 30-35€). Having it on Steam is a blast.
For 144hz users:
I've played it on a GTX970 on both single and dual screen and had no issues at all. Unfortunately, if you have an ASUS ROG PG278Q or a 144hz monitor, the game speed is tied up to the framerate, so i basically played 4 hours at something like 2.5x turbo speed (144fps instead of 60). To fix it, just lower your hz on Nvidia Panel/other before starting to play.

Twin monitor mode is incredible.  Turn the lights off, sound up, and you're in an arcade.  It's an amazing game.  My only criticism is too many of the same bosses.  But I love the idea of all the levels in chronicle mode-  I always found that shmups tend to have too few levels.  The 3000 level feature just brings the shmup in line with current more-is-more thinking (even though I don't necessarily agree that is always the case, it depends on the genre and feel of the game).  But when I play shmups, I kind of drift into a hypnotic state, and I appreciate the subtle differences of having so many stages, even if many of them have the same bosses.  I wonder if they used procedural generation to do this.  It's a great idea, seeing that shmup backgrounds are usually a pretty simple thing, and enemy waves could easily be randomly generated. This is worth $40.

You adore QTE-based gameplay? You hate dancing? Congratulations! You have just found the supreme incarnation of your dreams.
I mean, the game is moderately funny & colorful, but.. It's a QTE-fighting, you know. So you have to press the combo-buttons with ideal intervals, which ain't hard for a musical person, but boring as hell for a dancer. It's like a metronome simulator, people don't dance like robots in real life. All the variations your dancer performs are pre-programmed animations, he just dances automatically while you watch & your role is to push the arrows cold-heartedly, without a blink or a break to kick, shield, accumulate energy etc. No percussion, just the bass drum. So if you happen to like the track & it really turns you on, you are doomed to loose, while a totally phlegmatic person low on emotion, all intellect is almost sure to win.
It tries to mix dancing with Mortal Kombat, but both activities suppose unpredictable motion sequences, sudden pauses & stuff, while this one's like a rhythm-based card game, where you can lay a card only if you manage to beat the metronome.

I'd like to post what I was thinking to myself for the first few times I played the game, but most of it would be censored!
You might not think a shooter on Steam is worth 40-50 bucks. You'd be wrong in this case. It doesn't look like there's much here and yet I don't see myself exploring all of it for at least a few years right off the bat. You have several versions of a full size arcade game (complete with head injury warning!) and a new mode with 3000 (!) areas that spans the entire history of the Darius franchise including all the previous game's ships and nice snippets of story to flesh things out as you go. Beyond that there are some new ships with radical designs going as far as to add an omni directional controllable laser turret as a game mechanic. It has platitudes of options including the ability to remap buttons for each individual playable ship and more pedestrian ones like ship stocks. Also worth mentioning: this is the only shooter on Steam that not only recognized my gamepad instantly, it also configured every ship in a completely sensible way without my interference.
There is no online option aside from sharing cabinets which is both kind of cool and a bit strange, but If you have friends locally you're in luck! This has local multiplayer with FOUR simultaneous players at a time and the gameplay is suitably hectic as even under that amount of stress the game doesn't suffer from slow-down of any kind. The game is responsive and suitably optimized. That's not to say the visuals are tame either as some will actually bend your mind with the complexity of the on-screen action.
A magical soundtrack accompanies the face-melting action and serves as the perfect cap to an awe-inspiring game.
Few games, let alone shooting games can hope to approach the majesty of this product and almost none treat their fans with such a level of respect and service. If you love shooters you already own this. If you are a general gamer you should think really hard about checking it out.
If you are a Taito fan - welcome home.

Dance Magic, originally developed for the PS3 in 2013, is a dance/music & rhythm game now ported to PC. With three different game modes, including a unique Battle mode, prepare to dance your way through the 30+ pre-designed (or infinite amount of custom) songs! Local and online coop is supported.
Tournament mode is essentially a string of pre-determined AI dance battles, similar to Battle Mode. Your tournament begins by choosing one of three starting characters, after which 5 eccentric AI enemies will line up for you to face. A sort of progression element is included in the form of character, equipment, and music/song unlockables. The currency needed to unlock these items are attained through this Tournament Mode.
The controlled character has a set of 5 different moves to help defeat the opposing character by reducing their health to zero. These moves are:
These moves are individually performed by hitting four specific button inputs to the song's beat. Each character has a different pattern for each move so they are not truly interchangeable, but it is relatively easy to memorize the button prompts after a little bit of playing. Performing a specific combination of moves will provide you with a stun attack (ie. Attack + Shield + Dispel) which lasts for a few seconds.
This unique game mode is a very refreshing twist to the generic match-the-notes-to-the-rhythm/SHMUP-rhythm games. By forcing the player to adhere to rhythmic requirements, a lot of pressure and anxiety is created when you know what move you have to do, but must play to the beat. Although I am a huge fan of rhythm games, I always welcome new takes on beat-play.
A static chart (note board) will begin to populate itself with notes as a moving bar scrolls through the chart. Your goal is to press the required button input as the bar scrolls over the respective button prompts. This is very similar to other rhythm games (DDR, Guitar Hero, Rock Band, etc.) with the exception that the line (or receptors) moves as opposed to the chart/notes. Although the notes are presented well before the bar moves over it, in order to allow the player to prepare ahead of time, bonus notes are sporadically injected throughout the songs which appear at any time (sometimes right before the bar is about to move over it). This adds a very fun element of surprise and player engagement. When choosing a song to play (many will be locked at the beginning), the player has the option to select Beginner, Easy, Medium, or Hard difficulty levels. These are offered for play variety and are freely changeable in between songs.
My favorite component of Dance Magic is its support for custom songs in Dance Mode - BPM (beats per minute) calibration is needed. The BPM calibration is extremely simple; just hit any random note to the beat of your song. Although the BPM calibration will suffice, and comes handy as a cheap method for custom song support, the notes/chart could be much more harmonized with the music if they implemented a beat analyzer instead. As it is, due to the unpredictability of a song and note/chart generation off of a single average BPM, certain parts of a song will feel a little awkward/de-synchronized to play. Audiosurf does a fantastic job with song analyzation by deconstructing a song and creating a moveable track from it; something Dance Magic could take note of.

Either way, I am still very happy that DM supports custom songs, as there are only a handful (or less) of games on Steam that do. Also, it might be nice to know that no matter how many notes you miss, you cannot fail. This also applies to the native songs provided by the game. This feature allows you to enjoy your music at a high difficulty level without getting pre-maturely cutoff, like in many other rhythm games.
There doesn't seem to be much of an online community, if any, but I don't fault them for that. Dance magic is such a fun dance/music/rhythm game that even if I could only play it solo or with a local coop buddy, I would still be satisfied. Especially since there is support for
. I can't stress how rare it is to find a rhythm game with custom song support. With this in mind, I can easily recommend Dance Magic to fans of the rhythm and music genre, or people that want to interact with their favorite music.

Want to rule the world like a James Bond Villain?  Want to laugh maniacally as the world falls at you feet?  Want to show those James Bond wanna bes who's the boss?  Want to spend more time building your evil lair than taking over the world?  Want to spend most of your time waiting for your money to build up?  Want to micromange every little detail when your minions should be doing the job themselves?  Then this game is for you!
Ok in all seriousness even though this game has it's flaws I still think it's a great game.  It just has several big flaws that brings it down.  The waiting for money is my biggest issue.  You would think for a simulation game a fast forward button would be standard, not this one.  That's right you only have play and pause at your fingertips.  Well I hope you have something else to do whilst your waiting for that money to come in because there's little else to do whilst your waiting for the money.
The micromanaging can get very monotanous very quickly.  You see since your evil activities are causing the world to send their "very best" spies to put a stop to your activities you have to keep an eye.  Minions won't automatically attack spies without you tagging them first.  Meaning your going to be randomly searching your base to see if any spies have landed and you really need to keep an eye out otherwise your beautiful base will be ruined in seconds (and trust me that is THE last thing you want unless you enjoy the waiting game).
The basebuilding is the main part of the game.  Really this game should be called Evil Lair Architect.  Not that thats a bad thing the base building is very good.  It's the only simulation game I've played that allows you to plan out a building without it being built first.  This I like alot and other games would benefit from it, Simcity being one.  It's the optimazation of making your minions work hard and keeping spies out that make it a big draw for me however it's the waiting that makes it toturous.
The minions themselves are divided into classes that do certain jobs.  You start of with a basic construction worker that do all the building for you that can then level up.  Scientists can do research for you to get new items (you can decide how they research the items but honestly this system is just luck based).  You have security minions that will beat up the spies.  You then have the social minions that can confuse spies into forgetting their mission (just like mp's).
Taking over the world has little to it.  It's literly just a map.  Thats it.  You sends minions onto the map to complete missions or collect money for you.  Minions of different classes can do certain jobs better but honestly I would have appreciated a playable map similar to XCOM: Enemy Unkown.  Anything that makes the waiting more pleasant.
If your graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ then I'm afraid this game will not satisfy you.  Granted it's an old game but even for it's age it doesn't look good (Rayman 2 was released 4 years before this one and looks just as good).
The only thing that keeps this game up is it's charm and premise.  It's filled with humour (they interogate minions by dancing and putting them in a blender whats not to like?).  The premise itself is also interesting too.  Taking over the world who doesn't want to do that?  Honestly though these are the only things keeping it good for me along with the building mechanics.  If those aren't enough then I'm afraid this game is not for you.  If it is for you then I'd suggest waiting until this game goes on sale first.  Yes it is cheap to begin with at £7 but If your going to be dissappointed (and I wouldn't be surprised if you do) then get it cheap.
