There was a time where if you had mentioned to me that you either had access to DariusBurst Another Chronicle, either via an arcade cabinet or by playing it on an iOS device, I would have given you a weird look. And not just any weird look, but the look that I wanted to steal your soul type of look as I really wanted a chance to try the game, just for once in my life. And with no access to either an iOS device or a Japanese PlayStation Portable, I was forced to merely watch videos of the game in action on Youtube. That is until recently when Degica stated they were porting the game over to not just the PlayStation Vita, but also the PlayStation 4 and the real shocker, the PC. That’s all I needed to hear to get my shmup spirits lifted. Besides Darius, my other favorite shmups, Gradius and Thunderforce, were dead and buried, never to see the day of light again. And while Darius was still being carried on, its existence was always out of my reach, that is until now.   “Shoot-’em-up: a fast-moving story or movie, of which gunfire is a dominant feature. Also known as a shmup” DBCS is technically two games in one, which I believe was done to not only bring home that arcade experience but also to build upon it. Within the game, you have the ability to chose between DariusBurst Another Chronicle or AC mode, which includes all of the original arcade modes and original arcade screen ratio (perfect for dual screen or wide-format monitors and DariusBurst Chronicle Saviors or CS mode, which is the updated version of the game. And while you’re free to choose either mode, there are a few differences. In AC mode you have access to the original arcade game modes; Original, Original EX Mode, Chronicle Mode and Event Mode. Original (Easy, Normal and Hard) is what I call the starter zone while Original EX Mode is a tougher version, tailor made for shmup experts (Expect, Extreme and Exceed) . You know, the same people that are able to single credit an entire game.
Chronicle mode however is what stands out here as you are presented with several different missions and objectives to complete, as the systems are broken up into several areas. And speaking of those objectives, they range anywhere from completing an area with just one credit, completing an area with multiple players, playing with a specific set of equipment and so forth. It’s a definite time sink that’s for sure. Thankfully you’re not the only one who’s doing this, as everyone around the world who plays this game can also contribute to the AC progression via cabinets.  And just like it sounds, a cabinet is like a global progression save. For example, say everyone from a specific arcade was able to beat several areas, such as one of the specific multiplayer objectives. That objective would then contribute to unlocking more areas in the AC mode’s game, and everyone who is accessing that cabinet can benefit and contribute to that going forward. This allows access to literally hundreds of new levels and even exclusive AC mode only bosses that you likely wouldn’t unlock on your own.  And for those wondering, yes this is basically the NESYS  / NESiCAxLive Network being emulated at home. Oh, and when I mention hundreds of levels, I actually meant thousands! Yes, Taito is boasting that Dariusburst Chronicle Saviours’s AC mode will include over 3000 total stages. So you’ll be playing this for quite some time. No matter how you choose to play the game; Xbox 360, Xbox One, Dual Shock 4, Arcade Stick, as several other not very known controllers, you’ll be happy to know that the game supports just about every gamepad and joystick. I can attest to that myself as I’ve tested over 10 different configurations and were able to play the game with all of them.  And yes, you can even play with the keyboard, if you want to that is. I don’t see why, but at least that option is available.
However in CS mode, the game changes. Similar to the chronicle mode in AC, this is mode is also laid out in a manner that you have set paths to take, after first area is completed that is. And unlike AC mode where you can chose the next stage, once you start the area you’re stuck on until it’s completed. You’re also handicapped to an extent as you will find that some missions will not allow power ups to drop as well as restrict you to a specific ship. However you won’t go into a mission blind as the overlay will tell you from the start what your ship will be, power up status, how many zones make up the area, and stage make-up.  Another difference is that while you play CS mode, you accumulate points based on how well you do in the zones you play through. Eventually after accumulating enough points you can trade them in for a new ship which you can then outfit with lasers, bombs and shielding. Using this tactic, you’re no longer forced to use the preset ship, which will make certain levels that may have seemed impossible before a total cake walk with the new ship. However there’s also a down side to this and every time you use that powered up ship, you will consume however many number of points you put into upgrading it. So you’ll have to track how much you have or if you start running low, to take off some of that added power or simply use the preset ship. It’s a nice method to keep you from overpowering your way to the end of the game. Via every transition in CS mode, you’re provided pieces of the on-going story that you’re currently taking place in. And while CS mode isn’t as expansive as AC mode as it pales in comparison of possible stages (200+ vs 3000), it’s still a fun addition and more up-to-date take on the Darius shooter. Also worth noting that CS mode is a single player affair while AC mode will allow up to 4 players.
You want ships? Well you won’t be disappeared here, especially if you’re familiar with the Darius games as there’s a handful of them playable in-game; Gaiden, Assault, Next, Legend, Formula, Origin, Second, Genesis and one ship that isn’t related to the Darius universe, the Murakumo, which is a CS exclusive ship btw. Apparently that ship hails from an older Taito game, one that I can’t quite figure out. And while it’s not directly related to the Darius ships of legend, the Murakumo is clearly a fantastic ship in its own right and is fun to play with, assuming you can afford the points required to pick it up. Fans of G-Darius may be slightly disappointed with the Genesis Silver Hawk as it does not feature it’s capture ball. It’s not a huge deal and it doesn’t detract from the game, but it would have been nice to see it included. Even still, there are subtle differences between the ships, so each one is unique in that retrospect. If you’ve ever played a Darius title, then you should be familiar on how the game functions. You pick your ship and off you go, pretty straight forward stuff. Thankfully the controls of the game are very responsive, and while playing the game I didn’t have any issues as I dodge the incoming fire. That said, if I died it was due to me slipping up instead of the game.

A bit late to the party, but here are my thoughts about SOMA by Frictional Games. You play Simon who begins his day with a doctor's appointment for a brain scan only to wake up in an underwater station where something terrible happened. Everything is covered by some techno goo and the horror quickly begins when Simon meets the latest inhabitants: Robots. Some, who think they are human, others... well, you don't want to even look at them.
The levels change between the underwater station and trips to the outside seafloor, both are well designed. The references to Bioshock are obvious, although more in the beginning and not as colorful. Later on, the inside feels more like a space station and the wondrous world of the sea floor looks rather bleak with some occasional spots of really beautiful flora and fauna, the latter of course is best observed from a safe distance. But the bleakness adds to the overall mood of the game.
The graphics are solid, the creatures terrifying, but above all: the sound design is wonderful. It really ties together the soil your pants moments. Some visual effects which reminded me of certain japanese horrorfilms might have added to that too.
You get an idea about what happend and what is at stake fairly quickly, don't expect too many plot twists. This game is a journey of contemplation with the occasional butt clenching. the details of the story are discovered along the way in logs, reports, records of communications or personal stuff besides corpes. Gameplay changes between hide and seek horror, puzzle solving and quiet moments, where you discover more clues about what happened at the station but also get to reflect about identity, the world and all the rest. There are some boring fillers, but there is always time to appreciate ladders, I suppose.
Philosophical questions about identity are an aspect of the story in SOMA. There are some choices you have to make. But it is not the essence of the game, rather more of a vehicle to drive the story forward, and it works, supported by the voice acting and the dialogue. Although there is a "but": the ending. It didn't fit the overall mood of the story but more like an out of character compromise. And although there are some choices in the game there is only one ending. Maybe a missed opportunity.
SOMA is like a good short sci-fi story with horror-elements. Mood, writing and technical execution are well done. I recommend it.

I knew I would like it, but I didn't expect to love it.
Doom was always one of those "adult people" games for me back in the day. Not because it was violent but because only adults owned computers. Since then it became an obscure memory while I was being raised on Call Of Duty and Battlefield but I never forgot about it. Now that I've played it properly I can only say that I'm blown away by the impression it's made on me.
This game doesn't feel old fashioned or quaint to me, instead it felt more like I was playing something truly special. What struck me first was how much I loved how the levels were designed. I didn't expect to like this part of the game since I've never been a fan of not knowing where to go in order to progress. Doom eliminates this problem by rewarding exploration with essential items like ammo or keys. Any game can do this of course but in Doom exploring isn't a slog because of your immense movement speed and as a result combat never feels like a chore. It's just plain fun to move around and shoot demons in this game!
Thinking back on some of the newer shooters I've played, the fun never really came purely from the combat but seeing what happened next in the story. In Doom the story takes the backseat and fun gameplay is placed squarely in the driver's seat. It's a very sad fact that this kind of experience is mostly new to me, and in fact to a lot of gamers today. I'm looking forward to exploring the rest of the Doom series and more titles like it.

Grotesque yet gorgeous, Nidhogg 2 keeps the funny and tense gameplay Nidhogg 1 presented but with a few new tricks up it's sleeve by introducing several new weapon types and changes to how certain aspects of the combat work.
In Nidhogg 1 you essentially would divekick relentlessly with no real drawbacks apart from missing and possibly dying, however in Nidhogg 2 it's tuned back a bit to not be your ace in the hole in every single situation since you will also fall slightly after dropkicking your opponent which could hilariously drop you into a ditch if your opponent was on the ledge of a pit, so careful planning would be advised before you wantonly spam it to disarm your opponent.
An area of contention around Nidhogg 2 also seems to be it's more detailed pixel art style which has more characteristics and resolution as opposed to the blank and objectively featureless predacessor, the art style has no impact on gameplay at all and for me the style of Nidhogg 2 is much easier on the eyes for long stretches at a time and is genuinely beautiful to look at the various techniques used in this game like the pixel shading technique to illuminate the characters on screen from light sources within the arena, or the smooth animations of background environments casting actual god-ray lighting effects from the sunset behind you, the variety of stages in Nidhogg 2 absolutely floors it compared to the first game.
I'd also like to point out this game has a really good soundtrack as well, I don't really recall the music in Nidhogg 1 so I couldn't compare them but I will say I actually noticed the music this time around in Nidhogg 2 and wasn't compelled to turn it off in favor of my own music so props to the devs for the good tunes this time around.
So at it's core Nidhogg 2 still retains the fun (and funny) fast paced and tense dueling of the first game while offering improvements to the formula by mixing up the number of situations to handle with new weapon styles that have different advantages and disadvantages to them such as the bow, dagger, claymore, rapier. Bow can have it's projectiles reflected back at the shooter, the dagger is quick and good for sliding up under your opponent for a quick kill, the claymore will bash away the weapon in your opponents hands and satisfyingly blow their body into gory chunks upon impact, and the rapier still has the deadly long reach jabs and cruel skewering finisher to humiliate your enemies.
Anybody who is groaning and crying about the art style shouldn't have bought this game in the first place if they really don't like it so much that they're going to write sad and angry reviews purely because of the new funky visuals, because at it's core Nidhogg 2 brings what Nidhogg 1 brought but with a heap more for your enjoyment.

Just finished the campaign. Let's start with the positive. Would I recommend the game, sure, but I think its more of a $25-30 game. It brings a level of strategic space combat I heavily desired to have from being a fan of Battlestar Galactica. If you are a fan of the series you will feel the nastalgia from its small campaign. Bringing in both versions of the Battlestar class vessels into the battle against the cylons even gives you that warm fuzzy you are apart of the action and the series. The space compbat is somewhat cinematic and sometimes mezmorizing to watch.
Okay, the negative...more of a message to the developers. I'm sure I'll get some difference in opinion here. Took a few turns to get used get into it. The tactical gameplay is interesting and love the detail However there are a few items of note:
* Strategic Star Map has a lot to be desired. I wish the strategic fleet movement across the region had more depth. The Cylons randomly show up out of no where. It would be great to hold strategic points to hold off cylon growth. If there is a way to do this it is not very apparent.
* Be careful with your fleets early, later in missions its hard to build them up or at least the officers. Only large fleets can handle themselves against larger cylon numbers that show up later in game. So recruiting new officers becomes very difficult later on. I spent way too long building fleets against repetitive random attacks that made no logical sense to defend.
* Tactical battle management is fun but bigger fleets I wish I didn't have to micromanage so much. Would be great to create saved tactical maneuvers executed over several turns to give the ship rather than a turn by turn play of a turning the ship around.
* Wish there was a way to retreat during battle. Doesn't make sense to waste ships in battle because they have to fight if they can fleet the arena. Count it as a loss but at least allow my ships to jump out if the fuel is available.
* Could use some more complex benefits to officer rank advancement. Would love to have ship experience.
* Fighters? Think they could use some more fire power. Besides defending against missile attacks they always seemed in their own world and only for show. I know they can be deployed against other fighters but think more emphasis should be given to them especially out of carrier ships.
* If two or more fleets occupy the same planet it doesn't make sense I can't engage in battle. If my officer limits me to a certain amount of ships at any one time on the Battlefield at least allow me to jump more in after one gets destroyed. Best example of this Star Wars: Empire at War (Space Combat only). This could also solve the whole only 7 ships in any one battle.
* To continue on that note, Unless it provided more strategic options, weapons, ect this could have probably been a real-time strategy game, at least in the battle itself. Just a thought.
With all that said, here's hoping for an expansion or a sequel involving more aspects of the war that give the game much more depth into the gameplay. I think this was an awesome start to what COULD be a great series.

Full disclosure:  this game was gifted to me by a dear friend on Steam, though I do take price into consideration when mentioning certain aspects of the game.
1.  The artstyle is divisive, but I grew to be perfectly fine with it over time.  Consider this a much more bizarre, fever dream-esque version of Nidhogg 1.  I can say the only *technical* issue has been where certain body colors may not mesh well with certain sections of a level.  Speaking of those levels, they are technically very well done, but potentially very disturbing.  I'd argue Nidhogg 1 would be better suited for younger audiences, but the newest Nidhogg's art style may make it better suited for older audiences.  There's an aspect to it that may mess with very young kiddos.
2.  Controls are exactly the same as the first Nidhogg, but there are a few key gameplay changes.  Successful divekicks now knock down both combatants, keeping the aggressor from being able to spam them.  Jumping in general feels a bit more airy, but the Low Gravity rule still feels decisively different.  The new weapons do serve a purpose, but be ready to either practice with them or get used to them as your play.  I have seen several arguments against the bow initially, but after some practice, I was able to find a viable strategy that wasn't just chucking the bow at someone's head.
3.  Ultimately, I recommend this as an upgrade to an already-outstanding local multiplayer game.  Online - despite an input lag setting - still slowed to a crawl at times.  The price is entirely justified right now if you intend to play it locally (when tested on a wirelessly-connected Steam Link, it worked wonderfully), but online play is going to need some netcode patching.
BUY this FOR FULL PRICE if you want a better, stranger version of an amazing local multiplayer game.
DON'T BUY this if you intend to only play online.
Potential Quality of Life improvements:
-an online lobby system that allows for better spectating.
-the option to randomly select a level.
Edit:  After a bit more review, I have one other addendum:  go buy the soundtrack.  Outstanding work by the composer(s?).

This game lacks a lot. Gameplay is over-simplified, with only three spells for a caster and a very simple melee system. You can craft, cook and brew anywhere without using a workbench - hell, workbenches are in the game but don't have
, even if you turn on 'Roleplaying elements' in the options. There is no penalty for stealing stuff, you can't beat up friendly NPCs. Although you're playing in one big world, the pathing is painfully linear. You can't walk down edges (unless you jump), and exploring usually kills you - like when you touch the water surface of a lake you thought you could swim through. The new main character doesn't keep up with the previous nameless hero (how could he anyway?), the story is dull, quests are repetitive and most characters are unconvincing.
Most. What made this game for me was really was the opportunity to meet old friends. Especially Diego and Gorn really shine in this game, and seeing Lester and Milten again also didn't hurt. Besides that, the game is stripped down and shifted way more from the hard old-school RPG to a casual Action RPG, which - if you let yourself in for it - has its benefits: the game is incredibly intuitive, you don't have to put a lot of time to learn the skill system or whatever, and combat feels wonderfully dynamic. The game also looks pretty nice.
I started the game on difficulty 'Gothic' (of course...) which is the hardest one they give you. If you come from Gothic, do this! After about 3/4 of the game I put it down to 'Hard' and then 'Normal' because it started to get difficult and enemies had riddiculously high HP, making combats last forever. This made the late game kinda chewy. It took me ~21 hours to finish the game, which isn't incredibly long for an RPG, but some hours less wouldn't have hurt.
I'll give it a 6.5 / 10, mostly for 'nostalgic value', nice graphics and overall a very polished and smooth experience. If (and only if) you are into the series, it's worth playing!

Pyre is so obviously a very creative and imaginative exercise in world building, with similar visuals to bastion and transistor and a superb work in the soundtrack as is customary with supergiant games. However, I feel it's sorely lacking in the gameplay deparment.
Both bastion and transistor had a solid foundation in terms of gameplay mechanics, depth in progression, only heightened by a fresh take on graphics/visuals and an outstanding score and storytelling+narration. But here the GAME part seems shallow, a gimmick more on the likes of a minigame of a full-fledged game than a standalone thing. It gives the illusion of choice by proposing different paths, but in truth these do not change meaningfully the story or progression. Once you have completed the cycle once it really seems an unecessary grind to do it all over again.
I feel like supergiant dropped the ball here by trying to cover up with an imaginative world and pretty visuals something that at the core is not that interesting. It should have been the other way arround, you find a set of mechanics that pose a challenge and interesting decisions to be made (also at the level of storytelling) and then, on top of that, you build an interesting world to set your game in.
Although the price is very competitive, I found myself more interested towards minigames like GWENT or Blitzball / card games from final fantasy series than Pyre. I couldnt find much entertainment from this title beyond a handfull of hours.

I would like more variations of 'pets', depending on the combination of elements and growth stages. It's a best part of the game.
Despite of shortcomings, it's a nice game for its genre and price.

Friday the 13th: The game or better known as a glorified game of hide and seek. Survival consists of collecting parts for a boat or a car (two types), or escaping via the police (repairing the phone)– or simply just hide while Jason looks for everyone so he can kill them before they succeed.
Whether or not you enjoy Friday the 13th is going to come down to whether you enjoy the movies (the stunning attention to detail that pays homage to the franchise) and/or playing with friends that you can laugh with, screw over, and work together with, If none of those options applies to you, it may be hard to overlook its flaws. Such as the clunky combat system, glitchy animations, etc. As well as dealing with occassional trolls who will team kill you, team with Jason and lead him to you, escaping without others (car and boat escapes) or uncooperative teammates.
There are alot of choices involving the game I strongly dislike especially is that Jason can swiftly and easily kill a player using one of his finishing moves (aka instant grab kills, up to 4) that can be triggered almost instantly, which doesn't feel earned and cheap. Yes Jason like all serial killers should be a overwhelming force but the way these abilities have been implemented makes the game alot less fun. Resulting in players looking for groups to form custom games, where these sorta abilities are banned forcing Jason to use enviornmental kills only unless conselors are in groups of three or more. There is no incentive to working together as well as forcing players to stay to the end to earn 500 points for completing the match.
It's hard to recommend this game in it's current form due to techical issues right and left as well as unsatisfying gameplay, considering the fact the game is priced almost as high as major titles. Someday this game could potientially turn into a amazing game but as of right now, it's not reaching the level it could be as a game.

I knew I would like it, but I didn't expect to love it.
Doom was always one of those "adult people" games for me back in the day. Not because it was violent but because only adults owned computers. Since then it became an obscure memory while I was being raised on Call Of Duty and Battlefield but I never forgot about it. Now that I've played it properly I can only say that I'm blown away by the impression it's made on me.
This game doesn't feel old fashioned or quaint to me, instead it felt more like I was playing something truly special. What struck me first was how much I loved how the levels were designed. I didn't expect to like this part of the game since I've never been a fan of not knowing where to go in order to progress. Doom eliminates this problem by rewarding exploration with essential items like ammo or keys. Any game can do this of course but in Doom exploring isn't a slog because of your immense movement speed and as a result combat never feels like a chore. It's just plain fun to move around and shoot demons in this game!

A bit late to the party, but here are my thoughts about SOMA by Frictional Games. You play Simon who begins his day with a doctor's appointment for a brain scan only to wake up in an underwater station where something terrible happened. Everything is covered by some techno goo and the horror quickly begins when Simon meets the latest inhabitants: Robots. Some, who think they are human, others... well, you don't want to even look at them.
The levels change between the underwater station and trips to the outside seafloor, both are well designed. The references to Bioshock are obvious, although more in the beginning and not as colorful. Later on, the inside feels more like a space station and the wondrous world of the sea floor looks rather bleak with some occasional spots of really beautiful flora and fauna, the latter of course is best observed from a safe distance. But the bleakness adds to the overall mood of the game.
The graphics are solid, the creatures terrifying, but above all: the sound design is wonderful. It really ties together the soil your pants moments. Some visual effects which reminded me of certain japanese horrorfilms might have added to that too.
You get an idea about what happend and what is at stake fairly quickly, don't expect too many plot twists. This game is a journey of contemplation with the occasional butt clenching. the details of the story are discovered along the way in logs, reports, records of communications or personal stuff besides corpes. Gameplay changes between hide and seek horror, puzzle solving and quiet moments, where you discover more clues about what happened at the station but also get to reflect about identity, the world and all the rest. There are some boring fillers, but there is always time to appreciate ladders, I suppose.
Philosophical questions about identity are an aspect of the story in SOMA. There are some choices you have to make. But it is not the essence of the game, rather more of a vehicle to drive the story forward, and it works, supported by the voice acting and the dialogue. Although there is a "but": the ending. It didn't fit the overall mood of the story but more like an out of character compromise. And although there are some choices in the game there is only one ending. Maybe a missed opportunity.
SOMA is like a good short sci-fi story with horror-elements. Mood, writing and technical execution are well done. I recommend it.

Highly recommend this title, very engaging gameplay with an after action replay that never gets old. With an amazing soundtrack and 'realistic' dead sounding weaponry (you mostly just hear the thud of weapons rather than hollywood style explosions, as if you're hearing what the crews of the ships would hear from inside their vessels) the gameplay never gets old. Watching a Cylon Baseship explode in a glorious white-hot fireball is so satisfying, as is picking targets and giving orders to your numerous viper squadrons.
The Campaign does a good job of making you feel like you're fighting a seemingly unwinnable war against the Cylons, you will lose ships, lots of them. The 'feel' of the TV series is here, as you try to lose as few ships as possible with each encounter, desperately trying to get that last missile volley off before your ship is torn to shreds.
Despite a UI that could use some work (the fact that it has been designed to be released on consoles at a later date is evident here) it is an extremely fun and engaging game, it has plenty of replay value and it's not very often you get a good, easy to learn naval strategy game, let alone one set in space, and based on such good source material!

Right off the bat, I would have a hard time recommending this to my friends yet it was still able to keep me somewhat entertained for about 20 hours. I would give it 5.5/10 overall.
The game itself has surprisingly better graphics than what I thought they would be however there were some poor texture loadins and some odd texture spots floating around occasionally.
The main quest was very linear and besides some minor sidequests, you basically went in a line as you never revisited any other previous locations. The main quest itself got very disracted as at first, you're fighting for revenge (I am trying to avoid spoilers here!), and then you get distracted with trying to stop the paladins, and then you get distracted with trying to help the king, and then you get distracted by trying to save the city, etc. It felt like the quest was all over the place and when you finally accomplished one of the things, it was less than satisfactory. The sidequests themselves were mildly interesting. They actually rewarded pretty good loot and made them worth while.
It's listed as an RPG but the game isn't really one to be honest. Sure you can sort of focus on using swords or spells, but there are so few skills to upgrade, you end up getting all of them and it doesn't really matter what you're focusing on. The crafting system felt tacked onto the game as it doesn't really serve much of a purpose. I literally only used the health potions even though I could have made 30+ other potions. I also could have crafted some other weapons and armor but by the time I got the material required for them, I already had better weapons and armor than the thing I was trying to craft.
Some minor things I disliked about the game was that it seemed like there were only a few voice actors and there were only a few NPC models. There was basically no variation when meeting NPCs. Also it was annoying that I couldn't tell if I got hit by enemies. They would make a quick movement and I looked down at my health and saw they had somehow hit me.
The game itself was incredibly easy but I only played it on normal. After that, it can go up to hard and then gothic. I felt very overpowered and didn't really have to pay attention to my HP. I just pressed the attack button and rarely tried to dodge.
Some positive things about the game is that the bow mechanic was really cool. I also liked the overall lighting ambient in the game.  My favorite thing about the game however was probably that I was able to easily find better and better loot, from doing sidequests to doing the main quest. Normally games have a bunch of bad loot that you can get but this was a nice change.
As I said, overall 5.5/10.

For instance, theres a skill tree for stealth but it doesn't give you a bonus for a stealth attack until you've accumulated a lot of skill points which you don't get a lot of per level.
You can certianly build a mage if you prefer but the game is pretty clear in it's limitations in regards to how you build the character.
Otherwise, the game is fun. The characters are interesting but more or less pretty standard characters for a fantasy game.
If you're looking for an inexpensive RPG that will hold your attention, ArcaniA should do nicely.

To take the good stuff first: the space combat is very satisfying both to play and to watch (replays in-game are available), every single ship class fills a distinct role in your fleet which leads to a lot of tactical variation, the game has an interesting but not overly complex economic system (this isn't Civilization after all) where you have to provide fleets for security to different worlds so they keep the money flowing, good voice acting in the small but well-written story that feels BSG thanks to characters' conflicting morals and motivations and the ever-important political element.
Then to the bad stuff, and there are a pair of glaring issues with this game that you need to be aware of. There are some other minor things but I won't nit-pick too much. The first thing is that In space combat all ships have armour facings that need to be destroyed before the ship takes damage to its HP: left, right, top, bottom, front, rear. This system doesn't work however, because even if I'm presenting a near-as-damnit flat broadside to enemy gunfire they can still hit my ships' destroyed front facing and do HP damage, while my right-side armour remains undamaged, which makes the armour facing system largely pointless. The second, and biggest issue is that whenever you jump a fleet onto any sort of story mission, be it a side mission to rescue a freighter or a main story mission, the game doesn't tell you the odds you're up against. You're only ever told the odds when a roving enemy fleet jumps and attacks your fleet and you get the option to run away; never with story missions, and I've lost several fights when I jumped into one with the biggest fleet I had and found the enemy had a fleet twice as large and they wiped me out.
Do I still reccomend the game? Yes, but very hesitantly That issue with jumping in blind puts a very ugly tarnish on an otherwise very good game and they better fix it, but it is only -almost- a deal-breaker for me, because you can at least get past this problem partially by save-scumming.

I was hesitant about the price, mainly because BSG is a pretty much dead franchise at the moment and why would a quality game worth the full price be released now? Who knows, but my fears were averted once I picked it up and began playing it. The turn based gameplay has you constantly thinking and paying attention, checking your targets are focused, your raptors are prioritizing and most important your ships aren't crashing into each other. You can then watch in the autocam, which makes it look like it is directly from the TV show with the shaking and the zooming. There are hours of fun to be had here.
The criticisms I have is that the campaign can be rushed through very quickly, there don't appear to be many roadblocks in the campaign requiring you to research or make sure your fleet is up to scratch. There are a few of quality of life issues - most notably equipping your fleet with torpedoes/viper mk 2s in the battle screen, but also the whole fleet system, you have to level up officers which becomes increasingly difficult as you progress. For how fun and wonderful the tactics engine is, the CIC tasks are all very simple, mostly just building and moving fleets. While it would be nice to see a more XCom approach for outside the base, the developers clearly focused on the tactical aspect of the game and it shows in mostly positive ways.
In conclusion, as a fan of BSG and the newest XCom games, you will enjoy it immensely. Just a fan of BSG? Yeah, you'll still enjoy it. Otherwise, I'd wait for it to get cheaper, the whole game aesthetic is set up to put you into the BSG universe and it does it spectacularly.

I was disillusioned with Pyre at first, after expecting such a beautifully detailed and lush world like those in Bastion and Transistor.  Pyre feels as though it's keeping you an arms length from the scenery and the culture of the Downside, and at first, it feels strange.  I even had to step away for a couple months and allow myself to detox after getting through the first liberation rite.
However, you soon come to realize that despite the beauty of the game, where it ushers you into its arms is not in the scenery but in the characters themselves.  Winning and losing becomes encouraging, and you find yourself craving the interactions between your characters, your adversaries, and you.  The gameplay, even for someone who doesn't particularly care for sports, becomes hypnotic.  The spiral structure of the game itself, as the stakes rise and the action moves faster, becomes exhilirating.
If you didn't give a full playthrough a chance, I'd really recommend you try it - the lone first four hours of this game don't do it justice.

My only criticism of this game is that equippable items aren't well-adjusted in terms of strength, so you'll end up using the same ones over and over. That said....
This is a FANTASTIC game. Like previous Supergiant games, I absolutely adore the soundtrack and visuals, every piece of them tell a story, and you find yourself listening to the OST again and again once you're done with the game. This is definitely a game I recommend playing with sound on.
The game is a bit quirky at first, and it took me some time to figure out the finer points of performing the Rites and SLAM-DUNKING that CELESTIAL METEORITE into FIRE, but as you go on you slowly learn more and more mechanics, and can figure out strategies.
The story is beautiful and heartwrenching. Most choices don't feel like they have much impact, but certain choices (and you WILL know which ones they are) leave you almost in tears and wishing you had an alternative - but also knowing that if you don't do so, you're dooming someone to a fate they don't deserve.
I love how even if you lose fights the story still goes on, so I'd recommend playing the game without resetting. I wish there was a good online multiplayer mode, but it feels like it'd be a bit tough to implement. Either way, I definitely recommend this game!

TL;DR Avoid this abomination like the plague. Buy Sparkle 2 Evo instead.
I completed 2 Evo and thoroughly enjoyed it, so I bought this expecting more of the same but I was sorely disappointed at the stark contrast. It's as if the devs sat around a table and compiled a list of ways to ruin the atmosphere of Evo. Where Evo was a gorgeous relaxing experience with a few gentle puzzle elements as an afterthought, Genesis is a brutal, frustrating, rage-inducing grind.
Evo: Wide variety of organic deepwater colourful transparent prey animals; Sparkle has distinct evolutionary stages, everything has satisfying flowing movement and is visually stunning. No performance issues.
Genesis: Robotic modular affair with awkward, jerky pecking movement. It grows larger with no noticeable changes in development. Prey animals are few and uninspiring. The theme is overly bright, garish and uncomfortable on the eyes. It constantly stutters, poking you in the ribs to remind you what a miserable time you're having. I have a good midrange graphics card and never had a problem with any other games no matter how intensive the visuals.
They've attempted to transform this into an objective-driven challenge and failed spectacularly. It's tedious, extremely repetitive and there's no brainwork involved, just endless grind. Spikey Rivers is frankly impossible unless you "cheat" by grinding your points backwards to switch to green and use the Protection powerup. This is not a spoiler because a) you're wasting your time trying to do it any other way and b) nothing can spoil the game any further than the devs have already managed to do.
Unlike the flexible spine of the Evo Sparkle which lets you double-back and swirl effortlessly around the screen, Genesis won't turn sharply (which is necessary to catch prey) unless you keep the pointer close to the head at all times.
The noise when eating a jellyfish is INSANELY LOUD to the point where you have to brace yourself for it. The first few times it happened I nearly soiled my underpants. Remember what I said about the dev's ruination list? This is a prime example of the methods they've used to destroy the relaxing ambiance of Evo.
In Evo you can go deeper/shallower any time you like to catch your prey, which also moves up and down and has a wide range of terrain so you have to properly chase it. In Genesis you can only switch levels via whirlpools which often involves swimming long distances through barren wasteland. As far as I've progressed the prey never deviates from its limited position on the same level.
Most players discover that the whirlpools are broken and you can't switch levels. This is because it's set to use a controller, whether you have one or not. Every time you play the game you have to enter the settings menu and disable controller mode. Pretty inventive addition to the ruination list.
The in-game quests and achievements lists do not scroll so you can only see the first 4 items. FFS.
It has trading cards and achievements. I got 100% achievements on Evo 2 and every minute of it was a pleasure. With this I really did try and kept grinding for 10 hours but in the end I just couldn't stand it any longer and threw in the towel with less than 50%. Life is too short.

Frankenstein: Master of Death is a thoroughly average and unremarkable HOPA (
game, in which there is a mix of exploring rooms to gather items, mini-game puzzles, and hidden object scenes). While I think the developers did well in crafting a spooky atmosphere with the game's ~30 beautiful rooms (or scenes), the voice acting isn't very good (the protagonist's voice is especially awful), and the story is poor.
In fact, the storyline goes as follows: The protagonist, a friend of scientist Frankenstein, is tasked to stop Frankenstein's  monster, which Frankenstein greatly regrets creating. The protagonist then discovers that an evil man (an associate of Frankenstein) has a grand scheme to control this monster, and you basically go from scene to scene trying to stop this evil man. Ridiculous events occur in which this evil man slips from your grasp over and over. After awhile, I found myself not caring about what was going to happen next.
I play many HOPAs, and I finished Frankenstein: Master of Death in under 2 hours on Expert mode. This game simply wasn't a cost efficient purchase for me, which I could look beyond if the game had a memorable story and/or characters, which it doesn't. There are many higher-quality HOPA games out there with more gameplay hours for the same price, and a much more captivating storyline.
If you're a collector of HOPAs and really want to buy Frankenstein: Master of Death, I strongly suggest you wait until it goes on sale for a couple of dollars. To the general gaming public, I can't recommend this game at all.

Okay, so I finally got the chance to play this game and damn. I have two words for this game. FREAKING AWESOME! And this is coming from a person that doesn't play many first-person shooters, so kudos to Id Software for this amazing game.
First... The gameplay. I love the idea of just gunning down enemies and getting sweet weapons like a shotgun, plasma gun, minigun, rocket launcher and the iconic BFG 9000. Although incredibly simple, there's just something so addicting about it. And it's more than fair after you die, since even upon death, although you lose your weapons besides the pistol and knuckles, you can easily regain your lost weapons by gunning enemies down. Also, I feel like the game is tough enough to be fun, but easy enough for you to be able to pick it up and play it. This certainly is no game for casuals.
Graphics-wise... The game is obviously a product of its time, but I'm not a person to care too much about graphics as long as the game is great. And even for the simple DOS-based graphics, the game still seems to have aged pretty well... At least in my opinion, anyway.
Sound... Who knew that even MIDI typical of DOS games of its time could still get you pumped for the action? I also enjoyed the Doom Marine's digitized voice, even if it is just grunts and an agonized cry of agony upon dying.
Controls... Most enjoyable, since the controls are pretty simple and with the ability to aim only left or right, as long as you're shooting in the general direction of the enemy you're shooting at, you'll hit it. Otherwise, it's just your standard game of its time controls-wise.
Overall, I loved this game and can easily see why it's a classic. I'm hoping the Doom reboot is as awesome as the OG game. And one more parting thing with this review... If only modern shooters like Call of Duty and Battlefield could be this awesome.

I'm sorry to say that I'm not recommending "Frankenstein: Master of Death."  Looking at the individual elements of the game as stand-alone things, most of the pieces are OK.  But, when looking at the game as a whole, then the thing edges into the Not Recommended arena.
On the plus side, the graphics are good.
In the middle, the puzzles and HOGs are very easy (even for the genre) and the voice acting is tolerable.
For the slightly negatives, the story is very weak (again, even for the genre), the game is short (3.9 hours for me to finish it), a couple of items in the HOGs were mis-identified (cow <> antelope, forceps <> toenail cutters).  There also seems to be some kind of problem with some of the Achievements.  In my case, the game didn't give me the "Expert" Achievement (which we're supposed to get by playing in Advanced mode on Hard -- which I did).
But, the things that hurt the game the most are:
- An awful lot of the blocking items throughout the game are variations on keys.  Key after key after key after key.  Yes, you have to find the crowbar or something.  But, a very heavy trend is that those things you need are in a case or behind a door that needs its own special key.
- The chronological anachronisms strewn throughout it.  The story is a variation of Frankenstein and takes place around the year 1800 (give or take).  Yet, here and there in both the scenery and the HOGs are modern objects.  The big ones in the scenery are what look like a WWII airplane and a VW Beetle car.  There's no reason for this.  In addition to those, here are some of the other anachronisms I noted:  modern fire extinguisher, 1950's era toy robot, dynamite (not invented by Alfred Nobel until 1863), aluminum step ladder with plastic parts, movies, gramaphone (1887), digital numbers on a neon sign, reel-to-reel tape recorder, 1960's era camera, rubber dishwashing gloves, incandescent light bulb, and a foil tube of glue (complete with a recycling symbol and volume in milliliters).
So, I'm sorry to say I'm not recommending the game.  Definitely not at the list price of almost $9.  But, I'm still not recommending it at the dirt cheap price I got it at (less than $2).

Terrible first impressions.
Back Story:
To be fair I played this game in the beta and while quite a few things did get fixed there is still alot of work to go. This review may seem a bit harsh but from what ive seen i feel it is justified. I was a kickstarter backer from early 2016. The hype was almost instant, I mean all i had as a huge jason fan was the NES F13 game. Then after they met their goal all i saw was disappointment after diasppointment. Screen shots and alpha footage and then the beta, the hype rose, but then it happened. The updates from kickstarter started saying the same things worded new ways. All the social media had nothing to do with the game, more look where were going and watch us play other games on twitch,give us your money. Then came the news, delayed from Oct 16 to late 16. Then a short time later delayed again from late 16 to early 17 to work on the single player they were going to add ( also an additional kickstarter goal.... that wasnt reached). So using logic i divided the year into three parts early mid and late. Giving each equal time of 4 months i would have the game by the end of April... Nope. Missed it again by a month. And with no single player. Delayed for nothing.
Release:
Getting the game on release i honestly didnt even try to play. From seeing online a ton of people couldnt even play and there were major server problems. All things that should have been predicted and anticipated from doing a beta. When i did try and play days later i got in three matches. The first i was Jason. Killed two chased one in circles around a car (which is always a losing battle) and never even saw the others but i guess they got away. The next i was a counselor. while searching for items i pressed the button too close to a wardrobe as jason bust in the room behind me. As i entered Jason executed the kill for hiding people and killed me. BUT I didnt die. The game counted me as alive. I couldnt move my character or the camera and had no head but was still alive. It wasnt until Jason had killed everyone else and came back with sufficient throwing knives to kill me again from a distance. My third game i got off to a great start. Found a boat part and fixed it before hearing the ominous Jason coming up to get me. I ran around the small shack next to the boat and started around it to trying and head back into the woods to try and get away. That when i found my favorite thing in this or any other game (sarcasm). Invisible walls. There was clearly enough space for me to get through but yet it wouldnt let me. By the time i realized that i wasnt doing anything wrong and there was an invisible wall there i was dead.
Overall:
After spending some time with this game I would say that it can be fun. Watching this game has been super entertaining. Unfortunately thats where i feel it stops. When you take control of it things feel broken or illogical. Jason was an unstoppable killing machine until this game came out. Now hes stopped by everything from firecrackers to fences. In my own experience i also had the problem of the achievement counting up to be unlocked but never unlocking. Final thoughts on this game are that it was rushed. The game needs work. The achievements need work. Half or more of the game is promised at a later date. If you have seven friends to play this with it will be amazing. BUT so would anything else you can do with seven friends, so I wouldnt waste your time with this. Gun Media and Illfonic dropped the ball on this one and need to really put in the work now. As it stands, when people ask me what my favorite Friday the 13th game is, its LJN's Friday the 13th on NES. That was a Jason worth calling Jason.

This review factors in comments/reviews seen both pre and post release (as well as game play from pre and post release).
My overall impression of the game is overwhelmingly positive, but let's talk about the most popular/debated aspect of the game, the graphics/artstyle. I personally haven't played the 1st game (I've seen copious amounts of gameplay though), but I quite enjoy the style employed for Nidhogg 2.
Yes, it is drastically different from the original, but this was obviously intentional. The characters as opposed to a solid coloured silhouette, reveals fiendish, cartoonish looking characters.
Was this a reveal of the true characters from the original? I’m not sure, nor have I factored that in. But what I do know is that the visual likability of the characters did not affect my enjoyment of the game.

In general, the game has very simple controls, with various mechanics and weapons making it a game with a high skill ceiling - playable both as a couch and competitive game. Can easily be picked up and played, or have copious number of hours poured into it to master all the weapons.
Though a hotfix had been released already to fix a desync issue upon release day, it has been noted personally, on multiple occasions of various lag and stuttering issues. I have seen cases where both players experience the same lag, and also, where it’s only a 1-sided affair.

In closing, the artstyle, in addition to weapons, maps and music in Nidhogg 2 gives the game it’s own 2 feet to stand on, making it the successor to Nidhogg 1, rather than just a “DLC” of sorts – as such, it is quite the worthy and welcomed successor in my eyes. The controls feel clean, and the mechanics leave a lot to be explored with the help of several weapons, varying up the gameplay. However, the multiplayer side of the game has some kinks to be ironed out, but granted, this is release day +1.
I look forward to what the community will bring forth to this game, such as a mastery of the mechanics, leading to formidable and exciting tournaments!

THIS IS NOT MEANT TO BE NIDHOGG 1!!!!!!!
Just had to get that out there because many people seem to be confused by this.
I LOVE the original Nidhogg, it was and still is a great game, but content-wise, it was lacking. But the gameplay more than made up for it.
Originally, I saw the "awful" graphics for Nidhogg 2 and I told my self that I would never buy it because he completely ruined the appeal for the first game. But it grew on me. Now I have come to love them because it compliments the hilarity of the game.
As a original Nidhogg lover there has been a few changes gameplay wise. New weapons and quirks to them. Some have complained about the bow, I personally think if you know how to use it it works well. Some have claimed the broadsword is OP, but it has shortcomings. The dagger is amazing if used right and awful if used wrong. The rapier, however, is the all around choice. Either way, you can always turn weapons you don't want off, which fixes any of the complaining.
Alot of the original moves have been altered and I have heard the cry of avid fans and how it ruins gameplay. I would disagree and here's why. The original Nidhogg had a great swordplay mechanic (as does the second one) but I often found myself never using it because I didn't need to. I could cartwheel like crazy and then stab last second to kill nearly everytime. Then, if they caught on I would run and then roll-sweep the legs and get a clean kill. Add jumping and throw spamming and that was my strategy and it ALWAYS worked. A few times I would disarm MAYBE. But that mechanic was pretty much thrown out because you were just racing and the game was incredibly fast paced.
Nidhogg 2 changes that by adding more falling down doesnt allow spamming as easily. I find myself in this game being in more sword fights that actually use the brilliant mechanic because there is less rolling and sweeping and cartwheeling. Sure you can roll, but instead of sweeping there is a slide move that puts you on the ground (which animation wise is hilarious!). You can cartwheel, but it's more of a handstand then an elegant cartwheel.
The gameplay is less fast paced, but is still fast paced. There is more time for thinking to me at least. I find myself when I have a dagger against a rapier planning my attack. To me, it is a great idea to face off against other weapons that all have pros and cons and make you think quick. Other times, it is just a crazy frenzy. But that is what makes it great. Nidhogg 2 is great. It is replayable because everyone is different. It is a mind game that never gets old. Simple yet intricately skillful.
I played Nidhogg 1 competitively and loved Nidhogg 2. It is still a competitive game, there are just alot of new quirks and a slightly different set of skills to win then the original Nidhogg. Which I enjoy because it is a new game. I am happy it is just not a Nidhogg clone, but a whole new breed. At times it can be quirky and screw you up because something unexpected happens, but that happened in the old one as well. It makes it fun. Nidhogg has always been about fun and Nidhogg 2 is no different. It is so funny. The little um, Nidhoggins? Nidhoggians? Trolls? Simpsons? Aliens? Whatever they are. Their little determined, terrified bug eyed faces make me laugh way more than I should. I call em buggins cause of their bug-eyes but that's besides the point. The point is, the humor of this game is amazing. They are fighting to get eaten by a monster worm. Absurd. But it all makes sense when you are playing.
The original was great in my mind because it knew what it was.
Nidhogg 2 is great because it knows exactly what it is. It is hilarious. It is crazy. It is Nidhogg 2.
There is alot more that I could say that I am afraid will just bore you, so just go buy the game.

Siege is a great game with a great framework that becomes incredibly addicting, especially for those who are experienced in fps games. At the core of the game is the operators and their different abilities, with the full game, these operators are very easy to unlock, you get all the base ones within a few hours of gameplay, which is great as it allows you to unlock and learn individual operators as you go, making the process of learning the game a bit more friendly.
The starter edition makes getting Renown (the in-game currency used to unlock operators and weapon attachments) harder, meaning you have to grind out co-op missions just to unlock everything. Don't do it, the game isn't as fun when you lack all the options and attatchments the full game has, you'll have to invest way too much time into this game to get everything you need to do well, and the game's basic gameplay is good enough to the point where it won't really feel like that much of a grind, but you'll have way more fun with the full set of operators practically from the get-go. The devs really care about this game and are constantly improving it, buying the full game will help them with that too.

Real talk:
I really enjoy the first game and was excited about the second, but it is really hard to get into the sequel.
feel more arcadish, random and sluggish, and all of your reflexes and muscle memory from the first game will be thrown off. Honestly the animations are worse and movement strategy is almost non existent because the controls and movements feel more luck based than anything else. Also, hand to hand combat has been ruined since dive kicking causes both players to fall and you can kick weapons out of your opponent's hand. Also if you try to slide under your opponent's sword and sweep them they will kick your head into the ground so that move is useless... The actual controls and mechanics are a mess and are a huge downgrade from the crispness of the first game.
are a great idea, but only the basic sword and dagger are done well. The broadsword is too easy, and the bow is useless. The bow is a missed opportunity since you either hit your enemy or they deflect the arrow and hit you. The bow feels like a handicap since you can't swing or thrust it like a sword and the AI always deflects arrows.
the game is pretty but unpractical. I was looking forward to a visual upgrade since the first game was too bland, but Nidhogg 2's visuals are too noisy and distracting. Often time character's will blend in with the environment which makes things more confusing. There's a difference between adding nice details instead of vomiting neon paint all over the graphics. Also, the game does have some optimization issues so if you're playing on a conventional computer expect some lag on some of the maps with a lot of background effects. Character customization is very limited and the lack of variety gets old really fast.
If you're coming from the first game, prepare to be very disappointed. Game mechanics are sluggish, random and doesn't have the same strategy and energy as the first. The graphics are nice but way too distracting and too much stuff happening. The new weapons are novelties but are way worse than the classic sword. Character customization is a feature you thought you needed but don't use. All in all, a downgrade from the first.
*If you're new to Nidhogg, get the first game, not the second.

This is my first review an I will be as brief as I can.
The first hour of this game (campaign) was a very entertaining experience. The game mechanics a mix of realtime and round based strategy is refreshing and fun to use. The often criticised clunky controls and UI are not a gamebreaker for me.
BUT
what really destroys my motivation and is so damn frustrating, is the difficulty balancing of enemy fleets and missions in the campaign. No matter what difficulty setting you initially choose, the enemy seems to randomly start fielding fleets too big and too strong for what you can field at that point. In other words, the enemy doesn't properly scale in difficulty with your progress.
This has lead for me to many frustrating dead ends in the campaign. A BATTLESTAR Gallactica game is not much fun when you can barely move beyond unlocking the first type of Battlestar, not even to mention the Gallactica type.
(As evidence:
With 3750 the enemy has fleets nearly twice the size I can field at that moment 2000)
Right now I cannot recommend the game unless you want to pay that much just for skirmish and multiplayer.
Should this situation improve in the near future I will change my recommendation.

I barely recommend this game.  The game is a mix of Tactical and Strategy game-play.  The Space Battles are completed via turn-based movement in which the player has to arrange their fleet to best defeat the enemy.  The tactical component is actually pretty good.  The problem with the game is the Strategic level of the game.  You have to jump from system to system (there are essentially 4) trying to put out fires.  The strategic interface is very limited and generally detracts from the game.  The game provides around 20 hours of game-play to beat the campaign.
Strengths:
- Tactical Space Combat
- Music
Weaknesses:
- Strategic level interface/design
- Cost ($44 on 9 Sep 2017)
I'd recommend waiting until the price drops to $20 or less.

My first time, to give a thumps down.
This game is not recommended, and I am sorry to say so, becouse I acually liked some aspects of the game, and some of the lore in the game were really cool, but the games bad sides overrule the good, I will tell you some of the bad and good sides.
Good:
Some of the only good parts about this game is it`s atmosphere. At times the game gives us some cool locations, to look at. You can run around to explore more of the locations, and maybe find some secrets. Some of the lore parts are very cool like the three mages of power there are in a three, I really liked them.
Bad:
There are many bad aspects of this game if you ask me. I will take you trough some of them.
Loctations:
Didn`t I just say the locations had some good atmosphere? Yes and they have that, but it`s more of the boundaries of the game that bothers me. You have to go to special locations throughout the game, and when you get to them, you will feel that exploration feeling. The sad part is that the game feelt really lockt to me. I knew I could explore, but there were so little to explore, and the game makes you take it`s own route so fast, that you feel you have no freedom at all.
Gameplay:
The game is a RPG and it could easily be called a hack and slash, even though you also have bow and arrows. The gameplay is very simple, hit, block, avoid and it get`s boring fast. I don`t say simplisiti is bad, but this game purly used, what it could have used of diffrent tools, to make the combat more exating. You are constantly avoding enemys, only beocuse you will not bother to kill them, and that is a minus in my book, if you don`t wanna play the game, what`s then even the point? You can change gear and weapons throughtout the game, which is nice, but would it be to much to ask that the gear would change your appearance? You only change appearance a few times in the game, which is a bid wierd for a RPG, you wanna get the feeling that you got something out of the game all the time, but again the game falls flat on that part.
Characters:
I bounded to none of the characters in this game, not even the main character! I found the main character to be annoying, I did not feel free to answer anything in the game, my character would always be an annoying brat, who would be an idiot towards nearlly everybody in the game. I really hated the main character, but I am stuck with him, becouse he IS the main character. No other character said me anything, and when I finally found a character I liked, the games "stick to the story" acpect, made me leave the character and never see him again, which makes you forget them very fast.
Bosses:
I have to shortly talk about the bosses. All the bosses in the game, has a big lead up to them, which is good. You are hyped to fight them, but then something happens. Since the gameplay is so easy, the bosses are very simelar, and there are few changes to them. The most major changes is one of them can fly, and some can shot spells, and have minions. The first couple of bosses is some kind of hard, and one of the last bosses is a nightmare (the guy that burns down your city, I will get back to him). But the last boss was so anticlimatic, that I feelt an incompleted feeling inside, when I killed it.
The story:
This is the part I feelt the most angry about. For all RPG`s it is important to have a interasting story, so you can keep your player intertainted, and want him to search for more story, in order to experince how it all hangs together. But this game delivers a really wierd thing, I have never treyd before. The game start by telling you an evil demon of some sort, have sent out more demons in the world of Arcania, then you play as a king, who you then find out has become curopted by the demons.
Then your story start, and you are a person that have been washed up on a beach. In the beginning you are about to marry your girlfriend, and that starts a big tutorial to learn you all the basics, then you visit some witch who teels you, you are destent to do great things, and then your city is on fire! Everyone in the city is killed, even your girlfriend (which were one of the characters I liked). This makes you as the player want to revenge her, but then it start to go down hill. And that is wierd for me, I liked the story to begin with, and the it change into this:

An underwater story driven horror adventure set in the Atlantic that plays quite similar to their earlier title - Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬
Back in 2010, I was always looking for games that would run on my♥♥♥♥♥♥poor PC. Amnesia was pretty hyped (thanks to YouTube let's plays) so I got that and played it at like 15fps on that PC. It was an impressive horror game from a small studio that led to the monster chase horror game trend of which most were just as bad as my PC. SOMA however is one of the better story driven horror games from a small studio since 2010's Amnesia. It has the expected list of upgrades - better(okayish for 2016) graphics, smoother gameplay and no load screens other than when loading from a save.
I loved this story more than Amnesia's. The monsters also have some variety to them - some cant see but listen, some can - little variations like that. Even the underwater setting, at least for me, is spookier than a castle. It has mod support and thanks to a dedicated fan community there are already a few custom stories that you can play through.
This game isn't a masterpiece, it follows the usual horror tropes, in this case, waking up in an unknown place, something's odd and soon there are monsters blocking your progression through the level/story. Although SOMA does some improvements over Amnesia, it's pretty much the Amnesia formula. At least Slender and FNAF tried new things. Then there's the complete lack of an inventory system. In horror games, I find that running out of bullets/batteries and managing inventory space adds to the tension. Here, your flashlight battery never runs out. This makes the game very linear and discourages exploration and puzzle solving, at least for those who aren't so inclined towards it.

TL;DR below
I believe I have never played a game that has left such an impression on me. I absolutely love Supergiant Games due to the fact that they can create games with such remarkable and rememberable moments. Bastion's technological-yet-forgotten ambience, Transistor's cyberpunk-ish scenarios, and, now, Pyre's amazing storyline and world.
Let's start with the characters. Different from their previous games, where all the events are narrated by one or a few characters, Pyre has a full-blown cast of characters, each and every single one of them are unique. Not only that, they have interesting backstories,
The gameplay is the only part in this game where I find the game to be a bit faulty. To be clear, I loved every moment of it, but I though certain items in the game were a bit too overpowered to be used and made the game a bit too easy.
Aside from this, the game is pretty solid, being pretty challenging at times, requiring at least a degree of fast reflexes, specially in the Versus and True Nightwing modes.
Now, the art. The art of this game, to say the least, fits astoundingly well with everything. The incredible (presumably) hand-drawn areas are breathtaking, coupled with the well drawn character designs makes the game a treat for the eyes.
The story is conveyed mostly through the Book Of Rites, which you gain acess to in the beginning of the game. Aside from that, you gain snippets of information from red word on the dialog box, which can be highlighted to display the info (which is kinda confusing a first, but gets better with time). I have to commend the developers on this, because, compared to their last games, there is so much in this world for us to learn about us, our fellow exiles, and the past of the Rites. I am a person who loves a good fictional universe, and this is very cool.
Finally, the songs. Darren Korb, you incredible musician you. There isn't a single song, in my opinion, that doesn't fit the time they play in the game (
). The songs are expertfully crafted, having amazing vocals, that can be both calming and exhilariting at the same time.
TL;DR: The game is pretty good. It has good music, story, art and characters, and, last but not least, a quite solid gameplay which complements the rest of the game very well. Aside from some balancing issues, you should definitely buy this!

The game is amazingly good. At first I thought: "Man, a novel mixed with a sports game? Nah, can't be good." But you know what? It turned out to be something fresh.
The most important thing about the game are the dialogues. So if you haven't played this game before, you definately mustn't skip them! Of coure, if you want to experiance the Rites as they should be, turn on the highest difficulty level right on start, because on easy mode the first ones are
trival. Oh, and please, don't get me started on the music. It's gorgeous. Every track fits perfectly to the atmosphere at any given moment. The visuals are masterfully crafted. The characters? They all have been sent to the Downside, a place for those who broke the law of the Commonwealth, for diffirent reasons. Each of them diffirent, be it your companions or your adversaries. Each one of them has diffirent personalities, morales, background, motives and a story to tell. Throughout the game you really bond with them. They're no longer unknown Exliles who decided to help you, they start to be the ones that you care about.
But the question is: will you give your strongest, most Enlightened characters the chance to regain their  once lost freedom, or make them stay with you to help liberate others at the cost of their own chance of leaving? The choice will be yours, Reader....
I haven't mentioned the Narrator yet? Well, you'll going to love him, I can assure you...
TL/DR: Cool characters, cool story, cool gameplay mechanics. What are you still waiting for? Buy it!
(also, if you did, then congratulations for reading through all of those ramblings of mine...)

This is my first experience with a JetDogs HOG. Definitely not as good as Artifex Mundi, but still a HOG worth playing.
This HOG was somewhat more inventory oriented than others on Steam. Some items have multiple uses. A recurring theme is finding particularly shaped keys to open doors or containers (over a dozen).
The hidden object scenes are quite easy compared to most HOGs. The scenes are not very cluttered and the objects are placed normally rather than being hidden in clever but often unintuitive ways as many HOGs like to do.
A single playthrough takes only about 3 hours.
Pros:
* Nice static art
* Some scenes have some animations
* Hidden Object Scenes have many mini puzzles
* Hidden Object Scenes not too difficult
* Puzzles are straightforward/easy (there is a sliding 9-puzzle, though, that I'm not a fan of)
* Good cutscenes
* Good voice acting
* All achievements can be earned in a single playthrough (don't use hints or skip anything, and ensure that Advanced Mode is set in Options before starting).
Cons:
* 3D characters are a bit ugly
* Monster and some character animation is silly looking
* Somewhat weak writing (though not terrible for a HOG)
* Crude use of sound effects. Music is sometimes annoying.
* Some illogic (e.g. can cut chains but not thin bars with hacksaw)
* No replayability features (scenes not random, can't replay scenes).
* Crashed once during gameplay (progress auto-saves), once on startup, and every time on exit
* Some achievements are buggy (if you don't earn them the first time around, you may have to purge your profile data to earn them). I still haven't unlocked 2 of them despite seemingly meeting the conditions, but I haven't tried the data purge trick yet.

A hidden object game with a good storyline, beautiful graphics, and fully animated and voice-acted cutscenes.
A nice addition to the genre here is that there is both an expert and easy mode, with the easy mode allowing you to skip most of the hidden object puzzles and just focusing on the adventure item collecting/combining parts.
There is also a hint button on a timer, which helps you find the next screen to work on. Since this is a rather large game where you have to backtrack a lot, this comes in really helpful as a hint always works on a per-screen basis: once you can figure out where to go next, you can stop using it.
The voice acting is for the most part pretty good, except for the (few) lines voiced by the player character. Not sure what went wrong there, they sound too far away and don't fit the otherwise high quality design of the game.
Recommended for anyone who likes hidden object games, although parents of *very* young players should keep in mind the game may be a bit scary for them.

Frankenstein: Master of Death is the newest title from JetDogs to make it to Steam and is a nice addition to the hidden object catalog here.  An alternate take on the Frankenstein story, the premise is interesting albeit a bit hokey at the same time.  Granted, HOGs are not known for their great storylines as they're often just a base to build a game upon, but that's usually enough for me.  The time period offers us an amazing setting for gorgeously drawn backgrounds and artwork, my favorite aspect of these games.
Keys, keys and more keys.  A good portion of the game involves finding different keys for lock boxes, doors, and just about everything else.  Some open puzzles while others give access to new rooms and areas of the map.  While it gets rather tiresome opening door after box after door, once I realized that's basically the shtick of the gameplay I was able to sit back and enjoy it for what it is.  Fortunately, there are plenty of puzzles to play through, but nothing too difficult or mind bending. The hidden object scenes are interesting in that many include mini-puzzles within them as well, a neat addition that you don't see very often.  As for the scenes themselves, they're nicely drawn with no deceptively hidden items, just challenging enough to keep your eyes sharp.

If I had to describe Frankenstein: Master of Death in one word it would be "pleasant."  There are no leaps in logic needed to progress, no puzzles that completely boggle the mind, and nothing about the presentation that I feel was grating or annoying.  That said, If you're interested in something a little more challenging, you might want to look elsewhere. But if a casual experience with some light puzzle solving is what you're after, this may be the HOG for you.  Although on the pricier side for its length (it only took me 3 hours to 100% the game), full Steam integration adds a bit of value back into the package.  If nothing else, it's worth keeping on your radar for a nice sale.
Bottom Line - Recommended for casual gaming fans looking for a relaxing and enjoyable experience.

Take the base building mechanics of Dungeon Keeper with the overworld map of X-com and set it all to a parody of the James Bond universe and you've got Evil Genius.
In Evil Genius you play as an arch villian bent on world domination. You start out with a deserted island and a handful of hilariously inept workmen. As you build your base, steal money, hijack national treasures, kidnap specialists, and train your forces you'll move up the ladder of infamy.
As you become more notorious the forces of Good will grow increasingly aggressive. Expect the initial annoyance of investigators and burglars to give way to invasions by sabotuers, soldiers, and even super heroes.
Evil Genius is an easy recommendation to anyone who enjoys the dungeon building simulations ala Dungeon Keeper, or who likes the theme and setting of James Bond and doesn't mind a game that pokes fun at its foibles.
