Survarium takes place in the future of 2050, where a majority of Ukraine has been radiated by various sources. The war for the donetsk region of Ukraine still rages on, even though the world has gone to bitter ♥♥♥♥. Due to radiation, and the decrease of population in both sides, they have taken part in something straight out of a science fiction novel.
To continue the conflict, both sides have taken part to an illegal cloning project, which has spun out of control. The cloning produces millions, upon millions of middle aged men. And due to a unfortunate mishappening, each clone came with a copy of a Mosine and a Ppsh-41. With the coming uprising, the clones have taken control of both Ukraine Parliament, and Donetsk's Parliament.
With the end of the old world governments, you would think that both sides could come to an agreement, but no. Old grudges never go away. They declare war on each other, and send all their forces to attack each other. That's where you, the player, come in.
You take control of one of these mindless clones. You start out with a wool sweater, a PPSH-41, a Mosine, and a TT-34 for your sidearm. Unfortunely, your clone doesn't not come with a voice box, so you can not communicate with your allies vocally. You need to use hand signals to be able to communicate with them.
The combat is unique, accurately depicting the true struggles in the Ukrainian conflict. Everyone looks the same. Both sides have the same weapons, and the same sweaters. It's just like the real life counterpart, having both sides shoot each other while they have the same uniforms and weapons.
Shooting people isn't too hard, as each time you win a round you 'level up'. This means you are able augment your clone in to a type of super soldier unseen in modern warfare.
Dying isn't also a pain either, as each time you die a cloaked Matter Replicator brings a new you back to life to fight again.
The shop in game allows you to exchange US currency to a type of digital gold, to russian rubles. You can use the digital gold/rubles to further augment your clone, buy old world weapons/armor, or buy flags (Such as USSR, Russian Federation, Russian Seperatists, Ukraine, etc.). It is unknown in the story where the supplies come from, but the developers have hinted that Russia is supplying the clones. It has yet to be confirmed or canon.
My personal opinion is that it's an alright game depicting real life events, and a scenario which can happen in the future.
The clone I currently own is a level 20 Commissar, equipped with a gasmask linked to a gasoline canister, so that I can inhale the gas fumes and have supersoldier strength.
I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to see what it is like fighting on the front lines of the Ukraine Civil War. Thank you for this beautiful game.

For nearly two years VG have been promising something resembling an open world or PvE gamemode, and for two years they've focused solely on the PvP test element of the game, that was literally just supposed to be a test/tech demo to get the engine and netcode sorted.
I've clocked in a couple of dozen hours in the non-steam version over the past year and now thought I'd give the steam version a try having not touched it for 4 months and things are still looking dire.
It is currently on track just to be a generic pay-2-win model, with "premium weapons/clothing" that have slightly higher stats, along with making it impossible to progress without the usage of premium currency or boosters. This is extremely disappointing giving the potential this game had.
For all intents and purposes it is still a generic mediocre shooter. TDM, Capture the Flag and King of The Hill, in a couple of very small and bland maps, 8v8 and that's about it. It's recently added in perks (which give a clear advantage vs new players) and a faction system (just a daily rep grind for slightly better gear, also slow without premium) which is at least something to briefly hold your attention but it doesn't seem to be going anywhere past that.
The balancing is awful, the matchmaking out right never works, maps are poorly designed and bland and the gameplay model is geared towards rewarding people who pay vs people who play. This was lauded as being an extremely immersive post-apocalyptic MMO and it's turned into a Call of Duty mashed together with World of Tanks. The graphics are average, the sound design is very good, gunplay is not remotely satisfying combined with iffy hit-boxes and obnoxious hit markers appearing constantly makes for a sour experience.
There are a lot of guns to choose from, nearly all of them being russian based, with a single faction's rewards being western weapons but it's roughly similar to STALKER in variety. One of my biggest gripes with it claiming to be an immersive and realistic shooter, is that 10 different guns all use the same calibre of ammunition, and it is clearly stated as such, but they've all got vastly different damage values. People of a higher rank outright get more armour and have better weapons, and when you start out you have identical calibre weapons that can't touch them.
I, like a lot of people, saw this years ago as trying to lure in STALKER fans, and their website is very in tune with lauding on about how dangerous the "forest" is a long all of the factions, dangers and adventure to be had. The only thing even remotely similar to the STALKER games is the fact that they've added anomalies/artifacts to the maps that kill you when you get close, they contribute absolutely nothing to the flow of the gameplay and are a novelty at best.
Pros:
- Great sound design
- Large variety of weapons and clothing (that requires large amounts of grinding unfortunately)
- You can reach the main menu without needing to spend any gold.
Cons:
- Mediocre graphics
- Poor gunplay
- Grind heavy.
- Clear and major advantages to users who pay over uses who play.
- No fleshed out story, plot or context. (bar that you're in a dangerous forest filled with radiation and some scavengers)
- Poor netcode, hit detection and general network instability.
- Prone to crashing, FPS drops and graphical bugs.
To echo many others, if you take a look at the timeline we all saw two years ago -
We were supposed to have a billy bones basic version of the open world by the end of 2013. I predict at their current rate of progression, we'll probably see it fully released by 2017. Given that this game is very popular in CIS states due to the fact it's F2P and they are a major source of premium currency purchases in similar games, I don't see it dying out or crashing and burning, but it is still a massive disappointment and has turned into a cash cow.

NOTE: I try to spoil as few as possible about the Story!
„Pyre“ is the newest Game from Developer „Supergiant Games“ (Creators of the Games „Bastion“ and „Transistor“)
The Game plays in a World where the „Commonwealth“, a Union of many Races and Lands, punish Criminals with Exile in the „Downside“
This Downside can only be entered via a River which ends in a very deep Waterfall down.
Escaping back to the Commonwealth is impossible.
They are forced to spent the Rest of their Lifes in these Lands which consists mainly of Deserts, Bogs and other harsh Climates.
The Player was also cast down as an Exile. On the Brink of Starvation and Thirst, a Wagon comes the Way and 3 masked Persons come out. One of them gives some much needed Food and Water.
After being invited into the Wagon, a Question is raised if he can read a mysterious Book they have with them.
Through reading the Book, there is a possibility how to escape the Downside and thus the Journey to Redemption begins...
The Game consists of 2 Parts:
-          Story (Exploration, Dialogues, Party-Management, Choices, etc.)
-          Action (Rites)
In the Story Part, you travel with your Friends and other Team Members through the Downside to the Locations where the Rites will take.
The Wagon will act as your central hub where you can manage your Party, study the Book of Rites and interact with many other objects you later will receive.
There will be later an Option to train everytime against the AI for testing new Tactics/etc. Equipment/Artifacts which can be equipped on Team Members can be bought/sold at the „Slugmarket“ before the Start of any Rite.
During the Travels you will have the choice of selecting 2 different paths which will have different Events (Bonus) depending who requested the path.
Besides those Events you will also get the usual Story Events which can be also slightly random. At the Beginning you will find active Rites through the Navigation of a Start which indicate the Spot.
Later you can choose between different Stars and therefore also decide which Enemy Team you want to confront.
In the Action Part, 2 Teams consisting of 3 People each („Triumvirate“) tries to extinguish the Pyre of the Enemy Team.
To reach this Goal, a Character must throw or dunk the „Celestial Orb“ into the Pyre.
The Flame grows weaker afterwards (Default is 100 Units at Start). When a Character successfully weakens the Pyre, he will be banished until the Enemy Team scores a Hit or someone else from the Team hits the Pyre.
Every Character has also emits an Aura which will temporarily banish enemy Players.
This Aura can also be used as Projectile to send it as a Wave. If a Character takes the Orb his Aura will be absorbed fully by it, which then in Return makes him defenseless against enemy Auras.
Since this is a Team Game, the Orb can be passed to other Team Members, but only one Person at a Time can be moved while the others remain stuck and defenseless against Enemy Attacks.
Each Race has its own set of unique Movements, Aura and Abilities. Participating Characters gain Experience and unlock unique Abilities which are divided into 2 different Categories.
Every Character has 4 Attributes:
-          Glory (This Value describes how much Damage is dealt to the Enemy Pyre)
-          Quickness (This Value describes how fast a Character moves on the Field)
-          Presence (This Value describes how wide one’s Aura is)
-          Hope (This Value describes how fast, the Character can return back from the temporary Banishment)
During the Game i thought that it would get repetitive going from one Rite to another, but i was suprised how much the Story unfolds and new Events take Place. New Options also will get unlocked during the Game which makes it more appealing.
I also thought about the Action Part itself being stale later on, but was surprised how much depth it has and later gaining new options which makes it more difficult with also more stronger getting Enemy Teams.
Here are my positive/neutral/negative Points:
Positive (+):
-Excellent and very good Soundtrack!
-Good and tactical Action Part
-Your Decisions can influence the Outcome and Destiny of involved Characters in the Story
-Well written Characters
-„Fluent“ Artstyle and Graphics which remains in Future still good to look at
-Great Replay Value, since many Decisions and Wins/Losses can influence the Story
-Characters can Level Up and gain new Abilities
-No Real Game Over. The Story continues nonetheless how much you loose in the Rites
Neutral (o):
-This Game plays like a „Visual Novel“ since more then 60% of the Game consists of reading and making Decisions. For those who want more Action should be aware of this Fact!
-Character unique Artifacts, that can be earned during specific trials, can make the Items in the Slugmarket somewhat useless later on
Negative (-):
-No Possibility to talk with the Team-Members outside specific Events
-Versus Mode is only local with no Network Options
Fazit:
The Graphics and the Music are one of the Trademarks of this Studio which itself makes it worth getting it. The Characters growed on me during the Story and i also felt later their absence if they are liberated.
Since your Decisions can alter the End on multiple Things, it offers a great Replay Value!
For me its one of the few Games, which i can still play in future and still will be amazed of it!

This hurts me so much that I have to give this a negative review. Growing up I loved Warfare 1917 and 1944, and it's not just nestalgia because, as I've played both again recently, they're both really good games. This game, however, seems to forget what made the first two enjoyable to play.
First thing that's odd about this game is the free to play element. You cannot have a good base stratagy game with microtransactions, expecially with how the game incorporates them. You buy supply crates with money you earn in game, or purchased, and buy cards that are used ingame as abilities. These cards can be a number of things that include artillary, supporting your units, and even buying a unit immediately, ignoring the timer each unit has until they can be purchased. You can have up to a total of 20 cards in your deck at once for a battle. These cards break the stratagy, as it's completely random in what order you get these, and you can only use three at a time, or throw them away to get a random card, but lose the card forever. These cards are completely gone once you use them. If you run out of your 20 cards, like you're likely to do in a good match, you can't get any anymore. Not only that, but some of these cards are completely, and blatantly OP. Like the card that makes it impossible for a vehicle to fire for 15 seconds. Five seconds would be understandable, but 15?! I hated Halo Wars 2 for this exact same system.
In a match you can have five different units that you can select of your choosing. Infantry, vehicles, light tanks and heavy tanks. Infantry have a cooldown of around 15 seconds on selection, with tanks taking around 50 seconds. If you played the previous Warfare games, then how the game actually plays will be very familiar with you. There's one fatal flaw with this system though. Like cards, units have a limited amount of spawns, which means once you've spawned your tenth infantry squad, you can no longer spawn infantry, same for tanks. Cards have abilities that let you get more of a unit once they've ran out, but since you can run out of cards, eventually you're gonna run out of everything! That means in a good match where both sides are equally pushing each other back in a tug of war, someone is going to run out of units eventually and the game is over. That's just plain bad game design. This means the player with more cards that let them get more units will win every single time. That's also super pay to win, something else you don't want in a stratagy game. And it's super easy to lose units too, with not being able to retreat them (like seriously, why isn't that in this game?), and explosives and artillery descimating infantry. If your men are caught without cover, they won't run for the nearest cover, intead they'll act like dumbasses and just stand in the middle of nowhere. If you want to win a match, all you have to do is get like one, or two infantry squads and two assault squads at the start of the round. The assault class is broken, simply put. They can easily take out an entire squad with one well placed grenade. Then you have the fact that this game has an actual stat called "RNG." This game is an RNG fest. Sometimes tanks will one shot your AT squad, wasting your valuable time and now that's one less AT squad you can call in, and sometimes assault squads will one hit a squad as previously mentioned. Maybe this wouldn't be as noticable if it wasn't that you have a finite amount of units. AT squads feel really weak as vehicles automatically shoot them, and can possibly just one shot them, regardless of how far away as them. If you have an infantry squad trying to distract them, the tank will just ignore them. A better system would be to make tanks shoot the closest unit, or vehicle. That way you'd have a reason to keep units in the back, like AT and snipers, rather than rushing them because it's impossible to play defensively because of all the explosives. The only way you're going to win is by being offensive. In 1917, sometimes it could be a challange to take over a trench, however, in this one it's way to easy to advance. It's really confusing why cover is so sparse in this game when it's really important. You can't have a good defensive line because units like the machine gunner have an ever so slightly larger line of sight than your infantry class. This means that an MG team can wipe out an entire infantry squad without the infantry squad shooting back. Why would you take a sniper, when you can have MGs that kill quicker (though MGs still suck, like snipers, because defensive classes suck)? Every unit, besides the sniper, needs to have the same line of sight, but make units like the assault class do less damage at longer ranges.
It feels like this game was supposed to go to mobile, but for some reason came to PC. The controls are super simplistic, you only need a mouse to play. You can't chat, or use voice chat. The only chat options are premade chat lines. The controls for units should be more advanced at this point. Retreating and more advanced movement need to be included. The ability to individually select units to stand still is also a must, and shouldn't be a very confusing card that makes every unit stand still. I'd also like to see each class have it's own unique symbol above their head. At the moment each infantry class has the same symbol, making it hard to tell on the American side if I have an assault squad, or infantry squad because they both look the same. Until this game starts acting more like a stratagy game and less like a free to play game, I wouldn't recommend playing it for very long. If you're a long time Warfare fan, try it, but prepare to be disappointed.
I'd also appreciate it if you can earn XP when fighting friends.

Note that It is 12/31/16 at the time of my writing this, and as The Isle is in Early Access everything is subject to change. In a few days, weeks, months, whatever, there is potential for dramatic changes that may render aspects of this review invalid.
Revising my review from back in... November? It was a while ago, for sure, and there's been a few changes to the game that have made me rethink how I feel about the game.
I'm not going to give you information that's not already on the product information. Read the description and then re-read it again if you enter the game and are shocked to find it is unlike the videos on the store page. Anyways.
1) Community isn't all that great, both the developers and players have flaws-- as with every game. You can avoid this.
My rule of thumb is to generally avoid looking into the community forums with the exception of the Discord server and affiliated events such as streams, developer "pow-wows," and testing-- things aren't as ugly there, not taking into account the few personal nitpicks I have. My issues with someone's personality aren't going to affect how I judge the actual game, and certainly not how I choose to rate its functionality and appeal.
Avoid the rage threads. Ignore the people who whine in the forums and disown the game from their lives and then log 30 more hours within the next week. Read the rules and don't give the developers more reason to be wary and rightfully resentful of the community. Things will be unfair, but there's a purpose for Early Access and one of those purposes is to encourage feedback-- actual FEEDBACK and advice, NOT rage threats or meaningless vent posts. Do that. Don't be a prick. Done, next topic.
2)  As for the game itself, The Isle is pretty God damn solid. It's challenging, it's frightening, it's frustrating and it's super addictive.
On the flip side, hardcore survival is hardcore survival. You need to adapt, you need to pick your battles and know when it's time to leave an area because something bigger and with more teeth (or firepower) than you is approaching. Trust no one and always, always be ready to be backstabbed. It will happen. You will die, you will lose hours of progression, it's a game designed to kill you... but that's part of the charm. You need to think as an animal in some circumstances. You will need to put yourself first, always, not your packmates or herdmates or whatever group you may or may not have going. Kill your allies. Be deceptive. Trick people. Don't be afraid to think for yourself once in a while, it will (not might, WILL) save your♥♥♥♥♥in the future.
Learning to be cruel to keep myself alive was difficult, I wasn't used to that sort of playstyle and messed up plenty of times and was sent back to the bottom for that. It was frustrating! So I stepped back, thought about how to do better, and then did just that. It's a learning process, and if you keep at it you'll thrive! So don't let one setback ruin the game for you, think of it more as a learning experience. Once this game gets polished and finished, God ♥♥♥♥ing help you because you'll have more than predators and basic needs to worry about.
Not sure what else to say here. Game itself looks brilliant, creatures sound and overrall look wonderful save for a few scientific inaccuracies that I've been able to overlook. This is NOT a dinosaur simulator at its core. This is NOT dinosaur Club Penguin or Feral Heart or whatever. Don't play expecting to play without consequences.
Now, if all that's your thing? Get this game. It's been a ball seeing this game develop over the several months I've had it, and it's only going to get more interesting. Happy hunting!

Alright - time for another review of mine. :j2: :j2: :j2: :j2: :j2: :j2: :j2:
So, this is the typical "horror-game", what you see is basicly what you get. Friday the 13th!
- 7 horny councelors are camping at different locations near Crystal Lake, making Jason MAD and wants to smash'em all.
You get in a lobby with 7 other people - which means it's going to be a 1v7 match. One player gets Jason and 7 others get to be murdered. It's really "rng" but not really - once you get the hang of it, you can see in the lobby who's gonna be the next Jason. Let's say that guy nr.3 on the list - "Chaddy" was killer the first round.. then there's most likely 99% chance that nr.4 on the lobby list - "Hubert" - will be the next Jason. I can usually predict it anyway!
You need to organize a lot with people if you wanna play "serious" and escape, you can be altruistic and help the others fighting off Jason, protecting them - or you can be a piece of ¤%#& and run them over with the car or take off in the boat all alone. I myself do both, depending on how the team is. BUT I usually play with 2+ friends, so we usually end up fixing the 4-seater and taking it for ourselves or sacrifice ourselves for the greater good of the team. Also the ingame voicechat can be fun (making a dramatic death, screaming when you see Jason etc) but it can also be quite annoying with people insulting you for killing them - but I guess that's just online gaming in a nutshell.
ALSO you have 5... 5!!!! options of escaping!
- Calling the cops, which makes the cops arrive after a 5min timer after calling them; find the fuse, install it in the fusebox and call'em.
- Repair the 4-seater car (blue car); You need to install a battery, fill gas on it AND then you need car keys and drive out.
- Repair the 2-seater car* (yellow/brown car); You need to install a battery, fill gas on it and car keys - then drive out.
- Repair the 2-seater boat* (...boat...); Install propeller and fill it with gas, then start the motor and ... "drive"? out.
- Calling Tommy Jarvis and killing Jason; This.. is almost impossible with a fully random team, sadly. I myself have done it with 3 randoms and a friend! Look up guides on "How to" on either steam or youtube (or google).
- "Surviving" for 20 minutes; You will not be rewarded for surviving for 20 minutes.
*The 2-seater car and the 2-seater boat is a random spawn, there's only 2 vehicles on the map, where the 4-seater is a 100% spawn, so the 2-seaters boat/car is a 50/50% spawn.
Controls; Bit clunky at the beginning, but once you get used to it, it's pretty basic.
Sounds (Music & Sound effects); Sound effects are decent, some are however still delayed by 0.2-0.5 seconds, but I think they'll fix it within the next few updates! The music.... oh god, the music. It's the real horror in the beginning - but once you get to know the difference between the ambience music and the "he's here - RUN!!"-music, then it becomes less scary.
Graphics; Graphics are overall good, but you can tell it's indie developers with a lesser budget that's made the game.
Balance; This is probably THE MOST discussed topic on the forums! Personally I do think that the shift+grab+instachoke is bit overpowered. I genuinly believe that Jason should have 0.5 seconds "cooldown" on his abilities and grab after he exits shift. (BTW Shift is his "invisible fasttravel superspeed thingy"), but should still be able to HIT with his weapon. The game is also designed so that the survivors shouldn't escape, but in nearly all matches I've played AT LEAST 2 people have escaped. There's some balancing issues with Jasons traps at the moment (10th of June, 2017) where he can place 2+ traps on top of each other, so even if you disarm one trap, there will still be more traps under the disarmed trap.
Bugs/Exploits; (10th of June, 2017) Sadly, there's a lot of people using exploits to hack others perks and CP (points you use to roll perks), but the developers are fixing it. I myself have lost my perks and CP 2 times already! Luckily I do not need to play with perks tho. People have been exploiting themself onto a rock, under a bridge etc. so that Jason couldn't get to them - wasting others time. Luckily the match-timer is 20 minutes and they do NOT get a reward for surviving by time! If you see those players ingame and you're a councelor - KILL them. Screw the -200xp points you get. They deserve to die. If you're Jason and see an exploiter, go to the nearest councelor and tell him to kill the guy exploiting - and you will spare them their life (you can do that or you can of course lie and kill them after that... but I wouldn't recommend that, since chances are they will not help another Jason with that in the future).
Other; What I like the most about this game is the different ways that you can kill people as Jason! Each Jason has 3 different "special grab-kills" with their weapon, and additional.... 15? different grab-kills. You can only have 4 active grab-kills btw. In addition to this, you have at least 10+ ways of killing councelors with enviromental stuff, like drowning them in the lake or the toilet, burning them in the fireplace, throwing them out of a window etc. or you can just hit them with your weapon if you want a fast game! If you want to do enviromental kills then get a Jason with +grasp strenght so you can carry them to the enviromental-killinggrounds and sacrifice them to "Mother"!
- The beginner-Jason (Part 3) is good for that!
Edit; June 10th, 2017; I think I forgot to adress an ingame voicechat issue that I have: it would be REALLY nice if you could turn the volume up/down on each players mic, as some people have a REALLY high mic and others are like a whisper in the wind.
I will be updating this review once in a while and change it up.
If you're looking for a survivalgame where you WANT to survive everytime, then this game might not be for you.. if you're looking for some quickplay, then this is not for you either - this game is slowpaced and if you want the +500 endgame XP, then you have to wait approx. 20 minutes from match start, till you get your points.
If this game doesn't sound like it's for you, but you still want some survival-horror that will make you think "oh ♥♥♥♥ oh ♥♥♥♥ he will get me any moment now.. faaaaaaaak" - then I can recommend Dead by Daylight as it's in the same genre.

Sniper Elite V2 is a mix between sniper simulation, third person shooter and stealth. It has gorgeous graphics and a fully coop campaign of sizable length (~6 to 8 hours).
Both three components of the gameplay are intertwined to create an experience that is unlike any shooter. The sniping simulation part can take breath, wind and distance into account, but it can also be more arcade like, with extremely satisfying kill cams and various, creative ways of killing opponents (eye, testicles, enemy grenade, etc...). Thanks to its cover mechanics, it is beginner friendly. Stealth is entirely optional but well integrated, providing additional challenge and satisfaction for the sneaky types. Keep in mind that it is a scripted linear game though.

Pros:
+Same fast-paced, frantic, yet satisfyingly deep combat of the first
+Combat has been tweaked and balanced so things like divekick spam are less dominant
+3 new weapons, in addition to the classic rapier, that can change the situation dramatically
+Character customization
+10 absolutely gorgeous new levels, each with unique mechanics
+Ranked multiplayer matches
+Custom match rules
+Awesome new soundtrack, perfectly fits the vibe of the game
+Dev is quick to fix issues
Cons:
-The style of the new art is not for everyone
-The extremely busy background art can sometimes impair the game's readability
-Game has lost some of the sense of elegant, charming simplicity of the original
Overall, Nidhogg 2 is a massive improvement over the original in terms of mechanics, available features, total content, and graphics quality. The most divisive thing about it has been the change in art style, going from the minimalistic simplicity of the original to a grotesque cartoony look. However, the game plays smooth as silk, and the new levels, music, and weapons will quickly make you forget all about the Simpsons-esque character design. In fact, they've even started to grow on me a little.
Verdict - strongly recommended if you loved the original, you can see past the new look, and appreciate the quality game mechanics

Battlestar Galactica, Deadlock
BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)
I am really enjoying this game.  The turn-based style gives you time to think and recheck your actions before you act.  Graphics are great and the do an awesome job of putting you back into the reimagined Battlestar Galactica universe.  It's not a deep game, so that's good or bad depending on your expectations.  I'm good with the price I paid for it because it already gave me some gaming experiences I haven't had before.
I saw the clips, just like you did, I'm sure.  I'm a bit leary on those, so I also checked out a few youtube gameplay videos.  I was sold after watching the first.  I'll set this up by saying that I'm a huge fan of the reimagined Battlestar Galactica series.  I think the makers of this game followed along with some of what made that series a success in the Sci-Fi community.
This is a single-player game, with a multi-player option for skirmishes. I read somewhere that there's a Co-op in the manual, but I haven't experienced that yet.  The single player options have a skirmish mode against the AI, or the campaign.
The combat happens in segments.  Issue orders, movements, attacks, then watch as your orders are carried out.  Each segment is about 10 seconds long.  Orders happen simultaneously, so if you move and shoot, it'll take roughly 10 seconds to complete the move, while you're shooting.  Ships can collide and either damage or destroy themselves or others.
The best part about the combat (other than the feel of commanding a fleet and pounding your enemies to wreckage (yes, pieces are floating about when a ship dies), is your reward (or participant award, if you lose), the Replay.  This bit of genius allows you to watch your whole battle without the interruptions.  On top of that, the creators of this game used some of the same camera techniques used in filming the Battlestar Galactica series that gave it almost a documentary feel to it.  Camera angles and movement almost feel like you're watching a live video feed from a news camera, or a chase cam, or even a ship mounted camera in the case of the viper and raider views.  I watched as a ship that I targeted blew up, and as the pieces came apart, some of the bigger bits kept traveling in the same direction the ship was headed, with a slight shift from the explosion.  it nailed the illusion of mass...It looked incredible.  Pro Tip: you can pause the playback with the spacebar and take a screenshot.  My desktop is sporting a chase cam shot of a viper closing on the tail of a cylon frigate.
Pros:
-It's the Battlestar Galactica universe
-Satisfying ship destruction
-realistic damage (hit on left side, lose armor on left)
-Combat is not on a 2D surface.  You can go under or over other ships and do damage to those sides as well
-Combat is frequent, so not a lot of sitting and waiting
Cons:
-The difference between the potential complexity of combat vs the campaign map seems pretty stark.  Combat reaches simulation status and feel, while the campaign board feels like an electronic version of a board game.
-If you're not actively persuing the campaign missions, the side missions do feel repetative
-I think for 40 USD, the campaign aspects should be a bit deeper.  this is more of a feel than anything I have the words to quantify.  Feels like they spent most of the time on the combat portion, and slapped something together for the campaign interface.
To their credit, they've already mentioned content updates and addressing things that they've gotten via feedback.  It's not a AAA title, but it's fun, and the Replay....oh the Replay...  It's as close as most of us will ever get to creating a kick♥♥♥♥♥space battle to watch.

Hook is a short minimalist puzzle game with ambient music where you remove all the hooks and lines by moving certain sections of the "track" or "circuit" then pressing the buttons to remove lines that will not intersect or bump into any of the others. Each level is finished when all the lines and hooks have been removed.
It starts out simple and slowly gets more complex over the 50 levels that the game has. I wouldn't say that the levels become harder, but moreso that they become more chaotic. It may look overwhelming at first, but as long as you take it one step at a time looking at the lines to see which one is free of the others' influence and then follow the circuit back to the button, adjusting the sections so that it only moves what can be moved unhindered, it isn't all too difficult. The later puzzles, because of how complex they are, take much more time to finish than the earlier ones.
I definitely recommend this game for those who enjoy puzzle games, but also remember that this game is only $1 at its base price so don't expect a long experience. However, I think that the money spent is worth the 50 puzzles it has!

How would you like to see a combination between Fable [old school first game] and Elder Scrolls?
Gothic 4 - Arcania is pretty much the thin line that unites these 2 ideas.
I gotta say I have never had experienced the whole franchise before, only tried a bit of Gothic 3 after a friend told me about it [and wasn't bad at all].
Game was out around Oct 2010, which kinda made me expect a tinny bit better optimization regarding a few details than it had..
The story is intriguing at start and in the end. Buuut after having played a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of games in my age, can't say I had my eyes popped. But it was cute.
A few side quests reveal a few more details to you and some fun points regarding what's going on.
I don't know if it is connected with the previous games but it stands alone not leaving me with major questions... Well.. except the final seconds of the cinematic at the end of the game, wasn't sure what I saw and what it meant. [*cough* probably leaving space for a sequel *cough*]
In average it's a cool story to be told, there's much drama script-wise which adds to the suspense but you can say that most of it gets pretty much expected after a point.
It's balanced, not too original.
Also RPG-wise it's ok, though they could add a few elements regarding romance or key characters to connect more with your character and not have just one super hero that kills and burns and stabs and slashes through everything just to see what's going on afterwards. I mean this isn't the 00s any more guys come on..
The gameplay is pretty linear but seeing it from an open minded point of view it didn't matter.
And I mean linear because you are indeed in an open world [and a pretty nice one actually] environment, but you cannot go everywhere you want unless you unlock the area through your main quests. Unfortunatelly you cannot climb mountains and you drawn the moment you step into water [facepalming a bit] so when you reach a bridge or a gate, you cannot pass it unless you get the key or some official letter to show to the guard in order to go pass it.
Lot's of quests to do, many RPG elements like tons of items, a crafting system, gathering materials from herbs, teeth and meat from animals to ores from mines.
Leveling system with a not too complicated [and actually maybe too simple] skills tree.
3 basic classes to go through, warrior, ranger, mage. Some nice animations to attack, block, evade etc.
Not really bad but then again too easily to be repetitive as hell and make you a bit bored after a long while.
Few bugs to notice, though my weak CPU cannot go without noticing some silly moments like snaps from frames that show my character in a model position [open arms and legs frozen half gear on] due to loading, or stupid unnnatural dialogue moments due to the way the data is loading..
They are good for a 2010 game. Sweet open world filled with nature, forests, caves, dungeons, lakes, swamps, mountains etc..
People are nicely designed, though not really pretty faces. Maybe it's ok for being realistic, but sometimes I felt like I'd kill to see a pretty woman's face in there.
Armor and weapons are detailed and sweetly done, you can also have various effects with a few magical items.
Very nice weather system, animated nature depending how strong the winds are, rain with realistic sound and thunders and water that you can actually see the water dynamics even on your own armor [something not many games had achieved at that time].
Also has a night and day cycle, pretty neat when you see people going to sleep, then waking up to do their work or keep their shop.
Very nice music. Pretty well done and balanced. Suits every moment in the game. I was surprised that I felt like going through some sort of Elder Scrolls game here and then.
I have to mention that sound is realistic. Not just due to good environmental effects, but for a 2010 game noticing a realistic difference of noice and sounds betwee being out in the wild and in a town, or between being ouside or inside a house is something worth appreciating.
I was not really satisfied by the characters in the game.
I mean, they are all done very nicely, designed and animated well. But there's just that one thing, that one element missing that never helped me to connect with any of them.
I never cared about whether my character was a nice guy or a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I never got sad over a few dramatic events that occurred during the game.
I wasn't even noticing the change of character and his evolution during the story until some points were made by the NPCs at some times.
This was a bit disappointing for me because connecting with my main character in a game is a major and very important thing when I play a game.
I cannot give you examples cause I don't wanna spoil anyone, but from time to time there had been a few major events happening that really left me standing with apathy in from of my screen wishing the dialogues were a bit shorter or even skipping them so that I could go on.
The voices are ok. Seen worse. Seen better.
Meeeeh. For a 2010 RPG open world mechanism they were ok.
The game had tons of exploring to do. If you are the explorer type you would enjoy going around gathering materials or collectibles.
Fun fact; nothing is randomly generated. Every flower you gather, every monster you kill, they are all unique and will never respawn again. That was quite realistic for me and loved the idea.
Also there were a few elements that reminded me of Fable. Starting of from a humble young man from a village, growing into a uber powerful super hero of muscle and awesomeness badassery and heavy metal while holding flaming swords and magic shields♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ass through the plot. \m/
[at some points you can see people acknowledging as a hero figure and their reactions are fun to hear]
Tons of RPG elements, but not quite developed. I mean they put so much efford in everything, they could at least add a few more ideas about spells or increase the max level cap and let you try other classes since there's no free roam mode after finishing the game.
Another thing; You all know me. I LOVE ROMACE in my stories. And this game had nothing at all except a small flirty idea at the intro of the game. I was like, come on is there anything to help me connect with this guy? Even the action sequence was completelly stable; explore, kill, talk to NPC, do quest, explore, kill, talk to NPC, do quest, explore....
One thing I liked, since everything in the game is not unlimited or randomly spawned, being an explorer is rewarding in many aspects. For example sometimes i would first completelly explore the whole new area I unlocked and if i was done I would talk to the NPCs. That way I already had the quest items they wanted and I would farm exp instantly.
Easy to get some extra skill points and make you happy for a while? Yes.
Does it make sense to already be able to distinguish a quest item from the rest of the world without having taken the quest thus making the item as useful to you as a random rock on the ground? No.
But i ain't even mad ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

The voice acting sounds completely unconvincing and makes you feel like all the characters are cardboard cutouts. The female interrest of the (start)game is both annoying and a useless plot device.
All the characters look "decent" as long as you don't look at them. once you get into a conversation with them their weird blob faces come to light and show how horrible the faces look, combined with the voice-acting it doesn't make any of the conversations you have with the NPC's a good experience and sucks you right out of the game, hence i skipped literally ALL the dialogue in the game.
The before skillpoint system from gothic 1+2+3 seemed to be not "of this time anymore" since they threw that idea out of the window for a new fresh... aged system that even an MMORPG would laugh at. the skill window is ugly, unfinished and rightdown insulting to the series. there are no special talents for hunting, no different fight styles like two-handed, sword/shield or dual wielding. just 2 bars, one for flurries and one for heavy attacks.
The active HUD also is VERY aged and doesn't stand up. it's big, gets in the way and is ugly and takes away immersion and focus.
I obviously didn't play much of this game and i intend to keep it that way. 2-3 hours of this game have shown me enouth to know to stay away from this game. some may say that this game has a better story the longer you play it but i really doubt that.
so it gets down to this: if you can look aside ALL the flaws of the game, you basicly have a stripped down singleplayer MMORPG with less depth and a combat system so dumbed down that they actually reached a new low. then this game is absolutely for you. If  however you're looking for an intriguing RPG that is immersive and stands out from the rest, look further because this is not that kind of game.

A very solid sci-fi exploration game, touching on intellectual themes. Namely, the common sci-fi trope of transhumanism, pertaining to the idea of consciousness in this narrative. Nothing life-changing or thematic enough to question philosophically, but being a game brings this idea to an interesting perspective. The story will bring the player to decisions that will make them pause and reflect on their choices.
The devs being Frictional Games, they bring their brand of horror to this setting, and can still lay to claim their masterful craft at establishing atmosphere and mood. SOMA employs less horror than the devs' previous outings (Amnesia and Penumbra), but they more than make up for it in spades with one of their best stories, alongside a universe that leaves room for more. The setting, the sound, the immersion and plausibility of it all... SOMA's an amazing piece of work that works with or without the slight survival horror gameplay.
The puzzles are on the easy side, and the AIs of every one of SOMA's abominations are not difficult to outsmart, but they're still deftly layered behind the oppressive, bleak world that doesn't care what has happened. It's not overwhelming and suffocating like Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but SOMA effortlessly submerges the player in its world and inspires wonder and curiosity. There's no small amount of lore that aren't in the way, but answers as many questions as it does create them. Its near-futuristic world and its implications are chilling to think about.
The story has its holes, and its ending felt like it could have been better written (It seemingly forgot a few details) for a better delivery and meaning, but it's overall good and paces itself very well. The star of SOMA is not its scares or its gameplay, but it is the world that Frictional Games has created, and how it immerses the player in this world. Not really a replayable game or has a long length to its entirety, nor is it as much of an intense distillation of horror as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but SOMA is more worth as an invitation to explore and indulge.

A thought-provoking transhumanist sci-fi adventure game that delves full-throttle into its themes. It raises a lot of hard, disturbing questions about consciousness and leaves it up to the player to answer them.
While most of the game's enjoyment comes from its story and atmosphere, it succeeds gameplay-wise by having immersive puzzles that feel "natural" to the world, not placed in to create artificial challenge, and by never holding the player's hand. This is, technically, a horror game in the sense that there are "scary" parts. Keep in mind, though, that if you decide to play SOMA for pure horror purposes you may be disappointed when you find the monster bits to be few and far between. Granted, they are VERY effective when they come around, but for the vast majority of the game's length, you'll be solving environmental puzzles, exploring, and piecing the story together rather than running and hiding from Things That Should Not Be.
The only real criticism I have of the game is of one aspect of the writing: The main character, Simon, is far, far too relaxed  to a point that breaks immersion. Waking up in the far future and encountering horrific monsters seems to be met with a dull, resigned acceptance for most of the game's length. It's only about halfway through that he starts to become saddened by the implications of what he's seeing (when it was horrifying from the beginning) and it's only in the very last hours that he becomes legitimately upset. Everything from that point on feels more natural, but it also feels strange that it took so long for him to get there.
Otherwise, though, Soma is an amazing game I'd recommend to anyone who likes adventure games, science fiction, and horror. Atmospherically, if you're missing Bio/System Shock, this is absolutely the game for you.

I unfortunately have to downvote this game.  The worlds are too large for such a small player base, even on the highest populated servers.  The game doesn't feel full enough to even be in early access, it feels more like a prototype.  Don't get me wrong, the concept is amazing, the game looks nice, it's rad as Hell to run around as a raptor.  But here are my suggestions to make the game playable(in my opinion).
-Some sort of AI.  There needs to be other dinosaurs besides players, the world is just way to empty, even on the highest populated servers.  The addition of AI would in no way make the feeling of running into other players less awesome, simply because of the fact that it's rare.
-Expanding on the AI thing, carnivors and herbivors would be fun to see.  I'd like to play as an herbivore in fear for my life of AI and player carnivores.  But with the limited players(or too large of maps), there is no real threat.
-Possibly some sort of territory control would be interesting, give the players something other to do than just eat, drink, and sit.
-A health bar would be nice.
-Name plates appearing over other players when you're close enough, or something similar.
To sum it all up; add AI, add a health bar, and keep on doing what your doing.  Am I upset I paid for this?  No.  Only because I am tired of seeing all the good dinosaur games go to♥♥♥♥♥♥and dying.  Would I recommend this to anyone?  Not a chance, at least not yet.

Ok, here's the deal. You're playing an Evil Mastermind who wants to take over the world: Maximillian. Unless you're mad, female or cannot live without Lord Kane. You have bought an uncharted island far from any countries and now you're going to take over the world. Interested?
Thought so. The game starts out pretty bluntly with you, three minions and a henchman.  You get objectives that you need to complete in order to progress in the game. And the objectives kinda goes like this: Establish a base, Learn the Advanced Stuff, Prepare to take over the World and then you start building a doomsday device because... the most easy way to take over the world is to hold the world ransom apparently.
To your help you've got up to 100 Minions and ultimately 7 Henchmen that will ensure your security and that your goals become finished.
But of course the Forces of Justice would want to prevent you from this so they send you their "top agents" that got nothing else to do than to try and mess up your base. These forces are called
S.A.B.R.E: European Agency that also protects Australia, South Africa and India.
H.A.M.M.E.R: The Soviet Union. Protects Russia, Eastern Europe and Cuba.
A.N.V.I.L: Communist China, protects the Philippines
P.A.T.R.I.O.T: Americans, protects Japan too.
S.M.A.S.H: Middle Eastern Agency, protects North Africa, Middle Africa, South America and Antarctica.
I know what you're thinking: "What a bunch of cretins. How can they possibly stop my mastermind plans of taking over the world?" I would answer that they can't unless they bring in their super agents. Super Agents are agents that have sworn to demolish your base, kill your minions and steal that urn that you think would go well into your inner sanctum. The one you will find most annoying are the A.N.V.I.L Employed Jet Chan and he is your average martial artist hero that would love to run into a base full of heavily armed, evil minions without anything else than his knowledge of martial arts to back him up. And this isn't as suicidal in practice as it might sound. Jet Chan is pretty skilled at killing your minions and will with ease kill your toughest henchmen and taunt them afterwards.
But what is a henchman? He is a very loyal lackey that possess an extreme amount of endurance. So much so that he can only be killed by Super Agents. He does have three lives though so don't worry if he goes down once but if he goes down twice then you better load an earlier saved game. He is also very strong and can deal out loads of punishment. Some can deal more damage (Jubei, The Butcher), others have useful special abilities (Jubei, Lord Kane, The Matron) and others doesn't have so useful abilities and become useless tanks (like Moko, Eli Barracuda and Red Ivan).
In this game though, you don't control your minions. Instead they wander around the base and take care of themselves by their own initiative. So why do you have to be there watching your minions all the time? Because they're insanely stupid. They never take initiative and kill intruders, they always let them slip through your doors and even if they started to fight these agents they never seem to be in shape for doing so since they're prone to exhausting themselves in other activities, like manning the control room. If it wasn't for your evil intellect the whole secret base would fall apart. You do control them indirectly though: You can tag anyone except yourself and your henchmen which you want dead, captured or just confused. Your minions will then when they're either confronted by a tagged character or hear about a tagged character in the base loudspeakers, will drop everything they're currently doing and go and carry out the evil deeds.
So what do I think of the game? The feelings are a bit mixed. The game have several bugs which can be fixed by various members of the Evil Genius community. I have myself fixed a few in my bugfix file that you can find on the file page. The agent AI is quite poor since these guys likes to break into the base by force which alert you right away about their indiscretion. The gameplay tends to become pretty linear since it's often just the usual scenario of trying to man the control room and keeping the agents out of the base.  During the first part of the game it's pretty fun to try and take over the world but after a while when you get a more secure and impressive base you start to feel that the game starts to run itself. The agents kill themselves because of their stupidity, the minions go about their daily lives and you just sit in your chair and watch them wander around in your pretty base. You can try beefing up the game with more minions and funnier henchmen but that doesn't add variety to the game and variety is what the game so desperately needs.
The game is a pretty fun game that I enjoyed playing and although it looked more promising in the initial demo than in the finished game it still offers a decent amount of entertainment value. And this is one of these games that almost anyone can pick up and play since the difficulty is generally quite low. So I recommend this game for any casual gamers out there that wants easier games to play and those of you who just are looking for a fun game. If you're a hardcore gamer you might wanna skip this in favour for some other game like Dawn of War.

This is going to be a recommendation with faint praise. I sat down with this game last night after purchasing it on special and played through in about eight to nine hours on the second level of difficulty.
The game itself works very well on medium detail on an older gaming laptop (my system). Graphics style is 'comic book outline / film noir' and flow well with very little to no stuttering (I didn't notice but I wasn't looking for it). Gameplay mechanics are solid - shoot and you hit, something some games don't do well :) Enemy difficulty comes in steady progression but are quite predictable all up once you know their patterns. You can sometimes avoid an ambush and cut it down to manageable numbers by taking up space in a nook or corner out of sight of the opponents and popping out to draw in one or two at a time. Generally there is only one way to go and plenty of path cut-outs that allow you forward but not back (drops that you can't jump back over, etc). The 'on rails' feel is not really noticeable but certainly is not on a par with Halflife / Halflife 2 which for me sets the gold standard of set-path games, and is also not on a par with Deus Ex 1 or 3 (which has a more open path than Halflife).
Mild to medium story spoiler:
The game was engaging enough for me to play through in one sitting but I will not be replaying it and am uninstalling once I'm done with this review. Your mileage may vary though. My rating:
Graphics 8/10
Gameplay 7/10
Story 6/10

There is one thing you will have to remember if you buy the Isle in Early Access right now; the game will change drastically.

Though this game is still in early development, a lot of what is going on in this game is like reinventing the wheel in the most painful way for those trying to test the game. With no real deadline given to us and no real clue as to when this game will stop pulling out the trick falls, I am left very disappointed with how this game is turning out.
For those unaware, this is a survival game where you play vastly as an herbivore or carnivore Dinosaur (At the time of this review, humans are not an option). This in concept seems rather simple except that it isn't. Yes, you do play a surival game as a large formerly extinct creature, but you don't get to be large and formidable right away. To start either progression line, you need to become a velociraptor or a psittacosaurs (We just call them tacos.) As a velociraptor, you spend a certain amount of time as a small whelp of the carnivore line before you can progress into something a touch larger. In the mean time you enjoy a drink of water and run around pressing the friendly call to laugh at your fellow pack memebers around. As a Psittacosaurus, you roam around at the speed of a snail to find these special blue ferns. You eat two of them and you move to the next creature.
You may be wondering where the problem is. Your answer is simple. In the previous thirty minutes to progress into a larger dinosaur from velociraptor, your herbivore friend could already be halfway to a Triceratops and thus vastly stronger and quicker than you will be for a very long time. This has since changed for reasons unexplained to where thirty minutes is now considerably longer and in addition, your poodle sized meat grinder has to eat now.
Say you want to become the ever formidable Tyrannosaurus Rex. Well I hope you have 7- 13 hours of your day available to accomplish this without dying of hunger or thirst. Want to be a Puertasaurus instead? You can probably knock that one out within a couple hours and thats with a pretty rough start to the game.
My point you might be wondering is simple:
I want to play a game.
I know a lot of people want to play a game.
And I know a lot of people (like myself) have things we need to do outside of stare at the computer for 13 hours.
This means that if you don't have anything better to do, you'll be painful grinding your way to the top of the food chain for days on end. This assuming the various randomly added patches don't wipe the server which in turn wipes the progression you've so painstakingly clawed your way through. Even if you would want to be a creature that is mid way through the food chain like Allosaurus or Utahraptor, still be prepared to spend long hours just trying to get there. Meanwhile the herbivores are laughing at you from above as they've long since progressed to a large creature and had about two or three litters of babies to perpetuate their species.
And I know what you're saying. "It can't be all bad"
No, its bad.
The recent addition of bad map design and terrible spawn locations (At the time of this review anyway) make playing as any small and slow dinosaur a boring and arduous trek that almost always result in death because you couldn't get to water in time or there was a cliff drop and your little critter fell 60 feet to its death. In addition to that, when you do manage to find food and water, there is virtually nothing else to do. You are literally a dinosaur. Thats it. There hasn't been any form of teased storyline to us or real answers as to why we are a dinosaur other than "there will be things to look for and see as the game becomes more polished" (paraphrasing)
What it boils down to is this.
The game is boring and it is a chore. The only excitement comes from hunting down and killing other dinosaurs regardless being herbivore or carnivore. The game is incredibly buggy and in order to fix the problems, servers end up being wiped, or worse nothing happens. Being a carnivore is an absolute chore, especially if you dislike being a smaller predator with no real option other than to scavenge or hunt your fellow smaller predators.
Humans are anticipated to be added to the game which I believe will make things worse than better. The dev team is focusing its attention on making a game thats realistic to a degree that I have finally felt compelled to write a review about this. Realism does not always equal fun.

You are an evil genius who must manage a secret volcano base in the middle of the ocean. You will encounter tourists, spies, soldiers and super agents such as Jet chan and Sean Bond who you must defeat with clever trap placement. You automatically gloat and reveal your evil plan to these agents, should you capture them.
You're in charge of global operations, nefarious schemes and yet also tasked with managing your internal affairs, meaning that trying to micromanage too hard will cost you just as much as trying to micromanage too little. I thrive on these types of games, using your brain and outwitting the AI or exploiting little hitches in the game rules rewards your efforts tenfold, where as being lazy or intentionally ignoring certain things will punish you greatly. Games used to be challenging, Not hard, Not easy, and this fits that definition perfectly. The majority of my friends wouldn't make it past the first level because of the level of "skill" involved in learning the game mechanics, even though it teaches you as you play without holding your hand.
Zooming in to see the little details will often surprise you, everything in the game is animated and unique, as most games where before everything tried to squeeze onto an xbox hd.
A must for any Tropico 4 fan.

The game is a Dungeon Keeper clone, letting you build your lair, improving the various rooms and attracting and upgrading your minions. You only have direct control of your #1 henchman the rest of your minions working on their with you giving them overall objectives to complete.
Graphically it does for the same cartoonish look as Dungeon Keeper and it works quite well. The humor is great but often put too much in the background.
Evil Genius is a great game but marred by some unfortunate mistakes. Much of the minion management quickly becomes a grind and the difficulty jumps quite a bit once super-spies appears.
Definitely worth a buy from anyone that enjoys management games and/or mustache twirling.

If tabletop fleet gaming is your thing, or if you like fleet combat, Battlestar Galactica, or simultaneous turn based gameplay, this one's for you.

- Divekicking knocks both players down. If you divekick a wall, you get knocked down.
- Cartwheel thrusting is gone.
- Rolling into trip is now a slide, knocking down both players. Whiff leaves you in knockdown.
Personal nitpicks were the broadsword not having an active hitbox in neutral and the bows mechanic of blocked arrows returning to sender. Honestly the bow in general feels like it doesn't belong but I appreciate them trying something so new.
TL;DR If you have as many hours in Nidhogg 1 as me you should just keep playing that. If you just want a party game congrats, Messhof delivered.

By no means perfect, Deadlock is a wonderful experience for anyone whose seen the show and - like so many more of us - desperately want more out of the universe.
The UI could've used more work, the story isn't the best piece of literature ever devised and the voice-acting wasn't the best - but I have a hard time complaining about any of that around the time I get to watch 2 Cylon raider squadrons and a volley of enemy missiles disappear in a Battlestar's flak barrage while said Battlestar is firing in all directions. It's beautiful to watch, the soundtrack if phenominal, and the ships feel like true Galactica-style vessels.
The UI to be a bit of a challenge to deal with but otherwise there is a pretty deep strategy game in here; you'll just have to wade through a few questionable interface design choices to get to it. Having to tell 8 Viper squadrons individually to fire on the same target at 3 clicks a piece is annoying but not really game-killing.
Probably the most stand-out part of the game is the post-battle replays that do their best to emulate the Battlestar-y visual style, replaying the turn-based gameplay in a full realtime cinematic mode. I was concerned at first watching some of the preview youtube videos for the game with the camera-behavior that was in the preview builds but that concern was alleviated the instant I got into the game myself and saw it'd changed for the better. It's by no means perfect but when I'm smiling ear-to-ear, cackling in perverse glee as I watch 3 nukes reduce a Basestar to radioactive dust in glorious BSGcam mode, then something has certainly gone right. Kudos to whoever painstakingly set this system up.
If you're a fan of the reimagined BSG, the familiar names and setting of the BSG universe will quickly make you forget the issues mentioned above and you'll feel right at home and have a blast with the game. Non-fans will find a pretty alright all-around game with a few issues but enough going for it to justify the difficulties.
Basically: Get it if you loved the show, otherwise try it or wait for the 10% off sale to get it, because if strategy-combat sims are your thing, then you'll manage to sink a good chunk of time into this.
Now if you'll excuse me, I've got some frakkin' toasters to shoot out of the sky. So say we all~

Ok this program has it's good sides and bad sides but overall and before getting into detail I want to say the program achieves what it sets out to do and I'm very satisfied considering I got it during a sale and it came with two DLC's for $14 for the entire package.
I'm a writer and I'm currently using this program to design the cover art and illustrations for my book series, so I'm not using it for a manga or comic. I'm planning on using it as a supplement to my own hand drawn work. It gets the job done since I don't draw anime styles well.
Side by Side Pros and Cons:
Pro: Adding downloaded content is easy, just drag the file into CompiPo and you'll be greeted with an import screen.
Con: There is no option to "Batch Install" multiple downloaded resources at once, so if you're like me and install 300 items in one go, you'll be clicking for a while before you can get to using your new content.
Pro: Customizing characters is really easy, and if you know what you're doing you can make very unique looking characters.
Con: No sliders, and changing a characters skin color is not done in the character creation screen but instead is done after you have made the character and placed them in your scene (what???) I have high hopes that both of these cons will change in time and if they don't I'm sure there is a talented user out there who will create a downloadable modification to change this. Either way it isn't a deal breaker for me.
Pro: Quite a few scenes and items are included. Expressions are [nearly] limitless.
Con: Manipulating things to look exactly the way you want is time consuming and at times difficult. This program would become a favorite of mine if a feature to freely move characters eyes and arms would be added. As of now, while there are a good many poses available, leaving a creative user to depend upon these alone seems almost torturous.
Pro: Layers are easy to manipulate, snap assets, when messed with for long enough, are very useful for the interaction imagery.
Con: Characters are their own layers. I would love, LOVE to be able to have my characters interact physically without using snap assets. It doesn't seem like much to ask, having characters and other objects on a 3D plane instead of layering them would perhaps be a little more daunting to use at times, but would be SO much more affective in creating scenes. Imagine, instead of having to rearrange everything every time the camera angle changes, you just have to click and drag and BAM, the entire room moves with you, along with your characters and objects. A true 3D room. I hope to see this implented in future updates too.
Pro: ANIMALS!!!
Con: The animals have set positions and styles and cannot be manipulated in a heavy way at all.
Conclusion: The program is simple. When I found out the base program costs $49.99, my jaw dropped. I had the base program alone at one point, and it was NOT worth that price tag. Come on guys, don't be ridiculous. $14.99 for the base and the DLC was great, but the base program on its own is seriously lacking and is not worth $15 nevermind $50!
So, I was displeased by that, but I didn't have to pay that, so again, not a deal breaker (for me.)
To me, the base game is kinda like a burger, but without a bun or toppings. Having all the DLC I imagine would be like having a nice meal to do a lot of stuff with.
My advice to the DEVs, if they even really care what I have to say: Please quit it with these ridiculous prices. The program is not worth the prices you demand. The DLC does not add enough to the game to justify $12-$18 per pack, and after having TWO DLCs I felt like all I had was the base with a good, not amazing, amount of features. If need be, keep the prices, but ADD MORE! This program has so much amazing potential, but it leaves a lot desired. I have my burger, now give me my bun and fries, dammit!
This all being said, I do still recommend this program to those who are seeking something that will let them express their story without needing any drawing skills. The program can also help as a guide for those who do draw, a sort of advanced wooden mannequin type. It also serves its purpose with me as well, so I am somewhat satisfied.

I'll write this review for the sake of those who haven't followed the Gothic games.
See, long story short there was a divide between the old guard who liked Gothics 1 and 2, believing Gothic 3 was a poor sequel, and folks like me who agree that Gothics 1 and 2 were classic but 3 had a charm of its own. It's true, I enjoyed 3 and I still recommend it, even if I had some mechanical problems with its expansion (For the record I NEVER had any problem with the base game and although it could've used more content, I had a lot of fun exploring it!).
Now when Arcania (the de facto Gothic 4, under a new name for understandable reasons due to studio changes) was announced, the old guard of the former group were pessimistic and people like me were hopeful. I wanted a more polished game that offered the sort of open-world exploration, side quests laced through the main quest, secrets to find, factions to join or oppose and engaging choices that made the last games great, coupled with improved visuals and controls but especially more options and items and goodies in general.
What I got was an unbelievably linear, limited game that seemed to strip everything that made 3 fun while keeping everything the old guard criticized about it. I couldn't even finish it. I was bored out of my skull before I could even save the capital, let alone figure out what the nonsensical plot was about.
Maybe it's a little better if you aren't familiar with the previous games, but even then it's an unfortunate use of money to buy. You want to play Gothic, check out the previous three and leave this on the shelf. Fair warning though, I have trouble getting 1 and 2 to work on newer computers.

Nothing life-changing or thematic enough to question philosophically, but being a game brings this idea to an interesting perspective. The story will bring the player to decisions that will make them pause and reflect on their choices.
The devs being Frictional Games, they bring their brand of horror to this setting, and can still lay to claim their masterful craft at establishing atmosphere and mood. SOMA employs less horror than the devs' previous outings (Amnesia and Penumbra), but they more than make up for it in spades with one of their best stories, alongside a universe that leaves room for more. The setting, the sound, the immersion and plausibility of it all... SOMA's an amazing piece of work that works with or without the slight survival horror gameplay.
The puzzles are on the easy side, and the AIs of every one of SOMA's abominations are not difficult to outsmart, but they're still deftly layered behind the oppressive, bleak world that doesn't care what has happened. It's not overwhelming and suffocating like Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but SOMA effortlessly submerges the player in its world and inspires wonder and curiosity. There's no small amount of lore that aren't in the way, but answers as many questions as it does create them. Its near-futuristic world and its implications are chilling to think about.
The story has its holes, and its ending felt like it could have been better written (It seemingly forgot a few details) for a better delivery and meaning, but it's overall good and paces itself very well. The star of SOMA is not its scares or its gameplay, but it is the world that Frictional Games has created, and how it immerses the player in this world. Not really a replayable game or has a long length to its entirety, nor is it as much of an intense distillation of horror as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but SOMA is more worth as an invitation to explore and indulge.

A thought-provoking transhumanist sci-fi adventure game that delves full-throttle into its themes. It raises a lot of hard, disturbing questions about consciousness and leaves it up to the player to answer them.
While most of the game's enjoyment comes from its story and atmosphere, it succeeds gameplay-wise by having immersive puzzles that feel "natural" to the world, not placed in to create artificial challenge, and by never holding the player's hand. This is, technically, a horror game in the sense that there are "scary" parts. Keep in mind, though, that if you decide to play SOMA for pure horror purposes you may be disappointed when you find the monster bits to be few and far between. Granted, they are VERY effective when they come around, but for the vast majority of the game's length, you'll be solving environmental puzzles, exploring, and piecing the story together rather than running and hiding from Things That Should Not Be.
The only real criticism I have of the game is of one aspect of the writing: The main character, Simon, is far, far too relaxed  to a point that breaks immersion. Waking up in the far future and encountering horrific monsters seems to be met with a dull, resigned acceptance for most of the game's length. It's only about halfway through that he starts to become saddened by the implications of what he's seeing (when it was horrifying from the beginning) and it's only in the very last hours that he becomes legitimately upset. Everything from that point on feels more natural, but it also feels strange that it took so long for him to get there.
Otherwise, though, Soma is an amazing game I'd recommend to anyone who likes adventure games, science fiction, and horror. Atmospherically, if you're missing Bio/System Shock, this is absolutely the game for you.

Sparkle 3 is a nice casual game where you control a creature swimming in a kind of primordial soup. Your goal is to consume nutrients scattered around, slowly growing from a tiny creature into a huge (relatively speaking, of course) behemoth. You have full control over your creature’s evolution (which is largely similar to RPGs’ level-up system), and unlike in Sparkle 2, you don’t have to worry about eating particular elements if you want to evolve in a certain way.
To spice up gameplay, you regularly receive tasks from the scientist who created you, and completing all tasks on the level allows you to move to the next one. Some tasks make the game a bit action-y, but it remains fairly easy overall, and most of gameplay consists of casual exploration of your environment. (One particular kind of challenge – Spikey Rivers can be quite hard, but it can be bypassed effortlessly if you evolve in a certain way.)
If you are looking for a relaxing game with occasional bits of action, Sparkle 3 has my full recommendation!

In Pyre, you play the role of the Reader, an exile who's tasked with leading a group of fellow exiles called the Nightwings through sports-like rituals called the Rites.
Pyre is an RPG with real-time sports-like battles with fun gameplay, beautiful art, a wonderful soundtrack and a world that's easy to become lost in.
Pros
- Rites are a joy to play and require solid tactics at higher difficulty levels.
- Your strategies must constantly adapt to the growth and changes that occur within your party over time.
- World and characters are brought to life by the writing, the art and the soundtrack.
- Choices are meaningful and ensure a unique and rewarding experience.
- Difficulty can be changed at any time and can be further tweaked upwards for increased rewards.
- Game oozes polish out of every nook and cranny.
Cons
- If you don't care about storytelling in games then you won't have a good time with Pyre.
If you're looking for a game that will immerse you in another world with interesting characters backed by solid gameplay then you can hardly go wrong with Pyre.

I have beaten the third world (it has a HUGE spike in difficulty!) but with enough determination I got through it. You can go about it with the different skills (it all depends on how YOU play). But alas, the game doesn't seem to offer more than eating, growing, and getting stronger. I do recommend this though, especially on sale! I don't regret it at all, and I do see myself playing it more. I don't review games often, but I saw this game as reiew worthy (especially after seeing Mixed reviews). Everyone saying that the game is too hard on the third world just hasn't given it enough effort or just don't have a good enough grasp on the controls.
PROS:
*Graphics are pretty nice, and are pleasant to look at.
*The soundtrack isn't bad, so yay to that.
*Variety with how you level up is nice.
CONS:
*Lack of activities...aside from doing what you do, there's not much else.
NEUTRALITIES:
*Full controller support except for one button, and it's kinda annoying for those who use controllers.
*The difficulty spike on level 3; I personally had llittle trouble, but it seems a lot of people did.
I give it a 7/10.
NOTE: I played using an Xbox controller (I find this game more suited with the controller than keyboard and mouse, but that's just my opinion).

SIDE NOTE: Everything can be accessed by the controller except for the level up menu (which is tedious early game where levels are far more common, but I dealt with it).
TIP:
FINAL THOUGHTS:
This game is totally worth checking out (especially with sales!). I don't see the hate, I got a good amount of time in, and I plan on more time in the future, so I might have an update (soon...?).
If you fully read my review then thank you :)
I hope you get enjoyment out of this like I did!
