Disclaimer: I am a fan of both the BSG TV shows, so am probably biased to appreciate any fleet action game in this continuity as a result.
Second Disclaimer: Not a fan of Multiplayer, reviewed solely from the perspective of the Single Player campaign. Not completed yet (probably about half way - taking time to grind a bit). If you're looking for MP impressions, please check other reviews.
Overall: Not a naval/space fleet simulator by any means - but fun all the same. Similar to Victory at Sea in some ways - start with a small fleet, expand - handle individual fleet actions to the point of micromanaging ships as needed.
The Very Good: Battle Replay / Music results in sequences that feel like they're right out of the BSG reboot. Very nice if you liked said show. The particular camera shots appear procedurally generated, so if you use the recording function after watching one, you might not get a particular camera angle you really liked - and the procedural generation really likes Viper cockpit views for some reason, but those are minor nits. A little more major, had the only crashes so far after doing some recordings, so be warned if you try it. If it is this, I'm sure it will be fixed.
The Good: Battles are pretty balanced for your main fleets. Tutorial isn't too bad and is skippable on replay (if you do the campaign first as I am, you probably will start over at least once as you figure out some game mechanics). The Cylons appear to have infinite fleets who just pop up out of nowhere (no way to have safe routes or zones other than Ragnar that I can tell), but this is somewhat balanced by any surviving ships in a fleet being automagically repaired after a mission, so you don't have the headache of getting damaged ships back to a repair facility.
The UI is a little large, but not ridiculously so. It will bug you if you think about it, but if you're wrapped up in getting things done, it doesn't get in the way.
The battles themselves are pretty fun - I'm probably not the tactician I need to be, but I can hold my own pretty well and the game interface does allow for nice maneuvers, crossing the enemy T (several ships are best with broadsides), etc. Fighters are currently imbalanced -- the Cylon raiders apparently don't defend against Vipers and just go for their capital ship targets. As a result, it is very easy to take out all enemy fighter groups by around the same time the main fleets are getting close enough for action, allowing the Vipers to help a great deal in taking down the fleet or doing missile defense by the time of closing for ship-to-ship combat. Don't get used to it, I expect - that screams for a balancing patch in the future.
The Bad: The fleet/officer system seems problematic in the mid game, and I suspect it will be catastrophic in the late game (as mentioned, have not completed the campaign yet). There are two limits on Fleets -- first, raw ship counts (up to 7) and second "Fleet Points" which are related to the Officer assigned to the fleet. Officers also help reputation/resources for fleets fortifying planets, so you'll almost always want an officer assigned to a fleet. All reasonable so far -- but there are a few problems.
First - the same "RP" points used to hire/promote officers are also used to unlock any potential technical upgrades (like new ships / new weapons). If you don't realize that (or miss it if it was in the tutorial), you can easily be stuck with early/weak ships because you spun off several fleets/officers to protect colonies. RPs are only given to you from story or special missions, so you need to be very careful how you use them -- the tutorial having you burn some to promote your first officer right off gives the exact wrong impression. You'll want to let promotions come from combat experience, saving RPs for technology or new officers.
Which leads to the second/related problem: The default Fleet Points with a starting officer is WAY too small past the beginning of the game. Without a promotion, a fleet has 2000 points. That's enough for 2 Adamants (2nd ship you get, cruiser/carrier combo) and a single frigate. A good fleet in the early game up to the mid game. Your first battlestar (Artemis class) is 1550 points - so a starting fleet is that single ship. Any of these fleets is a sitting duck for the 3000+ plus point Cylon fleets you start getting once you unlock the Artemis class -- so any new officers/fleets are now very difficult to survive to get experience to level up enough to form a fleet that stands a chance. Either you have to really grind for RPs and burn them on promotions (which can take a while, the special missions aren't that common) or you want to plan ahead and farm RPs in the start of the game to form defense/fortification fleets over all the colonies before proceeding in the campaign/unlocking better ships (Adamant + Viper II seems like the sweet spot to me). That way you can use combat experience for all your fleets to have them ready for Battlestars later. Not terribly intuitive and you still have to grind story missions to have enough fleets to make that work.

Let me preface this review with this:
If you do not want to play a game that *is not finished*, then do not buy the game. Buy it when it is finished. If you are okay with an unfinished game, but do not like the current iteration of said game, then put it down for a month or two and come back later and check it out.
That said, this game has come a very long way since I first started playing it back when Region 2 was a thing. Back then, there was only sandbox mode. It was fun for awhile, but ultimately boring. Fast forward a few months to when the V3 map came out, and I picked the game back up.
At first I detested progression. I thought it was too hard and too time consuming, but as I played the game, it really grew on me. I learned where to go, what to do, and can even progress up the tiers without too much trouble. Yes, things are still broken. The collision bugs with bigger dinosaurs really grinds my gears, but I imagine that will be fixed in time.
The game is CONSTANTLY changing. It gets a little ridiculous how often patches are going in. And you know what? That's a very good thing. With nesting now being tested in a public environment, you can tell that the game is going to go some good places.
The dev team and community moderators are said to be on the irritating side, but honestly... Think about it from their perspective. Take something you're intensely passionate about, and think about people who are uneducated about your favorite hobby spewing a bunch of nonsense. You'd probably get irritated too, I know I would and I know I do. The team is working the best they can with the playerbase it has, and the team that it has though, in my opinion.
Yes. Things aren't finished. Some things are broken, some are still in developement. These things do not make this a bad game, and I very much look forward to the future of the game as it developes.

DOOM (Ultimate DOOM = DOOM 1) is one of my all time favorite games. This game is very repetitive, but somehow it never gets boring to me, really. I highly recommend purchasing this game, especially because it is so cheap.
Is it violent? Of course it is. But that shouldn't stop you from playing if you aren't too into violence and gore. This game doesn't direct its violence to humans as most shooters do, but to Demons instead (As stated by Id).
You play as the Doom Marine, a man in a powerful suit with powers and abilities. Your goal is to remove the Demon threat from the UAC facility in Mars. Portals to hell open as the plague goes on and you try to stop it. You end up having to go into these portals, which take you to the heart of Hell itself. Here, you must end the plague of Demons for good.
An additional episode released, Thy Flesh Consumed, is a DLC episode which takes place instead on Earth, where Demons have come back from Hell to torment you once more.

Sniper Elite V2 is a third-person action-stealth shooter about being a lone sniper, being released by Rebellion in 2012. It's supposed to be remake/reboot of original Sniper Elite, thus the name "Version 2". And yes, it takes same storyline basic idea and setting. It also isn't as grey. It also includes both cooperative and competetive multiplayer of all sorts.
It also came out PS3, Xbox 360 and WiiU. Never played them, but as far as I know, PC has better graphics. WiiU however omitted multiplayer completely, they say.
People tend to have issue with tutorial mission where you are supposed to lay down the mine. Game doesn't clearly tell you what to do next after it. It just sneakily makes a small tellow waypoint appear somewhere out of view, so keep looking for it, there isn't any bug. But I heard that some had strange issue where game would keep his character locked in same spot even after putting mine down.
Multiplayer community is alive and kicking. For cooperative it's automatically searches game and creates one if doesn't find any, no servers. It's for two players only anyway. But I still managed to get along with two friendly players from Internet this way. As for competetive it shows you usual server browser with all the filters you want. And you will see at least few near-full servers, with a lot of gametypes being played. By both new and regular people. The only thing that seems to be ignored is Dog Tag Hunt mode.
The plot of this game takes same basic idea of SE1 of being a lone American sniper who must murder all scientists for choosing to escape to USSR instead of the glorious America. Now with more rockets explosions, more cinematic, with less German Resistance people and without "Eagle Watch? Eagle Watch." password code. Headshot both Russians and Germans. 360 quickscope every tank you meet. At least I was able to follow the story this time around. Probably because it clearly told us main mission of our Karl Fairburne sniper right from the start.
You can choose a few difficulties, including the custom one. In custom you choose separately the difficulty of enemies, how much sniping simulation you want and if you want tactical assist or not. I recommend to pick the full sniping part, which includes gravity and wind. As for tactical assist, while hardcore-try-hard people are probably offended, I think that it's some fun neat stuff. You can tag enemies with binoculaur, which is a good reason to look around before shooting and revealing yourself. You can not only steady aim by holding breath, but it also will slow down time and give you aim assisting cross, so there are good reason to calm down and stay out of harm way. Plus ghost image of yourself pointing out where enemy belives you was before hiding and directional threat arrow indicator.
Then you also will get to pick loadout before each mission. Then again, you find lots of stuff during mission itself, so it's not as important. Just going to say that in Single there is no good reasons to pick other pistols aside from the first silenced one. The game now includes melee silent takedowns from behind, yes, but pistol is the only ranged weapon that allows you to stealth-kill anytime.
The main gameplay thing that you will notice how linear and confinig level design this time around. More often than not you have a linear corridor, with some more opened area. Now more scripted. There are some areas where close range encounter is forced on you, some areas where game clearly tells you that you can stealth. The first Sniper Elite had semi-open maps by comparsion, however they weren't designed good and flawed core gameplay wasn't making any use of them, so I don't mind linear structure here. Sure SE1 made itself look smarted, but it's just an illusion as far as I care.
In the best missions the game will start by letting you stealth as much as possible, letting you see the enemies first before enganging into fights, ending missions with the big boom. Thanks to the awesome soundtrack as well, at these levels I have nothing but pure blast of fun.
That, and just because it's about snipers doesn't mean that it's supposed to be only about attempting stealth. Action sure became much better. You now have a small regenerating health and can take cover behind things, possibly waiting for enemy to give up on searching you. Or to shoot them back with sniper rifle or submachine gun. It still means that you don't want to be in the open for too long. This game employes the awesome X-Ray camera to show you how the bullet penetrates poor guy's skull. And eyes. Awesome feedback for awesome shots!
And look, this game is mixing action with a bit of stealth, not about only one of those. It's all about surviving. Enemy may know that there is sniper around, but it's all good as long as he doesn't know where to shoot. While for pure stealth there are too many forced encounters. Not to mention that sometimes it's smarter to keep superior sniping position instead of trying to ghost your way. And for pure action it sometimes just doesn't make you change cover, becoming shooting gallery. Especially when it comes to enemy snipers, due to linear level design the fights against them are quite lame.
It all however can be forgiven as the game allows you to beat whole campaign from start to finish in cooperative play with your friend! I think you both have less health, but you can revive each other, like in a lot of recent coop games. Snipe together, sneak together, cover a buddy.
Cooperative play also includes few more game mode. Kill Tally is your endless waves invasion type of deal, also available in single. Spawned enemies are aware of your positions, but once they actually engange you they can lose the track of you. Bombing run is about scavenging vehicle parts on the map while getting ambushed, stay along with buddy at all the times. And Overwatch mode divides roles: Sniper is confined in small vantage point, while Overwatch is the one moving and completing objective, having only Submachine gun, pistol and traps, as well as ability to tag targets for sniper. Though most often Overwatch player just have to hide while Sniper is the one having fun.
And competetive multiplayer is a blast as well! While Deathmatch is chaotic and isn't much, Team based games are awesome.
There is nothing like hiding in the bushes and tagging enemy with binoculaurs. Because in this sniping game knowledge of position means a lot. You have to change it as the shooting from rifle also produces muzzle flash and bullet trace by which you can be tracked down. While tagging enemy helps your team, as target very quickly will be taken down, making you feel like a credit to team. You can lay somewhere and watch over battlefield as sniper. Being careful. Or you can run and punish enemy for not watching flanks by getting in with submachine gun. It all keeps what could be otherwise boring camping fresh and tense.
You can even find servers with Capture The Flag mode if you want to see people move around. So you could pick them off. Though strangely enough it keeps spawning teammates as if it was Team Deathmatch, so there hiralious times when teams would attack each other and then end up spawning on different teams side.
The sad thing is that most servers disable tagging or even enable "No Cross" or do other things to change this awesome balance. No Cross is quite horrible, it divides map into two parts so other teams can't cross, the only thing left is sniping. You may agrue that it's SNIPER game, yes. But it's also a third-person game, so people can easily just sit behind cover and wait forever for somebody to pop up, who also does the same thing. No risk of getting shot behind. It feels like winning this match depends not on your inciative but on opponent's boredom.
But yes, this Sniper Elite game has tight but linear campaign and awesome multiplayer of all kinds.

Comipo is an excellent special-purpose 3D tool: a way of creating web comics with poseable characters, static backgrounds, word balloons, the works. Its strength is the ability to quickly assemble characters and scenes from pre-built models and poses, without having to understand 3D modeling in detail. This is also its weakness: if you want to move past the initially limited library it offers, you will need to purchase DLC or install third-party models. Installing and using external 3D models is difficult. Fortunately, it's very easy to import 2D images for backgrounds or decoration.
Comipo lacks a polished user interface for anything other than the basic actions of adding models to a panel and moving them around. But for what it does, it's functional, affordable, and fun.

I do recommend this game, but don't get me wrong. Let's be honest, you're reading reviews because you want to get the game, and the only two things holding you back are if it is awesome, and/or what are the issues. (Note the date of this review, as games do get patched, in theory.)
Good game, and especially fun if you are about that proximity voice chat. I do recommend it, but not if you are on a budget.
So here's why not:
I know this is hard for a smaller company, but here's the obvious one for popular budget kick starter type games. As each day goes by, there are more and more hacks and hackers. This can range from perfect grabs, unlimited item use, and auto-aim. There's also glitches too exploit, not really hacking, but if you know how to do them, you can force at the very least a standstill. Great method for getting XP, but some people prefer the gameplay and mechanics. Expect to experience this 1/20 games, increasing. 5% of games, that's why this is not viable enough for a "not recommend" in my opinion.
The second one is a given for this game and really can't be fixed. If and when two or more friends play together (and they are a high level), they are most likely to grind some experience whilst playing. So expect to have more of a 8v2 or 5v5 match, as your supposed teammates will no doubt be helping Jason to come kill you. This, again, is probably are as common as hackers. Their loyal friendship will come in the form of same team betrayal to you. I don't warrant this as enough for a not recommend in my opinion, since you may do this yourself, unless you are actual real friends, in that case real friends kill each other first in game.
Thirdly, I would have to say content vs price. I'm sure you've read the other reviews. This game is over-priced no doubt, but the only ones who complain probably are strapped on cash. I'm pretty sure it's clear across the board with that one, even if not everyone says it. I wouldn't say it's outrageous. It's just a bit steep. I take that back, if you don't like unlocking outfits, then yes, this game will have gotten you.
All in all, I have high tolerance for hackers, friends who team up to kill everyone else, and I'm financially comfortable. So... yea, I recommend. If you have any deep issues with any of that, don't.

It seems that the developers have designed two or, maybe, three faces and decided that it's enough. If you have a 144hz monitor like me you should know that this game doesn't render at more than 60fps.

Even with vsync off, when the fps counter shows above 200fps, it still feels like 60fps.
If you know how a 144fps game feels like, you won't be fooled.
With so many high refresh rate monitors on the market today, it's a shame developers still haven't learned to make games run properly at those higher framerates.

A great horror game with even better storytelling.
It tells a story that's compelling and tackles some really intriguing philosofical questions.
The horror mechanics are great and fair. It's not the jumpscary kind of horror game, it's the amnesia/feeling of being chased kind of horror and it feels great throughtout the whole experience. It changes often enough to never feel boring or overstays it's welcome.
Great horror aside, what really shines in this game is the story of the world unfolding for the player. The way the game portays certain story elements to the player is refreshing and new, and the game really makes the player think about his actions unlike even a lot of storydriven games do these days.
With 30€ price tag, the game is a bit on the expensive side since it doesn't have anything more to it after the first playthrough, but for 20€ or less, this game is a steal. It's roughly 10 hours long if you explore all it has to offer, and I would absolutely recommend it for all horror, scifi and psychology fans out there. One of the best games I've played all year, and I'm not even a big fan of horror games to begin with.

I'm actually one of the newer users, not exactly sure how safely download the DeviantArt content, or to create my own items, but the latest updates and my DeviantArt findings keep this little program and my love for it alive. I myself have several test pages, character previews, and a PG-13 Fantasy series on the back burner.
Download the demonstration from the website, and see how you like it; practice like hell, then practice some more with the full version and DLC; then, once you've figured everything out, take a shot at making the comic you would like to read or to post on DeviantArt!

Don't worry, it's good. It may not be a big budget game, and it may only last five hours, but it feels just about right. There's lots of gameplay and moments packed into that time. It's satisfying, it's fast, and I'd say it's worth $30. We both know you've bought plenty of things for $30 that were way less entertaining for five hours than this game, so just do it.
The game does what it sets out to do; give you a way to tear♥♥♥♥♥♥up with cool powers and gunplay. The tentacles may feel weird at first, but after you get used to how asynchronous they are from your other actions, you'll probably want more. I liked it, and am a little surprised nobody else has been doing that. A lot of fights are made difficult by the placement and use of light (which disables your powers), which felt really refreshing. I'm a big fan of environments being part of gameplay, and while shooting out lights may feel tedious at first, the later fights really show off how well it can be integrated into combat.
But let's take a second and look at the story. It's skippable, you don't have to worry about it. I went through it, however, and i was really surprised how much time I spent wondering which reality was "real". They really tried to sell the different realities, and more than a few times i felt myself switching which one i thought was real. It may be a little out of place in a frantic shooter like this, but I appreciated it.
Overall, I'm surprised this isn't more well-known. The gameplay really sells itself, and there were a lot of innovations that were ahead of their time, or at least should have been more recognized. The fact that I hadn't heard of it until a Steam sale is a crime.

Having just completed the story-line, I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with Pyre.  It's a very story focused game; you find yourself immersed in the world and the lovable team mates you travel with,  which is frequently chopped up by action packed matches which the story is based around known as "Rites" (The Pyre universes own sport, where teams compete for there chance to regain their freedom and return to there homeland, thus relinquishing banishment) which allow for you to experience epic excitement preventing the game from ever becoming stale.  I found myself becoming utterly immersed in the games world, as the game does a great job of merging the playable character with the player which allows you to feel as a genuine part of the world which earnt the game major points from me. There are a wide variety of endings available, all being dependant on the choices made throughout AND how many Rite matches were won during the playthrough; this allows for massive replayability and having the new difficulty mode (Nightwing) being added ensures you get your moneys worth.  When it comes to the games soundtrack I don't think i could compliment the developers enough on selecting perfect songs to fit in with environments, certain characters and dramatic moments in order to alter your mood in such a way that makes every moment epicly unique to one another.  I highly recommend Pyre as you may be able to tell; and contender for best indie game of 2017 in my opinion.

I'm a huge BSG fan, and this game is the one I've been waiting for, but it is having trouble holding my interest in the present state of the single-player campaign.  About 10 hours in and I already feel like I've done it all and the autocam replays have somewhat lost their charm. It is great to see familiar names in the game and omg...young Doc Cottle!
The tactical layer of the game is just excellent. It feels like an actual, BSG, tactical simulation rather than a game. Which is what you want in a strategy game. It's something rarely seen in games in general, TBH. Nothing in this game is left to chance on the tactical level. There are no dice rolls and mathematics to try to tip in your favour; just physics, decisions, and strategy. It's entirely possible to win the day with just one ship and some vipers if you think like Adama!
But the strategic layer is seriously barebones and it takes too many missions to get blueprints for new ships and ordinances to add variety to your fleet. I already feel like I've done it all, but replay value is vital to strategy games. While the content that is here is suitable for competitive multiplayer, it's not nearly enough for single-player.
Thus, I keep finding myself returning to XCOM 2 when I know I'd rather be playing this if there was more to keep me playing — I will happily switch this to a thumbs up when/if they add more content to the game or lower its price.
*Given the recent announcement of the forthcoming improvements, content, fixes, and updates, I'm going to go ahead and give this the thumbs up now.

I'm a big fan of the previous warfare games and was hoping there would be something even greater developed in the genre, 1917 and 1944 were excellent games. Unfortunately this one is a let down in terms of gameplay majorly because of two things.
- Cards are incredibly powerful and extremely polarised in their effects, making RNG dominate the game almost entirely.
- USA vs. Russia in modern combat is about as interesting as watching paint dry, they should have stuck to historical wars as the theme, almost any war would have worked out; WWII with the various warring nations would have been excellent.
This could have been really good but no matter how much I tried to enjoy it I always felt either frustrated due to the RNG mechanics or the setting just felt unappealing.
Beyond gameplay, noteworthy is that:
- This game suffers from P2W. While theoretically you can at some point in your life reach top performance without spending, the grind so immense that you will spend months as cannon fodder to catch up to the whales to an equal footing and any casual player will likely never do that and will be perpetual cannon fodder served up to the whales.
In the end RNG, a very unappealing setting and P2W just sucks the fun out of the game.
Not recommended.

Overall 9/10 and a must buy for any BSG fan.
Game mechanics are simple, somewhat intuitive and the struggle feels real, game economics make every lost ship or officer hurt and it is quite possible for your losses to spiral out of control and dissolve the Quorum or be forced into a last-ditch fight where your shipyard is lost due to overwhelming enemy forces. And some missions you just can't win, I like that.
That said, there are several bugs and game mechanics that need tweaking, still feels like Beta was rushed.
Bugs:
Enemy capital ships occasionally dead-stop in space for no reason.
Second campaign at Admiral level with tutorials off wouldn't create some space lanes, leaving Helios Delta completely cut off from the rest of the system.
Ship names do not stick when changed while under construction. New name is generated when ship is complete.
Mechanics:
Vipers are too OP and Raiders are too squishy at all difficulty levels.
Navigation subsystems shouldn't stop your ship when hacked down to zero, lack of maneuverability is fine, but ship should still drift at momentum, even if decaying.
Squadrons are too small, I can understand an Adamant only having 10 or 8 fighters on board, but a Battlestar which in universe can field between 120-160 vipers, plus Raptors should have larger squadrons to make the game feel more immersive. so should a Basestar. personally I would love to have the feel of 40 Vipers trying to hold off multiple waves of cylon raiders that outnumber them 4 to 1.
Hopefully the devs will incorporate that into a follow-up game set later in the First War timeline.

Having now played the Campaign in full and gotten a real taste for the game, I now feel I can write an effective review. Please note that I played the campaign through on normal difficulty.
Let me begin by saying I bought this game primarily because I'm a BSG fan, and secondarily because I enjoy space based strategy games. I wasn't really sure what to expect when I started looking into the game until I watch EnterElysium playing the game on Youtube before release. I fell in love with the type of game being developed at that point. Never before had i seen a turn based space strategy game that played out in real time allowing you to see the consequences of your actions and also giving you the time to think out your every move.
The campaign was quite a journey. While the story was for the most part weak (Definitely left something to be desired), it was interesting enough to make it feel like each battle was for a reason. The real jem is in the journey with each battle having an unknown outcome no matter what you entered it with. There were several times I jumped into a fight with 2 battlestars and a reasonable support fleet that I was unsure if I was going to win the engagement let alone make it through with heavy losses, where earlier in the game it seemed like my frigates were doing better on their own. However, with a little more game time (And several heavy battlestar/officer losses later) I finally learned how to use those more expensive ships, thus securing a nearly clean victory in every battle there after.
The one exception to the victory rule above is when a Cylon Basestar fleet spawed on top of one of my smaller fleets consisting of 2 frigates and a corvette. While I got initially caught off guard, I was giving them hell until more ships jumped in, which again was unexcepted. That engagement caught me off guard, and I'll admit I was left wondering why that didn't happen to any of my larger fleets (Which would have made sense).
Anyhow, enough about the journey and on to my list of Pros and Cons:
Pros:
- Turn based system for tactical decisions (Made it easy to walk away when I needed to take care of something else, and ensured I had plenty of time to think about my decisions)
- AutoCam (Great beaty shots for the realime replay of the battle)
- The realtime replay feature
- Good balancing of ships and abilities (This one is up in the air for a lot of people, but I've found that spending some time with each of the ships and learning their strengths and weaknesses will cause you to adjust your tactics accordingly. Just because something is heavily armored doesn't mean in can withstand sustained fire from 4+ ships for long on one armor front)
- Intelligent AI that makes you think on both the strategic and tactical levels.
- Reasonable graphics for a game of this scale and type
- The tactical need to use different types of ordinance and fighter/utility loadouts
Cons:
- Interface was a bit klunky (Cycling through 10+ targets when selecting fighter targets was  a pain)
- I don't recall a tutorial talking about planet fortification. There was a bit about needing offensive fleets with officers, but it failed to explain the benefit of planet fortification. Trial and error is how I figured this one out.
- Storyline was a bit weak (If getting this game, get it for the gameplay, not the story)
Utlimately I feel this is a solid game with great visuals and tactical gameplay. It also provides a strong foundation for hopefully some great story content down the road. I paid the full $40 for this game and I do not regret it one bit.

The X-Ray kill cam is cool. For others it gets repetitive and boring, but for me it never really ceases to feel good.
Ballistics are pretty alright but definitely exaggerrated for reasons I'll detail below.
Those are about the only things good about the game.
So yes, it's a WW2 shooter with the !!twist!! that you're a sniper, and you have to infiltrate enemy territory and assassinate critical targets with (almost) no backup at all.
Maps are really linear, and don't offer the tactical opportunities an actual sniper would really like to get. They are also pretty damn small for real sniping, yet the reasons you don't want to go in with your secondary weapons are their abysmal accuracy, even when prone, abysmal recoil and little available ammo. Stealth isn't an option most of the time, or even something like relocation after firing a shot - kill or miss, doesn't matter, the AI will be permanently alerted, and no amount of hiding or moving away will stop them from repeating the same "Find him" or "Come out, sniper" lines over and over. Not to mention how they will just endlessly try to bumrush you on higher difficulties, again violating one's common sense to take cover then slowly move up and flank you. The real difficulty comes from them spotting you from absolutely anywhere you poke even a polygon through - a little crevace, in a dark room, a hundred meters away, it doesn't matter - they will still see you, and will keep firing in automatic bursts across that same distance and hit you 3/4 of the time.
Realism only really extends to the sniper ballistics, and even those are exaggerrated for the sake of giving the illusion the maps are really bigger than they appear to be. There's no sight zeroing but you do have a part bullet time, part "eliminate 90% of idle scope sway" hold breath mechanic. Sounds are exaggerrated as well with lots of echoing even in areas which shouldn't have echoes.
You frequently end up in shooting gallery sections, where enemies funnel down a corridor and you are expected to deal with them either with a slow(-ish) firing rifle (which can admittedly penetrate multiple dudes) or with the same abysmal secondaries mentioned above. This goes pretty much against everything a sniper is supposed to do in the area of operations.
Speaking of snipers, f*** the enemy snipers. They spawn in difficult places, with the only hint of their existence being an occasional scope glare and (on lower difficulties) an arrow pointing in their direction. Even when they are on the move, they have near perfect aim and WILL get at least one shot on you, every time, until you memorise their spawning positions and ice them.
I got this for free, and honestly I was really hyped the first time I learned of this game just before release. The sparkle and spectacle quickly wore down as it slowly turns like most other WW2 first/third person shooters with some mind boggling design choices.
If I were you, I'd not pick this game just because it advertises having wind affect ballistics, which many other such games seem to lack.

I do recommend this game, but don't get me wrong. Let's be honest, you're reading reviews because you want to get the game, and the only two things holding you back are if it is awesome, and/or what are the issues. (Note the date of this review, as games do get patched, in theory.)
Good game, and especially fun if you are about that proximity voice chat. I do recommend it, but not if you are on a budget.
So here's why not:
I know this is hard for a smaller company, but here's the obvious one for popular budget kick starter type games. As each day goes by, there are more and more hacks and hackers. This can range from perfect grabs, unlimited item use, and auto-aim. There's also glitches too exploit, not really hacking, but if you know how to do them, you can force at the very least a standstill. Great method for getting XP, but some people prefer the gameplay and mechanics. Expect to experience this 1/20 games, increasing. 5% of games, that's why this is not viable enough for a "not recommend" in my opinion.
The second one is a given for this game and really can't be fixed. If and when two or more friends play together (and they are a high level), they are most likely to grind some experience whilst playing. So expect to have more of a 8v2 or 5v5 match, as your supposed teammates will no doubt be helping Jason to come kill you. This, again, is probably are as common as hackers. Their loyal friendship will come in the form of same team betrayal to you. I don't warrant this as enough for a not recommend in my opinion, since you may do this yourself, unless you are actual real friends, in that case real friends kill each other first in game.
Thirdly, I would have to say content vs price. I'm sure you've read the other reviews. This game is over-priced no doubt, but the only ones who complain probably are strapped on cash. I'm pretty sure it's clear across the board with that one, even if not everyone says it. I wouldn't say it's outrageous. It's just a bit steep. I take that back, if you don't like unlocking outfits, then yes, this game will have gotten you.
All in all, I have high tolerance for hackers, friends who team up to kill everyone else, and I'm financially comfortable. So... yea, I recommend. If you have any deep issues with any of that, don't.

Absoloutely True History I learned from this game.
-Every house, tavern, and military bunker in 1945 Germany had the exact same 3 paintings.
-Gold was worthless. People just left bars of it lying everywhere.
-The Mauser 98K apparently did not exist during WW2 in Germany.
-The Nazis did not use the swastika as a symbol. Just the crucifix.
-The Russians won because roughly 33% of their soldiers had perfect, manly mustaches
On to the Mechanincs.
- Stealth barely exists.
After the disaster of a "stealth" system from the first game, they don't even pretend anymore. prone, crouch and stand are mostly for steadying your aim. Crouch and prone do allow you to move silently. Unfortunately this is only useful in 10% of the game, because the other 90% takes place in wide open areas with 10 enemy NPC snipers all apparently using wall hacks, bright skins, and aimbots. If you walk near an edge where even a few pixels get clost to said edge, the enemy not only notices you, but starts firing exatly at your head. Try getting a good shot off on Sniper Elite difficulty where you must account for bullet drop and wind stregnth while the enemy does not.
- Bullet Physics.
The only part of the game done decently, and only on "Sniper Elite" difficulty where bullet drop and wind are calculated.  Seriously, if you play this game on any lower mode you are wasting your time. Still not perfect though. Bullet drop is way too high. You drop a considerable amount at only 100 feet, which is odd for a rifle who's zero is supposed to be set at 300 meters. That said, there are no shots even 300 meters long in this game. This begs the question, why have a sniping game that has distances so short? Oh, and after striking theri target the exiting bullet will slightly change course on exit and may strike another enemy behind the first. This is rarely an opportunity to have this happen unfortunately.
- Enemy spawns.
Much like the first game, 90% of the time your enemies will only spawn once you move into a certain position. That position is typically right in front of where the guy with sub-machine gun spawns. Once again, why have a sniper rifle where your typical engagement range is 10 feet?
- Save system
This game drops the "save anywhere with limited saves" Hitman model and opts for the modern day shooter checkpoint system. The next checkpoint is past 20 aimbot snipers, and 30 SMG guys rushing you. Have fun replaying the same checkpoint 30+ times!
- AI
Enemy hears you throw a rock to distract him? Him and all his buddies on the entire map stay on alert the rest of the mission.  Ground enemies only have 3 modes. Patrol pre-set route. Run wildly back and forth between cover for no reason. Rush straight towards you.
- Pros
Decent Physics
Satisfying XRay Kills
- Cons
Trys to copy the worst aspects of Call of Duty and fails hard.
Sort of kinda prenteds to be a stealth game and fails hard.
- Verdict
Buy for $5 or less and you will be entertained for 10 hours. Spend more than that and regret will fill your soul.

We all know what happens when you dig to deep. Add to that reaching for immortality, and, uh, these things never end well, do they?
In Peregrin you are a member of a tribe in a post-apocalyptic world where humanity dug too deep and reached too far. You are sent alone to a dangerous area to try and get the gods to stop kicking your poor race while they're down, armed with your trusty fight-stick and the ability to possess critters.
The world consists of discrete screens, many of them linking together to form two or three-screen puzzles. There's an ongoing narration and points of interest, which give the game a nice storytelling vibe; it helps that the setting remains interesting throughout, and the writing is pretty good as well.
But at its heart Peregrin is a puzzle game. The two main puzzle types - possessing critters to manipulate the environment to allow you to move forward, and combat, in which you need to carefully pick the order in which you possess enemies and attack. There are some very light timing challenges (dodging turrets) but aside from one instance they're pretty gentle. There's a lot of wrinkles to keep it interesting; you can only posess animals within a certain radius of objects you need to activate first, and line of sight also plays a role; a lot of times you need to use objects to lure critters somewhere before you can control them.
The puzzles aren't particularly inspired, but they're always intuitive, well though out, and make sense within the world. They escalate nicely even though they tend to remain on the easy side. I'd say the whole game lasted me around four hours, and it never outstayed its welcome or felt like it was spinning its wheels.
The art style is great, with a scratchy style and an eye for striking vistas.
It's not a perfect package, but if you're in the market for a relaxed puzzling experience which manages to give you a glimpse into an interesting world, you can do a lot worse than this. Highly recommended.
Full disclosure - I know the lead animator for this project, but haven't seen him in ages (and I also only found out he was involved *after* buying the game).

Be careful with the likes of SOMA. Having finished both Amnesias, I was happed to delve deeper into the depths of SOMA (pun intented). While the atmostphere of the game, as well as plot, develop and intensify over time, the overall 'game' aspect is severely lacking. Much like titles such as Dear Ester you're tasked with simply walking to and fro to unravel the mystery behind your awakening, but once gameplay kicks in expect to be frustrated beyond believe.
Anyone who's a fan of the sci-fi genre in general will indeed love the story, but I'd suggest looking elsewhere if looking for anything else. What's technically a walking simulator becomes marred by the occasional 'monster' encounter that leaves you wondering what exactly it is you should do. Once you realize bypassing content is the best alternative you're left with nothing more than a series of events that you'll piece together to create a narrative.
The story itself is fantastic, bringing about questions any sci-fi afficianado can enjoy. I'd recommend this game simply on the grounds of plot, but unfortunately, from someone who has enjoyed many a Frictional Game, it sputters and fades out before it gets good. The climax comes to a definitive end, but as a GAME it's bittersweet.

For Honor does have some multiplayer issues. The connections are peer to peer, so if your internet is bad, you're gonna have a♥♥♥♥♥♥time. Its abuseable too, people can lag switch and host migrations happen.
Gear can be attained that alters your stats (Every stat change is a trade-off, for instance, increase your throw distance at the cost of your sprint speed), it only works in some game modes (Its disabled in Duels, for instance, but the cosmetic effect still shows). The real breaker with it is the high teir revenge gear, which effectively allows you to enter a super mode extremely quickly compared to other players and be more or less unstoppable while in this mode.
So why am I still reccomending the game?
Because the game itself is very, very good, and I think its positives outweigh its negatives. Look, you have a bad matchmaking system and a somewhat overpowered set of equipment. However, For Honor is a game based on skill. Unless you run into someone that is using internet ♥♥♥♥ery to cheat, and I haven't yet, each fight relies on the skills of the combatants. Combat is exhilerating and satisfying, filled with coutners and punishing attacks. And while the gear may allow you to become 'overpowered' quickly, you can see when someone has their revenge meter filled and back off until it drains, and even if they activate this mode, if they just mindlessly flail away at you, its wasted.
It reminds me of Dark Souls with its Love/Hate relationship you build with the game. I'd reccomend it if you're a fan of 3d fighting games. And if you're worried about infinite combos, don't, anything beyond two hits can be countered with the right timing.
Side effects include spontaneous erections lasting possibly longer than four hours. If you experience such an effect, don't worry, that's normal.

A beautiful game, with well-designed UI and a 30-second learning curve.  Much thought went into the ambience, the music, the tone and presentation.  This game is polished in a way that few games in its class are, the rough corners sanded down to create a truly pleasant experience second only to Osmos, IMHO.
So it was a surprise and annoyance to find that the level of care and creativity that went into making the game didn't map over to the pacing of the game.  The first two sections of the first level are excellent, everything I could ask for in a casual game like this.  Then the third section, the 'Spikey Rivers', jumps several orders in difficulty. You must navigate a slim river, without touching the sides, as it goes through a dozen hair-pin turns, another dozen tricky rapids, and ever-changing water currents coming out of nowhere, and if you touch the sides once you get sent back to the start of the river.
After the 20th try, I shut the game down and looked online to see: is it just me, or did the game really jump from something kids can play to something experienced hardcore gamers are abandoning after unsuccessfully navigating the Spikey Rivers?  As it turns out, it wasn't just me.  Every page of reviews I looked at, from many diverse sources, was full of posts filled with words like "frustrated" and "ragequit", and people resignedly abandoning the game because you cannot proceed further until you finish the Spikey Rivers quest.  The pacing in this game - in the 3 parts of the first level that are all most people ever see - is analogous to being taught to play checkers, then to play Osmos, then being told you can go no further unless you master Russian Roullette.
If you think I am exaggerating, look up any other review... the only ones saying they didn't stop playing after the frustration of the Spikey Rivers either say they'll try again later, or say they won't play again until the makers fix The Problem.  But aside from giving players the ability to treat some quests as optional, I don't see how they can fix it. The game is beautifully and consciously designed, every part fits the rest perfectly. Except for the part where any fun you were having falls down the oubliette never to be seen again.
Loads of promise, a few fun levels, and then... that.

Sparkle 2 was more of an ambient experience.
With the addition of quests, obstacles and the ability to actively alter your organism(*), Sparkle 3 is more readily identifiable as a "game (per se)."
*In Sparkle 2, you could sway evolution by what you consumed. Want to be faster/stronger? Eat more of the corresponding color. Sparkle 3 has a level-up system; eat all you want and decide afterwards how you'll progress.
From the start (from what I remember), your organism is much more tank-y in 3 than in 2. What with the multiple stats to consider when levelling, I assume it's possible to get as much maneuverability out of your organism in 3 as you'd in 2. Both movement and consumption (absorption) rates are slower. In 2, movement affected pretty much only your head - your body would coil around and follow it. In 3, the axis seems placed at/near the actual center of the body - no such turning-on-a-dime movement, thusly.
I've 0.6 hrs on record currently; 100% Sparkle 2.
I want/expect to do the same for 3.
I recommend this game to:
Those who enjoyed 2 and wouldn't mind more of a "gamey" experience; 3 is still casual, but what with obstacles and quests, it's not near as mindnumbing as 2 (though, that soundtrack though...).
Those who haven't played 2 and aren't after such casual-ties (heh... heh...) as 2; understand that - what with the slow movement and absorption rates - 3 is still chill, but you'll have to actually make an effort to get through, as opposed to 2, in which simply being in-game damn-near guaranteed success.

I was expecting a nice relaxing, slow-paced experience; I got confusion, frustration, and rage instead.
First two areas are mostly easy and enjoyable.  Your critter drives like a bus but slowly gets more agile.  Then they throw you into the third area of "spikey rivers" and expect you to expertly maneuver your slug down a long path just wider than it through currents and spikey trees that blend into the background and make you start over if you so much as come close to them.  After half an hour of attempts, I got halfway through and ragequit.  I came back later to try again and after another half hour ragequit again.
You can't bypass it.  You have to get through it in one attempt.  Could I have evolved my critter to better handle this challenge if I had known about it beforehand?  Maybe - too bad you can't change your upgrades without restarting.  If you look at the achievements, about half the people who get to this area make it past.  I honestly have no idea why they decided to make something so aggravating in a game that's supposed to be about relaxation.
The other quests weren't a whole lot better.  Save these eggs from the predators?  Okay, great.  I feel vaguely heroic.  Ok, now eat all the eggs because the omnipotent power says he doesn't like them anymore?  What?  That doesn't make any sense and immediately pulled me out of the experience.
Other than that, the in-game text is poorly translated with grammar errors in more or less every blurb.  Overall, it feels very unpolished and unprofessional.  The graphics are the only thing it's got going for it (they are quite pretty); the music is nice for five minutes but gets old very quickly.
3/10 with 6 stars for the first two levels and then -3 for the third.  Only get if you're an absolute fan of the series.

Evil Genius is what happens when you have Austin Powers and Dungeon Keeper make a baby. Traps, minions, henchment, and a secret island base are all meticulously run by your Evil Genius. You defend yourself against the ever increasing interest from world governments trying to shut you down to each region's top secret spy.
But what good is a top secret spy if you just shoot him? No, there's protocol. You gloat, you find his weakness, you cheat, you scheme, you start the unneccesarily slow dipping mechanism.
At it's core Evil Genius is Dungeon Keeper with a more simple RPG aspect and a wonderfully done 1970's coat of paint. You don't control minions directly, and instead give orders to build, buy, or work through various influences. While a little buggy, and sadly only supporting 4:3 resolutions, the game still does remarkably well if you're a fan of this type of gameplay.
It's definately a rare (be it unpolished) gem that has sadly been ignored by a the general public.
Controls can be hard for beginners, but a look in the options -> key bindings should help you out. It is highly recommended you download some mods for this game and the 3den Editor.

Again, this game has a TON of potential, and I really hope the devs continue to work on it.  With some work and pollish it could be incredibly fun.  But right now the "ooooo shiny" feeling fades pretty quickly as you run out of things to do.  If this game is improved upon I will happily revise my review. The Isle... was once one of the best prehistoric life games I have ever played. I would even go as far as to put it above ARK. I used to have all of the respect in the world for the devs, for making a game that resonated with me so well.
To me, this is not a survival game. This is not a progression game. This is entirely time-based. When I think of Progression, I think of actively being productive and creating a foundation of which you can survive. But The Isle is not progression. It is not productivity and it is not strategy. It is entirely based on luck, time, and will.
Now, there have always been problems with the game, but Sandbox and the old maps made these problems... bearable. They gave us ways to go around these issues, just like you would in any survival game.
Let me give a few examples.
The world is FAR too large, so much that it's hard to find anyone of your own species. Sandbox repaired this with Global Species chat. It did not enable you to talk to other species, but any of your own from any distance. It was easy to find each other and create a pack, making the large world no problem at all. Now that there is only local chat, you must play with a friend with some way to chat outside of the game.
Unbalanced dinos, not enough love for smaller ones. In Sandbox this was not very much of a problem as it took no time to get back to the exact dino you wanted to be. We had raptors, trikes, stegos,  gallis, shants, rexes, carnos, allos, all kinds of stuff. Now the only thing you can hope to see in a safe, stable situation is gigas and shants. Who would play as a raptor or small herbivore, or make a Nest as one when there's no chance of survival? Plus.. Raptors used to have places they could get to that larger dinos couldn't. They had to come down for food so they weren't invincible, and it was a good way for raptors to meet up with other raptors and make packs. That's all gone now.
Thats just a small bit of it.. I don't even need to mention how troll-y the devs are, and how disrespectful they are to their own community. People talk about that enough as it is.
I think.. You'd be best not spending your money on this. It went from being my favorite game of all time to a huge disappointment. What you see in the trailers and the description is not anywhere near what the game actually is. Keep your eye out for Saurian and Trials of Ascension (a game that does progression right...) instead.

At first, I thought it wouldn't be as fun as Dead by Daylight "although I hate people comparing the two games", however gameplay and social interactions have proven the opposite of that. I was terrified when I first got the game (and still am for different reasons), the ambient sounds and atmosphere make this game feel like a genuine horror movie. Although I haven't played as much as I'd love to, I've played since launch. This game is the most fun you'll have in any Asym Horror game.  There are many factors to this, personally I enjoy the challenge of playing Counselor against the super OP Jason (which the Devs stated was intended). If that's not your cup of tea, you can enjoy brutally murdering camp teenagers with various weapons and the environment. The social interactions are even better, you'll get Jasons screaming at you as they chase you down, counselors who scream at Jason to save you (or run away and leave you as bait for their own good). You get Counselors who manage to never leave until the rest are gone (and usually die trying that), and that is personally fun to me.
If you enjoyed Dead by Daylight's "72Hrs/360 Juke", you'll enjoy it even more in this game. You 360 like in DbD, but you smack Jason after he misses an attack on you, allowing you and friends to run for a few more seconds and (hopefully) survive until you find more windows to carelessly hop through, which is the most hilarious animation in this game.
The community is great, and Chad's inhuman beauty is even better. All the counselors fit everyone's unique playstyles, Adam or Bugzy are altruistic fighters, Vanessa is the bait player who can't fight, LaChappa is the nerdy kid who makes roleplayers like JFJ fun, AJ is the stealthy chick, Tiffany the chick for all you horny guys who think with your lower head, Chad's luck lets you jump from high windows or constantly block Jason's attacks, and Jenny will stop you from screaming at every dead body and getting terrifed, like bloody Chad does. Also Adam is hot ;]
The only bad parts I see in this game are team-killing griefers, who purposely queue to do that when their friend is or isn't Jason, breaking the point of the game, and Shift+Grabbing. Although Jason is supposed to be OP, there is too much control in that instant-kill maneuver for it to be fair.
If you can put up with those two, this game will be a hilariously fun time for anybody. Horror fans, and scared players.

Now, firstly, I just want to say, there are haters in the world, and there are lovers in the world. I do not know which side of them I'd like to pick, but I do see the game has some real potential.
Sigh, where do I begin with this? Well, I'll just like to firstly talk about the game when it first came to be.
It wasn't very big at all, but it was what I'd assume was one of the popular things of the month, a brand new Play-as-a-Dinosaur game. You're on this island, with many others as a raptor, t-rex, bronto, or gallimimus! So cool!
The dino fans of steam were completely thundering this game. Almost playing it 24/7... actually, they were!
It was so fun back then. Only 6 dinos,(Puertasaurus, gallimimus, shantungosaurus, T-rex, Carnotaurus, Austroraptor) but still really fun!
They soon after added the theri, then resting, multi roars, diablo, dryo, stego and trike. But, then, out of the blue, came the first ever added carnivore to be added to the game. Allosaurus. after that, they added the sucho, the herra, the anky, pachy. Then, footprints and bleed.
before you knew it, they added this new mode. "experimental"! It lets you play as the quetz. When they added that, v3 was just started to be made, then progression at the same time.
Not long after, the rexes lifestages were added. (Juvies, Subs, Adults.) Then a few days after. BAM, proggression. We still had the choice to do sandbox, but proggression had 2 new dinos. Utahraptor, and Acrocanthosaurus. At the time my computer had serious ♥♥♥♥♥ happening. So I couldn't play for 10 minutes without... crashing.
It didn't save anything, either. So I gave up on playing. Got a new computer and started playing with the 2 new additions, the taco, and the bary.
I played THE HELL out of the game. A bit after, they added... Giga, and Spino!
Giga just roams in massive packs and completely makes you want to kill yourself after spending all that time then wasting it.
Then there's the spino. When it came out, surprisingly not many people wanted to play as it, after seeing how weak it was. It was quite obviously underused.
Then giga came out, and BAM spinos became extinct. A phew minor updates have came since then, along with Christmas and New Year.
Now, the game has came a long way, and (according to reliable sources) it's only half way through development.
and I've seen the awesome kind of things that will be in the game when it's done.
People mainly hate the game a lot, ever since proggression existed, but I love it. It's just realistic, because, in sandbox you just picked dinos and had fun from then on. but there's nothing to achieve and there's just too many of the OP dinos.
Proggression, is realistic. Everything will be ballanced and there's lots of things to work up to.
Wanna become a giga? sure! Just wait a couple hours and not trying to get into fights as much, and... ta-dah!
But there are many downsides to it. eg: PP (proggression points) not saving when you die. Therefore, some people can just kill you without any hesitation and not caring wether you made someone waste almost 15 hours of their life. AT ONCE.
and, be careful with touch pads... you could accidentally kill someone about to prog.
So, since this guide is getting too long and I don't really have anything else to write about, I'm going to end it here, and, PLEASE support the game! The more support it gets the quicker things are added, and the game being complete. Heck, even if we're lucky, the devs might be able to finish the game in the middle of the year! (instead of new year)

I'm a huge fan of RTS games. I'm a big fan of the BSG show in the 2000s remake. A BSG RTS was a game I longed for, until this game released. The mechanics are usual of the turn-based RTS during field battle and the addition of a Z axis adds a 3D plane to the strategy but not much. in the galaxy map where you FTL from place to place, there's a Sins of a Solar Empire map strat to it, too, which adds to the fun. Making additional fleets to pepper the map and cut off cyclon advance is quite satisfying.
I am only a few hours into the game. So some quick pros and cons.
PROS:
-Graphics are pretty. not ground-breaking but def not ugly
-Replay camera makes you feel like you're watching the show!
-Strat relies on Z-axis and places importance of ship positioning (eg flak on the side of incoming missles)
-Fair amount of customizations that allow you to tailor your fleet to the situation
-Good voice acting
-Sound effects and BGM are nostalgic af
CONS:
-The HUD could use a little highlight (eg when selecting a ship a green reticle of the selected ship would help it stand out vs the double box it uses now)
-No short cuts to the commands for vessels
-Lacks multiple selection command to target same vessel (you have to click each viper group to attack the same target one by one)
-Short campaign. I'm on the 7th mission and I've been only playing 6.5 hours-ish as of this review. Hopefully they come out with DLC
-Price: It's a good and fun game but $40 for the content is a little steep
Otherwise, I enjoy the game a lot and even if the campaign is short, I'm opting to do as many side missions as possible to build my fleet and enrich the experience.
So, if you like BSG and enjoy strategy games, pick this up. The devs did a wonderful job recreating the BSG world and feel and making it into a game.

This game is not accurately described by its Metacritic score, however, the developers/publisher did not do themselves a favor in purporting the game as part of the Gothic franchise.  While the story is technically more interesting and coherent than previous Gothic games, the style of gameplay is significantly different as the design is aimed towards focused progression from point A to B.  The world is technically open, but there is never a reason to backtrack.  This design is not bad, however, as the developers make each step compelling enough with beautifully detailed locales and creatures to keep your interest.  If a fan of previous Gothics, understand that the structure is significantly different.  There are only a couple of decision points and there isn't a faction system to limit your abilities.  Abilities are also acquired via a skill tree rather than being trained and purchased from masters.  Still, this is a fun Action RPG and is worth a purchase when on sale.

Be careful with the likes of SOMA. Having finished both Amnesias, I was happed to delve deeper into the depths of SOMA (pun intented). While the atmostphere of the game, as well as plot, develop and intensify over time, the overall 'game' aspect is severely lacking. Much like titles such as Dear Ester you're tasked with simply walking to and fro to unravel the mystery behind your awakening, but once gameplay kicks in expect to be frustrated beyond believe.
Anyone who's a fan of the sci-fi genre in general will indeed love the story, but I'd suggest looking elsewhere if looking for anything else. What's technically a walking simulator becomes marred by the occasional 'monster' encounter that leaves you wondering what exactly it is you should do. Once you realize bypassing content is the best alternative you're left with nothing more than a series of events that you'll piece together to create a narrative.
The story itself is fantastic, bringing about questions any sci-fi afficianado can enjoy. I'd recommend this game simply on the grounds of plot, but unfortunately, from someone who has enjoyed many a Frictional Game, it sputters and fades out before it gets good. The climax comes to a definitive end, but as a GAME it's bittersweet.

I recommend this game. I really do, but I think the downsides of this game is worth a mention.
So, you play as a sniper rifle-wielding superhuman badass that can snipe a dude's nuts at a distance of twelve kilometers while blindfolded and shooting over the shoulder but can't hit someone in the torso at a distance of 12 feet with any other weapon.
I'm not even joking. Be the target moving, or stationary, or partially behind cover, or whatever, that guy is good as dead the moment you get your sights properly lined up. SMG's and pistols on the other hand are a different story. With crosshairs reminiscent to that of Moon River, you will be missing wider than a mile. Even at arm's length, you'll only have a 20% chance of hitting their bodies at best. May as well save the ammo for yourself, cause when you decide to commit suicide, it's likely that those rounds won't ever connect. Speaking of ammo... what ammo? You get one mag (or in the case of the PPSh, half a mag) of that stuff. Because of that, you won't be using them that much. In fact, you're better off NOT using them at all. The sniper rifle is the better choice in most cases.
Next, the AI. GOD DAMN are they broken, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly so. I saw one go prone, suddenly have siezures, stand back up, run to one place, go back to his original spot, and then repeated the process. They spawn just out of the blue, they run around like total autists, and some even mindlessly charge in your direction. Thank God those SMG's are as inaccurate as my answers during midterms, or you'd have an even worse time. Enemy snipers are kinda like you, except they come in either pairs or packs. Thanks to the broken spawning system, it's actually a tactic to die multiple times just to memorize where they'll spawn.
Moving on to stealth. I have one piece of advice for you. DONT. I don't care what you say, just don't do stealth. You get a suppressed pistol by default, and that's pretty much the only way to make any stealth takedowns aside from CQC. And as I've said before, the pistols in this game S-U-C-K. Just take your sniper rifle, and go crazy. You'll finish faster.
As for story, just roll with it. It's not very interesting. I'm sure you're not playing this game JUST for the story though, right?
Final verdict: solid 7/10 - Physics seem good to me, the x-rays are absolutely entertaining, and for a 2012 game, its graphics are outstanding. The cons kinda just dragged it down.

Since I played the first game in the Penumbra series, I was hooked on this sort of "horror adventure." I came from the world of Myst and it's ilk, so horror gaming combined with adventure was new to me.
Since then, there isn't a single Frictional Games release I have not regarded as epic. They evolve, and they continue to invoke more story into the experience.
A Machine for Pigs took a nice step in that direction, but nothing compares to the leap in story driven glory SOMA brings to the table.
As I played the game, I noted to myself how, unlike the prior games, this one felt less lonely; a companion was near, even if sometimes not in your hand or arms. The story will address that as well, in a very powerful way as it comes near its close. That surprised me more than just about anything else. I wondered, "Did the devs leave me thinking I had companionship, which I did in one sense, yet rip it from me and leave me alone?"
I won't tell you that answer, you'll have to see for yourself.
When the ending(s) came, it was the culmination of a brilliant story in a way that both saddened and elated. It was two endings in one.
The downside to SOMA is only one, as far as my experience dictates, and that is there is more long searching for locations than should have been required. Otherwise, the game is nearly flawless. It is beautiful, scary, scientific and futuristic like Dead Space meets Amnesia, and all around beautiful to view.
This is a story that will jolt the mind. Finish this game, and you will understand the depth of the dev's storytelling.
This is easily an 8 out of 10, and would be a 10 out of 10 were it not for the time spent figuring out where to go next.
Do yourself a favor if you choose to play this game: Get to the end, then
, then you'll see the brilliance in this story.

The Darkeness II is not perfect. But I think its flaws dont outweigh what I like, so here we are. I would reccomend the game on sale, as it is wont to go because the combat is fast paced and fun. Sometimes theres a little too little ammo, and especially when enemies can disable your darkness powers this makes some areas a bit too hard, but the combat is fun, fast and brutal. The guns are tight, the darkness controls well, and the cell-shaded look is pretty good looking, especially considering this is based off of a comic book, as well as allowing some odd character desgin, like victor. The villians are vile, and normally I would say this is an attempt to make jackie seem like the better guy-and to a large degree thats true, but the game also never really pretends jackies perfect, so its not as obnoxious as it normally is. The story is ok, not great but not awful, and after reading some of the comic book plot summary, the veering away seems like a good choice. Everything is pretty solid, though I think they could have expanded the story and world a bit more and it would've fleshed it out a bit more.  Perhaps they couldve, but this games biggest problem probably had something to do with that-length. The game is just too damn short, and considering I enjoyed that it makes me sad that this was the case. The length is not ok, the FOV needs to be adjustable-this game is best on PC for the number of buttons that you use in combat, and not having a more adjustable FOV is unnacceptable. Also on PC, there are still bugs that don't let you get through certain areas unless you turn on Vsync, which makes the game look blurry if you leave it on by accident. Thats not ok, escpecially in this day and age of patching. The co-op is enjoyable, though the characters are all flat stereotypes, and  I can understand accusations of racism, though  I chalk it up to laziness more than anything. Still its a fun game, and I would highly reccomend it, though it may make you sad when you beat it to realize they may not make another one, considering the silence around it. Fingers crossed they do.

Having just completed the story-line, I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with Pyre.  It's a very story focused game; you find yourself immersed in the world and the lovable team mates you travel with,  which is frequently chopped up by action packed matches which the story is based around known as "Rites" (The Pyre universes own sport, where teams compete for there chance to regain their freedom and return to there homeland, thus relinquishing banishment) which allow for you to experience epic excitement preventing the game from ever becoming stale.  I found myself becoming utterly immersed in the games world, as the game does a great job of merging the playable character with the player which allows you to feel as a genuine part of the world which earnt the game major points from me. There are a wide variety of endings available, all being dependant on the choices made throughout AND how many Rite matches were won during the playthrough; this allows for massive replayability and having the new difficulty mode (Nightwing) being added ensures you get your moneys worth.  When it comes to the games soundtrack I don't think i could compliment the developers enough on selecting perfect songs to fit in with environments, certain characters and dramatic moments in order to alter your mood in such a way that makes every moment epicly unique to one another.  I highly recommend Pyre as you may be able to tell; and contender for best indie game of 2017 in my opinion.

SOMA is a masterpiece.
I won't tell you about the story to avoid any spoilers, as you need to experience it for yourself. To give you only the premise, a routine scan at the university hospital turns into a nightmare when you wake up in a dark, claustrophobic, biomechanical place with no signs of human life around.
The story is the centerpiece of this game, what starts just like another survival horror grows into something much deeper. It is told with much finesse; there are hardly any cutscenes and forcefed dialogues. The most part can be discovered by exploring the surroundings, searching computer terminals, looking at objects.
The game itself is linear, but there are some open ended actions you can peform - they are inserted into the game so delicately that you will only notice afterwards, or perhaps not at all.
These smart storytelling mechanics, letting you unravel the plot at your pace really help you to connect emotionally with the characters, and will leave you with a lot of food for thought.
As for the gameplay it is spot on for a horror game. It is not based solely on jumpscares - although be warned that there are just a couple - but instead is based on a constant feeling of terror and anguish, which masterfully builds up. Just like a good horror movie, you hardly get to see any monster at all. However the fear that a monster may be lurking around the next corner, or behind you, is omnipresent throughout, and will keep you on your nerves.
The actual encounters are terrifying, but smart. Similar to "Alien - Isolation", you'll have to figure out the best way to stay unoticed and tiptoe past the horrors that lurk beneath.
The Graphics, Sound and level design are also excellent. All the way throughout the game (count 10~12h to complete) you will not get bored, with varied realistic environments to keep you enthralled, and scared. Some of the levels actually had me split up between the need to explore more to see if I could find more interesting views and story items, and the urge to get out of there fast or something horrible might happen.
It's a barren and silent world out there, where the scary noises steal most of the show, but the few dialogues are well written, acted and poignant.
Whether you are into psychological horror, sci-fi, or simple thrillseeking, I recommend SOMA wholeheartedly.

Let me start by saying that, at first, I was against buying For Honor because I was expecting bad connections and was sceptical of liking this new title from Ubisoft. Little did I know I would be so surprised.
First and foremost, yes there is connectivity issues. I've met them and it screwed some of my games. Alas, it's not as bad as some people claim it to be. It would help if some players weren't so salty and left mid-game, which triggers a connection synchronization. This, my friend, is the bane you'll encounter (with conquerors and warlords) since everytime it happens, your game can start kicking players out. Hopefully, it doesn't happen that often where I'm from. (Hint: Canada)
If Ubisoft ever decide to go dedicated servers in tandem with a nice content patch, like some characters coming out, I'm sure they could get back and retain way more players while also getting new ones at the same time. Do it, Ubisoft!
The gameplay, one of the most important aspect of most games. I tend to pardon some flaws in games if the gameplay is good. It is the case with this game. If you like pvp and outsmarting (or going ham 4v1) your opponent, I can easily recommend this game. There is a good enough amount of depth in each characters, even the easier ones, that you can master to triumph over your opponent. I've played most of the classes and despite some of them having more love than others (conqueror and warlords...), it is still entirely possible to win and dance on their slain bodies.
Right now, the game is really rewarding defensive play and some equipement bonuses are borderline unfair in a 1v1 scenario (Revenge build, I'm looking at you...), but the devs are pretty open to constructed criticism and are actively making the game better. Let me be clear, the game is still plenty playable and enjoyable right now

The program is pretty basic. I've read other reviews that have said similar things, but I was still pretty neutral until I looked around the program myself. I agree with them. I bought this game for 10 bucks and I don't see how this game is even worth the full $50 it originally sells for.
Character editing - It is extremely limited and not very diverse. There is no adjusting the eye sizes, no making different body types, and no changing skin tones. As far as it goes towards making characters with unique physical features, you're out of luck. No busty heroines, no dudes with scars, no people with rippling muscles... I can't even make my characters look all tanned up from a vacation in Hawaii. All the characters look pretty generic.  A saving point is that 3D mods like hair styles and facial expression can be imported from external sources, but the character-making feature still leaves a lot to be desired.
Character poses - There are somewhat of a variety of making characters pose differently, which is good if you're an artist and want some reference. All the models are set in stone, only allowing you to change angles from which you view them. You can't adjust the poses manually.
2D models - There isn't much to work with. Luckily, images can be imported.
As I said earlier, it can be used for basic things. Maybe it can be used for a project or presentation, maybe it can be used as a ref for drawing. It's not a very compelling program to use otherwise, at least for me.
