Surprised to see a lot of mixed feedback for this game, wanted to throw in my two cents.
Let me start by saying I didn't follow the development. I wasn't on any hype train. Tried the beta, liked it. Bought it. Have enjoyed it very very much, and think I've put a good 40 hours in now.
For me personally, and for the group of friends who bought the game, connectivity has simply not been a big issue. I've been kicked maybe once since I started played, though I do see people drop from games relatively often. It is an issue, but one that doesn't make the game unplayable or significantly diminished in quality.
The community is relatively split between decent people who want to have fun and want you to have fun and the occasional toxic player, tryhard player, etc. This is true of any community that involves a keyboard and directly tests your mettle.
There are a lot of playmodes available at varying sizes. If you want duels, they're there, if you want 4v4 team fights, they're there.
The overall game balance for the vast majority of the player base is good. Some classes are frustrating to play against (I'm looking at you PK!) but almost everything has reasonable counters and reasonable "toolboxes" to draw from. From my understanding, the very best players tend to disturb balance -- at that bracket, warlord, warden, and PK seem to stand out. The chances that your average player who hasn't been a lifelong fighting game player will ecnounter those specific issues are fairly low IMO. If your fundamental skills are superior to your opponent, there is a very good chance you'll succeed regardless of class (Parrying, blocking reliably, GB and GB interrupting, etc).
Matchmaking is fair -- a lot of people really desperately complain about gear score and insta-revenge and, yes, to some degree it can be a problem when any 2v1 flips revenge on. However, revenge is relatively easy to play around with two people (depending on class). Throwing in GB's, shoves, etc, can counter it effectively, as well as dodging and simply blocking your opponent. The core issue with a game like for honor is that even if the enemy team has one player who is signficantly better than your team, things can get very swingy and steam rolly off the back of that one player.
Thus far my review seems fairly washy, I would say -- the game has real issues. However, I am comfortable truly endorsing this game.
The core game mechanics are fantastic. This type of gameplay is vastly different than anything else I've ever experienced and to some degree feels like how a real battle between equally armed and skilled combatants might play out. The environment is a huge part of game play, position matters, the psychology of you and your opponent play a huge role in how your battle and strategy will develop and even though each class has a specific tool kit, there is a lot of variation in playstyle you'll see against varying players (some less than others, unfortunately, for instance, Lawbringers have basically one very effective combo chain and that's about it).
The game needs a lot of balancing, fine-tuning, and generally speaking more of a focus on offense. As it stands, the most effective paths to victory often stem from playing as defensively as possible -- which is a problem for a game based on smashing each other to death.
There is tremendous potential in this title and despite all of the issues I've described (and others I'm sure I've forgotten) I've had a ton of fun with this game. Visually it's amazing, the animations are smooth and perfect and feel visceral. The classes and cultures draw from authentic sources, but aren't afraid to add in dashes of fantasy. The sound design is great, the battlefields are impressive. I'm out of stuff to say.

This is pretty damn good tactical gameplay. From top to bottom that's what the game offers. If you are into turn based tactics and sci-fi? then look no further than to try this game. It's good.

Text:
But its not perfect.
First, the technical side of things the game is lacking a proper full-screen mode, and its video options are woefully inadequate. While performance is fine, its not stellar.
Visually, the game is okay - if you were intrigued by the  tactics or turn based strategy, this isn't the end of the world - its not a focus of the game, but visually.. it did let me down. Both in visual fidelity, but also in overall fluff. Explosions were... ok, not great. ship detail is ... ok, but not great. Quality of the maps is ... adequate, but not great.
So you might think this a bit of a lackluster game then, reading that - but that's far from the truth. because the meat of the game is in the depth and complexity and sheer tactical capabilities of the combat encounters. With various ships costing different number of army points, requiring smart compositions being the very first bit of the entire layer upon layer  of tactical power.
From the way ship movement (and hull strength) works, to the way you can position ships in (somewhat) 3d Space and the way turrets, attach squadrons and everything else works - it creates a methodical, but fast paced (due to timed turn limits in multiplayer) way of having a fantastic battlestar chess... that has explosions everywhere.
Not a perfect game for sure - but one that's damn enjoyable and worth looking into if you like tactics and turn based strategy.

I will make this short:
The game is a Kinetic Novel, which makes it a dialogue heavy book with background und characters drawn out for the reader and some BGM to listen to. The kinetic means there are no choices to be made.
The world is quite interesting, the character are well written and fit the story, the drawings look good and the soundtrack is fitting to the mood. If you are interested in a story about the stock market, high frequency trading and the economy in general you are pretty limited to begin with, but World End Economica delivers an above avarage experience in all points (if you like points you could say everything can be located between 6-8/10) and is a good choice.
Now to the negative part:
There isn't that much here to discuss, but i think the main point is the fact that World End Economica is in fact a kinetic novel, which means that the reader has no influence whatsoever over the direction the story and characters are going. There is still something that makes this a negativ point for me and that is the fact that you can see some scenes where choices would have been in the game and it feels like they cut them out on short notice. While i can understand why they would cut out the choices (choices are a lot of work if you want to implement them in a meaningful way; you have to make sure the choices matter and every branch and decision has weight behind them, which is especially hard when you consider multiple episodes and more and more branching), it is still a bit sad to see them cut the influence a player (instead of a pure reader) could have on the game.
But that is my only gripe with the game and if you are even remotely interested in a beginner friendly introduction to any of the topics mentioned above you should check out this kinetic novel.

While this is it's own game, the basic mechanics of the previous game "Starhammer: The Vanguard Prophecy" are there, with vertical movement now included. Players of that game wkill feel right at home....but wait, there is so, so much more. The price? About $10 too high, as is usual with Slitherine follow-up sequel-esque titles ("Vietnam '65" and "Afghanistan '11" are good examples). Ship models are very reminiscent of the BSG Mod for "Nexus - The Jupiter Incident" which is no bad thing - they were killers, but could only be played in limited skirmish. Leaps and bounds ahead of the "Homeworld 2 & Remastered " Mods if you've played them, frustrated at losing missions for who knows what reason.
This has it all. From ship to fleet management to the tension of wartching if your nukes hit home or a wave of Cylon nukes end the life of your Battlestar at the end of a turn/movement. That's how you play the game. You plan out your ships or your entire fleet's movements, and ghost-like images show where your ships/s will be and allows you to set firing arcs for your hevyiest hitting weapons. Or you might just be manoevering your sjip to evade or pursue. Hit play, and the movement and combat phase takes place and here's the tension. For the few seconds this phase takes place you must wonder did you do right or walk into an ambush? This is strategy, and that it's BSG is icing with candles.
The music, the immersion it's all there.This sill be a top shelf game for BSG fans who have longed for a game such as this for eons. It really is that enticing for a Sci-Fi/BSG/RTS fan....like me.
Recommended, but a lower price would have been appreciated. Oh, and if you haven't picked up the previous game - it's worth it, and cheaper.
8/10
EDIT: A special mention of the Replay Camera. You'll want to watch your replays as it's like watching a battle from the 2004 re-boot of the series. The camera zooms in and out and sways around from ship to ship, just like the battles were shown in that series. It's a real treat!
**One drawback though is the difficulty. It ramps up quickly and to my mind unfairly. Some missions are more puzzles than battles, and it is here that the game falls down. Balance needs to be looked at by the Devs.**

This game WAS good by a good amount, one of the best dinosaur games EVER! But now, as of December 7th, this game has gone from good to trash.  Here are the reasons. But i keep it around for the hope, one day they'll reintroduce sandbox. If you have it, keep it. One day sandbox might come back.
-The Updates
This game gets updated around twice a week, pretty good. But the updates themselves are pretty trash. New dinosaurs are added pretty quickly. But there are a ton of glitches. And the updates barely help. Instead, all the updates do are fix the plants.
-The progression system
This is really hated by many people. The progression system is where you have to earn a number of points as one dinosaur before becoming another. In the Isle, if you're the carnivore, you earn a point a minute. Whether you're sitting in a bush or hunting, one point a minute. And the really good carnivores are over a hundred points. A hundred minutes! If you're a herbivore you can eat special plants that help you progress faster by giving you points. So many play as a plant-eater. And the funny thing is, it's not the progression system idea that's bad, it's how they put it in. The progression system itself is good, surprisingly. Games like Mope.io have a basic progression system, and they are far better than the isle. In The isle, when you lose, all your points are gone. No matter if you played for an hour or 5, you lose them all. In mope, if you lose, you retain some. I could say more, but I have to log off. I'll write a better review after some updates.

I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of this game. I ran into absolutely zero bugs and the program did not so much as stutter once. No lockups or crashes ever. Runs like butter even on highest settings on my PC and my PC is about 5 years or older. I do run a gtx 760 gpu.
Mechanics are solid in the game and controls are pretty good. It is a bit awkward walking around when you are taking shelter behind walls but ive had worse. Graphics and sound are great IMO. You can really use the sound of the soldiers voices to help locate where they are. I am running dolby 5.1 and the surround sound works really well. I bought the game for the 1 player and the campaign is very good and challenging with plenty of levels of difficulty to accomodate all players. The DLCs are really hard. Ive finished all but the Assasinate Hitler mission and will be doing that next.
Stealth is pretty hard in the game since you really have to duck down right away after you shoot a round otherwise all of the enemy on the map seem to know where you are. Stealth can be pulled off during times when there are loud noises like thunder and bombs dropping, the sounds mask your shot so that is a lot of fun to time. The AI of the soldiers can be really good at times and other times not so much. I did discover that if you just injure a soldier when you snipe him that his mates will try to come to his aid and carry him off and then you can pick them off too. This aspect of the game reminds me of the scene from "Full Metal Jacket" and is a nice feature for picking off multiple enemies. Another cool feature is the ballistics of the bullets and how if you get lucky you can pick off two guys with one shot. If you pick at a group of soldiers clustered closely together you may hit one target and then the soldier behind him may catch the bullet after it passed through the other man.
I also bought the zombie trilogy and will be moving on to that next. I am getting many hours of play out of this. I have 18 hours in the game now and havent done the Hitler mission yet. The hours are all in 1 player. Got the game on sale so it was well worth the cost, great deal!

Overview:
how do you Do It (actual capitalization) is a "game" that involves a girl trying to figure sex out on her own by removing the clothes from a male and female doll, and repeatedly mashing the dolls together while her mother is out of the house.  There's no other game play.  Same scene of the girl's mother leaving the house, then controling the movement and rotation of the two dolls, and the scene ends with the girl hiding the dolls from her returning mother and a counter as to how many times the dolls may have "did sex."  I may have given up too soon, but I couldn't even have the girl get caught.
Graphics and sound:
This is a free to play game, so what exactly are you expecting?
Positives:
If WTF kinda humor is your kinda humor, then there's a chance you may enjoy this game.  I was brought up on crude sexual humor encountered in the schlock movies shown on USA Up All Night back in the early 1990's, but even the humor value this game immediately lost it's value with me.
Negatives:
There's virtually no gameplay to speak of, and you have to use the keyboard.  But don't fret.  Unless you're the same age as the girl in this game, you likely won't find yourself needing to use one of your hands to touch yourself as you mash the two naked dolls together in an attempt to have them possibly do it.
Conclusion:  It's like what Rowan Atkinson said in Blackadder's Christmas Carrol:  One massively disappointing bang, and the whole novelty quickly wears off...  Only there wasn't much of a "bang" between the two dolls, the girl mashing the dolls together has the same (childhood sexuality) thoughts every single time, and yet never seems to wonder what's between a boy's legs.  This game may be perfect for people who live in households that consider homosexuality wrong, because there's only one male and one female doll, and with no ability to have the girl try and mash two naked dolls of the same gender together.  And since there's only two dolls, both of them are white, which means no ability to form interracial couples.  If you want sexual encounters from a child's perspective, your best bet is to look for the Alter Ego games outside of Steam.  Even while those two are text based, at least you'll get more amusement from it's portrayal of childhood sexuality.

I found this program disappointing. Like many others have said, character creation is painfully limited. The poses are fairly wooden, and while there is a large variety of stock manga expressions, there isn't true flexibility in that either. The various elements (e.g. backgrounds, accessories) tend not to match the style of the characters. I had the feeling of trying to create art using clip-art. The colour filters are also limited. Either one would need to be skilled in creating one's own content, or rely heavily on DLC or CC - and I am not inclined to go searching for that when the base program has so little to offer already.
What you CAN use this program for, I imagine, would be as a base for your own art, to divide pages into panels and add effects (e.g. drama lines) and speech bubbles to.
However, if you have any artistic ability at all, skip this program and draw your own manga/comic. It will look more consistent and be far more rewarding and less frustrating. Whatever you do, don't get it at full price.

This game, Unexpected Day, was not that bad of a game. It did have bad things about it, but also good things about it. The game itself wasn't that clear in what was happening, or where you needed to go. It was a very unique game, and had an interesting story mechanic.
So, I am going to start off with a bad point in the game, but the game itself wasn't bad. The game was not clear in where you needed to go, and what you needed to do, outside of providing onscreen cues. Often when playing this game I had to take a few tries to figure out what it was expecting me to do, and sometimes these actions were a bit unstable, for example the swing. And it was not always clear that you had to do something, like jump on rocks, because they had no distinct outline. The goal was quite, as you could say, unexpected. One more thing about the game that wasn't fantastic was that you cannot save, or take screenshots. But the game is short enough that saving is not relevant.
This was a very unique game. I really enjoy games that don't conform to the norm of video games. This game was unqiue in many aspects, it had minimal controls, which didn't at all feel trapping. It had a very surreal setting, which is always refreashing for video games. The game itself felt like I was watching a movie, not because it didn't let me play, but it was quite theatrical in its scene transitions, often fading out and fading in, as well as automatically controlling certain actions sometimes. This game achieved a feeling of being dreamlike very well in its uniqueness.
The game used no words as such, instead it told the story through visuals (and if there was voice acting, I could not hear it), the story of what is actually happening can be read in the game's blurb on its Steam Store Page, but it is much nicer to figure it out yourself. The game's blocky graphics did not do anything to hinder this visual storytelling, no object was too blocky to see what object it was. The game itself is quite short, but enjoyable. If however you measure the value of the game by time taken to play, and not enjoyablility, you may think this game too short. The story itself is quite good, very abstract.
Overall this game is a nice little quirky gem for anyone who wants to quickly experience a unique game and enjoy some unconventional storyline.

In addition to the single player part, it also has got a "multiplayer" part called "Vendettas". It's merely one campaign consisting of five or six missions which can be played either solo or with up to three other players. Outside of that it also has got some "Hit List" missions which can be played solo or with others as well.
By completing the main portion of the game, you unlock "New Game+" which allows the player keeping all powers from previous playthrough and to choose which chapter to begin from (only want to play the end boss battle? Sure thing). I think that's pretty nice.
All in all, I really liked "The Darkness 2" and I'm hoping for a third installment in this series. If you like FPS games with a twist, then buy it whenever you have a chance of doing so.

SOMA had me asking questions from the beginning, and 48 hours after finishing the game I still haven't stopped. Thinking about the game during and after playing, for me, was the hallmark of a great game. I'm sure my friends and family have grown tired of me filling them in on the story and asking questions about what it all meant!
I would thoroughly recommend the game. It confronted ideas of existence, AI and personhood, causing me many hours of philosophical debate internally and with others, in an engaging and challenging manner. There are many threads on Steam and Reddit going into these at great length, if you are interested I would advise you look them up! The characterisation of NPCs and the player through these ideas is well handled and believable (though sometimes Simon comes across a bit naive I feel). The voice acting to back this up I also felt was top-notch, along with a very nice soundtrack/environmental sound stage.
Graphically the game looked fantastic. Water effects were obviously key and handled very well, including rarely used underwater effects (such as blurring at extreme water pressures) that were very nice indeed. Game mechanics were good as per usual with Frictional's efforts, rewarding exploration with detailed information and useful advice.
The monsters are the main sticking point for some. Yes I agree that they felt, at times, like they had been added because it's Frictional's style and that it added little to some points in the story. Overall however, I felt that the tension generated from the encounters was a benefit to the story arc and made the environment feel a bit more alive and oppressive.
TL;DR: Recommended game. Great story, challenging ideas, nice graphics and sound to go with. Short but sweet and wish there were more out there like it!

This was the mmo that I played for the longest time; it's incredibly fun (although frustrating sometimes), but the community always kept me playing. Cons:

Comipo is a program you're either going to get a lot of use out or nothing at all, depending on what you think you're going to get out of it. Since the reviews for this program are all over the place, I thought I'd honestly write about what you can and can't do with it so you can realistically decide if it's any use to you or not.
At its very core, Comipo is a very simplified drag and drop comic creator, letting you place 3D models of characters into various situations. The interface is actually very easy to learn, and every object is loaded into a separate layer in each panel like Photoshop or something. If you've ever used the Mac application Comic Life, it's a very similar experience, as you can pretty quickly make a simple comic using only your mouse (save for a keyboard for writing in text balloons).
The main problems most people have with the program are mostly focused on the limited resources Comipo offers. By default, Comipo only has 4 characters you can use in the comics (1 male and 1 female character in two different outfits each). While you can change a fair amount of features on each character (changing the outfit design, hair, coloring, etc) and save them for later, you're definitely going to have a hard time differentiating from everybody if you plan on using multiple characters in a comic, mostly because everybody is based on the same character builds. Comipo does have the ability to import 2D images and 3d models, and while most images import without any issue, I never managed to make 3d models import correctly, as they used a very specific filetype and usually come out incomplete anyways.
The limitations also spread to what the characters themselves can do as well, as while most characters have a pretty good selection of poses (with the ability to tweak the hands and head slightly with each one), odds are pretty good you'll have to make compromises in your comics. A lot of the poses are really focused on a school and general conversation settings with only a few "action" poses, so the chance of you making any sort of fight scene is near-impossible.
So what is Comipo actually good for with its limitations? Well, if you just want to make a silly comic where some characters talk or argue and maybe publish it for fun on your blog or twitter, this is honestly a fun and simple program to use and you really can't go wrong with it (you can also export at absurdly high resolutions, eg bigger than 5k per panel). If you want to make any sort of serious comic, you really shouldn't bother, because the whole comic will feel artificial with the built-in assets and the limitations in the program will probably frustrate you.
If you're still not sure about Comipo, they placed a demo on their website you can try for yourself. It's not listed on Steam, and I can't link it here because Steam gets mad at you for putting links in reviews, so just google "comipo demo"

Apparently there are a number of reviews from people who either don't understand the purpose of Comipo or just want to troll. I thought I would provide a review from a professional. I bought Comipo on sale to play around with it, to see what its capabilities were. I am an artist, so I don't strictly need Comipo to create my work, unlike some. But I think that many people will probably really love Comipo, and it will allow them to bring their ideas to life. It is not, however, a software for anyone and everyone.
Comipo comes with a good number of resources, and it's easy enough to learn the basics. Drag and drop, click and move -- all these things should be pretty familiar to anyone who uses a computer regularly. A great feature, which is easy to use, allows the user to import photographs and other materials to use in the program, making it very easy to accommodate all kinds of settings and situations.
Most all of Comipo is highly intuitive and easy to figure out, and if you're willing to experiment a little, you'll probably be delighted by the sheer amount of variety possible with it. Yes, you are limited to the options you're given, but there are just so many combinations and possibilities that I would think most users who understand what the program is for will be pleased.
My only real concern is that there is not a huge amount of variety in the models, so there's a kind of youthful, school-age appearance that most every character will have, although it is possible to add age lines and such. There are also different characters in the DLC packs that make it possible to have very different-looking characters, so even that concern is dealt with at least to some extent. There are some features and aspects of the program that are less than intuitive, but these are mainly going to be more advanced ones I think, so it would be a more experienced user who will be able to figure it out.
Overall, however, Comipo is an excellent program for what it offers, and it has a thriving and supportive community full of original assets just for the program! It's possible to create a huge variety of comics and tell your story. As a creator, I find it really exciting and fun to play around with, but I can imagine too that if you are someone who loves to write and create stories but cannot draw, Comipo will be a godsend. You may have to be a little imaginative and work within some limitations, but the potential for you to realise with Comipo is massive. It's huge. There's so much you can do with it.
To address the common complaints from some: no, it's not going to just magically generate your comic for you. There is some work required, but Comipo all but hands everything to you on a silver platter. You basically are a few clicks and some typing away from a perfectly good comic.
Yes, there are limitations in variety. Yes, you have to work within the choices you are given by the program. Every kind of program, and every kind of creative project for that matter, has boundaries that must be creatively addressed. However, for what it is, it's amazing. I get the impression the Comipo crew are a small group of dedicated people with a passion for creation that they want to share with others. The community certainly supports this feeling.
So if you are a mature creator who wants to put your imagination into realising your stories, give Comipo a try. If you can look at the different items, characters, and tools presented and find your imagination bursting with possibilities, Comipo is definitely for you. It reminds me of the game/early machinima software The Movies, and all of the exciting things that were possible with it, from original creations of the community to the resources provided by the game itself, or the various versions of RPG Maker that have existed through the years.
If, however, you expect effortless realisation of your whims, this isn't for you. If you aren't going to put in anything, you certainly aren't going to get anything out of it. It's the easiest and most accessible software it can be, and it has the capability to do phenomenal things. For that, I recommend it to people who really want to create but don't have the ability to draw. Comipo is for you.
As a side note: I see so many writers in need of an artist to help them create their dream comic story, but few serious artists have the time or inclination, and artists who aren't serious tend not to stick with projects. Most of the time, these writers can't afford a decent or fair pay for their artists, and we artists have to make a living. Comipo can help so many of these writers to show that they can write, and well, and it can help them to make a real comic and see their vision become reality. Because of that, I wholeheartedly endorse Comipo.

Written by Isuna Hasekura - best known for his
series -
is a slow progressing three part visual novel with a heavy hit on one's psyche, sense of justice and emotional durability. This first episode and the second one following are currently accessible for the community, and it is announced that with the translation complete, we can see the third episode here any day now.
In this elaborate science fiction/economic thriller, it's been 16 years since the mankind embraced a new frontier and built a colony on the moon. That colony declared its independence to take on to become the financial capital of humanity. Kawaura Yoshiharu - a young boy who was born on the moon and never has seen the earth - ventures out to follow a big dream: gathering enough capital fund to go out and establish a new frontier for the mankind: Mars. For the purpose of gathering enough money, he runs away from his home and lower-mid class life style; and starts margin trading in stock market. As he goes after this own dream, his life crosses with a bunch of others, making him a witness to both the hollow and the ugly side of any glory. Will the boy who is already living on the moon be able to reach Mars one day?
This first chapter of
narrates Haru's backstory by introducing the fundamental structure for a powerful metropolis set on the moon, and not so prosperous lives of other individuals that Haru grows attached to as a powerful contrast to the seemingly flawless wealth of the setting. The setting is unique, and the storyline - even though dreadfully slow building at the start - grows to become a marvelous thriller that will present you a sleepless night. The narrative is heavily relied on financial terms and a bit hard to follow at times, so I advise taking time to read slowly. Considering it is a kinetic visual novel with no actual participation from the player, this is most certainly not a "one sit to go" story. Threat it like an anime series that you'd be excited to see the next chapter of.
As a visual novel, the display is decent enough. While panoramic art are various and breathtaking, character design and art are somewhat mediocre. For a visual novel with this size and playtime, I'd expect a certain variety with CGs and artworks, yet it feels like there was a shortcoming about that department. The music is fittingly moody/exciting at every turn though and establishes a successful tone for the narrative.
I cannot recommend this first chapter to everyone, with its slow progression and heavily dramatic plotline structure - but for the one's that would be interested with a plot driven drama on a mid-sci-fi setting, this first episode was a very well-done choice. You'll start reading it lazily and hope that something exciting would soon happen for the first half; and then suddenly you cannot stop reading by the point that you are halfway done. It is a heart-wrecking experience.

Okay so, after writing the review I left below, I sort of felt like a wuss for backing down, especially since I tend to think I never like to back down for a challenge. So after a restful night after writing said review, I loaded up Pyre again and continued on. I don't know what the hell happened, but during the next rite, everything clicked. The cumbersome controls suddenly all resonated with each finger press, and I was able to actually outsmart the A.I by doing certain maneuvers, even on hard mode (the biggest reason for my negative review below.)
"Wow gi99les, it took you 4-5 hours to get used to the controls?"
Yes. Yes it did. Isometric RPG's (Supergiant's Forte) are not a genre I play very often. Pyre originally frustrated me because I felt that I was being left in the dust because I could not get used to the controls well enough to combat the A.I.
So basically, my point is: to anyone with my past predicament, PLEASE continue on. You WILL get used to the controls, and you will then FULLY appreciate the enjoyment that is to be gotten out of Pyre.
Pyre is probably not my favorite Supergiant game (It's REALLY hard to beat Transistor in my eyes,) but It is surely one of the most unique games I have EVER played. This being a Supergiant game, I already knew the music and storytelling aspects would be top notch, and I was right on the money. The story is incredibly well written, having different scenarios written for the different choices you make, making you feel the weight of your decisions. The Rites take a little while to get used to, but once you do, you'll feel unstoppable, even with 12 Titan Stars enabled (This games version of the difficulty modifiers that Supergiant are known for putting in their games.)
Basically, don't be a fool like I was, and possibly miss one of Supergiants most ambitious projects to date. They have released another masterpiece to their portfolio and I will ambitiously await their next game with wallets at the ready.
ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW (For reference)
____________________________________
I WANT TO REITERATE THAT MY REVIEW IS BASED ON THE EXPECTATION OF THE HARD MODE DIFFICULTY FOR NEW PLAYERS. IF YOU PLAY PYRE ON NORMAL OR EASY, YOU ARE PROBABLY NOT GOING TO EXPERIENCE THE SAME GRIEVANCES I DETAIL BELOW.
I. Love. Supergiant. I have 23/24 of the achievements from Bastion, and all the achievements from Transistor. It is clear from the start that Supergiant put a lot of love and care into the creation of Pyre, and the storytelling and artwork are on a whole nother level of engagement and beauty, but what ruins Pyre for me is the Rites (The main gameplay aspect of Pyre.)
I want to clarify that I usually play games on the hardest difficulty possible whenever I get the opportunity, so I set it to Hard. It just seems as I progress through the story that the A.I gets cheaper and more strategic while the player struggles to keep up with everything going onscreen. The story progresses whether you win or lose, but if you hate losing, I feel that Pyre will frustrate you to levels you didn't even know you were capable of. I understand you're really not supposed to win them all, but the difficulty curve RAMPS UP TOO QUICKLY from rite to rite. The Rite with Udmildhe nearly made me shatter my desk in half, and that's only 10~% of the game! If this early on I'm getting schooled by the AI, then I honestly do not want to progress through the rest of it.
You can argue that the hard mode is for when you beat the game on the easier difficulty and "master" the game so to speak, but If so, then why didn't Supergiant implement the NG+ mechanic from Bastion and Transistor? Why allow us to play on the hardest difficulty if the AI is just going to abuse the sensory overload players get from trying to keep track? I love Pyre's world, but as a game, I cannot recommend it.

One warning, this is not really a "game", rather it is a kinetic novel, which means it is all text (no choices) accompanied by character images, CGs, and music.  If you like visual novels you may like this game if you are okay with not having any choices.
As for the actual game, it's worth noting that playing just this part alone will probably leave you disappointed.  Part 2 of this series is already available on Steam and Part 3 is supposed to be coming....sometime.  On its own, this is still a great story that is full of detail.  The characters don't seem great at first, but they get more interesting as the story goes on.
The action in this novel all revolves around the trading of stocks.  You will discover just how exciting this can be (but so risky that it didn't really encourage me to want to invest, haha).  If you like Spice and Wolf, you will probably like this.  If you don't like Spice and Wolf or have no idea what that even is, you will like this if you like character-driven stories where the action revolves around principles of economics or the stock market.  Some of it can get pretty meaty, so if you are the intellectual type it will probably be pretty satisfying.
Some of the technical aspects of this novel are where it suffers.  The music, while nice, often does not loop well.  A track will be over and suddenly restart instead of having a seamless loop like most video game music.  Also, when a character expression changes in the middle of a sentence, the text briefly disappears and then reappears, like it would when advancing to the next screen, but this is really annoying when it happens right in the middle of a sentence and is quite jarring.  There were some typos and grammatical errors, but I would say the amount of these is pretty standard for most translated visual novels.

TL;DR -  About 10 dollars too high, if you love BSG/Turn-based (WEGO) (preferably both, b ut either or) - then this is a game you should get.
Pros:
- You feel like you're in the BSG universe.
- Actions have consequences, you can lose ships - even if you are in a situation you cant lose
- 6 directions versus 4. Most games allow you 4 directions (forward, back, left right) - BSG gives you six (up, Down, Forward, Back, Left, Right) to fight from. This adds a dynamic that makes it a lot of fun.
- First Cylon war - This does have a war feel to it, it can get desperate.
Cons:
- Missing that 'extra' to it. Story, Outside combat feel, characters, et. al. feel unpolished. This gives it a 'beta copy' feel.
- About 10 dollars to high given its lack of the extras, in my opinion (though I would suggest every BSG or Turnbased/WeGo fan get it)
- Bugs: While rare, you will get the random bug. Nothing game breaking.. but things that you know aren't supposed to be there. A ship randomly floats in a direction, you FTL in and the ship is inverted for a moment.. etc.
- Story: I put this at the start, but don't buy it for the story. I wish I could say the opposite, but buy it to be in BSG if that's your flavor.
This is a game that I really do enjoy. The game has a gritty feel to it, no matter what level you are at - or what ships you have - it is quite possible to lose them. There are tactics that do help gaurantee a win, but there is always a real risk of ships being lost. The game really excells in its combat piece. You can move in six directions (Up, Down, Left, Right, Forward, Back). This adds a great element to it, and also a difficulty as you can have ships run into eachother from both sides.
Outside of combat, everything else is manegable. So it's turn based, you can research ships and weapons, you can build ships and weapons, and you move your forces around a map.  There is nothing spectacular about this and what it does have feels like battlestar galactica - so its passeable.
While I am a youtuber as well (under the Lore Reloaded brand) - I do watch other youtubers and would agree with Enter Elysium's opinion that this game would be considered a 'Good Beta'. What I mean by that is that it is really well done, the game as sold will do it for you if you are a BSG/Turnbased fan. But it's missing the little things. There are nit picks here and there, and a few things that could be explained better in a tutorial. Additionally, the story could use some work. They put together a game that works well as a Battle simulator, but didn't take just the little bit of extra time to nail everything else down.
Also, the price is, for me, about 10 dollars to high. I think it's a solid 30 dollar game. 40 dollars seems a bit stout with out all of the little things. It's like buying a car at the standard price, but the radio isn't installed. Still, I would personally pay the 10 dollars more because I love strategy and I love BSG. If you are the same, I suggest you get it.
If you are on the fence? Might wait for a steam sale. Either way, this ultimately should be in your library.

If you are a BSG fan of the 2000's series then you are going to have a good time.
A nice turn based strategy game in on of my favorite sf universe.
The music, the ships, just perfect.
Combat is turn based and you can position your ships in the direction and height of your choosing depending on your ships current heading and speed. And be careful of other ships because ramming another ship does great damage, for instance a jupiter class battlestar will barely survive an impact of an cylon carrier (as i found out the hard way).
Combat its done by planning your moves and then press play, no direct involment during the combat phase. So if you dont plan your moves accordingly, you are going to have a bad time.
Be carefull of hacking attacks as these can cripple your ships, best way to deal with that is to blow the offending ship into spacedust. After the battle you can get a replay with nice BSG style camera work.
After the battle you are brought to the strategic map where you have an overview of colonial space where you can plan your next move and build new ships etc.
The graphics are decent but the skybox could use a higher resolution texture, this is especialy appearant during replays when the camera is zooming in on vessels.
I love the working turrets and the vipers launching from their tubes.
TL; DR
Pro
- Battlestars light up space with flak
- Music you come to expect from BSG 2000's
- Cool ships that have working turrets
- Ships are carried over to the next mission (so dont break them)
- You decide fleet makeup.
- Combat can be challenging.
- Game itself not demanding, could play on potato.
Con
- Skybox could be of higher resolution.
- Currently still some bugs but nothing gamebreaking that i know of.
- Why are you still reading this, aren't you a BSG fan?

I'd say this game is far from perfect, right off the bat. There are netcode issues and the game still isn't fully optimized (my FPS goes to hell on two maps in particular, but stays at a stable 60-70 on every other).
Unlike other FTP games, the pay-for weaponry isn't any better than the ones you can earn, aside from perhaps one slightly useful stat which, if you're lucky, you can get when you upgrade the normal variant, and aren't stuck with two other semi-useless traits (let's face it, reliability isn't all that useful as of right now).
I'm on the same train of thought as everyone else in one aspect: give me freemode! But unlike others, I can wait. I'd rather they release a more whole product than a completely unfinished version of it, as people nowadays are as likely to flock away from an unfinished product in beta as they are in full release.
In short, if you don't mind an arena-like shooter with somewhat realistic mechanics and some technical issues, I'd recommend this. If you are having problems dying to SMGs or the like (as of 2.7), I recommend coming back with the next update, where every faction and several guns are being rebalanced.
Edit as of 2.8: Okay, so 2.8 hit and the game has been rebalanced. I see far more variety of weapons in the field, and that is fantastic; no more is the rifle-SMG combo dominating til super high tiers. Now I see shotguns, SMGs, rifles, assault rifles, etc - all of them and beyond. But, not all is sunshine and rainbows.
North American servers are still MIA, and as a North American player, I'm one of those suffering from it. Not to mention hit detection and the like. Still, I can keep my vote positive if only due to my only like of the game - but everyone should take it with a slight grain of salt at this point in time.

If you're looking for easy Steam achievements, then 'Ambre' is the way to go. It's a short story, not a game; there aren't any choices to make, there is nothing to customise, and the story can be completed quickly (I completed it in under an hour). If you really want, you can just keep hitting the spacebar to finish the game even quicker.
Ambre suggests psychological themes but doesn't actually address them in a deep or meaningful way. The concept is fine, but the delivery and length [of the story] fall short of a rich story and substance. The writing style is simplistic and you may find yourself rushing through the story, as I did. The dialogue, especially before the climax of the story, had me cringing a lot. It's only later that I understood why the story was written in this way; I don't think it's an accident or the product of an inexperienced author. Having said that, there are better ways of spending an hour of your time.
Spoiler ahead:
In a nutshell, Ambre is about mental illness and the social pressures of society, which affect women. Other media cover these aspects in a better way.

has made big promises, and while the ideas that have been put forth are certainly appealing, the development of the game has given me little faith that much of the promised content will even be implemented, let alone implemented well. Many of the development team’s planned features have yet to be incorporated into the game, and the content already in the game leaves much to be desired. While I understand that
is an Early Access title, I cannot recommend the game at this point in time.
The gameplay has always been barebones, and development has not added much to make it exciting. While new dinosaurs are released often, the excitement wears off quickly, as they don’t offer anything new or exciting in terms of gameplay. Dinosaurs are differentiated by basic stats more than anything, not unique abilities. This may change in the future if other factions are added and the current roster of playable creatures is given more unique abilities, but considering the incredibly slow development process, I can't say that I'm confident these steps will be taken any time soon. The tedium of playing turns to frustration thanks to the frankly awful networking, both in official and community-owned servers. I’ve never experienced such severe lag so frequently in a game. Rubber-banding and freezing were frequent as to render the game unplayable, even if I picked the geographically closest server possible. A dinosaur that should have taken one or two bites to kill often took a dozen due to the lag.
The progression system as it is now discourages active gameplay, as the risk of being found out and losing hours of progress is too high for many players to stomach. Players can progress to the highest tiers simply by filling up on food and water and waiting, and, as of the last time I played, hunger and thirst were so forgiving that I had simply alt-tabbed out of the game while sitting in bushes for long periods of time before progressing. This made the already barren official maps even lonelier as players hid away out of sight for hours on end in order to reduce their risk of dying and losing progress. Workshop maps may help some of the problems that come with such large maps and low population densities, but it doesn't help the core issue of the game not providing enough incentives for people to play actively.
For reference, I am running all graphics on the highest possible settings. Framerates are smooth for the most part. Overall, the game looks good, though not phenomenal. The game does cause my graphics card to run hot, which most other games, even graphically intensive and beautiful games, do not do. Other players I have spoken with regarding performance reported similar problems.
As of posting, the available map is incredibly large. From what I saw of Dondi’s streams, the sheer size of the map seemed to be a bragging point, with little consideration, from what I’ve seen, for the effects on gameplay. It seemed as if he wanted the map to be huge for its own sake. The map, from the time I’ve given exploring it, was lacking in diversity. There were few landmarks and features that I could recognize and use to navigate. Whenever players congregate, it’s typically around a few specific lakes. All the large map size seems to do is make the travel to these hotspots more tedious. It’s my understanding that the developers intend to add a smaller map, more landmarks, and more biomes, so the current lack of diversity in the map design may be remedied in the future. Update: the addition of a Steam Workshop can help tremendously, as players are now more free to play in a setting better tailored to their wants. The return of region 2 is also a positive change, in my opinion, as it was a smaller map than the map I had previously played on and had more noticeable landmarks.
The dinosaurs themselves are great. Most of them are aesthetically pleasing, and it is clear that great attention to detail was put into their design. The animations, textures, anatomy, and sounds are all top-notch in my opinion.
For some players, an enjoyable Early Access experience entails actively taking part in development and feedback. For such buyers, satisfaction comes from putting forth valuable feedback, seeing that feedback implemented, and fostering a positive relationship with the developers and the community. For such players,
will probably come as a disappointment. Feedback is frequently met with hostility, whether from the community or the developers themselves. The developers often mock the game’s players, whether on the Steam forum, Twitch, or on their Discord server. I’ve seen developers post screenshot after screenshot of Steam posts they considered “stupid” without even editing out the poster’s name or avatar, ban players for minor – or even merely perceived – infractions, rant about specific players on their streams, incite the community to grief a player-owned server, participate in griefing themselves by purposely breaking server owners' rules and spawning overpowered dinosaurs that were inaccessible to other players, and so on.
The development of the game has not instilled confidence that it will appreciably improve in the foreseeable future. The development team clearly had a lot of ideas that they wanted to include in the game, such as humans, cannibals, strains, and so on, but it still feels as if there's little direction to the game's development, and whatever development is taking place has been slow. Numerous playable dinosaurs have been released, but the core gameplay hasn't improved substantially despite the years this game has spent in development.
As far as I understand, a new survival game mode is being worked on that will restrict playable creatures to a smaller number in order to focus on making these playable characters a unique experience. Again, as far as I understand, the progression game mode is being scrapped in favor of this survival game mode. It does make me wonder why this mode hadn't been talked about much earlier and why such a significant amount of development time had been put into the progression game mode, especially considering the scope of the game as originally planned was far more ambitious than most, if any, AAA teams would consider taking on. Examples such as this only lead me to believe that the development team can't set realistic goals for themselves.
I bought the game in March 2016, and while it has changed, it doesn’t feel like it’s changed much, and the changes that have been made haven’t pushed the game into a positive direction. Many of the promised large features such as playable humans have yet to be added, and the game at its core remains a large cast of dinosaurs with some slight variations roaming around mindlessly or sitting in a large, lifeless map, the same as it was when I bought it. The changes that have been made haven’t really refreshed the experience, and considering this, the pace of development, and the developers' treatment of their own players, I would strongly recommend against purchasing this game at this point in time.

Taking a break from austrian castles and industrial age cities, Frictional games have jumped to the future in their continuation of the true horror genre in Soma. A game set in the 2100's when mankind has all but been wiped out and you play as Simon Jarett a man from another time and no less confused to his current situation leagues under the sea inside an experimental marine facility known as Pathos II.
In the previous titles I have had to meticulously ration out supplies to survive and when all else failed run for the hills, the Amnesia games never wanted for suspense or atmosphere and the same can be said for Soma, straight off the bat I cautiously examined anything and everything to get a better understanding of my locale which wasn't difficult as yet again clues, logs, and backstory was weaved into the very level design but as I better understood my surroundings the ambient sounds around me did a fantastic job in making me feel apprehensive, in constant danger and that i wasn't alone.
As with the second Amnesia the control scheme and UI is intuitve and intergrated into the game rather than displayed on a HUD as with most titles, which in my opinion allows the player to become more absorbed into the world around them, unlike the Amnesia games however your journey through the bowels of Pathos will not just be filled with monsters of varying design looking to gank you, your character Simon is fully voiced and will communicate and comment about his situation with others as well as himself which makes me feel like im controlling a person and not a robot.. Ahem.
Anyway graphics having continually evolved since the last game, Soma in high doesn't disappoint I myself risked life and limb to take screenshots whenever the oppurtunity presented itself as the possibility of roaming the sea bed doesn't come about very often in games except for Bioshock of course.
At any rate between the always pervasive ambient sound and music to the gloomy but sharp graphics and lighting you will never be happier to be running and hiding at the bottom of the sea from violent monsters looking to tear you a new one.

A brutal FPS with a few psychological thriller elements, the Darkness II is not for the faint of heart. The game puts you in the shoes of tormented mob boss Jackie Estacado, hereditary host of the malevolent supernatural being known only as the Darkness. Struggling to keep the evil contained within him, Jackie is pushed to his breaking point by a powerful organization interested in drawing that evil out. And so the game beings.
With the Darkness unleashed Jackie is a force to be reckoned with. The Darkness is extremely powerful and dispatches of enemies in the cruelest and most horrifying ways imaginable, while at the same time nourishing Jackie and keeping him alive. The Darkness fears only one thing, the light. So whenever you see a source of light, you should destroy it right away. But with all his power Jackie's fragile state of mind can't take the stress and soon he finds himself unable to tell reality from hallucinations and that is the highpoint of the game's narrative. Is any of this even happening? Is there really a Darkness? Yes the story is gripping and very very interesting indeed.
So highly recommended? Well, no. Regardless of how great a story it tries to tell, as a game it could still be much better. At its core this is an FPS, but despite Jackie's outlandish abilities it is still too limited. All you can do is stand in the middle of a dozen enemies and shoot them or use the darkness to destroy them. That is all, no real tactics, no sneaking, nothing. After a while it just get tedious. Thankfully the game is very short, so at least you won't notice this as much. But still with a story as interesting, I wish they had paid some more attention to the game itself.
I will still recommend this game. If only for the narrative and the atmosphere it creates. But this is a weak recommendation.

I have held off writing this review for a variety of reason, most of which I will address but I want to begin by saying that at its core, Nether is a fun game. A vast, beautiful world that although seemingly barren is jammed full of things to explore. The possibility for looting is everywhere and the nether that inhabit the city make for fun opponents if not the most challenging (this is of course after getting a few guns, otherwise you’re in for a rough time).
By far the biggest impact of the game comes from the player base and how you come to interact with it. I started off by reading a bit and prepared for the usual spawn campers that inhabit all survival games. The first 5 hours of gameplay were terrible and I am sorry but there is no other way to put it. A combination of the fore mentioned spawn campers and lack of gear resulted in countless deaths for no gain. Eventually though you will survive enough runs between safe zones to get a small stockpile of weapons and ammo which gives you a few options, continue exploring deeper into the city, collecting as you go or become that which is hated by entering the pseudo pvp. I call it that because there is no give or take by investing in the melee tree, you have a gun or you die and even then you will still die but only to other gun holders. Sadly this game seems to center too much on murdering other players for their stuff. I am about 20 hours into the game and although there are servers where people will work together and explore this possibly great game, for the most part it’s just people who get their rocks off by spawn camping. I have read that a pve environment may be in the works but unless the AI is improved then that will be the ultimate care bear of this game (making courier package runs is reasonably easy already minus the players that snipe everyone entering or leaving a safe zone).
So the long and short of my review comes to this, Nether is a fantastic idea that with enough time and tweaking could have been the fallout mmo that some gamers like myself have been waiting for, but  a combination of in-game bugs which ranged from my flashlight never turning on to ramps and platforms not actually being between building so all you get is a nice 50 foot death fall, as well as a dimwitted AI and terrible player base which are trapped in the "I am l33t you are n00b" mentality ruin this game for continued play.
As I said before I held off reviewing this because I wanted very much to enjoy it with seemingly small problems ruining my experience. Unfortunately the slow development cycle, player base, and almost laughable enemy AI have finally pushed the game past the point of enjoyment. It is a chore to find playable servers with minimal bugs and players that have more social skills than road kill. I wish the developers the best because there is a solid idea here but it needs a lot of work.

Let me start off by saying this: I played through Soma once via a non-Steam copy, then bought it on Steam because I wanted to show my support for Frictional Games and hopefully fund more games like this.
If you're a fan of the first Amnesia, of System Shock 2, or of story driven games with philosophical elements, you owe it to yourself to check out this game.
Set in an underwater facility that is equal parts BioShock and System Shock 2, filled with audio logs and ghostly remnants of those who came before you, one might be forgiven for thinking that Soma is a horror game; It's really not. Soma is a psychological thriller, closer to Silent Hill 2. Except in Soma, there is no combat. Like Frictional's previous game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you are expected to hide from the various monsters. The monster encounters, however, are not numerous - though there's just enough of them to keep you on your toes and wary. Instead, the game's main focus is on exploration, story, atmosphere, and a smattering of puzzle solving.
I don't want to even outline Soma's overarching themes because I believe that they are much more interesting to discover organically as you play the game. But the story is one that will stick with you long after the last cutscene plays, leaving you pondering its implications and the questions that it raised. Soma is not innovative, and it's not particularly scary (though it can definitely be tense at times), but if you're a fan of moody, psychological, mildly philosophical games, it is absolutely worth a purchase.

World End Economica definitely met my expectations, although I'd still say I prefer Spice and Wolf if given the option between the two.
The story is kinetic VN about a boy who has decided to go to the stock market to make money and his journey. The author clearly knows what he is talking about when he wrote this VN. However, if one is not very financially literate, the VN will be a bit of a challenge to understand. Considering that I am a finance major and know about stocks and how the market works, I understood everything that was happening in this VN. In fact, I can say that the VN made the stock market look way TOO simple compared to the way it is actually. Futhermore, there was some nice references that some people would have caught. For example, Daniel Trap who bought a tower in Manhattan who had gone bankrupt 3 times... HMMMMM Also Carlyle Group is an actual company although in the VN it was Carlyle Investments. One other thing was that the stock market in the VN followed the Japanese market time from 9-5 instead of the US one from 9:30-4. Finally, the ending of the VN really laid the cold truth out there and I really enjoyed that realistically because before that, it just seemed like the stock market was a place where people can profit easily. But those detail aside, the VN presented a nice thought stimulating experience, especially for someone like me who is interested in the field.
Aside from the good parts of this VN, I thought the character development was a bit shallow to say the least. Some of the parts seemed a bit forced and the connection was surface level from one to another. Although you can see the growth in the character relations, I still felt like it came too sudden and sometimes too unexplained. That is one of the main reasons why I'd choose Spice and Wolf over World End Economica, because in Spice and Wolf, the character development was amazing.
Overall, definitely worth playing/reading this VN because it is really good. I look forward to better character development in episode 2 and 3 and for an amazing conclusion!
Rating: 8.4/10
Recommend: $5 or under

Unlike most of the people talking about this game, I didn't come across this thanks to
, but rather
, which I (mistakenly; see above) thought was from the same author.  I've heard
's more contested quality-wise than
, and it does have its issues, but if it's so much worse,
is some kind of masterpiece, because
was able to render me full-on bawling for fifteen minutes straight thanks to the climactic speech in the ninth episode of the anime.  It's pretty difficult for me to cry at stuff these days, and this thing had me going harder than the first five minutes of
!
So, with the kind of anticipation that could inspire, I tried
out, though I wasn't sure how it was going to be.
Lemme just say, it started cold.  Hal/Haru is a terrible trash pile of a person loaded with Social Darwinist machismo and casual misogyny.  His internal monologues left me wanting to throw his laptop into a bonfire.  Credit where credit is due, though, he's far from unusual when it comes to teenagers, so I let the story unfold, hoping that Haru's worldview wasn't being supported by the narrative.
I'm glad I stuck it out.
The characters developed slowly, but that's fine.  When I wasn't yelling for Haru to take the hint from Lisa and stop being an♥♥♥♥♥ouroburos, I was enjoying the other characters (Lisa especially - she's got the patience of a saint) and the world-building.  It's rare to really get legit hard sci-fi as opposed to sci-fantasy works, and this one delivers on that.  Back to the characters, though; when Haru finally starts to take the hint (thanks to a plot spoiler that had me teary-eyed), things became more enjoyable, and other characters began to open up through his eyes.  Hagana in particular became a favorite.  Her trauma and mental issues spoke to me, and much of my initial dislike for Haru was because of his failure to truly understand what she (or anyone else, for that matter) was going through.
Still, by the end, while remaining a flawed person, Haru had me rooting for him in some of the most tense moments I can remember in a story like this, which is a real feat since the combat, so to speak, is largely cerebral.  The stock trading scenes, especialy the ending, had me glued to my screen, hoping as Haru did for a happy outcome.
It takes a lot of patience, but I would call this a worthy experience, espcially for fans of hard sci-fi and/or economics.  More than an exercise in world-building, this ends as a powerful story about hope, compassion, and what to value in life.  There are some problems, mostly the rough translation and the lack of variety in artwork, but they didn't interfere too much with my experience.  With interesting (eventually) characters, a strong if slow plot, and a focus on a more cerebral form of conflict,
stands as a worthy addition to Hasekura's library.

Pyre paints a beautiful, vibrant fairy tale full of memorable characters. You play the role of The Reader, exiled from the Commonwealth for the crime of literacy. This is a great narrative device that leans up against the fourth wall in a clever way. The game uses it throughout, with much of the lore and color in the world filled in by literally (excuse the pun) reading the in-game Book of Rites as you help guide your companions to salvation.
This redemption is earned by conducting the Rites, essentially a form of magic 3v3 basketball. While this may seem out of place, gameplay is engaging and flows well, and I enjoyed the tense competitions as well as the need to change strategies as you confront different situations and use different characters. As with titles from Supergiant Games, the difficulty (and rewards) can be increased in-game, if you want more of a challenge.
The art and animation has a delightful whimsy about it, and the music and voice acting are compelling. Fans of Bastion or Transistor should pick this up immediately. Anyone else wanting to share a grand tale, well told, with a great cast of characters flung into fantastic world should also get this game; it is well worth your time.

I want to love this game more than I do.
This game is 75% reading and 25% actualy gameplay. Which started off fine because the world is colorful and interesting. The characters are very well done and their personalities are varied and engaging. But after a while, the game gets to a point where it's just too much. Nearly all the information and dialog is more or less inconsequential. And you sometimes get bonuses for slogging through optional dialog so it's detrimental (albeit, only slightly) not to engage in it. I just want to play the game, darnit. All the significant plot details are buried in an endless sea of pointless information.
The actual gameplay is really pretty fun though. It's similar to Transistor and Bastion where you are encouraged to adapt and pursue different strategies with different characters, and it's done incredibly well. The short games you play would be perfect for a quick game session - just hop on, play a game, hop off - except that that's impossible because there's so much dialog and time spent both before AND after each game. It's frustrating after a while. I respect Supergiant's efforts to create something like Pyre and I think if you're interested in investing in a visual novel, then I highly recommend this. They've done an incredible job at creating an amazing world. I just would like to play the game more.

WORLD END ECONOMiCA is a kinetic Visual Novel made by Isuna Hasekura, which is known for being the author of the renowned Light Novel, Spice & Wolf.
Like the author's previous work, this kinetic Visual Novel has the economical drive within it's repository, joining in the mix of tragedy and love. Isuna Hasekura's previous work, Spice & Wolf, revolves around trading. This time, WORLD END ECONOMiCA episode.01, revolves around Stocks and it's Market. I am amazed at how the author succinctly mixes different genres in this Visual Novel, much like Spice & Wolf.
WORLD END ECONOMiCA has three games, namely episode.01/02/03.
However, one should not compare Isuna Hasekura's Spice & Wolf and WORLD END ECONOMiCA, as the former is a Light Novel and the latter being a Visual Novel. Of course the manner of telling the story is significally different, as a Visual Novel introduces music and accompanying CG to maximize the tone of the current atmosphere and situation but with less words to further balance the narration of story by giving the personality to the CGs and sprites, while the words supply the story itself, unlike a Light Novel where the artworks are introduced at the start of reading, but it just introduces the setting and vibe of the story being told, with the descriptive narrative giving most of a Light Novel's shine. Nonetheless, one should not underestimate Isuna Hasekura, and one should know that the author would definitely give a story that is rich and fantastic.
- Fantastic setting and atmosphere
- Rich character development
- Character personalities are well-developed, and makes them stand out at each other
- Nice soundtrack that optimizes the tone of the current situation
- Cute and well-drawn character art and CG
- Length of the Visual Novel is enough to deliver the story
-
- The opening to the story is a bit bland in my opinion
- The Main Character has an unlikeable personality, and makes rash cynical decisions (but this will be remedied later on)
- The explanation about Stocks are long and a bit confusing if not understood clearly (Seeing the Visual Novel is about Stocks, I'd recommend anyone to have atleast a very basic information about Stocks and its workaround)
- There are very few soundtracks to begin with. And a few of these are incorrectly looped.
- This Visual Novel does not yet support Steam Overlay, and its current engine does not yet support Achievements and Trading Cards (However, this will be also remedied later on)
-
-
Overall, I would recommend WORLD END ECONOMiCA episode.01 to those people who likes Light Novels and Kinetic Novels in general. Please be reminded that there will be an update that makes it compatible with Steam Overlay, Steam Achievements and Trading Cards, though. The stories are long, too. I'd advise you to wait for Sekai Project to release all the episodes, because then they would patch them to a different engine.

I thought long and hard about this review as Arma 2 and it's expansions were probably my favourite computer game of all time, and that's largely why I'm unable to recommend Arma 3 straight out of the box. Let me explain:
Arma 2 (complete) was/is an amazing modern day combat simulator. It contained a hugemungus range of modern weaponry from many nations, all beautifully researched and recreated lovingly. There was an editor, but you didn't really need it because of the outstanding "armoury" feature which IMO was one of the best ideas ever implimented in any pc game. All the weaponry was historical too, so any number of modern day conflicts could be recreated. There's nothing comparable in Arma 3 either, so no excuses guys.
By complete contrast Arma 3 has failed on two levels for me; make believe weaponry from 2035 - why? I can't imagine a less likely place for WW3 to start than some idyllic island in the Mediterranean either! And worst of all no proper and wide ranging armoury feature in-country, allowing gamers to unlock new weaponry, leaving SP gamers like myself feeling more than a little short-changed from what is not, for most of the time anyway, a cheap game.
It seems to me that too many developers these days are using the MP ability of their games to save a lot of work on their own part, though this is often not reflected in the pricing policy. Even if the over-priced dlc for Arma 3 was included in the main game, then the equipment would still fall alarmingly short of the hardware on offer from Arma 2. So perhaps that's why they dropped the Arma 2 armoury feature - because there wasn't much to unlock by completing those fun randomly generated missions!!
HOWEVER because of the modding community out there Arma 3 is still worth getting. Why? Because the community has done what the devs should have done and included all the content from Arma 2 plus more in the outstanding CUP mod (duly updated too with stacks of maps). Ok so there's still no armoury feature, but if I can recreate those missions, and new ones, from the editor then anyone can - and it's fun too.So battles can be fought in more likely places and avoid upsetting the tourists!
Why the heck Bohemia couldn't have done that in the start is beyond me, it would have catered for everybody and likely increased their sales too. I'm not interested in future wars, if I was I'd buy a science fiction wargame...
So thank you the CUP project for bringing most of my favourite game into a more graphically updated setting. There is one final complaint to the devs though; what's with the weird combat animations? I shot several prone enemy recently, and they leapt to their feet before going down again dead WTF? How could that be released in a game?

I'm lucky enough to not really be affected by either of these topics very much, but if someone else who was stumbled upon this game, it would be terrible. I don't mean to bash, but I think it's very important that you tag this game. Thank you for reading. ♥

Not exactly the most thrilling story. It's uncomfortable to sit through in the beginning. It has a pretty slow build up and what it was building up to wasn't too groundbreaking. Once the twist is revealed, naturally things start making more sense. Though they only make sense in the context of the story and don't hold up much in reality. (Which isn't always a bad thing, but this story takes place in the real world so the character interactions and events are awkward.) Honestly, I was sold on the title screen since it gave off such a mysterious, melancholy vibe. However, it didn't hold up through the rest of the novel. The storyline became bland and boring, just making you wait for the huge twist you expected from other reviews. The ending dragged on way too long, I feel like it should have ended on the twist and let the reader speculate on the impact. Instead, it explains the situation to the point it where becomes dull and you wait for the game to end. (Much like how I'm writing this review oops...)
Maybe it was just the English translation, but the writing was kind of...empty? I guess that's the right word for it. There were some lines of text that intrigued me, but then they were over-explained and made me go "Okay, I get it already. We can move on." I would've prefered if they kept it subtle instead of shoving it in your face.
In terms of characters, there's not much depth to them. The novel is more story based than character based, but for something like this, it should have been more balanced. You don't get a chance to establish a bond with the characters. While Ambre's intentions are fully described, her motivations behind her actions aren't clear enough and are hollow. The portrayal of mental illness and the treatment system is shallow, like the author wanted it to be overly dramatic without actually looking into the subject or simply disregarded facts.
Overall, the storyline had potential, but the way it was executed felt odd and underdeveloped. Sad circumstances? Yeah. Heartbreaking? Eeeeh, depends how sympathetic you are. It personally left me disappointed since I went in thinking it would be emotionally provoking. I went out of it feeling like there should have been a lot more or a lot less. Could've been great. Not the absolute worst, just wish it was better.
Would recommend if you want to make your friends feel a little uncomfortable. Otherwise, you won't be missing out on anything big.

I bought Nether when it was $3 and I still felt ripped off.
Even though they are marketing it as a "stable release", it feels like I'm playing a game that has never left the alpha stage of development. You sit and watch your character hopelessly glitch and twitch through an annoyingly large landscape with long expanses of nothingness except for the noises of yourself russling through the bushes alone; Minecraft lends itself to be more suspenseful than this.
And at least in Minecraft you feel the satisfaction of striking iron ore once every four minutes. Whereas I'll spend half-an-hour meandering around and scrounging piles of garbage without receiving any reward for my time spent.
The factor that intrigued me most about the game has become the factor I loath most about the game. It was pitched as an MMO where you bump into new players, and then have an intense moment to decide whether to fight, go your separate ways, or attempt to build alliances and hope your trust is true. Yet, without microphone capability there is no time/way to explain your hopes/intentions/truces, so the game becomes more of a PvP shoot-em-up-free-for-all-deathmatch-thing. Sure, there are the occasional "Nether" (the NPC bad guys) scattered about, but they are the least of your worries in this game. THERE IS NO ONE YOU CAN TRUST IN THIS GAME, SHOOT EVERYTHING THAT MOVES.
Permadeath is a fun idea, until you watch 4 hours of your work go down the drain on a regular basis. The game throws level 1's with level 30's and expects things to go smoothly. But I built my character up to level 12 only to watch him get insta-killed by a bully level 30.
I could complain more, but I'm tired. I'll hopefully come bacm to this later.

This is a kinetic novel, where you don't have choices and basically just enjoy the story. There are some points where there will be no backgrounds or music, and though these were probably used to have some sort of effect on the reader, they felt out of place to me. There are also a few typing errors. Overall though, I still very much enjoyed it and am looking forward to playing/reading it's sequel (it is part of a three part series).
