Be warned tho, it's not perfect: I will try to explain my reasons here.
The good stuff:
The game itself is a lot of fun. The main objective is self-explanatory: if you spawn as Jason you have twenty minutes to exterminate the eight counselors walking around the camp. If you spawn as a counselor you have the same amount of time to find a way out by fixing cars, boats, radios and calling police backup or the iconic Tommy Jarvis.
Playing as a counselor is easy enough: run, hide, find tools and weapons, call the cops, stick together, bring war to Jason himself.
Playing as Jason is a lot harder than it looks, at the beginning: You need to master all of Jason's abilities to become the ultimate killing machine, otherwise you will warp into a fence and be stuck for the rest of the game while other players laugh at you.
Each character, Jason included, has a lot of skills to unlock via gameplay points: that is to say perks, executions, abilities and so on.
The main advice I would give for the game is DON'T RUSH IT. Everyone has a decent amount of time to do everything, and rushing like a tornado means phocking things up for good. Take your time, especially when you are the killer: study your prey, try to anticipate their movements, stalk them and still fear inside their hearts with mind tricks.
BTW you can't compare Friday the 13th with Dead by Daylight: yes, they have the same root gameplay, but the dynamics are so different there is literally no relation between the two.
Now for the bad stuff:
The price is goddamn insane: the game is barely a 3 map / 6 Jasons / 8 counselor game right now. Paying almost 40 USD/Euros for this is a joke. I bought it because I'm a huge fan of the series and at least this game wasn't a disappointment, but I wouldn't risk it if I wasn't a fan.
People are storming the servers everyday: that means connection issues, random kicks and stuff. Also, people seem to be leaving the game if they don't spawn as Jason or if they don't get their favorite map. It's very very disappointing, this means that people don't buy games for fun anymore but to achieve something at all costs, and that's ridiculous.
Teamkills are a big issue as well: some counselors just shoot other counselors in the back to steal their stuff and to run solo all over the map, or a Jason player might leave the lobby when he feels powerless against other players. No joke.
All in all:
Great looking game (lacking content for now), bad players sometimes.
I'd give it a good 7/10, if it wasn't for the price and the skinny structure it presents. Let's go with a 6.5/10 for now, hoping the devs will add more stuff in the future.

So for this I originally rated it a thumbs up, which was my fault because after playing a decent amount of time I realize that one does not get $40 worth of game with this.
Pros:
1.  It's something to do while waiting for another game to download
2.  Fun with firends once you get pass all the game crashing, bugs, and exploiters.
Cons:
1.  3 Maps, all pretty much the same and they require the same tactics for Jason and counselors.  The RNG (as far as items go) is there, but it's pretty much the same thing with a different name
2.  Speaking of RNG.  Great thought, bad execution.  RNG can really screw you.  Regardless if your Jason or a counselor, the RNG can screw you bad.
3.  A game where success is completely based on communication (and luck), and doesn't require a microphone nor is a text to chat option available.
4.  It takes nothing to play as Jason.  I appreciate the efforts put into all the environmental kills and grab kills, but a rare few ever use them.  Jason grabs, button mashes the hot keys and there is no way to break free unless you happen upon a pocket knife, which again, RNG can screw you on that.
5.  Tha game becomes dull, monotenous, and a gamble.  This game seems to be 70% luck and 30% skill.  Imagine playing the slots where a win amounts to a high five.
6.  Bugs, not just cosmetic issues, but game altering/ending issues.
7.  Objectives.  Boat, car(s), or cops.  Same thing each time, same fix each time.  (I am aware you can "kill" jason through an elaborate process, but honestly, I am sure that most people who have gotten that coordinated it.
My Hopes:
I wish this game the best, I do.  The developers spent much time and effort on it and I would never wish ill on their work.  As it stands now, this game is worth $15 in my opinion.  The way ahead, there does not seem to be any growth to this game.  It is so tightly spun around a single theme that expanding will either A:  Be cosmetic (i.e. RetoJason) or B:  Anger the die hard fans.  I hope this game continues to grow, I do, but being realistic, with the problems mentioned above and the options of expanding very limited, it does not look too promising.

I think its about time i were to write an updated review on this game.
Alright, For Honor is a complete piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥in nearly every aspect. There is almost nothing positive i can say about this game or its community. Now some of you are going to say "hur dur look at yur hours" but ill go into that in a moment. So lets break this down piece by piece

The game does require a learning cuve but it is very satisfying when you pull off a victory. Because you cant just recruit new guns or troops with resource or base building it forces you to care about your men and to think your decsions through more than most games. For those coming from Operation Star its still a learnign curve to where it is a newer game but still has the spirit of the original. In my opinion this is how a sequel should be done.
If you dont want to take the time to go through learning and are used to always winning agianst stupid A.I. this game may not be for you. It takes time! It will be frustrating and there is no formula for winning. There arent specific counters built into the game and artillery isnt always going to come down where you call it. Its a simulator not an arcade game. And it wont be fair, if you want fair tank on tank combat go play War Thunder Arcade mode! Also if youre expecting a graphically beautiful game dont buy, it has its moments but the animations are clunky and vehicle models do look good but it isnt BF1.
What the game sets out to do it achieves. And that is a realistic depiction of small/medium unit engagements in WW2. Not for everyone but if you take the time then it will grow on you and you'll never go back to other strategy games.

As an older gamer in his mid fifties who is obsessed with WW2 and especially the Eastern Front, this game is a dream come true. So far with only 16 hours in I am still on the steep learning curve as to how to do things but, that said, with every hour played and with helpful tutorials, especially on You Tube, even those for the earlier Graviteam game  Operation Star, I am understanding more. With this understanding you realise just what depth and knowledge this game has to offer, There is a saying that the Devil is in the details and there is one huge Devil in this game. The Binocular and magnifying glass view of your tanks taking AT fire, of hits and brewing vehicles with molten steel sparking high into the air as ammo cooks off makes the game worth the price alone. The inclusion of German and Russian as the language being shouted by the soldiers adds to the historical depth that runs through the veins of the programming that has been lovingly coded into this creation.
I could go on for many paragraphs about the attention to detail here but suffice to say, having a library of over 300 books just on the Eastern Front alone, Mius Front beats the oppositon in so many ways showing the War in that theatre of operations. Get over your concern about how to actually cope with all the menus and control options as they will make sense over time. I am still learning and will be for a few days if not weeks but who cares. Buy this game and Operation Star and a smile as wide as the Russian front will appear on your face.

After a very very very rough start, i have come to like the game. It is absolutely unforgiving, and you will die a lot in the beginning. But there are ways to get Experience, Money and Equipment quite fast, if you know how. Also, the game has quite a lot of glitches and bugs still, but they sometimes make for hilarious moments. Other times, they make for a quick death of your player character.
The development team is really bad at communicating with the users, though, but at least they are quite active with two patches in a little over a week since i have been playing.
Glitches and Account creation issues aside, Nether is actually quite easy to get into. There are not too many different items and weapons in the game, but enough to make for a healthy variety. Stuff you can loot is glowing, which may take away from the immersion for some, but also can make lootable objects, especially in the open, an easy to spot target for all players in the vicinity. There are "World Events" like loot drops, especially strong Nethers appearing and Safezones becoming, well, unsafe. The risk vs reward mechanic in the game works really well: should you engage that nether and try to kill it for its body parts, despite the possibilty of the sound of combat attracting other, potentially hostile players? Should you take the direct route to a safezone, but risk getting ambushed?
The Tribe and territory control system is kind of lackluster, mostly because you cannot tell what tribe another player belongs to until you are very close to that player, and so Players killing other players from the same tribe is quite common. As is players killing players in general. This game features full loot (except for cosmetic items and golden keys) when it comes to players. Well, there is a global inventory that persists through player deaths, but the space is very limited and to access it, you have to get to a safezone. Trust no one. I tried to be a friendly player in the beginning, but once you get steamrolled and killed on sight by other players a few times, you adapt to that playstyle yourself. The game is best played with friends that you can trust for that very reason.
So, if you can take getting killed and losing stuff a lot, if you like intense survival games and "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;-moments, and if you can look past bugs and glitches, Nether can be a great experience. I'm not sure whether i would say it is worth the full price, but if you are really open and willing to give the game a chance (especially if the game happens to be on sale) i' recommend trying it out!
PS.: There is a lot of talk about cheaters on the forums. So far i have not come across anyone that i really suspected of cheating, but maybe i just was lucky.

The Anime Sale a short while ago put my eyes open and looking. Isuna Hasekura's name brought my eyes here.
I can say without a doubt that I would have paid full price for this now, and I insist to anyone that has bought and read Hasekura's Spice and Wolf series, that this is right up your price alley anyway.
-CLARIFICATION-
This is not a multibranching Visual Novel Game.
This is just a Novel, with Visuals.
--
The length blew me away. Even more importantly, I saw the episode one, so I was expecting the story to end and just about every major plot development. While not an intentional effect...I feel this ultimately added to my enjoyment, even if it's not an easily or sensible reproducable effect.
As I felt it important to provide that clarification up there, you may have guessed but I was expecting a multibranching VN game. I was skeptical, because while I trusted Isuna Hasekura's name on any book, I wasn't sure if he could translate from book to game. Certainly, the industry doesn't have a massive success record for such things, albeit I'm still very shallow in the Visual Novel genre, so I speak there with no authority.
This is not a concern, as this is essentially, a Book, enhanced. To be perfectly emotionally honest...I feel like this is an improvement, with how well it was used. Certainly it's not for everything, I can't even begin to imagine how Spice and Wolf could be made into a similar format with matching use of medium, but I suppose I'm not an author or a game designer am I?
At the minimum, I will always be on the look out in future for Visual Novels that aren't multibranching story games, thanks to World End Economica. Previous to this, I would have thought it defeated the point of it being a Visual Novel. Now, I appreciate the value of the effects and emotions the additional medium power on the table.
Potentially Spoiling Insight for the still undecided below:

Great game, I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys the "assymetrical multiplayer" genre and doesn't mind a difficult learning curve. The music is awesome, game looks nice, and the gameplay is exciting! I admit, it is still glitchy at times but oh well, usually most games are nowadays upon release. If it makes you feel better, the glitches are sometimes hilarious so it's not all bad. Teamwork is a MUST so I would NOT buy this game unless you have a mic. It's still fun but its easily 200% more fun when you talk. Now I'd like to dedicate the rest of my review to answering a few of the common things I see people saying are unfair/OP in the game because there is a LOT going on mechanic-wise that is not so obvious at times. The overall complaint/source of bad reviews for this game is that Jason is too OP. Here are the reasons I see people listing off most:
1) "Stamina runs out to quickly!"
TL;DR answer:
Stand absolutely still to regain your stamina. The only real time stamina is necessary is to re-distance yourself after Jason's SHIFT ability and to avoid being grabbed by same SHIFT ability, which closes distances faster than you can run. His MORPH(teleport) is not nearly so dangerous, as he will most likely not be able to teleport directly on top of you as he can with a SHIFT. Also, Jason's SHIFT is really only useful outdoors. Houses are your best friend for stamina recovery AKA standing still.
How to GIT GUD:
best way to help yourself recover stamina is:
1- always have a house to escape to. The only way Jason can enter a house is to break down the door. This time allows you to chill out and recover stamina
2- hang around a teammate! take turns distracting Jason so that your other mates can stand still and recover their staminas too. Using your mic is a hilarious way to get Jason off your friends so they can stay alive, be creative! Taunt his♥♥♥♥♥ Insult his mummy >:'D
3- use your stun weapons wisely. along with having group members to help you hit Jason with melee weapons, there are many weapons that are 1-time use that stun Jason well enough that you can afford to stand around and recover your stamina
4- don't waste it in the first place! So many people are running full speed when they could be briskly jogging(press X to toggle from walk to jog). Save your stamina for those SHIFT uses because that's the only real time Jason has to close in extreme distances and grab you. Also, don't run around in the open so much. Use your stamina mainly for darting from house to house.
2) "Jason's grab is inescapable! Even with a 10/10 composure character!"
TL;DR answer:
low fear and strength is what actually makes escaping a grab possible, not high composure. Composure is just a skill that allows you to recover from fear easier but composure will NEVER be able to decrease your fear fast enough if Jason is pursuing you for long periods of time. A lot of high composure characters have low strength so they simply cannot be relied on to break grabs.
How to GIT GUD:
if you are not playing Tommy, Jenny or Adam, or don't have a pocket knife on you, always assume you will NEVER escape a grab. And even if you ARE playing Tommy, Jenny or Adam, assume that you are ONLY SAFE from the FIRST GRAB! Jason persuing you increases fear too much, you cannot possibly escape 2 grabs in a row, just not how the game works. Every other counselor has too awful of a composure+strength combination to escape reliably. Try to think of it from a Jason perspective, too. Why would he grab anyone if it took more than 2 tries? He may as well swing his weapon at you instead as the weapon damage makes counselors slower and it only takes 3 melee hits to kill most of them. Grab is a fun mechanic, please don't hate it ):
3) "Shift grab is OP"
TL;DR answer:
the balancing factor in the SHIFT move for Jason is it's cooldown rate and the fact that the game provides a spooky sound hint + static effect that alerts you as to when these super dangerous abilities are back into play so you can plan to avoid them successfully.
How to GIT GUD:
ANYTIME you see static on the screen, take 3 seconds to run around irradically to avoid a potential grab until you can spot where Jason appears. USE YOUR MINI MAP! Jason lights up as a red icon with arrows indicating where he is facing. It is difficult for Jason to turn and maneuver around in the SHIFT mode because of how god-awful fast he travels, so use that to your advantage! See where he is facing and determine the best way to avoid where he might be going.
4) "Jason always traps the objectives! I can't call the phone or repair the car because theres always traps there"
TL;DR answer:
When you see the spot is trapped, don't bother dealing with it immediately. Drop your objective items near the spot and go find a weapon and friends to bring with you when you attempt to repair it. Friends can help stun Jason and he will most likely attack whoever is caught in the trap because they're easy pickins and that's your chance to save them AND stun him. You don't really have to actually repair anything, you can disable the trap, all spread out and run away, then come back later. If he has new traps up(some Jasons have more than others), just rinse and repeat till all his traps have been used up. Easy! It takes a while, sure, but as a counselor you are in no rush! As a matter of fact, you're pretty much rewarded for dicking around and eating up time so why not?
How to GIT GUD:
Either ignore that thing altogether or be strategic on how you take it out. If it's a car that's being protected, is there another one? Usually the four seater is trapped so sometimes people make it their strategy to avoid that car period. For the phone it's a bit more annoying.. Someone has to REPAIR it and then someone has to be inside to call the cops. I'd suggest having 3 people in your party for this one, one to be the BAIT(aka trigger the trap), one to fight off Jason and get that stun hit in there so BAIT can escape (one of these two people can choose to repair the phone while the other holds Jason off) and finally one more additional person who is ideally already inside the house to get on the phone instantly so Jason doesn't have time to re-disable the box again.

I’m going to go out on a limb here and say this:  Soma is the best narrative experience ever in a video game.  Sure, it’s got the standard Frictional Games tropes of hiding from scary monsters, creepy environments, fast breathing, and audible heartbeats when your character is supposed to be scared.  And all that works perfectly together, as it should.  But the story… the way it makes you really consider your actions.  The way it makes you ponder between gaming sessions what is really going on.   That’s simply spectacular.
Frictional Games caught me a little by surprise with “The Dark Descent.”  As a character who awoke in a dark and scary castle with no recollection of prior events, I assumed that I was a decent fellow who fell into bad luck.  I loved the way that game slowly revealed what a cretin I really was.  And part of the fun was the tension between self-preservation and disgust.  In A Machine for Pigs, I suspected I was a jerk at the start, and the game slowly revealed how much of a jerk I really was.  (By the way, I am one of the few who vastly preferred a Machine for Pigs to The Dark Descent).
In contrast, Soma tells you what kind of person you are right at the get go.  What you don’t know, and spend much of the game finding out, is how you got to where you are.  And what “you” actually are.  And why you are.  And that discovery is done at so many levels.
The game has many choices, but only one ending.  Sound limiting?  It’s not.  Because the choices make you think.  And as the game progresses, I understand what the choices I made meant – I didn’t need the game to tell me.  Even now, after completing the game, I still wonder if some of the choices I made were the right ones.  Have you ever heard of such a thing with a videogame?
Now, about the horror… there’s really no such thing in videogames, IMO.  Sure, environments can be creepy, and things can jump out at you.  But, as with most games, you have infinite lives.  So, for example, in Outlast (another wonderful game), fear turns quickly to frustration as you die over and over again trying to get through a tricky spot. Not so with Soma.  I only died a few times, and only once did it feel repetitive and irritating.
I like storytelling in videogames.  I think that the medium introduces new ways of promoting immersion.  In particular, the trope of being alone in an unfamiliar and dangerous environment is done better in a video game than any other medium (Remember Myst?).  And Soma does it better than everything else.  The graphics, sound, script, everything made this as immersive and thought-provoking game as I have ever played.  I can’t recommend this game highly enough.

TLDR; Negative review that could easily turn positive with updates, unfortunately they're few and far between.
I love survival games, and the theme is really good in this one. I wouldn't recommend it simply based on the bugs.
This game could be awesome with mod support, fog of war bug and experience gain bug fixes, user interface improvements, a revamped inventory system based on weight and shelter size, and most importantly a bug fix for disappearing expeditions.
The game is still playable, and I can't imagine you won't get your money's worth just learning how to play.
By then, when you have your overall strategy in mind and really dig in, you'll encounter bugs that would be acceptable in an early access title. However, this is a full release and has a slow update cycle. I don't have high hopes of being able to return to a fixed and fully playable (if clunky) game anytime soon. I would say it's currently in the "lots of potential, but still needs polishing" stage of development.
My personal incomplete "want" list:
-The ability to remap keys and addition of a scroll bar or "book pages" for inventories. Compare the time it takes to scroll through a 300 item inventory and decide what to trade, to the time it could take if 1 click changed the "page"
-Borderless windowed mode
-A combination of weight, cubic item dimensions, and shelter/character inventory slots so that item stacking makes some sense
-The ability to create and change waypoints while a party is on the road, with rations/water being an actual factor instead of a way to cheese the hunger/stats mechanics being different if you're in your shelter
-"Camping" and "Searching" mechanic for expeditions to allow map interaction
-A mechanic swap between faction areas, loot sites, and quest encounters for fluid random interactions
A-Towns could have a representative icon displaying they exist, with randomly sized areas around them where 'urban' loot sites are statistically more likely, influenced by perception stats/gear. I think a map graphic for towns would be better, and icons could be utilized differently tho (outlined below)
B-Caravans/Roaming quest encounters could have a randomly sized (invisible) area like towns in "A", where exploring or camping in an area implies scouting missions and roaming sentries of the camp would encounter the caravan or quest NPC if in that area at the right time
C-Faction area's could have an icon like quest targets, but with invisible area's of affect as well, improving rate of encounter while in their domain
D-These areas could be mobile and dynamic to represent changes in faction territory posession, areas of town rich or deficient in loot, trade caravans being persistent and nomadic
E-These would all factor into what happens if an encounter occurs.
trigger encounter- determine local, determine faction or neutral, loot event or NPC encounter - determine strength of NPC's in event based on their faction size/power or randomly if NPC is neutral - determine nature of encounter (combat, trade, recruit, special etc), present to player - Local is city street, faction is matriarch and they are presently weak so gear/stats are inferior, this is a combat encounter
This would simulate walking through a city while scouting, allow controlled chaos in what you find and the area it's found in, remove the static buildings mechanic to broaden the mystery and necessity of exploration even without fog of war, and give the game essentially biomes where you can reasonably expect to see rural/urban/forest/mountain/wasteland etc types of encounters but not be able to fully control, exploit, or avoid any particular one.
-Fog of War reappearing over time but town names remaining on top of the fog when it reappears. Either once it's explored it's explored (since what's there remains static) - Or if you haven't visited an area in a while it makes sense to not know exactly what you'll find (if locations were dynamic) but for you to know that the town exists in that general area.
Icons would then be representative of what was found, but not exclude finding something else next door, making the mechanic of "finding different loot at the same spot indefinitely" make sense since you're just exploring the town area and finding random places within it (or middle of nowhere, or forest, mountains etc).

Alternatively, I think the icons themselves could be recycled into event locations of importance, but that a relief map with random town outlines giving a rough estimate of the "Area" the town events are likely to take place in would ultimately make the game more interesting. Perhapse a way to prioritize what your party should be looking for so that hospitals or airports are more likely when looking for specific gear, but the randomness lends tension and difficulty.
-Everything outside of core mechanics to be stored in a modular library indexed format allowing player mods and custom artwork to load alongside (or instead of) vanilla code. This game has all the basics, mods can take it the rest of the way.

Where to begin?
A wonderful piece of software, made with passion and expertise by a developer that knows the subject matter and strives to recreate the grim reality of commanding men on the field of battle.
This is not a wargame, neither is it an RTS, it's a coldly unforgiving battle simulator that does a terrific job of placing the player in the shoes of a battalion commander, this is a game where actual knowledge and understanding of military doctrine and of the tools at yours and your enemies disposal will be advantageous, real world tactics not only work but are necessary in order to succeed.
Look, we are talking about a very small independent developer with other projects on the go, this masterpiece, this labour of love represents a truly staggering achievement, which frankly puts the paltry offerings of many so called 'Triple A' studios with their multi million dollar budgets to shame.
If you are interested in military based strategy and fancy yourself as a master tactician then look no further, there is no better or more satisfying challenge out there.

Summary: Nether is one of thoese games that sound good on paper but are horrible executed. It is utterly boring, clunky and luck-based; you level up, gather stuff and lose them for an enemy that didn't register hits or a random player sniping new players. As  for the performance of the game, it runs horribly: it is badly optimized and textures are low resolution ones. Overall, it is a poor overpriced game, and it is time-consuming on top of that. It relies on community and RPG-elements, but the community is filled with players who prefer boring approach (that is killing new players with overleveled characters), and the RPG elements are irrelevant and leveling up/gearing up takes a lot of time for little reward.
More in detail:
Gameplay is clunky. Animations are lacking, there are various physics glitches (I got behind an idiot on top of a building to either communicate with him or kill him but I couldn't drop down a ledge and he detected me) and it  is unresponsive. Shooting mechanics are horrendous and require no technical or tactical approach. The enemy design is boring as well; teleporting enemies with poor hit detection.
Quests or objectives are dumb, and the game does a poor job of guiding you or whatever. Just carry this stupid package to a place, then get killed by an overleveled player with low ping or a stupid group of Nethers. The game is pretty much aimless; it would be much better if you can group up with people to make small camps/factions and have a mean OF A BIT MORE FASTER TRAVEL.
Graphics:
The game is badly optimized and it looks fine in some places during specific times of day/night. The whole game needs some sort of filters to define it, and it requires better textures. Also better ambient occlusion would help, but that is demanding on performance.

I had high hopes for this game as a fan of turn-based strategy, but those hopes were quickly dashed.  The only thing Garden Tale has going for it is the artwork, though some suspect character designs (Meryl) manage to tarnish even that.
Garden Tale prides itself on a trap system revolving around Bonions, exploding vegetables that can harm both enemies and allies. The videos and images show large-scale chain reactions that seem exciting and fun, similar to games like Disgaea or La Pucelle. The videos, however, lie about these possibilities in a shameful way, including fabricating combos for show on maps that, in practice, aren't possible to pull off. Indeed, one segment of the advert video shows a combo on one of the first few maps you play on, with a starting point that would require a long-ranged attack. The problem? There aren't any long-ranged attacks, particularly not at that point in the very beginning of the game.
And there lies the biggest issue with the trap system; there is no safe way to work within it. Bonions require an attack to detonate them and they explode over a large area, and several hours into the game and 5 characters acquired, I still only have melee attacks. Essentially, bulding a series of explosions thus means sacrificing a character to the fallout afterwards.
Except, that assumes the traps are worth building in the first place! Enemies are many per map, and they hit very hard, an issue exacerbated by the forced progression from map-to-map without opportunity to grind and level one's characters up. Bonions, further, cannot be pushed, pulled or thrown, they can only be moved with certain attacks done by certain weapons wielded by certain characters. This means, in order to set up traps, you have to spread out your characters, take several turns moving Bonions into range of each other, and then sacrifice a character to detonate them.
In practice, this will get you killed long before them just from enemy attacks, enemies which have your characters beat both in movement and attack range. The solution? Ignore the Bonions, and just attack the enemies. Not only is this easier, it's the only real effective strategy. Unfortunately, it's also the most boring one.
In the most aggregious lack of enemy diversity I've seen in any game in a long time, there are only two types of enemies, and fittingly two types of enemy sprites; a melee wolffoxthing, and a ranged wolffoxthing. Further, while there are a variety of skills, they mostly function on the Bonions which have since been established as effectively the most falsely advertised form of a gimmick a game developer can get. So, enemies are uninteresting, and skills - given that they function on a nonfuctioning system - end up uninteresting as well. In the end, the game comes down to hacking and slashing enemies in a very uninteresting, monotonous way alongside some of the worst, uneditable control and camera systems in modern gaming.
There is little else to save the game from it's badly thought-out battle system. Animations have no flair, music is forgettable, and the storyline and character development are on par with Creative Writing 101 alums at best. There's no way to grind, defeating the fun for people that enjoy that, no real way to strategize, defeating the excitement of one coming from better-made TRPGS, no multiple paths, no exploration, no choice, no point.
Even at under $10, I wish I could get my money back. There are far better experiences even in this price range for RPG fans. Skip this one until it's in the dollar bin where it belongs.

If this game would be 10€~ and had an “early access”-tag, I’d probably not rate it negatively.

Unfortunately however they charge you 37€ and quite honestly, if this is the “finished” version of the game that I just bought (and refunded), I’m glad I never had to play the beta.

The core question for most people will most likely be Friday the 13th or Dead by Daylight?

If you don’t own either of the games yet, start with Dead by Daylight.
And here is a reasonable conclusion why:
DbD is cheaper and offers way, waaaay more content than F13. (look at the bottom of the review)
DbD lets you rebind your controls, F13 does not. (and F13 requires way more control-keys than DbD does)
DbD lets you play solo as Killer, solo as survivor, survivor group from 2-4 players or in a private match. F13 lets you set a preference on whether you want to be Jason or a Survivor, so it comes down to luck who you end up being and of course you can play in private lobby too, if you got enough friends in your steam list to fill it up that is.

Engine / Performance / Control / Gameplay experience wise .. or however you wanna call it, DbD and F13 feel equally clunky, they work for the most part but neither feels like a polished game.

Both games require grinding/farming to unlock stuff (DbD more in the longer run, but it is present in both games nonetheless).

And last but not least, both games had a very crappy release. DbD had one and F13 has one too, in fact a lot of indie games suffer from this.
Anyway, the point here is that you can either buy F13, go through the “we have no idea what we are doing”-release months filled with problems & bugs OR you can just get DbD for half the price with 2-3x the amount of included content and on top of that (compared to F13) also get a “finished” game that actually works by now.
Once you get tired of DbD after a few months you can still revisit F13, which should be enough time for the devs to improve upon the game and hence provide a better experience. (plus you probably will pay less too or end up getting a fair amount of content for the money you pay)


So just to clarify I’m not saying DbD is better than F13, I’m just saying it's the better investment for the time being, especially if you don’t own it yet.
And even if you do own DbD and are tired of it (or have been hoping F13 is the savior of the franchise) then I still would not suggest you to buy it yet, because quite frankly F13 is nothing more than an alpha game sold at full price. (and yes DbD kinda did this too but more on that later)
The matchmaking does not even work properly in F13, the price to content ratio is hilariously bad, especially when paired with the obviously unfinished state of the game. The “fear face” of the survivors is just a joke, so is the physics, collision, combat, netcode & aim system in the game itself.
If the devs are serious with the game and want to provide a good game rather than making a quick buck, I have no doubt that all of this will be fixed in due time and the game will become playable and a suitable competitor for DbD and the likes. However at the current state it's not worth more than 10€ and honestly steam should force them to put the early access tag on again.
Obviously it is not fair to compare DbD and F13, because DbD had way more Dev time and had an easier time getting started because quite frankly it had no competitor in the genre. But hey, it sux, but that is business.
I mean honestly, if you like to support "trick your customer" developement like this and dont have a problem with anything I stated, go and get F13, they probably will need the money anyway.

DbD: 20€ base game, no DLC  (or for like 13€ on ebay..)

DbD: 41€ with all DLC's (excluding cosmetic & soundtrack DLCs)

I like Visuals Novel in general and while I was a bit disappointed by the lack of choice in this one (making it pure story and then not so much a "game"), the story was really great. It moved me much more than I expected. I could really feel the world and imagine how life would be on the Moon.
The story brings some uncommon themes such as trading (and it's explained well enough so you don't have to be an expert to follow), space colonization on the moon and the social issues arising from it. The Moon is now the centre of wealth, which happened only because of the hubris of every big corporation from Earth which decided to move there. The Moon is forced to import resources massively from Earth and would actually die fast if the space elevator were to shut down.
The main character ran away from his home and seeks to make money with the stock market to achieve his dreams. This game is only the first part so the story keeps going and you will have to wait for the translation to be completed before you can enjoy the end.
I do have one thing that bothered me in the story about the scientific accuracy. While I won’t argue with how human colonization on the moon was possible (since it is still after all a subject of research), the errors in high school physics (Newton’s law) was a bit more troubling and people ought to remember that while the weight changes on the moon the mass doesn’t and a punch has no reason to be delivered with a different force.

This game is fantastic if you like the Half Life franchise. It consists of the almost identical progression system where you are introduced to more and more guns as you progress and soon figure out which guns work better for which scenarios.
It's not a fantastic game over-all by any stretch of the imagination but if it only costs you less than 2 and half a buck there's no reason to pass on it. It'll definitely make the money worth, especially if you are hunting for more games like Half Life.
The most evident flaws I have with the game is that half-way through, only then, did I realize that you could peek around corners and shoot, which basically kept 90% of the damage away from you while you could still shoot perfectly fine.
This made a HUGE difference, and even on hard I started to feel that the game became a lot more fair. What makes the game seem unfair to begin with is the unforgivingness of the AI, and it's dead-on accuracy in some situations. But if you just cover around corners and utilize the Q and E-keys, you should be fine for the most part through. The game may or may not have explained this mechanic to me that clearly so that I would realize it's there, but nontheless.
I did encounter a single enemy that was completely invisible, in the same moment that I found myself almost completely out of ammo, which really made me question if the game was mean't to be beaten or not. Nontheless I decided to minorly cheat past him, which is totally possible by the way if you feel bamboozled in some areas. It didn't really affect gameplay much after that and it kept playing along fine.
The melee option is not that useful and I think they should've made it a lot more viable to get ammo back.
Because of the non-regenerative health system, it's hard to get back into the game once you're behind it, but it is certainly possible with the tips and tricks ab-fore-mentioned.
Health is not terribly rare to come accross though. Usually every other room of enemies has a health station, or a medkit, that keeps you in the fight, and you can almost completely cap out before you fight [any/the] boss(es).
Just make sure that you quick-save a lot in this game if you are going for the most daring of difficulties. F5 and F9 are your best keys to use throughout the game.
The hacking mechanic is a nice touch but it loses potential further into the game once you pass half-way, sinc eit becomes rarely used, but it's fun to mess around with at first and definitely is refreshing. If you can grasp it's usefulness properly, you can probably play the game out almost stealthly in a way, which feels nice.
The story is certainly compelling, a little typical of a story in some ways, but it works alright, and it's not terribly difficult to keep up with.
I never ended up using the
though because it was simply too terrible to use in every single case. I would not recommend it at all.
Over-all it's not an awful game. Great for a weekend. Not enough to justify on paar with Half Life, but it's certainly worth picking up on a sale if you have nothing of the sci-fi genre left to play. Runs fine on Windows 10 too.

This is the first game by Frictional Games I've played, and I'm highly impressed. The story was brilliant and the atmosphere was so intense that I felt a sense of dread when I would boot up the game, but I wanted so badly to press on and get to the end.
A few times, I had to pause the game and tab-out to watch someone else complete a section on YouTube before I felt comfortable continuing. This was mainly due to the monsters. I agree with many that they could have been left out. I don't think they added a whole lot and toward the end just became a nuisance. The atmosphere was so tense that I still would have felt unnerved if I hadn't been trying to avoid anything.
[SPOILERS]
What I really liked about the story were the heavy ideas addressed and the emotional punch delivered at multiple points. I felt really guilty harming robots, and Simon coming to grips with the "copies" was rough. That being said, sometimes Simon's voice acting failed to properly convey the tone of what he was saying, and several times he seemed far too calm considering what had just occured. Overall, the performances were excellent and I really liked Catherine.
[END SPOILERS]
Performance-wise, the game ran great. The framerate usually dropped when transitioning to a new area, and there was some hitching at times, but that may have been due to my GPU and the lack of a Crossfire profile. These minor issues ruined the immersion a bit, but the quality of the game just pulled me right back in.
SOMA is an amazing game and I am really looking forward to whatever Frictional release next. I'll definitely be playing Amnesia at some point in the future as well. For now though, I think I need to play something a bit less serious.

What makes SOMA great is that it keeps you thinking.  Something too few horror games do.  And the ideas it presents are often far more terrifying than the monsters themselves.  Because the monsters can be beaten (in a sense), but those ideas stick with you long after you finish the game.
The ideas are not new.  Any freshman Philosophy student will identify them right away.  But they are delivered in a way that I don't think has really been explored before in video games.  And it's all hung on a wonderfully realized framework of sci-fi psychological horror.
If you are paying attention, you will be able to figure out the ending.  This is my only complaint with the game.  I knew how the game would end because the rules were laid out fairly early on.  Following them to their logical conclusion meant the game ended exactly as I expected it to.
That being said, the journey to get to the end was absolutely fantastic!  SOMA is designed to stir discussion.  Again, something too few horror games do.

I really enjoy this game. It's very ressource-management -ish but that is not ment as a negative. It fits the whole apocalypse theme. I've played with several families, some of them did better than others. The worlds are randomized - sometimes you get a very "hard" world where you have to travel far and sometimes you get a much more manageable world.
When someone goes exploring it costs water yet they don't consume food or water while gone. Your family gets to have a pet at the start of the game and depending on the pet there are various advantages and disadvantages to each. Say a horse or a dog can go with you exploring, a cat catches mice etc.
People can die from starvation, radiation sickness, wounds from fights with strangers, dehydration - and they can (if you really mess things up) get traumatized and go insane.
It is a bit annoying that the rain is so randomized. Sure, that's more realistic. But that doesn't help when one of your guys die because it hasn't rained in forever. And then, as if to taunt, it rains five times in the next three days.
But if you focus on setting traps and building water containers and sending out expeditions as soon as possible - you can get a decent start and survive.
To sum it up: I really recommend giving it a go. Once you get a hang of what's going on and are able to survive it gets very entertaining trying to build your shelter and explore the world aound your bunker.

Supergiant Games’ new game, Pyre, in the simplest of terms is a mystical 3-on-3 basketball league where everyone is seeking redemption. The gameplay is a series of 3-on-3 basketball matches to gain the right to play in the liberation rite. Winning the liberation rite means being returned to the Commonwealth and released from all previous wrongdoings. The matches are called Rites and the goal is to deal damage by scoring slam dunks/shots into the enemy’s pyre. I would recommend playing to learn more about the story. As a player of this game for a while, I decided to throw my two-cents into the game. It's not an easy game. You'll die a lot early on. It's a game where a lot of the frustration comes from the random roll of events and the loot you get. Yes, you can do everything right and still lose. That's life. It's very rogue-like in the sense that you're always learning from the randomized elements.
If you're the type of person that can't get over an indy game's visuals, slightly clunky controls (which mostly have hotkeys), and a rather ruthless RNG...then the game isn't for you.
Lemme tell you what I find enjoyable with this game. Firstly, it's got a lot to do. You can expand your base to four sub-levels, giving you loads of oportunity to make the game your own. The base essentials (generator/air/water/contruction) can all be upgraded 3 tiers (and except for construction they can be leveled in different ways). This game also loves to ♥♥♥♥ with your ingrained video game logic. You'll rarely bring enough containers to carry most things you find. You'll never have enough space to store everything. This means you're always looking for certain things. It's not like "these items are rare so always get them". Some games you're always hungry. Some games you're not. Some games you can get loads of materials to upgrade. Some games you're struggling to get enough water to go that far! It's not easy, but god damn it's fun.

(Very) good games are pretty rare nowadays, especially for PC gamers. I have been looking a long time for a game that can hold my attention span for more than 10-20 hours. Few games could, like Fallout: New Vegas, Diablo 3, CoH2 and some others. Lately I’ve rather been collecting games instead of playing them like many others on Steam. Just playing them for a few hours and thinking “no, this is not it…” and ending up with 1.5 – 10 hours played and already getting bored. So which game could pull me in for more than at least 200 hours?
When Graviteam Tactics: Mius Front came out I already played around 10 hours on Graviteam Tactics: Operation Star. The controls, the confusion about what’s going on, the lack of a good tutorial, it all added to putting the game down and thinking: “Nice game, but I’m gonna try a few others first”. But when GT:MF came out, I immediately bought it. I guess something in my unconscious, said: “Buy it. Just buy it! And give it another try!” It still took a few months, but after being disappointed by another bunch of games, I started GT:MF, and this time with the determination to not let go before I got the hang of it.
And after another 15-20 hours, it struck me thinking: there is absolutely no equivalent to this game when you like RTS war games. GT:MF (and also GT:OS) will leave you speechless. If and only if you persevere the first few hours playing this game. And with “first few” I probably mean the first 100 hours and more. It is so much more than a RTS game, it is a real battlefield simulator. And a damn good one too! Don’t rely on the fact that when you issue orders, your soldiers will simply obey them. If your commander is too far away and you don’t have telephone and wire cables set up, your orders will not be transferred among other things.
GT:MF is no click-fest like most other RTS games with intense micro management. No, it focuses on careful planning, creating strategies, coordinating combined forces of infantry, cavalry and anti-tank units, setting up defenses, entrenchments, fire archs, calling in air strikes or artillery, which shells to use, reinforcing units, line of sight etc, etc, etc. Everything is done during three phases: the strategic, the deployment and the operational phase.
Replenished your units and carefully planned your defenses during the strategic and deployment phase? Well, you can bet the AI will try to circumvent you and attack from completely other directions you thought they would attack. When you thought they only had a few tanks, suddenly there are ten T34’s crushing your only three PAK’s you set up in the villages of Marinovka or Stepanovka. Key points can switch hands multiple times during the campaign.
Because the campaign is long! Very long! I only played part of the Marinovka – Stepanovka campaign as Germans and I am still playing it. After reinforcing my units at strategic phase Turn 1, the Soviets attacked my positions from… Well, almost f****** everywhere!  All these battles you have to fight before you can replenish your troops and start Turn 2. I played for 20 hours now and I am still in Turn 2. No campaign will be the same, so the amount of replayability is huge!
GT developers made it possible to transfer your units under AI command and I must admit, I do that a lot. But when the Russians come too close I take over command. But the AI is smart and you can sometimes sit back, relax and watch all hell break loose. Most of the time I use the “helicopter view” to direct my troops, but when you zoom in, the physics of the explosions and hits are so good. I always zoom in after the battle to see the statistics and devastation on the battlefield. You can watch the statistics to see which hit did most damage and which hit knocked out that tank or PAK or whatever. Which brings me to the level of detail.
The game is so insanely detailed: everything is carefully crafted and added to the game: weapons, calibers, tanks, anti-tank, artillery, armour penetration diagrams (ridiculously detailed), ammunition, morale, command level etc, etc, etc. If you’re a World War 2 / history fanatic like me then this is definitely a (no, THE) game for you.
Another thing to mention are the carefully crafted environments and staff maps. Heights play an important role and you better plan your strategies based on these on the information on these staff maps. It is all there on the maps: the gullies, hills, rivers, woods, farms, bridges. I immediately believe it if they say it is exactly the same as it was in 1943. The surroundings, the atmosphere, the tension during night battles with tracers flying everywhere. Man, this is a tactical wargame! Nothing comes close and all other wargames are redundant / unessential for me now. I am not saying other RTS war games are rubbish but no game can ever live up to the standards of this one for me.
DLC will bring you new campaigns and I just bought Dawn of Blau as well as a few other expansions for GT:OS (some depict the Afghanistan campaign and one does the conflict in Angola bringing you new tanks and units). Do I need it right now? No, but the DLC for GT:OS is sometimes on sale like it was this weekend. Was the DLC for GT:MF also for sale? No, but these developers deserve my money for this one. This is the game I was looking for to sink more than 200 hours in. And I will!
Most of the stuff I found out myself. But if you’re stuck or confused (and you will get stuck or get confused in the beginning) there are plenty of good tutorials on YouTube. I recommend the tutorials from Arch Warhammer or Agrippa Maxentius. They explain a lot and it’s worth to put some time into watching these videos as they make it a lot easier to get into the game. Be as tenacious as the Germans or the Soviets in this game and you will be rewarded with some very memorable moments. After twenty hours I can’t count them anymore as I won and lost various battles but each and everyone of these battles had it’s share of the finest moments in my overall gaming experience.
I am still confused about some partsof the game: buttons, movements by the AI, artillery strikes off target although I planned it carefully, replenishment of troops and lots and lots of other things. But never ever has an RTS game with a slow pace given me so much excitement and joy. It keeps me on the edge of my seat and I found myself sometimes staring at the screen whispering: “Take out that bloody T34, for heavens sake!”
Totally and highly recommended! I can not praise this game / these games and the developers enough! I already collected some medals during battles but if there was one with the Order of the Ukraine, it should be pinned on the chests of these wonderful men and / or women of this game studio. You deserve it!

DISCLAIMER: Despite showing only 1 hour of game time on Steam, I have been playing the game quite frequently using the desktop launcher because of early issues linking my Steam account to my Survarium account.
At first I was really skeptical due to mixed reviews but it's actually a decent game with plenty potential to improve! It's not P2W but you can pay(a ridiculous amount of $) for premium or weapons and such. Premium may help with leveling but the weapons you have to pay for aren't going to make you any better than the next dude who only has F2P weapons. On the topic of purchasing things, with the in game currency you can permanently purchase weapons+equipment to swap as you like! This is a huge deal maker for me because in previous F2P games that I've played the big deterrent was buying 7-day use gear/weapons that you'd have to purchase again and again to keep them. This game doesn't have that issue at all!
Now, like every other beta/early access game there are going to be performance issues. There are periodic bouts of lag/rubber banding and the servers aren't exactly what I'd call rock-solid... But the only real gripe I have about the game is the users for the most part. It's the lobby queing that makes other game modes nearly inaccessable(especially with the influx of new players). I wish the lobby system was set up better so that you aren't locked into TDM all the time just because everyone else only has TDM selected. I love research mode and haven't even gotten a chance to play the 3rd available game mode...
All in all it's a decent game in my opinion. Lots of room for improvements but that will come in time I'm sure! It's free, just download it if you're even remotely interested and make an opinion for yourself!

Characters

Narrative
This a mixed feeling where the narrative can be improved. The story is been told by the main character, Hai. He was introduced as arrogance young boy who became interested in the stock market. At times, Hai can be childish and annoying and many new reader can start to hate him. Personally, Hai's narratives helps show his character and personality and better understand him on how he view things and his thought. This is a plus in my book but the thing that annoy me is how Hai described economy terms, the stock market and the setting. The narrative did explain the reader of their situation to better understand them but it intend to be long and may have to reread it to understand. Not very easy to catch up with the explanation and few times i have to reread it. Not a huge minus but it can be improve to make it easier to read.
Visual/Sound
Mostly good on both the visual and the sound. The artstyle is very good quality and presented the situation in story very well. There were many rememberable artwork in the story and love everyone last of it. My only complain of the artwork is not enough. There are times in the story where i just see pitch black and block of text. This frustrate me because i want more artwork rather than leaving it to my imagination to image the artwork. The music helps set the mood of how story was presented. It helps feel the emotion of the character and situation. The music has like few rememberable songs I like for example, Escape.
Story

Overall

Where do I start?
I strongly recommend this game to any petrol-heads or car fans out there. I might not be a good competitor for racing simulators, but it keeps its title as one of the most realistic soft-body physics games ever to come to public release.
The physics in the game are insanely accurate and precise, you can replicate real-life crashes with surprisingly similar results.
I would not really call this a game though... I would call it more like a Simulator, or Tool for soft-body physics.
Again, for the petrol-heads and car fans, this game can teach a lot on how a car works, both outside and inside. In this game you can answer those weird questions about cars that you had in your childhood. How does a driveshaft work? How does tire-pressure change handling, all of this you can try out here, on any road surface you like.
After spending half of my "precious" life on the internet, you can see that there are a lot of unanswered questions about cars, and how they behave. Back then in my childhood I used to have Mythbusters running and watched them do these experiments, from which I asked more questions. Like as an example:
A car travelling at its top speed hitting a wall head on! Yeah, you can find this safety footage stuff on the internet with cars going city speeds crashing to weirdly shaped obstacles. But what many of us want to see is... Destruction! And it's true!
You want to see how small you can crumble a van? BeamNG is for you!
You want to test how big of an engine you can put in a small 3-wheeled car? BeamNG is for you!
What about a drag race between identical cars with different tire-pressures? BeamNG is for you!
Want to replicate popular race crashes? BeamNG... Yeah, I think you got the idea now.
It is a great game with good balance in simulation and just having fun. You can not complain it to be too boring, because if that is so, it is not the fault of the game, it's the fault of your imagination. Because honestly? You can test pretty much anything related to vehicles in this game.
Enjoy the game as much as you can, as there is lots of fun things to experiment with.

I have been holding off on writing a review for this game because I've had some tech difficulties which I've still been unable to solve - I got an error that caused Windows to force close the game, and when I restarted it my cursor had gone missing! I tried changing the settings.ini file to turn it back on and checked the cache, neither of which solved the problem. Luckily I have a combination laptop/touchscreen, so was able to continue playing. I still have quite a few achievements left to gain, but I finally worked my way through all of the puzzles just now, and when the music at the end began playing I knew I had to stop and write my review right that minute! If my online name is puzzling to many (elpfan), it stands for Emerson, Lake, and Palmer fan. They were a prog band who began their career together in 1971, and whose second album release was their adapted and added to version of Modest Mussorgsky's "Pictures At An Exhibition", which also happens to be the closing music to Collisions! And while the devs didn't use ELP's version, I love the music regardless of who performs it, and greatly appreciate the fact that someone else loved it enough to make it the finale for this game.
I know - as a game review, this one sucks. But honestly, it's a physics based get the ball to go places game, having a nice ambience, beautifully understated background graphics throughout, and an everchanging soundtrack of music and sound effects that soothe rather than intruding. Even with my disappearing cursor, I can easily give this game a 4.5 out of 5. I'm going to have to find the solution for the cursor though, if I plan on playing it much more...the pad of my forefinger is practically numb from trying to  bounce and spin and flip and otherwise maniipulate the flippers and buckets and wheels that move the balls around. Imagine playing an old-style pinball machine, but that you have to flip the flippers each time with your fingertips. There are times when speed and reflexes absolutely make a difference, and, while I have a sore finger, I also noticed that my gameplay improved considerably when using the touchscreen as opposed to controlling play with the touchpad and buttons.
I'll be going back and playing more - if for no other reason than to make it all the way to the end again! Besides - I haven't gotten to kill any bugs yet, and I have a lot of frames that haven't turned yellow. (perfect solve) If you're looking for some relaxing, yet somewhat challenging playtime, give Collisions a try. Or if you happen to also be a Mussorgsky or ELP fan! ;-)

Alpha Prime is a very basic scifi first person shooter. I'm going to start off with the pros. The story got me hooked, it's the only reason I kept playing. It was easy to follow, there were a few plot twists, good stuff. The Italian prospector you meet early in the game was ridiculous. The stuff that happens will keep you entertained. The game has many faults though, and most of them are in the mechanics. First the AI. It's very unfair in how good it's aim is. Other reviewers are not kidding. Either the path was way too hidden, the corriders look alike and I was going in circles, or I couldn't drive the sensitive buggy where they wanted me to, etc etc.
Overall, I believe you can get better similar scifi FPS games like Doom 3, Half-Life 2, Fear for the same price as this. I already had this for years when I started playing. I was one of the people trash talking the game when the beta footage was released, but now that it's come out its a ton of fun. I played the game for 11 hours straight in my first session.
The game actually has a lot of depth that isn't initially obvious. every character has varying stats that make them good at some things and terrible at others. For example, the goth chick is a stealth character who can easily hide, but is a weak fighter. Other jock type characters are good at fighting Jason and stunning him, but make a lot of noise as they move around.
There are several different ways to escape, and teamwork is a big part of most of them. There are even alternative ways to win, such as killing Jason through secret means, or simply hiding and surving until the time limit expires.
Performing various actions in the game will earn you experience points, unlocking new counselors and Jason variants. You also will gain "CP" every match to spend on new Jason kills and counselor perks ranging from "Poor" to "Epic" Rarity. Perks have both negative and positive effects, so knowing which perks to assign and which perks to sell is part of the learning curve.
In closing, the game is just fun and plenty of people play it right now, so you don't need to worry about not being able to get into a lobby. you'll easily get your moneys worth out of the game if you buy it now.

I recommend it though, I hope the developers are going to fix some of the problems, and add PvE servers.

There aren't many games I can compare the overall experience of Pyre to. Perhaps The Banner Saga, in parts, but nothing else really comes to mind. The game oozes creativity, and feels like such a fresh experience. It's easily one of the best games I've played this year.
Pyre is nothing short of incredible. The artwork & animation are absolutely beautiful - some of the most beautiful I've ever seen. The music is lovely, and complements the atmosphere of the game perfectly. The quality of the writing throughout the entire game was phenomenal, honestly better than 99% of the books I've read. The game gives you choices that can actually have a significant impact on the outcome of the game - yet you're never left feeling like you made the wrong decision.
The characters have clearly been designed with meticulous thought, and are full of personality. The narrator of the rites is one of my favourite video game narrators of all time (if you loved the narration in Bastion, then you'll have an idea of what to expect).
I wasn't sure how I felt about the rites at first, with the reviews of others having left me prejudiced. I quickly grew to love them. The rites can be incredibly intense. They begin relatively simple in order to tutor you (as expected), but steadily develop into a complex, genre-defying sport/game that works fantastically. There are a whole number of options for perks, talismans, characters and more which keep the rites feeling fresh and interesting throughout the game.
Having taken the time to write this and think back on my experience of the game, I would rate it 10/10, on the basis that I can't think of anything I would consider a flaw, or in need of improvement.

Commonwealth is a fantasy land where you can get a life sentence for stuff like terrorism, war crimes, literacy or having no family. Exiled into the dark Downside, your only chance at freedom and absolution is to collect a team and win a game of magical football.
Well, that's about it. The game is a mix of interactive novel and sports, quite a new experience from Supergiant. On the other hand, you get all the good stuff: the sense of fleeting beauty, longing and desperation, music that is a vital part of the game and changes along, breathtaking visuals. But the best thing so far is the characters: your teammates and opponents have their personalities and agenda, and the more you get to know them, the more their history is revealed. Both your wins and losses progress the narrative in a very natural way, the relationships between the charaters develop, and you get to make some hard choices.
I found the beginning of the game to be a bit slow-moving, with some empty dialogue and little meaningful interactions, but that changed for the better. The action itself can become a bit repetitive, but the diversity of charaters and an urge to change things up from time to time barely fixes that problem. The world was a bit too heavy on lore, but that one's completely optional.
I also found myself not caring too much about the “big picture” of the game mission, and getting overly attached to particular characters. I'd say overall music, action and emotional impact worked better in Transistor.
Pyre is beautifully made, with plot variability and nice replay value, and full of living creatures of all shapes to get your sympathy, compassion, hatred, disgust, admiration — anything except indifference.

So I just finished the campaign and the whole experience left me kind fo puzzled, but in a good way.
It is certainly interesting from a game design point of view and I think it is almost worth playing just to see the unique way the story and gameplay are presented.
The game really provides you with a flavorful and different outcome for all your choices and while the overarching story is short and straightforward, they really took giving every player a different experience to an extreme - even the music that plays during the credits is customized to your personal achievements. Of course the depth of story is going to suffer a little if so much breadth is provided, but in my eyes this was done very carefully and didn't devalue the experience. Rather it left me wanting to know more about a fascinating world that I'm still not even beginning to understand and wondering, what other facettes of personality the characters I learned to care for might have, which I didn't get to see in the short time we shared.
The core gameplay of the rites is very interesting and works well. The performance of the computer controlled enemies is a bit all over the place - sometimes mercilessly exploiting your weaknesses, sometimes just staring puzzled at what you are doing. At higher difficulties or with a few boni to the enemies attributes the game is seriously challenging. At normal difficulty I managed to only lose a few games, but there are many options to make the game easier or more difficult and I suggest you use them to find a level of challenge that is enjoyable for you. I am kind of curious how the story would have turned out had I simply played on a higher difficult setting. My biggest complaint is probably that the filler matches outside of certain key points in the story don't really feel like there is much at stake.
Other notes: I definitely recommend playing with a controller. The graphics look great and fit the style and tone of the game perfectly. The soundtrack is simply amazing and beautiful!

Comparing the games, Doom and Half Life there are actually quite a few similarities in the mechanics and gameplay. Half Life follows a sort of linear open world, or rather, levels that the player is left to explore and progress.  Doom contains open levels with areas to be discovered and an exit to find to progress to the next level.  Each game is absent of regenerating health instead the player must find heath themselves.  In Half Life the player can find heath dispensers and suit chargers (like armor) on walls.  Holding the interact button will recharge the player’s suit. In Doom, the player can find health and armor lying around maps, just walking over them will equip them to the character. There are major mechanic differences between the two games. In Half Life the player is able to look in 3D directions, jump, and crouch. In Doom the player can only look in 2D directions, cannot jump, or crouch. Each game’s mechanics work well for them respectively. With each game, the player must slightly alter their play style to adjust for the differences.
In Doom the player progresses through open ended levels searching for an exit. The player must find different colored key cards corresponding to colored doors to progress. The only way the game is progressed is to finding the exit of each level. After finding the exit the player is shown an overworld of levels cleared and levels remaining. Because of this open world design there is a lot of exploring left up to the player and quite a bit of getting lost as well. Visual cues will tip of the player that they have been to an area before, such as the bodies of demons already killed, as well as different room textures. One helpful thing about the game is the map (which I discovered late in the game), which can be accessed with the tab button. As the level would be traversed, the map would be created.  However, the player can find a map of the area which would reveal all rooms on the level greyed out, then once the area was traversed the map would go red. The mapped helped me out, although even after discovering it I still got lost, part of the fact for that is the heavily pixilated and dated graphics walls sometimes blur together making the 3D illusions of the game hard to discern. I did find a few secrets in the game, some by pure accident, others because I had a map of the area.  Sometimes I would stumble into a part of the map and after exploring further I came across a heaping pile of loot. Other times I could see on the map a yellow section (indicating a door) after pressing interact with the wall it would slide revealing its secrets. All in all I felt Doom had mediocre flow.  Sometimes levels were very easy to get through other times I was completely lost.  However, the faster I got through the levels the more things I missed, sort of a trade off.  I also played a bit of Shadow Warrior, quite different than Doom and Half Life. I’m not going to talk about it though, so I don’t even know why I brought it up.

I've never played a 'Graviteam'  made game before, so I'm totally unfamiliar with this developer. I have played Battlefront published games like the original Combat Mission series from 15 years ago or so. This game is somewhat comparible in style, however it is more or less a live action game after the pieces are set. This is not a RTS type of game like Company of Heroes, it's really a battlefield simulator with a God's eye view of everything and the ability to pause and speed up.
Unfortunately, the developer sort of dumps you straight into a main menu with a couple of large scenarios right off the bat. If you're inexperienced, don't try to play these, use the quick battle option and you will find several tutorial type of scenarios to run. These are extremely sensitive to deviation from the instructions. If you misunderstand an instruction or click the wrong button, you will probably have to start it over again to complete it. Fortunatly, these scenarios are small enough to avoid overwhelming a new player.
The game interface is quite difficult to understand and the overall presentation is not well thought out. However it is configuable and if you're willing to spend some time watching experienced players play this game on Youtube, it is not an insurmountable task to get to a point where you find it playable.
The sound quality is fair, but not great, I get a bit of popping and crackling with button clicks and other actions that is annoying with headphones on. The music is awful and I had to turn it off within minutes of playing my first scenario. The graphics would have been cutting edge 10 years ago; today they are passable.
The game play is actually quite fun. There is a setup phase, then a battle phase. The setup of your forces is a bit simplified, however there is a decent amount of complexity and you can do an adequate level of fine tuning of positions. The line of site tool is extremely valuable, especially during the deployment phase.
Once the battle begins, your task is mainly scanning your God's eye around the battlefield and prioritizing targets or adjusting force maneuvers/positions. You never control anything directly, you can issues orders. There is a great deal of complexity and some battles are so large, that micromanagement would make the game too tedious.
If you're looking for a good WWII battlefield simulation with lots of complexity and accuracy to details, you will like this. This is not the type of game most would enjoy or take the time to understand, but as a wargaming veteran, I am enjoying it.

Review edited after completing Episode 03.
World End Economica is a fairly lengthy kinetic novel (non-interactive story) that has a rough start but becomes rather engaging, and through its three chapters has become dear to me.  The fact that the story is about economics is at once both entirely tangential and ridiculously important:  Economics serves as the framework, the catalyst, and the bane of the characters' hopes and dreams.  The story makes dry, complex, or possibly alien financial concepts like stocks and financial crises both accessible and interesting, even while those same take second stage to the characters living in them.  I wish I could have gotten in on the kickstarter for this years ago, but I had no idea at the time how important this series was going to become to me.
The characters are engaging, sometimes loveable, and sometimes infuriating but also full of surprises.  They are easy to grow attached to for good or bad.  The mood music is spot on, and some of the artwork is breathtaking, both visually and emotionally.  As education, as literature, as art, World End Economica is an amazing product.
It was hard to find words to express how important World End Economica has been to me, so even with my own shortcomings I hope my review has helped you decide whether or not to invest in World End Economica.
I hope you have chosen to take the risk.

I was very reluctant to buy this game at first, it says episode 01 and I know there are more to follow. I was not sure how long it would be and if the story will end or just leave me hanging for a sequel that might or might not ever happen (been there, done that in the past).
However, I ended up buying it because of steam sales and oh boy was I wrong. Why did I not play this before?
The story is great, the artwork is amazing (aside for some secondary areas and backgrounds). This is
a "choose your own story" visual novel with multiple choices and paths, this is just a story. Do you like reading books? Do you like getting immersed in good stories? Then you will like this.
Do you play dating sims and visual novels with "routes" and choices? Do you just want some h-scenes? Then I'm sorry this is probably not to your linking.
The story is long enough to keep you entertained  (I clocked 13-14 hours), it is very interesting and at times not so easy to follow so it will require your attention most of the time. If you think you might not like economics and stock trading... well, you might be surprised because this story really makes you want to get more into it. I myself do not really enjoy stock trading but this story almost made me want to get out of my way try my hand at being an investor,it really is that interesting.
The ending fits well with the story and provides somewhat of a closure so you won't be left hanging in the middle of the plot only to be told "yo sorry, go buy the other episodes". Without spoiling anything, it leaves enough space for the following episodes, but at the same time you will feel content with what you have. Just like reading a good book of a trilogy, so do not be afraid to give this game a go. It is totally worth the money in my opinion.
