Bite Size Review - Velvet Assassin
The Good:
- Punishing but rewarding
- The setting is good and I enjoyed the voice acting (also the Germans spoke German, as someone who has played many WWII games, all I can say is thank you for this)
- Graphics are good, and the level designs are interesting and varied
- The morphine mechanic I found to fit the story and work really well (it acts as a free kill if the enemy finds you)
The Bad:
- Saves are checkpoint based, which can suck in some levels
- Missions from level to level can sometimes be boring/unclear
- Aiming is inaccurate, with enemies more than 10ft away being a problem to shoot with any of the games weapons
- Your inventory is limited to 1 primary weapon, 1 secondary, and a knife - so pack-rats like me will be leaving stuff behind whether they like it or not
- Leveling up Violet depends on finding in-game collectibles, which I found hard to do, meaning I felt under leveled for some parts of the game
- You can sometimes dress up like one of the German's and walk around like in Hitman, but you only really get to do this 2-3 times in the entire game
- AI is pretty dumb, and to compensate for this, the developer has given each one over powered weapons
The Verdict:
I really can not understand how people hate this game so much. Maybe if you've played nothing but splinter cell your entire life and felt like the lack of gadgets and climbing from those games made this game too punishing I can see someone being frustrated enough to give this game a negative review.
I on the other hand really enjoyed the game. It really forces you to pay attention to enemy movement and to see and wait for openings that allow you to kill them or move past them entirely. Even though it was an option however, to move past them, I found myself mostly having to kill them all in the hopes of finding one of the few collectibles in each level that are the only sources of EXP in the game, which is used to level up Violet. I wish leveling up was more based on completing the level than it was on these collectibles but the system worked well enough. All in all I had my issues with this game as you can see above but I did enjoy it, and beating each level was really satisfying. For $5 or less on sale, I think a lot of people will enjoy this game.
(P.S. I highly recommend searching online for ways to disable the blur effects the game turns on by default, the game runs and looks 10x better without this blur)

You could go into the game knowing that you didn't have to sink hours into it just to have fun let alone find anyone cause the maps weren't as big as they are (and they're constantly getting bigger it seems). I got food from those who died.  Yet once I learned the game giant herds started to become more a thing of the past, carebearing was just starting to become a target for public shaming, and I had grown personally bored with it.  So I became a part time KOSer and explorer, as the current maps got updated. I averaged playing Theri, T.Rex, Austro, and Trike. It was fun. There weren't any rules, it was just for fun, yet, deep in my heart, I knew this would all change, Nesting (at the time thought to be breeding), Survival, etc, were already known to be coming, and I had hopes that these would only make the game more entertaining to play, but as time progressed, I started to notice this wasn't the case, and soon many of the issues that would soon plague this game like a disease.

An amazing 7vs1 horror/survival game!
Having the Jason theme adds to the atmosphere, making you enjoy it more, and be more scared.
GAME SUMMARY
-You either play as counselors or Jason Vorhees.
-There are many counselors, each having different statistics (stealth, stamina, strength, composure, etc.). You can also buy perks (extra boosts/abilities) with in-game points, which you earn through playing; you actually get a lot (NO SPENDING MONEY).
- Counselor objectives are to escape (through boat, car, or police rescue through gathering items and fixing them), or survive the whole 20 minutes (which is hard to accomplish).
-There are also many different types of Jasons, each having different abilities and weaknesses.
- Jason's objective is to kill as many counselors as he can (there is no losing playing Jason).
-There are only three maps so far, but within each game the houses/cars/boat/etc. are randomized, making the gameplay different each time.
-IT IS FUN PLAYING BOTH JASON AND COUNSELORS!
OVERALL RATING: 3.5/5
- This is a super fun game! Interactive, cooperative, and even uncooperative! You will be scared running away from Jason, hiding from Jason behind bushes, trees, doors, under beds, and inside closets. You will enjoy playing as Jason killing others in creative ways, and even feel frustrated when they fight back.
- YOU NEED A MIC! Having a mic will add to the fun, and also make the game easier in your favor by being able to communicate with others (i.e. seeing if others have certain parts for cars). I believe any mic will work. I use a cheap $6 earbud with a mic, and it works fine. You can find out by going to settings on Steam and checking voice settings.
FLAWS
- $40 is quite pricey for the game due to the little content is has as of right now (although developers are working on more content). If you feel like you can live without this game, then you can wait for a sale (which will be forever). If you have the urge to play this game, then get it. You won't have any regrets because the gameplay will keep you engaged.
- It has some annoying gameplay flaws. These flaws consist of: closing the door while trying to stay in the house but you actually walk outside the house while closing, and getting stuck in rocks and bushes while trying to run away or chase.
*** Although there are flaws, I would highly suggest the game. It is still super fun.

Take note: my play time on Steam does not reflect my actual play time.  Steam's DOS simulator is incredibly buggy and not worth its salt, they seriously need to try and make a better port for this game.
That being said, once you manage to get a decent port working (mine being GZDoom) this game is amazing.  When you read the stories about the original PC gamers blowing up demons and tearing through the depths of hell you often take it for granted, but after playing this game over the course of a two-day period I've found that those tales are not exaggerated.  For a game that's as old as Doom it's aged quite well, and the game as a whole is immensely difficult even in the 'normal' difficulty later on.
By itself, without the extra mods thrown in, I'd give Doom a 7.5 out of 10; it's a fun shooter that's shown its age, but it's playable and guaranteed to give you a good time.  However I lowered the score largely because it takes forever to find the right ports to use and much of the tutorials that can be found that shows you how to play Ultimate Doom, the ports, plus any mods you want to have fun with have largely been lost in the annals of the internet, which meant getting everything set up took much longer than necessary.
However, throw in some basic mods such as, say, the Metal pack available among the downloads on Brutal Doom on the ModDB website, and I definitely raise the score to a 9.0.  This game's a ton of fun, and even more fun when you throw in the ridiculousness of some mods (Hunters Moon, for example).  Now that I've started, I can't wait to purchase Doom II and Final Doom and give those a try.

Welcome to my review of Settled!
-Intriguing Storyline, with plot twists!
-Retro-licious, 8-Bit Graphics.
-Simple, easy to play, and not demanding in requirements.
-Dark, macabre themes (if you’re into that ;)).
-Extremely Short (Under an Hour most likely).
-Errors with the program keep it running in the background after closing.
-No true Replay value
Settled is a Retro-style, Pixel graphics Adventure game, similar in style to Point-&-Click titles in that you wander around interacting with objects as they appear. The story is the most compelling aspect of Settled; you begin as a father who has lost his only daughter, and as the plot unfolds, there are some satisfying twists and turns that leave you guessing as to what exactly has happened. I don’t want to give away the ending, but the story resolution was intriguing and well worth the play-through.
The trouble is that Settled is an extremely short game -- although my hours played shows 18+ hours, I was able to defeat it easily within an hour of actual playtime. One aspect of the game that frustrated me is that, upon exiting through the in-game menu, the actual game program remained running in the background on my PC unbeknownst to me. When I finally realized that Steam had me flagged as in-game still, I was unable to find the Settled program even in task manager (despite other reviewers saying that worked for them) and I had to actually restart my entire ‘rig to get past this. The developer has stated that this should be fixed in the future.

The price point for Settled isn’t bad at all, even with the short duration. There’s little to no replay value here, unfortunately, but it’s still a ride I’m glad I took. If you’re on the fence, maybe wait until a sale pops up, but honestly, even at current price, it’s not a bad way to spend 60-80 minutes.
If you enjoy training your brain and your reactions in the same time go for it.!!

Half visual novel/RPG, half fantasy "sportsball".
This is the first game I played by Supergiant. I must say, I was a bit conflicted how I truly felt about this game. Most of the game is a very simple RPG, while the conflicts/battles are played out in this fantasy style sports game. Picture a traditional basketball or soccer game, where you can only control one player at a time, while your teammates remain motionless, and you can shoot your enemies to remove them from a game for a time.
I loved the look of this combat system and the idea, but when I played it at first, not so much. It just doesn't feel very smooth or easy to control. The game rules are very simple to understand, but I feel the combat system has a huge learning curve when it comes to controling the game mechanics. After playing it more and more, trying out different control schemes (which is extemely easy and offers mouse driven, WASD, or Gamepad) I found myself really enjoying the "Rites" (the combat system). I don't think the system is perfect, but I believe the devs are on to something. Keep in mind, I didn't come to this realization till just before I beat the game. The learning curve for controling the Rits was that high, at least for me. In the end I settled on mouse driven controls. You would think a Gamepad would be better for a game like this, but in the end, the mouse controls proved to be the least frustrating once I got used to them.
The RPG side of the game is nothing special, but does tell a good story. Simple choices will dictate upgrades, loot, or  story outcomes. This along with the epic soundtrack, surprisingly creates a lot of drama. Makes you more emotionally invested in the characters, even some of your enemies.  That fact that you can't lose the game facilitates this. There is no failure state. If you lose a battle, the story just continues. So it's more about trying to get the best ending, while seeing what happens or what stories you create with all the characters based on your decisions, and  your success.
The game comes with a Verses mode, where you can just make your own match-ups from all the characters in the game. It's unlocked right away, so beware of spoilers if you jump right into that first. I recommend not touching it till you beat the game. Verses mode has tons of options, but it's local mutliplayer only, or against the AI. For me, I don't think the Rites by themselves are enough to keep me interested long term. I need the backdrop of the story to keep it interesting to me.
Overall, I liked this game. The art direction and music is top tier. The game is almost worth the price for that experience alone. The RPG and combat system aren't the greatest by themselves, but i think the whole game comes together in the end. Out of all the games Supergiant has done so far, I hope they consider going back to Pyre someday. Either as a sequel, or just an evoltion of the gameplay they have created here.

Everyone is aware of the connection issues. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
I can only recommend it if you have friends to play with and can be fun to hang around with. The game servers usually test our patience with the constant disconnects, sudden lag advantage, and the occasional loading mid-battle (it seriously affects the battle everytime). Why I'm able to play through this is because of my friends alone. It can be frustrating, but we're not alone on it. Just me and my four bruddas having some fun.
What I can say is that the gameplay is intense. It requires you to not only use skill but with "mind games". From there you can create interesting scenarios in combat and play with your foe's mind. The game features a "feint" mechanic for faking hits and a parry to keep the edge in combat. Guardbreak is a wild card though, as you may not guarantee a free hit (due to counter guard break) or just end up falling off a ledge.
Oh and ledges, Jesus Christ just avoid them (or use them in a jiffy). They are an INSTA-KILL. It's ironic to have honor in this title because of environmental kills alone. But hey, just gotta get used to it and develop surrounding of maps. You wouldn't want to be caught in a spike trap on low stamina.
Matchmaking is another issue too. This game has not been noob friendly for early release. Often I was matched up with Rep 1+ experienced players, whilst me and my pals were only levels <10. It was hectic but we kept sparring on private matches and got gud (yeah you heard it). Eventually we were not so afraid of the higher reps. Just practise with friends or bots. What I personally like to do is spar with my friends and critique or moves. There's a bunch of meta to know for such simple movesets.
Moving on, I can say the gear score is another odd part of For Honor. Random drops for items with stats and cosmetics. This can be seen as P2W in this aspect, which I can agree is true. Even so you can still win by mind games, skill, environment kills and human error. The fact that you can purchase steel (a currency) to buy random crates is absurd though.
In summary: Matchmaking, balance, microtransactions, p2w random drop gear, and NETWORKING (the essential argument against this game) is terrible. But if any of this is fixed, then I would recommend the game very well for its interesting mechanics and combat.
I can only hope Ubisoft does a "Rainbow Six: Siege" all over again, by fixing all these Godamn connection and balance issues.

I love Arma 3 to death, and I'm not going to stop playing it for the forseeable future. The community really makes the game fantastic via mods and such, which drastically increases the replayability factor. Playing on a server with a group of friends can be endless entertainment. By two most substantial gripes are two generally shared by the entirety of the playerbase; collision physics and AI.
The collision physics are absurd and often lethal. A rework is a must, and I have not found any mods that rectify the issue. If you accidently ram your HEMTT into a Hesco barrier you're liable to take off into orbit and re-enter, taking the ISS down with you. Intertwined with this is the issue of serverside vehicles being dangerously fused together post-reset, which can injure or kill a player walking nearby without warning. Servers rarely place things in the right spots, and vehicles are no exception. Expect to lose a lot of time in multiplayer when a server gets reset.
The AI in this game seem to just be ported Arma 2 AI, with fairly non-dynamic tactics and a profound lack of adaptive strategy. There are mods that help with this, like GAIA, and make the AI less linear and predictable, but for those looking for a smart enemy that can take advantage of a situation strategically, set your expectations low for Arma 3.
That being said, this is one of the very best shooters out there. The mod potential, the weapons, the gear, the terrains, and all that are all quite good (You're gonna want all the RHS mods however, they're pretty vital). I would say that Arma 3's greatest asset is its potential, and for that alone I will gladly recommend it to all.

Sheltered definitely has some rough edges and flaws, but the game rewards players that pass the steep learning curve. The core survival strategy hinges (pun intended) on maintaining a sufficient level of resources, while collecting new resources to create improved equipment and upgrade systems. Survival can be brutal as a single mistake can destroy the shelter. I dismissed a recruit with poor stats who contaminated my water supply, and then came days of rain and black rain maintaining the contamination. Within a few days, everyone died of either dehydration or radiation poisoning. Lesson learned.
The scarcity of resources is simultaneously frustrating (hinges!) and rewarding. You have to constantly send people on expeditions and broadcast to traders to gather the necessary resources to build crucial equipment, such as freezers and beds. Learning what resources are common at what locations are key, as lumber mills unsurprisingly provide wood and school surprisingly provide plenty of rubber. Some survivor equipment unlocks additional resources, like the lock pick that allows survivors to find guns and ammunition in houses and farms.
Sheltered’s most significant flaw is the brutal learning curve and insufficient tutorial and documentation. My first two game experiences were brutal learning experience, moving progressively further to unlock . By my third play-throug and after plenty of discussion board reading, I’ve easily passed 60 days over several hours, with a strong group of survivors and plenty of resources.
Perhaps the beginning of the game, the steep learning curve coupled with the inefficient equipment, makes survival in the first 30 days so challenging, but the reward is worth it.

I doubt that you have ever heard of 2006's console exclusive
or the comic books published by Top Cow Productions (yes, that's the actual name... I couldn't make that one up) of the same name, so let me tell you a little bit about the unpopular
.
Or The Darkness 2 if you don't know your Roman numerals. If you don't, shame on you.
In
you play as Jackie Estacado, a member of the Franchetti crime family. He was adopted by the former Don of the Franchetti's, Frankie Franchetti at the age of six and matured quickly; he lost his virginity to a female officer durning an investigation at the age of fourteen and killed his first victim at the age of sixteen. His presence in the Franchetti family helped it to expand, as predicted by the mysterious Sonatine.
When Jackie turned twenty-one, he revieved the powers of the Darkness, a timeless power allowing the Host to form basically anything out of darkness (for example, the Arms) that will crumble to dust in the light. To keep it short, lots of sh*t hit the fan in a short period of time, causing his true love Jenny to be killed.
Years passed since then, and Jackie forced himself to keep the Darkness locked up inside of him after blaming it for Jenny's death.
That's where the second game begins and the Darkness gets unleashed again.
Sound interresting? Well trust me, it IS interresting.
The Good:
· Very solid shooter mechanics.
· An upgrade-system that will make you feel more powerful as the game progresses.
· You can control Jackie's sentient demon arms to grab enemies and objects and perform brutal finishing moves. (For example splitting a guy clean in half or ripping someone's spine out of his sh*tter. I know. His f*cking sh*tter. They just rip that open harder than Kim Kardashian's c*nt.)
· A surprisingly personal and meaningful story that will keep you interrested until the very end.
· The Darkness 2 plays with light in a unique way - standing in light will blind you and make you more volnurable, but being in the darkness makes you brutally strong.
The Bad:
· The co-op missions can easily be forgotten.
· Besides tha campaign, collectibles and co-op the game offers too little content to keep you coming back to it.
· Unfortunately unsuccesful, meaning that the chances of a third installment is highly unlikely.
The Ugly:
While the comicbook-esque and gore-filled visuals are a joy to look at, there's nothing too stunning about it. It never looks bad, but it doesn't look as good as it could have.
Final verdict:
This is a title I will always remember for its dark and unique setting, plus it's one of the forgotten "good comicbook games" out there that needs to be played, simply because it's an thrilling experience. 8.5/10

The following is a review for people who will likely play The Isle alone. Strap yourself in because it will be lengthy.
The Isle is a hardcore survival game that will test your sanity and perseverance if you play by yourself. You will be killed by nature, players, and happen to die by your own hand due to stupid mistakes. This will happen for the first 100 hours of the game, give or take.
The Playerbase:
The community many types of people, however, for simplicity, and time, I will split them up into two categories: Angels and Demons.
The Demons are only sated in the pain of others. They will kill without a second thought because it makes them feel better about themselves, and it inflates their ego. Trying to join them is pointless as they already have a close knit group of friends.
The Angels can be a blessing, if you aren't playing as a carnivore and starving. They will come to your aid and save you if they are in a protective mood, or if they think that the dinosaur you are playing is cute. However, if you are a starving carnivore they can be worse than the Demons as they will prevent you from killing anything.♥♥♥♥♥♥them off by killing a member of their herd/pack and you will have hell to deal with.
The Community:
In general the community is extremely, and I mean extremely self-entitled. They will press their ideas to the game developers without a second thought. Ignoring the fact that maybe someone has already come up with that idea, or maybe, just maybe, that it is a terrible idea in the first place. This has caused most of the developers to go from optimistic, excited, and ready to listen to the community, to pessimistic, annoyed, and demoralized at their continued work, due to the community's constant harassment. I know I would be going crazy if I had to deal with that everyday.
The Game:
As I stated in the beginning The Isle is a hardcore survival game, so if you are thinking that buying this game is a free ticket to go around as T. Rex, and rule The Isle, think again. You will spend hours of your life trying to reach this goal, only to have it foiled by a player who wants to murder you for fun. In its current build The Isle only has Dinosaurs, however, the developers will add mutated "strains" of certain dinosaurs, modern humans, tribal humans, and "Cannibals" which are almost alien like. I have no doubt in my mind that the final product will be a must have for survival game lovers, but in its current state, if you play alone it will not be a fun experience, not because of the developers, but because of the playerbase.
Verdict:
If you don't have any friends that play this game, and you don't intend to make friends while playing this game, avoid it in its current state. Wait a few months and come back and see if the good reviews have changed (Good reviews are ones that go into detail and explain why the game is currently playable, or unplayable).
I hope I managed to give a good explanation of why you should not get this game is you are a solo player.
Break down of my hours spent:
1/2 of my over 1000 hours have been spent cowarding in fear gaining "Progression Points" (this is needed to get to the next dinosaur) or watching YouTube while I gain "Progression Points".
1/4 of my time has been spent playing the game, and the other 1/4 has been spent talking to friends.

A fantastic and unique game. Playing as dinosaurs and having to think like them to survive. Not run around in a tiny arena playing deathmatch. Though that is possible in one of the game's current sandbox maps, but that's not the meat of the game.
Where the game really shines, in my opinion, is in progression. Where dinosaurs are tiered. So you start small and work your way up to bigger dinosaurs. And to unlock your path to the next, you simply have to survive long enough. With some paths being harder than others. Such as the rex. You have to go from a baby rex to subadult and then adult. And alone, a baby rex has to both be careful and cunning to survive.
The game also has a lot more planned than is currently in-game. More biomes. Humans, both modern and primitive. A strange unique cannibal group as well, adding an entirely different, more monster-like approach are yet to come. Along with more biomes and more dinosaurs. And not to mention, dinosaurs nesting. You'll be able to raise young and then invite a player to play as the young dino, once raised to a certain age.
The game has a lot of promise and things I certainly look forward to. And offers a unique take on the dinosaur theme, where you can actually play as one and try to survive.

TLDR: Buggy af. Jason is OP af. Combat is broken af.  But hey. Booty. Laughs. I'd get it again.
I am well aware that there are ten devs or whatnot working on this game and I highly respect that, and the fact you have a lot of work to do with bugs and future content etc. I get that. I definitely do.
Here are some things I think could be improved, if you'll see this at all:
1: Jason's grab. It's fun. Yes. It's hilarious and it's great to have those amazing kills. But his grab is so over powered. So many times have i had someone teleport on me, and grab me instantly and that's it. Game over. Pocket knife used? Ok, wait a few seconds, and then another grab. I think, that Jason should have to hit someone a couple times before being able to grab them and use the special. Get less points for just axing them down, and get more for using the special. Like a pokemon! You have to bring their health down before you can catch them! It should be the same with this game. The survivor should have low health before you can grab them. Otherwise it's incredibly frustrating and overpowered. I get it, Jason is supposed to be strong. But we need SOME chance of survival. I think that would improve this game IMMENSLY.
2: More ways to escape. We have a few, that's great. But many times if survivors die, or leave, or even escape, the rest that remain have practically zero chance of escaping. I feel that there should be ways for single survivors to escape or two even, that can be tough to find. Obviously you don't want it too easy otherwise the balance in the game will be too much in the counselors favor. Currently it's too much in Jason's favor.
3: Stealth. It's lovely. It's great to hide with.
Or is it? The mighty power of Sense renders even the stealthiest of characters quite painfully easy to find. Thus, lately people are just using the louder faster characters, because if you can't hide you might as well just fight Jason until you die or rush escaping. I feel that a 10/10 stealth character should be able to hide their fear.
4: Combat. Currently, with Jasons grab being slightly overpowered, combat is basically useless unless you can dodge his grabs and hit him with a sucker attack. That's okay I suppose, but I feel like if you were to folow the previous "advice" and make it so that Jason had to hit them a few times before grabbing, combat would be a lot more fun. We know we can't kill Jason without a loooot of work and organization. So this would more balance the combat as opposed to leaning in survivors favor.
I highly respect the devs for what they are working on and going through. I hope that they see this and at least listen.
Other than that this is a fun game.

I tried to like this game, I really did. But every chance it got it would screw me over, either putting me with team killers who don't get punished, or hackers who don't get punished, or crappy servers being hosted from some Russian guy's mom's basement. There are lots of things I like about this game, like the atmosphere and the sounds and the customization. But the cons far outweigh the pros. Here are a few examples,
- I finally get enough money and experience to afford the next bolt action rifle, so I buy it, I take it into a game and get lied to by the gun's stats. For example, "Damage: 110" the health of a player is 100, so I figure this is an instant kill, right? Never have I been so wrong... As far as I could tell, the damage actually means "11.0" because I have to fire multiple times into the backs of heads before they BLEED TO DEATH. 110 damage can't even kill a person with five bullets before they die from blood loss, not actual damage caused by the gun that fired the high velocity 30.06 round that obliterated their brain stem, "No, no no, that would make too much sense!"
- Servers are hosted deep in some gulag, probably, so I will constantly see someone skip around as I hopelessly flail around trying to hit him before just falling over dead with nothing to give me a hint in order to make an educated guess on what just happened. I once shot two people in the head (Multiple times), and killed them, only to have the server catch up and I end up getting practically gang banged by their whole team.
- The game starts you off with a Mosin Nagant, which does 100 damage (Supposedly). But it also gives you a submachine gun, which does 30 damage per shot. The Mosin Nagant has a fire rate of 36-40 rounds a minute, the PPSH has a fire rate of 1000 rounds a minute. The PPSH also barely has any recoil, and can expend its 35 round magazine (Which the 1941 model never had) in less than five seconds. Just let that sink in for a little. The Mosin Nagant has a damage per minute of 3600 - 4000, the PPSH has 30,000. So for someone like me who prefers to hang back and snipe, it gets frustrating when I get swarmed by a squad who have a collective fire rate of 3000 rounds a minute.
- I get into a situation where the guy I'm shooting at has a Mosin Nagant, and I also have a Mosin Nagant. I fire and hit him in the chest, he fires and hits me in the chest. Keep in mind that both of these guns have 100 damage per shot. I die, which didn't annoy me as much as the fact that he barely took any damage. When you hit someone the size of the hitmarker tells you how much damage you do, and if you see a red hitmarker it means you killed him (Most of the time, keep in mind servers are in some gulag). So when I see the smallest possible hitmarker on him but I die immediately, it makes me wonder. Mosin Nagants fire 30.06 ammunition, which usually will kill anyone instantly if it penetrates the chest cavity or neck or brain or whatever, simply because of its size and velocity. So when my round seemingly bounces off of his barrel chests with minimal damage, his explodes all of my internal organs and liquefies the skin where it entered. So... why does his gun, which is the SAME EXACT GUN as mine, actually follow the statistics that the game gives the gun, while mine just says "Here I'll roll some dice and see where that takes us". Why is his 30.06 better than my 30.06? They're both over 100 years old, both were dragged through two world wars and both were fired probably hundreds of times before they fell into our hands, so how come his can kill me instantly while mine barely rustle his chest hairs? (This has happened on MULTIPLE occasions, most of which are when the servers actually work)
- The game constantly reminds you of how much of a free to play game it is by flaunting deals that you can buy in order to get premium and gold, which you can use to buy MUCH better guns and armor for you to seal club with.
- When I first started this game I thought it was pretty fun, so I asked my friend to download it and start playing it, but there was one problem. There was absolutely no way to add friends. There was a friends list with a search bar, that I soon realized was to search through your own friend list, given that you have so many that you have to do more that scroll for half a second. There was also a squad button, which allowed you to search for players, but not to my surprise it was also to search through your friends list. So as far as my friend and I could tell, there was absolutely no way we could play in the same game together. I searched up online and grazed over the forums to see if I could find anything on the subject, but found nothing. By some miracle we ended up in the same game together and afterwards clicked on each other's names and clicked the very prominent "Add to Friends" button, which for whatever reason was literally the hardest thing to get done in this game.
- Map design is pretty good, until you realize its made for close quarters battle, which requires you to use the PPSH or any other extremely high rate of fire weapon, otherwise you're pretty much a free kill.
- The game has factions; Scavengers and the Black Market. I liked the sound of the Scavengers, because their armor and weapons reminded me of Fallout, but quickly realized that the scavengers are MASSIVELY underpowered until they reach level 5. We are graced with the presence of no armor, close range capabilities, or actually useful items like traps. At level 5 we unlock the Remington 700, which is the only scoped weapon in the game. I set my eyes on that but quickly lost track of it due to my frustration with the games inability to do anything correctly.
- The game reminds me of Nether.
- Team Killing and hacking, people not understanding what teammates are and people who snipe me from across the map through walls and obstacles. The teamkilling really bothers me because I'll find a nice spot to set up camp (Yes, I know, I play like an actual sniper instead of some small child with a .50 Cal jumping and spinning), and then suddenly some guy comes up and shoots me in the back of the head. It frustrates me even more when I realize its my own teammate! I quickly realized that the game does not punish you for slaughtering your own team and granting them the loss. So I attempt to get away from my team and go lone wolf, but alas, the giant bright triangle above my head that people can see through walls lets everyone know where I am. I only encountered a hacker once, but it was the most depressing things to ever happen to me in this game. I just sat there and watched as less than a second after I spawn I get gunned down by some 5 year old with a PPSH at his spawn. Our tickets ran out in about a minute, the child went 175 and 0, and I just watched as my death counter went up and up and up. It was at that point that I just gave up trying, I really wanted to enjoy this game, but I find it an impossible feat to accomplish.
Yes, there is a lot of hate behind this review, and I have a right to express my feelings towards this stool sample of a game. If you enjoy whatever this thing is trying to pretend to be then by all means play it, I'm not telling you what to think, I'm telling you what to expect. You can form your own opinion, and I'll gladly listen to it.

First of all it is very alike to "Survivor Stories" aka. "WarZ".
The UI looks similiar.
The Economy is simliar and so is the ingame market.
Pay for cash currency and ingame obtainable currency can be traded for items  in a "safe zone" in both or either currency near a global inventory market stall.
You can buy consumables, backpacks, vanity items and melee weapons, after purchase they get deployed in your current character's inventory.
You start with a server list.
After joining a server with max. 64 players you can choose your character's appeareance,
some appearences require gold obtained with real money.
Then you can choose to spawn in the world or you can spawn inside a safezone.
You start off with a knife and a box, which you can turn in inside a designated safe zone or outpost at a specific market stall's NPC.
For turning in the boxes you get experience, ingame cash and/or items.
These boxes can be obtained inside those outposts, they have abbreviations like WTO to WTM,
which indicates where the packages is obtained and where it needs to go.
Inside the safe zone, you can turn items found or given by delivery assignments into various weapons, some "junk" items can be exchanged into ingame currency, if you have enough of those items, if not store them in your global inventory for later.
The crafting system is simple. It's more like a turn in quest, you have item x + y + z, you can craft the "can gun" which fires shotgun rounds.
Outside the safezones it's very likely to be shot, chopped, stabbed or clubbed to death by other players.
Istead of zombies in "Survivor Storries" aka "WarZ" you get to fight different kind of monsters, apparently called "Nethers",
so far I encountered two types, first one attaks you via melee attacks and teleports around, the second one uses some kind of ooze on you and teleports around, both are easily killed and drop tongues, spines, vials of blood, skin and other entrails.
After death you loose your character's experience, but you get to keep your money, most of it, but your inventory is lost, except for mission items, I don't know though,
if vanity items or backpacks will be lost.
Loot is distributed by either containers or items direcly, in the case of containers you have to "open" it and then various items appear around the said container, then you just need to pick them up.
The game currently seems to be in some stage of early developement, but the level design is seems to be quite good and fitting for a post apocalyptic game, except for the largly scaled doors and ceilings, some things make less sense like the lights of emergency vehicles and traffic lights are always on even though the power supply should be dead by now.
Performance wise I didn't have any issues.
I haven't seen any warping or lagging players. The graphics don't seem up to par with other current gametitles, but seems to be in the upper range with simliar games of this genre.
Gunplay and Meleeplay is simliar to older titles (Half-Life), bullets hit targets immdiatly, fly straight lines in a fire duration dependant cone of fire.Melee weapons hit when the animation is finished and when the target is in range.
Currently I won't recommend to anyone in buying this game, either turn away forever or you wait for it to be more polished.
We'll see what they'll make with this game.

Sound design and graphics are pretty alright and really the only redeeming factor. Story is not particularly riveting as far as horror games go, and there isn't enough 'meat' to it to really call this a story-driven game.
There's no option to exit from or skip through text so everytime any appears on the screen (CONSISTENTLY only one or two sentences at most) you have to wait 5-10+ seconds.
The game would definitely benefit from ALL of the interactable items having flavor-text, not just the coat. It's not the only thing that changes so it doesn't make sense for it to be treated as such.
(SPOILERS)
You play as a regular old dad who's very upset his daughter died and has resorted to killing people and collecting cow heads to bring her back! Except, not really. The story is very unclear and the 'twist ending' where it turns out you're some random dude that killed the father because he wanted to have his daughter for himself did not clear anything up at all.
There's a motif of cow skulls and and sacrifice for what seems to be no real reason. There's a specific instance in the game (and in one of the preview screens) where the Star of David / Seal of Solomon is used in place of where a pentagram would be in a spooky game like this, but I couldn't find any correspondence between either symbol and cow heads so it doesn't make any sense. Literally the only thing that's cleared up by the """BIG TWIST""" are the scenes where you approach 'yourself' from behind all spooky-like (you as the killer are approaching the father from behind). Everything that isn't extremely obvious to piece together by just playing the game doesn't make sense at all.
If the twist was instead that the daughter got murdered and the father is sacrificing people to bring her back the game would make a LOT more sense (especially the scene where the wall says 'DAD LET ME DIE'?? like that doesn't make any sense in the context that you're playing the random killer).
The story is just a goddamn mess.

Settled is a pretty little game (that is if disemboweled people hanging from the ceiling fit your definition of „pretty”) that I have great many mixed feelings reserved for. Firstly, the gameplay is very limited even for the standards of an indie adventure game. Namely:walk left, walk right, interact. That's all there is to this game.

Furthermore, I can not really make up my mind whether I like the art style or not. True, that it is a brown-greyish (and ocassionally profound red), low-res, pixelated and rather fugly for the most part. And then there is the „devil” who looks surprisingly awesome for all his classic, horned, red – eyed image. Oh, and he is,but of course, symbolic, like it should be in a modern, ambitious, indie horror.
Then there is this rather frugal use of sound. Still, I'd rather argue that the player hears exactly as much (or, more specifically, as little) as needs to be heard and precisely in the right moment. Furthermore, the game never stoops so low as to employ the jump scares. The atmosphere is built by … oh, let me have it in a separate paragraph, k? Trust me, the aura that Settled manages to create deserves a paragraph of its own.
Well, the tension that Settled manages to build up and maintain is, unquestionably, the game's selling point. Although short, Settled manages to preserve that fragile balance between tension and gore without feeling cheap or incongruous for a moment. And in my opinion, that is enough to carry  a horror game through. Truth be told, I think that it would be prudent of Frictional Games (you know, these dudes behind Penumbra, Amnesia and lately Soma) to consider employing Allen Dayan (Settled's author).
Whether you sway towards psychological or gore, there are plenty horror games on Steam. Truth be told, the only reason for this review's existence is the fact that Corpse Party hasn't downloaded yet. Still, I believe this game is worth attention. Sure it is a half-an-hour experience, but that's more or less a price of a hamburger. And for the most part, there is more meat in Settled.
Wersja polska.
Settled to taka mała, urocza gierka ( jeżeli wypatroszeni ludzie przybici do ścian mieszczą się w twojej definicji słowa „uroczy” ) która wywołała we mnie sporo mieszanych uczuć. Po pierwsze, rozgrywka jest tu bardzo ograniczona nawet jak na standardy przygodowych indyków: idź w lewo, idź w prawo, użyj czegoś na czymś. Tyle.
Dalej; grafika. Nie mogę się zdecydować co o niej myślę. Przez większość czasu utrzymuje tonację szaro-burą ( z okazjonalną domieszką głębokiej czerwieni), atakuje oczy pikselami na pół ekranu i jest, co tu dużo gadać, zwyczajnie paskudna. I wtedy pojawia się „diabeł”, który to w całej swojej klasycznej, rogatej, czerwono okiej okazałości jest całkiem za*ebisty. I jest, oczywiście, symboliczny, jak przystało na ambitny, niezależny, współczesny horror.
Dźwięk jest zdecydowanie oszczędny. Powiedziałbym: słychać dokładnie tyle ile trzeba i we właściwym momencie. Dodatkowo gra nigdy nie zniża się do straszenia jump scare'ami i chwała jej za to. Settled buduje atmosferę w … pozwólcie że opowiem o tym w oddzielnym paragrafie. Nastrój jaki panuje w tej grze zasługuje na swój własny akapit, k?
Do rzeczy: napięcie jakie Settled buduje i jest w stanie utrzymać aż do samego końca jest głównym powodem żeby zapoznać się z grą. Settled nie wystarcza na długo, niemniej jednak jest w stanie osiągnąć ten niesamowity balans pomiędzy napiętą do granic wytrzymałości atmosferą a wiadrami krwi bryzgającymi z ekranu bez uciekania się do tanich chwytów czy wywoływania uczucia niespójności. Prawdę powiedziawszy, w mojej opinii Frictional Games ( czyli goście od Penumbry, Amnesii czy ostatnio Somy) powinni rozważyć zatrudnienie Allena  Dayana (czyli gościa od Settled) do projektowania cut-scenek. Serio, dokładnie takie miałem wrażenie grając w Settled.
Niezależnie od tego czy wolicie psychologiczny horror czy juchę lejącą się z ekranu, na brak gier na Steamie narzekać nie możecie. Tak właściwie, ta recka powstała głównie z powodu przeciągającego się downloadu Corpse Party z którym planuję się za chwilę bliżej poznać.Ale wracając do Settled, niby starcza na pół godziny ale kosztuje mniej więcej tyle co buła w Maku. A dużo więcej w nim mięsa.

Having played through the game end-to-end, with a handful of reloads in-between to try out different options, I feel like I've had enough time now to enjoy and put together a halfway decent review.
To preface, I loved Bastion, I played it (and the bonus/side-content) through three or four times. The music, the art style, the story, it was fantastic. The gameplay wasn't groundbreaking, but it also wasn't the focus. The world and story was, and rarely did the gameplay get in the way of that.
Transistor, on the other hand, I felt as though I spent way more time thinking about the game than enjoying the story/music/art, which to me is a major minus. I'm not buying a Supergiant game for gameplay, at least that isn't the driving force. I'm buying it for the art, music, and storytelling.
So. Pyre.
Let's get the negative bits out of the way first. I felt like the "tutorial" part of the game, which is essentially all the way up till your first liberation rite, is a little long. If it were up to me, I'd have back-loaded the longer "seasons" of the rites instead of front-loading them. That said, the snappy dialogue and likable characters make it enjoyable despite the slowness, and you'll reach your destination soon enough.
There are a couple of rite locations that can be buggy, depending on your actions, but it's nothing game breaking. I also found that the in-game things keeping track of locations you've visited and pages you've found for your book to be lacking and it makes it hard to be sure you've gotten everything.
I also feel like the end "villain(s)" were introduced a little bit late in the story, but that depends on how you look at it, and what choices you take.
Mostly, my issues are nitpicking, not any real fatal flaw.
On to the good stuff...
The rites can be a lot of fun, especially if you're rotating lineups to try and keep all your characters pretty even on XP/level (which you should). The variation in play styles, when you add in different trinkets and what-not, really allow you to figure out how you want to make your different teams work.
I especially like some of the late-game items you get from the slug market, even if they do kinda feel like joke items more than the high-risk/high-reward they're positioned as, it was entertaining to play around with them.
The cast of characters is fantastic, and while I feel like there were 1 or 2 that were sort of unnecessary, that may have been the point? Some of them have grand ambitions, others are just along for the ride, but that would make sense given that all the exiles are not created equal. You've got everyone from the corrupt rich to volunteers to rebels and war criminals, not everyone is going to be a hero or villain, some people are just trying to get by.
In the end, Pyre made me care a
about more characters than I thought I would end up caring about, so much so that I really wish I'd had more "seasons" and time to get to know them.
In summation, Pyre is great game that might be a little too long in some places, and a little too short in others, but the experience provided is more than enough to make up for any small shortcomings in one area or another.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have an alternate plan I need to try on another playthrough.

Something I believe I should note right off the bat is that
That doesn't mean Pyre is bad. No, it's the direct opposite of that. However, compared to their other games, this one might be harder for some to enjoy due to its heavy visual novel elements. Now that that's out of the way, I think the one word to describe how I felt after finishing this game is
Even if this is a more niche title, it doesn't change the fact that
is one of the best games 2017 has to offer.
By Supergiant standards, this is the best they've done in the visual department. While all of their games look great, this one was eye candy from start to finish. All of the different areas really set the tone, and the character designs are extremely diverse and unique. There isn't much to say here, but there isn't anything about the graphics I can fault. I don't think there's any way they could've done it better, because the game is absolutely gorgeous to look at.
Pyre's weakest aspect is its gameplay, however it's not bad at all. At worst, there was a lot of missed potential, but at best, you have an extremely interesting and unique take on football/basketball. There's no denying that Pyre's gameplay is extremely unique, and it's extremely fun. It's not completely polished, as certain characters like Ti'zo and Fae/Dae/Bae/etc. are ridiculously OP, but the concept is there and it works. I loved experimenting with the different playable exiles and adapting to the fairly dynamic (and constantly exciting) Rites, and the game encourages flexibility. That being said, the Rites themselves don't actually get all that interesting until about 1/3 of your way into the game, where more gameplay options are provided to you. It's quite understandable if you find yourself slogging through the first part of the game. But once you get passed that, the gameplay becomes far more complex and interesting. Also, it's important for me to mention, this game has awesome online multiplayer potential. I was surprised to hear this game didn't have online multiplayer, because the Rites are very enjoyable once you get through the beginning stages. Overall, the gameplay's still good, but definitely where Pyre falls short.
story made me feel a wide range of emotions. At some points, I was getting teary-eyed, and at other times I was audibly yelling at my monitor in excitement. It felt like a real journey, and it was so fascinating to watch all of these problems unfold and see how the characters respond to it. But that's where
is at its best - the characters. I loved every single one of them. Every single Nightwing who joins you is fleshed out and three-dimensional, you can tell plenty of time and care was put into making them lovable. One thing I also liked is that the game did take certain character clichés and flip them on their heads, one example being my favorite character, Rukey. The way he's portrayed at first gives you the vibe that he's going to be a shady, self-centered, and annoying prick who will want to make you bash your head into a wall. Instead, without getting too much into spoilers (but I'll censor it anyway just in case),
Anti-trends like this are pretty common with all of the characters, and it made me love everyone, even the exiles you face off against.
is probably one of the most deep and open-ended games I've ever played, with there being a ridiculous amount of lore and ways for the game to play out. It's definitely going to overwhelm some, but if you power through it, you will find that this game is very immersive and keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.
Supergiant games have always had a great soundtrack to back them up, but they went above and beyond with this game. Each piece feels different and fits their intended tone. There wasn't a single piece that felt out of place. The songs with vocals, however, were the highlights. Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett have beautiful voices, and every time they sang, I got goosebumps. While some might be disappointed by the lack of Logan Cunningham's normal narrator voice, the one they had for this game fit the theme a lot better in my opinion and I was perfectly fine with him. This game's narrator especially got more entertaining as the game progresses, although explaining why would lead to spoilers. To conclude, just like the game's story and visuals, I can't find anything to fault here.
The amount of replayability in this game surprised me. There's a LOT of different outcomes to the game, and with the incredible story, I'm considering going through it again just to see what other interactions I can find between the charming ensemble of exiles. It's a shame that the game doesn't have online multiplayer, though, otherwise I would be even more hooked on this game than I already am.

While

Supergiant has given us yet another high quality game, and if it appeals to you, dear Reader, you will be more than satisfied with this incredibly brilliant and enthralling emotional rollercoaster.

Reminiscent of the atmosphere, storytelling and obvious pixellated aesthetics of
, it is unfortunate that it doesn't fall into a more specific and mainstream genre.
lacks in length as a laid back 40-minute experience which isn't interactive enough as a game to be called much more than what people call a walking simulator. What excels is the execution of the narrative and the strange, eerie tale itself which would have all been marvellous to build upon as a point and click like the aforementioned horror series.
Using the arrow keys to move and back out from interactions and spacebar to interact with highlighted objects, you are introduced to the story much the way you would reading a picture book. You move your character mainly through a house among other locations whilst looking at objects and a variety of scenes to easily grasp a timeline to put together your own version of the events that seem to have unfolded. Excruciatingly tempting as it is to unveil a little bit of the story, it is the core of this game and as someone who went in without an ounce of knowledge about
I am glad I went in blindfolded and came out with a sense of uneasiness as I doubt I would have felt as intensely had I known any of the story beforehand.
This is what I yearn for badly written narrative reliant games to turn into, namely poorly penned visual novels or bland exploration games that lack any literal composition.
uses an elegant method of telling stories with minimal text yet still emphasising a narrative rich experience. You are presented with flashbacks or self reflection and these snippets of thoughts and scenes are accompanied by a bare minimum of text. Many indie developers have a wealth of creativity in them but don't possess the skills crucial to relay it effectively by utilising written word to the extent of a novella or even an anecdote. This leads to winning plots quickly morphing into indecipherable and wasted gobbledygook within an otherwise well made game and a mistake so many incompetently written games make. Even though it plays like a 2D version of
where you move through rooms and open doors to interact with objects that tell you a story,
is the better version since it refuses to use traditional narration and walls of text instead substituting it with visuals much more meritoriously. This game proves once again that even without intricate game mechanics, you needn't be so reliant on words to tell a worthy story and create a solid narrative experience.
Having played
a day earlier (basically a mini-me version of
) and it being half an hour shorter, with absolutely no world-building and yet pulling off making my heart heavier than this game did, I am optimistic that the developer could easily build a much more comprehensive game with an even creepier universe for a more satisfactory experience. An outstanding example of gameplay and mood is
(also a first time for these developers) which is a surreal pixellated adventure horror game set in the dark depths of the ocean, which keeps your hair on end all throughout and is a true hidden gem. If you are a fan of the horror game genre and have played a good number of similar games, it is unlikely that
will scratch that horror itch or scare you much even with the eventuality of it being a psychological thriller. Even so, the ending does make most of it worthwhile and though up until that point you'd have wondered when the game would end, you'll be saddened that it is so short despite it managing not to feel abrupt, and just want more. Hence, as an indie game made by someone inexperienced in such endeavours, it is well done and makes me look forward to future work from them.

Half visual novel/RPG, half fantasy "sportsball".
This is the first game I played by Supergiant. I must say, I was a bit conflicted how I truly felt about this game. Most of the game is a very simple RPG, while the conflicts/battles are played out in this fantasy style sports game. Picture a traditional basketball or soccer game, where you can only control one player at a time, while your teammates remain motionless, and you can shoot your enemies to remove them from a game for a time.
I loved the look of this combat system and the idea, but when I played it at first, not so much. It just doesn't feel very smooth or easy to control. The game rules are very simple to understand, but I feel the combat system has a huge learning curve when it comes to controling the game mechanics. After playing it more and more, trying out different control schemes (which is extemely easy and offers mouse driven, WASD, or Gamepad) I found myself really enjoying the "Rites" (the combat system). I don't think the system is perfect, but I believe the devs are on to something. Keep in mind, I didn't come to this realization till just before I beat the game. The learning curve for controling the Rits was that high, at least for me. In the end I settled on mouse driven controls. You would think a Gamepad would be better for a game like this, but in the end, the mouse controls proved to be the least frustrating once I got used to them.
The RPG side of the game is nothing special, but does tell a good story. Simple choices will dictate upgrades, loot, or  story outcomes. This along with the epic soundtrack, surprisingly creates a lot of drama. Makes you more emotionally invested in the characters, even some of your enemies.  That fact that you can't lose the game facilitates this. There is no failure state. If you lose a battle, the story just continues. So it's more about trying to get the best ending, while seeing what happens or what stories you create with all the characters based on your decisions, and  your success.
The game comes with a Verses mode, where you can just make your own match-ups from all the characters in the game. It's unlocked right away, so beware of spoilers if you jump right into that first. I recommend not touching it till you beat the game. Verses mode has tons of options, but it's local mutliplayer only, or against the AI. For me, I don't think the Rites by themselves are enough to keep me interested long term. I need the backdrop of the story to keep it interesting to me.
Overall, I liked this game. The art direction and music is top tier. The game is almost worth the price for that experience alone. The RPG and combat system aren't the greatest by themselves, but i think the whole game comes together in the end. Out of all the games Supergiant has done so far, I hope they consider going back to Pyre someday. Either as a sequel, or just an evoltion of the gameplay they have created here.

Platformers. The beginning of my dive into video games was Super Mario Bros. I've since played most Mario, Sonic, Mega Man, and countless other platform games over the years. I have an extensive history with them.
Based on that, I have to say that Rayman Legends is one of the best I've ever played.
- The controls are very responsive and the gameplay just flows effortlessly from move to move making it your own fault if you screw up.
- The art style is amazing and is something I will never tire of looking at.
- Extensive number of very well designed stages that are extremely fun to play
- Time Trials, Daily and Weekly challenges, and most of the stages from Rayman Origins can be found here.
- Musical stages, where you run and jump to the remixed beat of popular songs. I play these over and over they are just so enjoyable.
Basically, if you don't already own it, buy it. Yes it requires Uplay, but so what? The game is so darn good, I honestly don't see why it matters.

Never before have I been so consumed and immersed in a videogame. As far as I'm concerned, this is a masterpiece of storytelling. It is a first person horror game which mostly has you exploring an underwater scientific complex of laboratories, listening to audio logs, solving an occasional puzzle and avoiding monsters (the avoid the monster bits were my least favourite, they were tense but I often found them fairly frustrating, fortunately they are not too frequent and they are incorporated into the story quite well.)
The game has amazing atmosphere, voice acting that breathes life into the characters, the story is original and extremely interesting (at least to me, I'm sure something similar has been done before but I haven't heard of it).
The game overall does a really good job of making you want to find out what happened. It starts off in the present time as the main protagonist, Simon Jarrett goes to take a brain scan that's supposed to help him recover from brain damage he suffered after an accident. However, right after the scan, Simon finds himself in what seems to be a decrepit space-station. At first I thought he was just hallucinating but it turned out his situation was much more complicated (and interesting...and much less cliche).
I won't spoil anything though, If any of this sounded interesting to you, you can get it in September 2016 Humble Monthly for $12 along with 5 or so other games. As of writing this review, there are still 4 days left on this deal. Don't miss it, I personally never play horror games and I was almost positive I wouldn't finish this one either but it kept me nailed to the chair all the way through.

One of my favorite single player FPS, the combat has more fluidity than any shooter I've ever played. (Apart from when you run into lights, which happens fairly rarely.) The quad wielding mechanic of having your 2 darkness (snakes?) and having 2 guns makes combat feel reallly good. The story isn't my absolute favorite, but the ending is pretty good. I would have to say though that the game's biggest issue is it's linear design. All guns are a straight upgrade from the last in their catagories in every way, and there's no choice to any situation. I've heard of people having issues with this game but I played through it and only had 1 bug, (an infinite loading screen) although your experience obviously may vary on that front. The game is also kinda short though, but has good replayability. One thing that I find incredible is that each collectible Relic in the game has it's own unique backstory. Such as at one point you can find a dagger forged from 3 nails in the crucifixtion of Christ. If you see it on sale I'd definitely recommend picking it up, but for the 5 or so hours I got out of it (that includes me trying to find hidden stuff throughout every level) it's definitely not worth 30$, but if it is on sale for a good price it's a must grab.

Arma 3 is a love / hate relationship to the extreme. For someone like me, I always recommend the game to anyone who is a fan of tactical shooters and squad-based gameplay, but I tell them to expect a steep learning curve as well. The short is - this game is probably the best game I've ever played in terms of its community, the mods, the gameplay, and the memories I've made. Nothing comes close. If you manage to grab it on sale definitely don't hesitate to buy it. Just expect a few odd crashes and weird glitches that I like to classify no other way other than just saying "#Arma".
The long version:
Pros:
- Game runs fairly well if you have a mid to high tier PC, Bohemia have released many updates to stabilize the game. Crashes are very rare nowadays.
- Longevity / value for money - this game has so many spin-off game modes, and hundreds of high quality mods that honestly the base price is a steal. Get the APEX expansion when it goes on sale, still not quite worth the $35 imo, but definitely worth $20.
- Tactics / simulation - no other consumer game comes close to this. Squad replicates the "boots on the ground" experience better imo, but nothing touches Arma's ability for combined arms warfare.
- Serious fun - If you're a nutjob like me and like communicating with someone with the mental capacity larger than a grapefruit, this game is for you. The community is the best community out there.
- Graphics - while this game was known to be hard to run in the past, most modern mid-tier hardware will have no issues at all running the game (though I recommend having it stored on a SSD for noticeable performance improvements). This game is straight up beautiful at times.
Cons:
- This game is a labor of love - sometimes it'll do things that just annoy the heck out of you like memory crashes, or weird connection issues in multiplayer. Most of the serious bugs have been fixed at this stage.
- Performance - Get a good CPU if you want to run this game, but even so especially in MilSim environments the framerate may not be ideal (even with an i7 6700K don't expect greater than 60-70 FPS in a standard multiplayer server). Singleplayer runs great however.
- If you're like me and use a crap ton of mods, expect to allocate almost 100GB for everything.
- If you are the run-and-gun type, this game is most likely not for you - there are a lot of times where patience and tolerance for boredom (i.e - kitting up, planning out an attack, inserting into the AO, calling for exfil) are not commonplace, but they are frequent enough. Those with a higher maturity level are definitely what this game's core audience is.
Summary:
If you've read this far into this review - I have 3500 hours, help to run and design missions for a now two-year old MilSim (91st Special Forces Group) #shamelessplug, and regularly work to make this game better for everyone - I might as well be a dev at this point - get this goddamn amazing game. Find a good clan or group of friends to play with - you will not regret it.

Maybe I made a mistake by going into this game thinking it would be decent, because mostly all it did was disappoint. I couldn't even start the game because of an error message, so right off the bat I was getting a
impression. After searching the forums and finding the solution on some old threads, I had to download some missing files for PhysX, of which you'd think they could have bundled with the game's download, but whatever.
After all that I finally got the the main menu... which you cannot navigate with your mouse. Must be a console port. Oh, but my gamepad doesn't work either. So it's a
, fantastic. I configure settings and start up the campaign, greeted with one of the most boring intro videos I've seen in a long while. Once I'm in the game, it runs pretty terrible, so I have to quit entirely to change the video settings that can only be set from the launcher's splash screen before you actually launch the game itself, because why would we want to configure video settings from the in-game options, right? My specifications far exceed the Recommended System Requirements, good components made after the game's release, but I still have to turn things down, so evidently optimization wasn't a priority. You also cannot use the Steam overlay by default, and the "fix" for this is to rename the executables so that Steam will launch the actual game instead of the launcher, meaning you won't be able to edit your video settings again as readily.
Now for the gameplay itself. It is a stealth game, first and foremost, but it isn't a very good one. Oftentimes the game puts you in situations where it's near-impossible to sneak up behind someone before he turns around, mostly because your movement speed while sneaking is far slower than an enemy's casual walking speed. You can increase this movement speed through an arbitrary level-up screen, and while I normally don't mind RPG elements in non-RPG games if they're done right, this one feels out of place and like it only exists to handicap the player. The effect of increasing the skill is hardly noticeable too, even at the maximum value.You're supposed to be playing as a badass operative, alone and far behind enemy lines, but I'm not sure how she got that far if she's slow as a snail.
You can also increase how tough your character is so you can take more damage before dying. Your character is already quite frail in terms of how quickly you can die if caught, but if the goal is not to be seen, why is there even an option of increasing your health? They certainly don't give you enough ammo to have the freedom to go in guns blazing. At least, not until
You have to rely on sneaking and stabbing. In some cases, you can simply avoid enemies, but the game rewards you with stealth kills, so there's incentive in trying to take out your enemies. Not only does the game rank your performance for each mission based on stealth kills, but you also restore a small amount of health for performing them.
Of course, because the game puts you in situations where you're likely to get spotted from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, you're probably going to take some damage every now and then, assuming you aren't killed outright, which is just as likely. It feels like the game tries to make up for this, not by correcting its mistakes, but by almost admitting it has them. There's medkits and morphine littered all over the place. You'd think those two items might serve the same purpose, but they don't. Medkits heal your damage taken while morphine is essentially your Get Out of Jail Free Card. The morphine won't save you from all situations, but if you're caught (and you will be), you can kill the enemy as if through a stealth kill. However, no matter the duration, you can still only kill one enemy during your morphine rush, so if there's more than one guy together, you're still screwed if you try to kill one. In these situations, you're better off using the morphine to reposition and hide elsewhere. Both of these items can be found frequently, as if to say, "You'll probably need these because the game isn't exactly well-designed."
There are no manual saves. I can understand this from one perspective, because it's really easy to cheese a stealth game if you can save at any time. But on the other hand, reloading from the last checkpoint will sometimes feel like it's disrespecting your time. For example, there's one part where you enter an area where two guards blocking the path will immediately start talking to one another. Despite talking to each other, rather than facing one another, they both face player's direction. There's no way around them and you're forced to wait a solid minute or so for them to shut up and move on before you can even progress. Dying at any point before the next checkpoint means you'll have to sit through this conversation in its entirety, every time. Actually, these conversations you must sit through happen frequently, not as a one-time thing.
Speaking of chatter, the dialog in this game is just awful. The voice actress does an okay job at best (except for this one particular letter she reads quite poorly if it's found in a shack), but the script she's reading from feels like it was written by a child. In the mission briefings, the choice of words comes across as dull, predictable, and repetitive. And throughout the levels, your character will occasionally chime in with a statement basically telling you either what you know you're to do next, or what you're already doing, which is entirely unnecessary.
Also, you know how I said this is primarily a stealth game? The developers must have bipolar game design syndrome, because at the end of every operation, you're forced into firefights with enemy soldiers. I guess they must have thought that ending a mission by successfully being covert was too boring, so they had to throw in things like a rushed escape scene or a shootout to keep your interest. Nothing says congruent design like sneaking through enemy ranks only to attempt to turn your squishy stealth operative into an action movie hero at the very end, surely alerting anyone nearby who isn't dead.
Although, when it comes to alerting others, the game isn't exactly convincing. When spotted, your enemies will open fire and shout, "Alarm! Alarm!" or something similar. You can even hear what sounds like maybe an alarm going off briefly. If another enemy was in that same room, or maybe the next room if a door was open, they'll come searching too. But anyone else nearby in the level will remain oblivious that there is an intruder. Part of this may be because guards are unable to enter or leave most rooms. Seriously, if you get caught, you can go through a door and the enemy cannot follow you. After a while of peeking through the keyhole, you can see them give up, exasperated with their designers for having given them such a shortcoming. Then the enemy will go back to singing that same dumb tune as if his comrade wasn't just murdered. You may find yourself retreating to previous rooms often when the game shows its incredibly unfair level design.

This game feels very unpolished and incomplete. There is no manual, and most of the features are undocumented. The only documentation available is the wiki, which nobody has bothered to fill in; and the tutorial, which only explains a small fraction of the game's mechanics.
The controls are very unintuitive. Clicking on a character should select the character, but usually, this fail to work correctly. Instead, it will command the already selected character to move to that location. Only the "move" command is left click, while other commands use right-click. This notably contradicts most RTS games, making it difficult to learn. Sending a character a new command doesn't replace the character's old command - it adds a new command to the character's queue. This could be useful, if it used shift-clicking, for example, as is common in other games; and if the command queue length wasn't limited to 2 commands.

Remember back in the NES days, when games were all about trial and error?  You'd play a level over and over until you learned the timing of the enemies and the pattern of their movements.  The AI was unrealistic and often pretty unforgiving of mistakes.
That's basically how Velvet Assassin plays, and some people will like it for this reason, and others will not.  It's also very unhurried because you're slowly sneaking around for 95% of the game.  For me, it was a nice change of pace after playing a few action-oriented games in a row.
Some of the old-school video-gamey aspects are:
- Enemies basically pace between 2 or 3 points on a set path, and will stop and stand still at certain points in their path.  Your job is to enter an area, observe their movements, and figure out the correct timing to kill and hide an enemy without the other enemies seeing you.  Repeat.
- You are hidden when in the shadows.  You can be 5 feet from an enemy, right in front of him, out in the open... but he won't see you if you're in the shade.
- If you do alert the enemies but manage to hide, they will basically walk a few steps in one direction and look around, a few steps in the other direction and look around, then just shrug their shoulders and go back to their set path as if nothing happened.
-Enemies don't follow you through doors, so if you are seen and can manage to go back through the last door you came through, nothing will happen.  The enemies will just go back to their set paths after a few seconds.
If you need a break from the action and can embrace the out-of-date gameplay, go for it.

After the success of the first Knights of the Old Republic, LucasArts saw to it that a sequel would be made immediately by Obsidian Entertainment, a company featuring the creators of the 'Fallout 2' and the 'Baldur's Gate' games. However the short timeframe LucasArts gave the developer resulted in KOTOR 2 being rushed; a great game littered with bugs that the player must tread carefully.
The biggest difference between KOTOR 2 and its prequel is the story. Instead of a familiar Star Wars story about the fight against an evil army with a doomsday weapon, we are instead treated to a morally gray story that not only focuses on the hypocrisies of the Light & Dark side of the Force but also the very thin line between both sides. You are a former Jedi, exiled from the council due to past crimes and begin the game hiding from the Sith actively hunting down and killing all the Jedi from the galaxy. The story twists and turns from this starting point and subverts common Star Wars tropes along the way.
It is worthwhile to play the game just for the story itself as it is more intricate and self-reflective of the Star Wars mythology than any other material I've seen/read so far.
The gameplay is the same as before with a few changes. The combat is the same real time round based action involving DnD rules that calculate how effective each of your attacks are against enemies from KOTOR 1. The gear you use can either be obtained from fallen enemies or with a crafting system depending on your stats. If you were a fan of this gameplay before then you'll enjoy it this time, if not then be warned as there are prolonged combat sequences in this game.
The biggest change to the gameplay is the influence system; one that tracks the relationship between the player character (PC) and their companions throughout. This system places importance in the idle banter between the PC and others as the trust between the group can grow or diminish. Gaining the trust of your party allows you to influence their behaviour from changing their light/dark alignment to training them as Jedi/Sith. This system makes the relationships in the game much deeper than before by adding gameplay benefits to actively having an effect on each characters ending.
Despite the post release effort from modders, the game still suffers from some awful bugs as a result of the rushed development. If you do play this game then it is absolutely necessary to create multiple saves and enable cheats to overcome any gamebreaking bugs like what I had to do. It's a shame as these issues can detract from the games quality despite everything else it does so brilliantly. Looking past these issues there is a game that is worth your time but I believe its absolutely necessary to bring these issues to light.
- A fantastic RPG with a morally conflicted story to keep your interest.
- A bitter reminder of LucasArts' later year incompetence.
