What do you do in this game?  It's a nice, simple stealth game that takes place during WWII.
Like many stealth games, you creep around in the shadows, staying out of the light, you can sneak up on enemies to silently kill them, and you can hide their bodies to keep the other enemies from finding them.  Other stealthy things include wearing a disguise, whistling to get  your enemies' attention, breaking fuse boxes to knock out lights, shooting flamable/explosive stuff to kill your enemies, wearing a gas mask and releasing poison gas to kill a lot of enemies at once, pulling the pin on their grenades to turn them into walking time bombs, and a few other exciting ways to kill, confuse, and evade your enemies that I'm probably not thinking about.
In terms of gunplay, most of this game involves stealth, so you won't be doing as much shooting as you would in other games.  You do get a silenced pistol on most missions, but very little ammo.  Other weapons include a flare gun, a Lugar pistol, a shotgun, sniper rifle, and an STG-44.  The noisier weapons tend to be rare, and only available at certain points in the game.  The lugar is semi- common though.
Overall, I did enjoy this game and much of what it had to offer, but as usual, every game has its cons.  As many have stated, checkpoints tend to be spaced a little far apart at times.  This means that if you get killed, you will have to redo quite a bit of gameplay.  It's not quite as bad as some of the other reviews have stated, but it can be frustrating.
I'm not the most patient person when it comes to games, but I can honestly say that I never wanted to "rage quit" at any point of this game.  Sure, the checkpoint thing is frustrating, but the good gameplay more than makes up for it.  In other words, I really loved this game.

Possibly the most underrated stealth game to ever have a Triple-A style release. Velvet Assassin has faults, but with those are some of the best stealth mechanics and level design that you can find. You can't go in guns blazing and expect progress. You have to follow the rules, move unseen and kill quickly. Mistakes are rarely forgiven. The high difficulty could be the largest factor as to why it's not more popular. Velvet Assassin has a gritty, realistic vibe which can be very unwelcoming unless you're accustomed to the genre. But this is where it excels; Many games have stealth oriented gameplay but don't place focus on it like this one does.
However where things succeed, they fail elsewhere. The last two levels are combat oriented which is a dramatic change in pace and gameplay. Combat is clunky and due to how unforgiving being seen is, having to acitvely fight against enemies who are aware of you becomes a nightmare. Glitches are few and far between but they do exist and you can be forced to restart a checkpoint because of them.
In all, It's a fun but tough as nails stealth game. The artstyle can look absolutely gorgeous at times, but the rare instances of combat and the focus on it in the last two levels really bring the whole experience down. It's not of the quality that it presents itself to be but it's a great experience. Anyone who is a fan of this genre should really try it out.  It's tense, frustrating, but also so rewarding when you make it through each area.

This is a review of the game without the lost content pack, as I feel that is more fair to those that may have not played this game prior.
Is this game good? -Absolutely, one of my top 3 favorite games of all time.
Is it dated? -Graphics and mechanics wise, sure. However it aged extremely well.
Does it reflect well on Star Wars? -I think this game covers the deepest, darkest elements of Star Wars, and only in the best way imaginable
Good characters and companions? -Some of the best written, as well as philosophically challenging.
I can't compliment this game enough. Before playing it recently on steam I had beaten this game over 20 times on xbox many years ago, and as such was not as good at the game since I did not understand the DnD type combat system. Now, replaying the game I can say the game is comprehensible to any average gamer, though some of the terminology you may need to research in order to understand a lot of the combat mechanics. That being said, don't let that discourage you from playing the game whatsoever.
You play as a character that is a veteran from the Mandalorian Wars. Though this character is covered in the Star Wars extended universe, you can craft him/her however you see fit. Playing as a male vs female gives you different dialogue options as well as companions, and you can pitch from 3 Jedi classes, later able to change that class to a prestige class. This offers decent replayability, not to mention the light side dark side options, and even allowing one to be a Grey Jedi, taking no moral side, even if some of the game options force you to make light or dark side decisions. If you thought the first game lacked in any way, this game takes every aspect to a whole new level. Discussions about the nature of the force are referenced often, and if you wanted more feats and powers, they sure expanded on that.
What I personally enjoyed, were the musings of your beginning companion Kreia, and her evolution along your journey and her lessons that even carry a modern outlook on the weight of our actions. Anyone playing a goody two-shoes like I did my first playthroughs of this game might even find themselves looking in retrospect at their decisions prior after heeding Kreia's advice. Other companions I found I liked were Atton, T3M4 who they gave more personality to, and my favorite, Bao-Dur, who's seemingly gentle nature is often times shattered by his moral outbursts. I also thought the handmaiden was a great addition to the game, as she is handled well and gives a delicate view on the echani values and how you as a character eventually can shatter them. Who also could forget the hilarious hk-47? With enough influence with most of the human companions, you can also train them to use the force, which I found pretty damn cool.
Overall I think even someone who is not a Star Wars fan should check this classic out, simply because it is one of the best written games with a lot of dialogue and story that will stick with you long after you play it.

Ultimate Doom and the Doom franchise itself was an extremely popular game back in its day with more copies of the game being installed on computers than the current Windows operating system at the time. Does it still live up to the praise it had back then? To an extent the Ultimate Doom does a good job as a first person shooter, its fast paced filled with numerous weapons each with their own unique function and use. It is an older game however and some of the puzzles or map layouts can be confusing the first few times through. The story is decent all throughout the game with updates at the end of each episode. The one episode I did not enjoy as much as the others was "Thy Flesh Consumed" which acted as the last chapter of Doom and the prologue of Doom 2. A few of the levels are confusing, and have puzzles that are very frustrating. The difficulty level of this chapter skyrockets with little in the way of easing you into it. As a result I turned the difficulty setting down to even make it past the first level of the chapter. Ultimate Doom is a great game filled with fast paced action and decent gameplay, if you are looking at playing the final episode I would consider lowering the difficulty to prevent frustration.

How high is your tolerance for slow-paced weirdness? 'cause that's gonna determine how much you'll enjoy this game. If it's high, you'll enjoy this little story. If it's low, give it a pass.
The gameplay in this game is just a process of moving from one checkpoint that moves the story along to another. There's enough minor things changing along the way that looking at objects multiple times is worthwhile, though if you're only interested in getting through the story you'll find that searching for whatever object gets you back to the story is annoying. Fortunately, there isn't a large swath of objects to interact with so searching is decently short. It's a plus that the gameplay caters to both the person who will click on every interactable object just to see what's there and the person who just wants to get through the game, but the latter type of player will find the gameplay unpleasant.
It's clear that Settled is more focused on its story and setting, because both are quite well-done (if a bit thin at times). There are a few semi-traditional jumpscares, but they don't come out of nowhere - they're built up to using the environments you go through and the sounds you'll hear. Things moving out of the corner of your eye, minor graphical changes in an object you think you've seen over and over - it's the little touches that really give the game an eerie atmosphere. It's good, but nothing in this game is going to seem revolutionary. Without spoiling, blood and guts get thrown around pretty liberally but I sometimes wondered why it was even needed. This is where your tolerance of weirdness is really going to come in handy. The designer clearly has a good understanding of how to build atmosphere and move a story along in a way that feels genuinely strange and uncanny. The somewhat gratuitous blood doesn't always seem in line with that. People with a high tolerance for weird will probably enjoy the story and be able to forgive some of the weaker points in the narrative. You just want some well-made weirdness? You'll get a decent dose of it from this game.
Personally, I had a great time with the game. I like a good short experience and I always enjoy seeing a game with a good horror foundation. If that's what you want, give it a try.

Settled
Short Story-Driven Horror
Allen Dayan
Allen Dayan
is a short story-driven horror game developed and published by Allen Dayan.
To avoid spoling the plot, I'll just say that you play as a father whose daughter died some time ago, and he explores his house after hearing some strange noises.
While at first I wasn't all that into the story, after a while a constant state of dredd started creeping up on me, until I was fully invested on the f*cked up things that started happening in this game, till you get to the unsettling (albeit predictable) ending.
Developed in Construct 2, the game's pixelated art style is very simplistic, while the hand-drawn look of the cutscenes delivers a more creepy vibe.
Pretty simple: you walk around the house and you interact with highlighted objects. Again, the focus is on the story, and its gameplay is the best and easiest way to tell it.
Pretty weak: not that much of a soundtrack, and the sound effects are royalty-free. The game relies more on actual creepiness rather than jump scares.
Unfortunately, there are no achievements or hidden secrets: after 30 minutes, you are done playing this game.
If you are going to play this game, you are in for the story. If you like story-driven horror games that will unsettle you for a cheap price, then buy this game right now.

I bought this game due to the history of the studio's previous releases, a pair of games that had been by far some of the most moving, fun, and beautiful games I've ever played. Bastion and Transistor had deep colorful backgrounds told through talented narration, combat mechanics that felt fun and made one think about every situation, and music that fit the setting. I found little of what I enjoyed in the two previous games here, nor anything new that was interesting or moving.
While the whole basketball thing was definitely new, the slow pace and limitation on character movement hampered what could have been a fun and interesting section of gameplay. Considering that the bulk of the game rotated around this game mechanic, found myself repelled by the thought of having to play it more than a few times.
As in the previous two releases by Supergiant Games, the world in Pyre promised to be large and deeply interesting, with colorful characters and environments. A few minutes into the game, I came across a choice to travel through one of two areas. I made my choice and found that while the game had these interesting areas, you didn't actually get to see any of them, just hear about them.
I dunno guys. I love this company but I refuse to prop this game up on a pedestal like Valve fans have with Half-life. A bad game is a bad game.

Is this game worth $29.99?
I will make a series of statements. If you agree by saying YES to 8 of the 12 statements, this game is worth it to you.
#1 - I enjoy horror/thriller games and movies. Y/N
#2 - I take things at a slow-pace, soaking in the details. Y/N
#3 - I'm okay with not having much action. Y/N
#4 - I really enjoy Sci-Fi. Y/N
#5 - I play a good game more than once. Y/N
#6 - I'm too impatient to wait for a sale. Y/N
#7 - I sometimes prefer Single-Player Only games. Y/N
#8 - 10-15 Hours of Gameplay is enough for me. Y/N
#9 - I'm a sucker for a good story. Y/N
#10 - I'm a sucker for great visuals. Y/N
#11 - I've played and enjoyed Outlast, Amnesia, and/or Silent Hill. (Any) Y/N
#12 - Storyline is more important to me than Gameplay. Y/N
If you answered 8 of 12 with Yes then this game is worth the purchase.
Side Note, though: Although there isn't much technically wrong with this game, it is still pretty isolated, like Amnesia was, which makes it a bit of a one-trick pony. But it's a mind-boggling trick. For gamers who love a mysterious plotline that keeps you hooked until the end, this one is replayable, but like rewatching a TV Series (Game of Thrones, Breaking Bad, etc.) once the twists are revealed, it isn't the same experience the second time. You're buying it for that first experience, and if you truly did answer 8 or more of the statements above with yes - it is well worth it.

The most important thing to remember when judging Velvet Assassin is that it was a middle-market release. It admittedly does have some weaknesses, but most of these are things that are pretty well guaranteed to crop up in middle-market games, and it would be absurd to judge it by the same high standards as its big-budget AAA competitors. Once you allow yourself to get over these few niggling little problems, Velvet Assassin emerges as a superb and memorable stealth game, which definitely made the most out of its measly budget.
In short, it's not the perfect stealth game (see Thief II: The Metal Age), so I wouldn't recommend it to absolute beginners as their introduction to the genre. Conversely, if you're a stealth purist you might be frustrated by this game, because while the narrative and atmosphere have both been crafted with painterly precision, the game's few faults do tend to be concentrated in the actual stealth gameplay itself. But in general, if you're a fan of stealth and dark atmospheric games then this is definitely recommended. Well worth the price!
Pros:
+The dark and dreamlike ambience of this game was perfectly executed, and its atmosphere is deeply immersive and unsettling.
+Borrows mechanics from some of the best stealth games ever made (particularly the Thief and Hitman series) whilst also innovating with several brilliant new approaches to stealth gameplay all its own.
+This could easily have been "just another game with vaguely symbolic, dark subject matter". But it's a testament to how expertly this game was written and designed that it still manages to be profoundly upsetting and truly horrific at times, even to someone who's played many games that touch on similar themes before. This is particularly impressive given that everyone already knows bad things happened in WWII, so they can't simply fake it by surprising the player with unexpected dark twists.
+By 2009 standards this game really punched above its weight in the graphics department, especially its beautiful lighting effects, which hold up even today.
Cons:
-This game features a checkpoint-based save system, which is unbelievably frustrating in a stealth game, and therefore indirectly shatters immersion.
-The light-and-shadow-based stealth system is completely binary, and occasionaly glitches in a way that renders certain rooms essentially impossible to traverse stealthily. However, it would be unreasonable to expect a middle-market title to be completely free of little problems like this.
-Much of the narrative and atmosphere is communicated through overheard conversations between Nazi soldiers. Unfortunately for non-German-speakers, it's very easy to miss parts of the English subtitles for these conversations whilst you're still in the middle of gameplay at the same time. Consequently I felt like I was missing much of the rich worldbuilding and narrative these conversations conveyed.
-This is not a pure stealth game, and at fairly regular intervals it forces you to gun down waves of enemies. This schizophrenic design choice means there are some sections of the game which can't be completed stealthily, and other sections which can't be completed violently, and you're often not sure which of the two you're in at any given time. This often leads to punishingly difficult scenarios, where you have to ask yourself "Am I failing because I'm just bad at the game, or am I trying to be too stealthy in a scenario where the designers have arbitrarily decided I have to be violent?" or vice versa. Unfortunately the worst instance of this problem takes place in the final few minutes of the game, where the only way you can finish the game is to gun down wave after wave of absolutely merciless enemies. I found this frustrating, punishing, and just simply not fun in any way, and it honestly ruined the ending of the game for me.
-The level design, a feature of crucial importance to stealth games, is sadly quite linear most of the time, and the levels themselves are not particularly large. It wouldn't be realistic to expect significantly more from a middle-market title, but it's still a weakness.
-The enemy AI is somewhat robotic and "gamey", and is especially unrealistic when you're using the social stealth mechanics. Again, little problems like this are understandable in a middle-market game.
-The gameplay is quite regularly interrupted by cutscenes, although most of them are mercifully short.
-There are no non-lethal combat options whatsoever.

My GOTY for 2014. Seriously.
A play-through will take you five minutes, tops. You'll replay it two or three times.
But those moments are transformative. Transporting you back in time to an era in your life that you remember well; old enough to realize that Sex Was A Thing, but too young to have more than the most innocent, half-gleaned knowledge of it. It was in those eras we earnestly sought to know How Do You Do It? But our sources were few, and fewer still reliable.
It's a game about that feeling, that innocent curiosity and discovery and being hilariously inept and so far off the mark. It captures it, and delivers it, with a purity and earnestness that I can't resist. We laugh as we play, but we're not laughing *at* her. We're laughing *with* her, years later, as she remembers what those fumbling first attempts to understand the threshold of adulthood that lay ahead. We laugh not in spite, but in joy and celebration that there was a time we could engage in that learning without baggage or the larger concerns of society.
It's short, it's silly, you'll laugh, and then afterwards, you'll think back about it and smile. And probably hit Play again.
And you'll wish more games could do this, with the magic of a simple premise and purity of purpose.

The most important thing to remember when judging Velvet Assassin is that it was a middle-market release. It admittedly does have some weaknesses, but most of these are things that are pretty well guaranteed to crop up in middle-market games, and it would be absurd to judge it by the same high standards as its big-budget AAA competitors. Once you allow yourself to get over these few niggling little problems, Velvet Assassin emerges as a superb and memorable stealth game, which definitely made the most out of its measly budget.
In short, it's not the perfect stealth game (see Thief II: The Metal Age), so I wouldn't recommend it to absolute beginners as their introduction to the genre. Conversely, if you're a stealth purist you might be frustrated by this game, because while the narrative and atmosphere have both been crafted with painterly precision, the game's few faults do tend to be concentrated in the actual stealth gameplay itself. But in general, if you're a fan of stealth and dark atmospheric games then this is definitely recommended. Well worth the price!
Pros:
+The dark and dreamlike ambience of this game was perfectly executed, and its atmosphere is deeply immersive and unsettling.
+Borrows mechanics from some of the best stealth games ever made (particularly the Thief and Hitman series) whilst also innovating with several brilliant new approaches to stealth gameplay all its own.
+This could easily have been "just another game with vaguely symbolic, dark subject matter". But it's a testament to how expertly this game was written and designed that it still manages to be profoundly upsetting and truly horrific at times, even to someone who's played many games that touch on similar themes before. This is particularly impressive given that everyone already knows bad things happened in WWII, so they can't simply fake it by surprising the player with unexpected dark twists.
+By 2009 standards this game really punched above its weight in the graphics department, especially its beautiful lighting effects, which hold up even today.
Cons:
-This game features a checkpoint-based save system, which is unbelievably frustrating in a stealth game, and therefore indirectly shatters immersion.
-The light-and-shadow-based stealth system is completely binary, and occasionaly glitches in a way that renders certain rooms essentially impossible to traverse stealthily. However, it would be unreasonable to expect a middle-market title to be completely free of little problems like this.
-Much of the narrative and atmosphere is communicated through overheard conversations between Nazi soldiers. Unfortunately for non-German-speakers, it's very easy to miss parts of the English subtitles for these conversations whilst you're still in the middle of gameplay at the same time. Consequently I felt like I was missing much of the rich worldbuilding and narrative these conversations conveyed.
-This is not a pure stealth game, and at fairly regular intervals it forces you to gun down waves of enemies. This schizophrenic design choice means there are some sections of the game which can't be completed stealthily, and other sections which can't be completed violently, and you're often not sure which of the two you're in at any given time. This often leads to punishingly difficult scenarios, where you have to ask yourself "Am I failing because I'm just bad at the game, or am I trying to be too stealthy in a scenario where the designers have arbitrarily decided I have to be violent?" or vice versa. Unfortunately the worst instance of this problem takes place in the final few minutes of the game, where the only way you can finish the game is to gun down wave after wave of absolutely merciless enemies. I found this frustrating, punishing, and just simply not fun in any way, and it honestly ruined the ending of the game for me.
-The level design, a feature of crucial importance to stealth games, is sadly quite linear most of the time, and the levels themselves are not particularly large. It wouldn't be realistic to expect significantly more from a middle-market title, but it's still a weakness.
-The enemy AI is somewhat robotic and "gamey", and is especially unrealistic when you're using the social stealth mechanics. Again, little problems like this are understandable in a middle-market game.
-The gameplay is quite regularly interrupted by cutscenes, although most of them are mercifully short.
-There are no non-lethal combat options whatsoever.

Problems aside, this is a very fun game, even without friends. It's a very social game where it's key to talk to fellow counselors, though as a fellow European you will run in to russians (Mostly) and sometimes other nationalities who refuse to talk english which is very annoying. Socializing IS key and luckily sometimes you'll run in to great and fun people.
The game feels varied, much so compared to games like Dead by Daylight where you just have to repair a couple of generators and get through the gates and you're done. Here you can escape by either repair and fuel 2 different cars (One 2 seater and one 4 seater) or a boat. You can also survive by calling the police and wait for them to arrive at the gate to rescue you, or you can wait for the match timer to run out.
But here it comes, you've probably already read this hundreds of times, Jason is a bit overpowered, but only thanks to his shifting ability. One second you can be running away from him and be 20 meters ahead and the next he grabs you and insta-kills you, it's very annoying. I don't think he should be able to shift while you're looking straight at him and his shift ability should have a longer cooldown and/or a shorter period of time he can stay in his shift mode.
Some problems you should know that plauges the game at the moment:
-Servers are inconsistent (While I have never been disconnected from a match, sometimes I haven't been able to get pass the title screen)
-Achievements doesn't work at the moment (A bummer but shouldn't prevent you from getting the game)
-Price (I understand why some think the game is too expensive, I personally think the game should've been $/€29.99 at most, though if you're a big fan of Friday the 13th and have friends who are on the fence on buying it, you should buy it)
-There's no penalty for quitting (Annoying when you're playing Jason and the player you're about to brutally murder quits mid-animation, it means the kill won't count and you get no experience)
All in all, the core game is a lot of fun and I'm looking forward to future content and tricks/fixes.

At first I was sceptical of spending 40 bucks on it. People said it wasn't worth it, repetative, boring,
Well its extremely clear these people... aren't fans nor can appreciate this game for what it is.
I tried a match an councillor first. After seeing gameplay vids I had an idea of how it worked. And I died, helping my teamates repair the car, sneaking away, securing parts and it felt scary, paranoia packed and so cool being able to see Jason whilst hiding behind stuff knowing he can't see me. The stealth mechanic works really well.
2nd match I tried I died doing the same but my teammates actually managed to kill jason and it was epic as ♥♥♥♥ to behold. Good teamwork and unlike gamer websites argue... its not that convoluted at all. Get the sweater, get a machete, stun him, hit him from behind boom done. Sure easier said than done. for SURE. But... still doable :) And extremely fun when it works.
3rd match I played as Jason and it was the most fun I've ever had. Impossible not to laugh at your victims as you chase them, continuously talking to them via mic. " Im gonna get ya!!!!!!! Run!!! Run for your life!!!" Its just amazing fun.
This game is nevertheless something that should be enjoyed in relatively short bursts. Say. 1-2 hour gameplay sessions. Its not that the game is repetative as such. What hurts it the most is when your team doesn't play well and your effort feel for naught. That makes the repetative sensation magnify greatly.
Play with friends, communicate, and your gameplay session will be awesome. With Jason you can just chill and kill whoever. Its a nice break from Councillor gameplay when you're chosen.
Overall. The price tag is really not a problem to me. A heard a guy talking about it, saying the game gets criticism as if it was a tripple A game when in truth its kickstarted and the dev team is small. Something that highlights that that kind of criticism is unfair. That being said, I can understand people wanting a functional game.
However. The game is not at all as buggy as some reviews argue. The devs are working on it and considering their size and abilities, I'm giving them patience because the core concept here is outstandingly good.
I'd really love to see a singleplayer campaign here and more skins appear. Customization at the moment is good and fun. Being able to control Jasons special kills via perks is great. Choose the ones you like.
Lastly the game has amazing atmosphere. Its dark, feels like the movies. Familiar music plays and you will never stop feeling on edge playing.
The graphics are to my liking. Jason looks fantastic and the councillors do as well including the surroundings. I'm impressed personally considering this was a kickstarter game.
The facial animations are still a bit wonky but honestly, its fine to me. The devs even made an in-game joke about it through an achievement.
Reach 100 fear and still make it through the night. Achievement is called the " Chad Face" and we've all seen it :)
Its a fun game. Teamwork reliant to huge extent. Still a bit buggy and in some ways mechanically Jason as well as the councillors can act somewhat broken. Via dodging, moving at the right time to avoid being hit and more. can feel quite cheap at times but it'll probably get fixed later on since the devs seem passionate about this.
Fun in relatively short bursts, best with good teammates, and thank god we can mute the players that hate this and whine about it but play anyway. Met a few of those. Dont worry. You can mute them and if they really annoy you in game, you can teamkill them as well. Unsure if there is a pentalty for that but its not recommended doing so because you wanna win and need people to do that :)
So yes. Try it yourselves. Got 2 hours to refund it. Matches last in between 10-20 minutes. Depending on you either escape, jason kills you or the timer just runs out. And honestly. 20 minutes is enough. Once you're in it... time moves really slowly because you never relax for a single second :)
The game has 1 issue with quitters that aren't Jason or those that quit after dying that could potentially be chosen as Tommy jarvis resulting in the Tommy character just being playerless and not able to help people.
We need a ban mechanic for the quitters because winning against a good jason with less with 4-5 is really hard. Sometimes your matches drop to 5 from 7 councillors from the start. It makes things a lot harder. Really sabotages the team.
But yes. Try it yourselves. I had great fun being a fan of the franchise. ♥♥♥♥ing love to see Kane Hodder here as well. Its an extremely scary game when you're really trying to survive or get chased in the car or boat. Heart racing really. Fantastically scary :)
The good outweigh the few minus' it has by far.

Combat is tight, and weapons seem pretty balanced, since every weapon will kill you in one or two hits, which does help reduce any pay-to-win aspects. You get given the mosin and PPSh to start with and both will do the job no problem. I seem to get killed by people with mosins more than anything else. Weapons are pretty arbitraraly walled off to you depending on what faction you join, but it is possible to "find" weapons on the battlefield, that is to say, you get given them after the match is over, you can't pick up dropped weapons.
It doesn't feel to "grindy", credit rewards are decent and missions give boosters and are pretty easily achievable, though this should really be counted as a flaw, since if the devs have any plans beyond the current state of the game the only reason to put this out is to generate money, and if there's no reason to buy premium currency, no angle grinder to the taint forcing you to buy premium items just to coninue, then its not going to generate any revinue. There is a character upgrade tree, which adds a little something to the standard shooter mechanics.
All this sounds pretty good, especially for a free game, but that's my real problem with Survarium (other than the clunky awkward♥♥♥♥♥name). Its too polished, too well defined as a deathmatch shooter to ever be anything else. Its also free to play, a payment model that I dislike. Mentally I slot in in with games like War Thunder, Heroes & Generals and World of Tanks; free to play deathmatchers with 90% of the content available to grind, and the rest in the real money shop. Games that exist in a constant state of development, never really being completed, with a long list of upcoming features, where the line between open beta and full release is so blurred it might as well not be there. As I said, I can't imagine this game ever becoming the mmorpg with faction based PVP combat, scavenging, trading and surviving in a hostile open world that it claims it wants to be.
If all you want is a free deathmatch shooter with enough extra mechanics to elevate it a little then I would recommend, it is free after all, and a pretty small download as well (though every game seems small after Shadow of Mordor), but if you want something more, or are hoping that this game will one day become the game it was supposed to be, then just forget you ever heard of it. Its not going to happen.

Doom: The OG FPS. Here with all the episodes in tow. This game came out about the same time that I was born, yet it still feels fantastic! I grew up watching my big brother play this game, alongside other classics like Diablo 2, and I can fully understand why this game is considered one of the best games ever made.
This game does everything I love about games: It gives zero s***s about story, and just throws you into Hell itself to mop up in the best way possible: With guns. BIG guns.
Just about everything in this game is classic, from the weapons and monsters, to the unnamed space marine you play as, commonly referred to as Doomguy. Heck, for a long time, this game was the only thing on peoples' minds. Workplaces had to put in specialized bans to prevent people from bogging down the servers with Doom. And this was back in the 90's, when computers with gigabyte storage were considered huge and the internet was "just a fad". It even took a while for games similar to Doom to be called FPS', rather than "Doom-clones."
Its cultural impact aside, is Doom still a good game? Oh Hell yes! Even compared to modern FPS', this game is still my favourite of its kind, because of its fast pace, its satisfying bloodshed and badass protagonist. For a guy who says nothing, Doomguy is damn well aware of how awesome he is; especially when he whips out the BFG 9000. (Yes, it's literally called the Big F***ing Gun 9000.)
And the track record for Doom has always been good. You won't hear anyone except pacifists and idiots complain about Doom or its sequel. The third entry was admittedly polarizing, with its reliance on horror over badassery, but with the arrivial of Doom 4 (known only as Doom for some reason) this franchise is now stronger than ever! Heck, I might say that Doom 4 is GOTY for 2016, even with its disappointing multiplayer. Because f*** it, I don't give two s***s about multiplayer anyways!
But back to First Doom...
If you're a fan of retro games, you've already played Doom. If you're a fan of FPS', you need to play Doom to see where it all started. If you're a casual gamer, you must try Doom at least once. If you're a crybaby with a weak stomach for blood, get over it! This game needs to be played! So play it! I honestly can't give this game enough thumbs up! It's Doom for f***s sake! Now go out there and kill demons!

For fans of the dev's previous works, this game might be divided on opinions and preferences. As a new IP that is judged on its merits, it's a high quality and incredibly detailed indie game that is clearly a labor of love. No matter if you dislike sports games or visual novels, or have a staunch fondness for anything similar to Bastion/Transistor; you cannot deny the amount of effort and passion that was put into Pyre.
Pyre is many things: a basketball/blitzball/reverse-CTF game, a fairly lengthy and branching visual novel, an Oregon/Amazon Trail adventure, a MOBA-ish party RPG... Genres that don't seem to have much in the way of blending together, but somehow is all combined into something cohesive and logical, an experience that is easy to approach, but can satisfy cravings for something a bit deeper. Every system is polished and well-thought out. Nothing seems out of place or cobbled together. It all fits together as if the stars aligned for them.
A huge part of that is how much context and worldbuilding are used to not only explain every single thing in Pyre, but tie it all as a story, a natural part of the game world. The story is very accomodating of the typical game victory or defeat states; failure and losses do not result in a game over screen or starting over. The game tells you to move on and accept it as a lesson. The characters and story will take these into account, to the point where certain events and revelations reveal themselves only through defeat. Pyre is one of the better examples in the video game industry where the story has been exhaustingly adapted to the media's operative structure.
Loss, regret, redemption, justice, ambition, forgiveness, humility, acceptance, piety, camaraderie, loyalty, sacrifice, mercy, liberty. Many words for a tale set against Supergiant's peerless craftsmanship for the senses. Their artistic touch and their hauntingly beautiful music. Their meticulous attention to detail everywhere, from the audiovisual to the lore and characters, even to how the game plays. Not much escapes their eyes.
I only have a few strikes against Pyre, and the most significant one is there is no New Game Plus option, like Bastion and Transistor. Out of those 3 games, Pyre by far would be most fit to have a NG+ mode. Being able to start a new campaign run with all your RPG progressions and facing off against high or max-geared adversaries right off the bat would do wonders for replayability in the campaign. Getting bonus objectives (Feat of Glory) or having the ability to choose any of the large choice of increased difficulty modifiers (Titan-stars) at the start would boost that replay value even more. It's a huge oversight in what is otherwise a great game, and one I can't look past.
The other problem I have is no online multiplayer for Pyre's Versus mode, otherwise limited to local multiplayer. Now, that's not much of an issue for me as NG+, simply because I tend to not associate Supergiant Games with multiplayer. But with the action gameplay they poured their efforts into creating, it feels quite a waste to only have local multiplayer working in that mode, which is the only other option besides facing off against AI. An online multiplayer mode with its own leaderboard/matchmaking and private/custom matches would be an incredible feature to have, to expand on this game's potential with its audience. Combined with NG+, it'd be quite a complete game and a huge value for its $20 USD pricetag. As it is, without those two features I mentioned, it's a very good game even at that asking price. Hopefully Supergiant Games can look into adding those in later, either as free or paid DLCs.

SOMA is one of the first horror games I've actually beaten. Granted, I played with the Wuss mod installed to avoid the "hide and seek" gameplay that Frictional Games is known for with previous games like Amnesia, but the experience was still very unnverving and something I can see any horror fan enjoying.
Honestly, if you're in the market for a horror game, I don't know if there's a better one than SOMA. Sure, the horror elements aren't the jump scares that entice Youtubers, but the haunting locations, terrifying monsters, and the huge plot make for an even larger horror experience. The game is also incredibly well polished and feels like a AAA title that is well worth the standard 30 dollar price tag.
On the topic of the plot, not only is it absolutely horrifying, but it's just pretty dang good, which is one of my major gripes with this game since I'm not typically a horror guy: the horror element can potentially drive people away from the thought provoking narrative. I've heard people online say that the gameplay elements of running and hiding can be tedious in some sections, but removing them makes the game a "walking simulator" in a sense. Because I had the Wuss mod installed, I was able to pretty much tailor the experience to something I much prefer (since I don't do jump scares and the gameplay sounded frustrating) but it's something to think about before purchasing.
Even with the Wuss mod installed, the game is super spooky, mainly because of the ambience that permeates throughout the game, the rich narrative spread throughout small tidbits of collectibles and secrets, and just the world itself deep within the ocean. Tight corridors, creepy looking facilities, and darkness are commonplace along with... other things...
tldr: SOMA is the best game I'd never play again

First let me say I somewhat enjoy this game and everything written below is not meant as negative criticism.
This game is a standard budget FPS with lame plot and dumb yet unforgiving enemies.  You are John Prime (or whatever his name is) who is lured by his ex to save her current boyfriend from what can only be described as the biggest cluster♥♥♥♥ of trouble ever. Yep , stuck on a mining planet with a bunch of crazed miners and hostile robots. And then the corporation owning the mine sends swat teams to clean up the mess (you included).
Gameplay is pretty standard- you've got your shotgun , machinegun , sniper and stuff. Oh , and bullet time. Bullet time is pretty much useless , cause unlike other games that use a slowing time mechanic , here your bullets and you get slowed down the same amount as the enemies. You know how in Max Payne you trigger bullet time while falling so you gently soar like an oak leaf in October , but you still can aim with almost the same speed as outside bullet time , and your bullets travel a little bit faster than the enemy's. Well you wont see that in Alpha prime. In bullet time you move and shoot just as slow as your enemies , you still aim at normal speed , but it seems the AI does too. What you can , and should use are the lean buttons. Yep , [Q] and [E] are going to be your best buds again after all these years (ok you might have used E for Use , its bound to F now). I have found that you take 5-10 times less damage if leaning compared to popping out using A/D. Your health does not regenerate , but there are med kits and med stations (a-la Half Life/Jedi Knight) scattered around.
Oh , also , dont let the screenshots fool you - the game has 1080p
In conclusion: OK game if you like generic FPS , can be a little unforgiving at times , but the first few levels have more than enough med kits.
Also , I read someones review , that said objectives pop up for a few seconds and then you cant check them afterwards. Not true - you need to hold down the Z key (redefineable , I use TAB)

I'll start by saying i really enjoyed the first Darkness game. The story was really well done and the game had an atmoshpere of darkness and despair that really matched it. While this sequel is a decent game it didn't quite live up to it's predecessor for me.
First of all the game's cel-shaded looking visuals while not bad looking, just didn't seem to fit with this game. What should be quite a dark game ends up looking cartoony and it just isn't the right fit. It also makes the game feel a bit more arcadey instead of the visceral feel the gameplay of the first game had.
The story while interesting didn't reall captivate me as much as in the first game either and Jackie is also less likeable (though you could argue this might be to reflect the effect of the experiences in the first game on him.)
The gameplay and combat isn't too bad. There's a bit more variety with combat in this game and your darkling follower can be quite useful and adds a bit of comical relief. There's also more variety with enemies which require different strategies to deal with.
Overall all it's a decent game but nowhere near as good as it's predecessor. If you enjoyed the first game i'd say maybe give this one a go if you can pick it up cheap but but be prepared for the fact that it's not as good. If you didn't like the first you probably won't like this either. It's a 6/10 for me.

Hook is a rather short but interesting puzzler!
If you enjoy puzzles in general or little puzzle minigames than Hook is definitely something for you!
Pros:
+It's easy to jump into without needing a single sentence throughout the game.
+The puzzles are really short, so you can jump in even if you only have less than 5 minutes time.
+no tutorial needed, the first "puzzles" are the introductory.
+Price! Just about 1€ is definitely worth it, if you like puzzle games(And you don't mind the short game time; look below).
Cons:
-It's to short. You just need about an 1 hour(maybe 2 if you really take your time).
-It's too easy at the start and the last puzzle isn't too hard either. It could be way more challenging.
-The first 20-30 puzzles are really just the "tutorial" since the game is really easy at the start. So you really just get about 20-30 "real" levels(there are 50 in total).
-Feels like a "home-made" university project(although a good one), since there is really little content.
Ideas for next time:
-A level editor would be great so you could play with the interesting mechanic and share harder self made levels.
-Definitely harder and bigger levels so you would need more than 5minutes per level.
-Part 2 would be appreciated.
-maybe a timer or some sort of measuring device, but that could be also a con.
Thanks for reading, give it a try!

The scenery is breathtaking during the daylight hours and the dinosaurs wonderfully realistic. One might wonder whether such grand spectacles would be easily managed by lower end computers. ~Spending 20minutes running towards a friend in the hopes of reaching them before progressing takes the fun out of playing. I've been wanting to play this game since 6 years ago, and finally I got a copy of it.
For 2009's game, Velvet Assassin already have all the basic stealth action game needs: sound, light and shadow detection, (limited) evirontment and tools utilization, enemy manipulation, and most important among them are all of those stealth kills. It also offers gunfights in some occassion, which my noob skill in FPS game like Counter Strike turns out to be very helpful. Because, suprisingly, this game gives you the ability to do instant kill with headshot and recoils control. Like playing CS games, all you need to do is just tweak your mouse sensitivity, aim right, and learn each weapon's recoils.
The graphic and sound in this game are pretty good for its time. Especially for the ambient sound and music. It almost sound like early Silent Hill games.
As for storyline department, Velvet Assassin have a non-linear plot, with no multiple choices/endings, and often went fastforward to a different timeline. This non-linear plot makes the game a bit confusing at the begining. But if you keep following the story, at the turning point event everything that has happen will be explained (including her dress(?) and those srynges, maybe?). It's just... there is one thing that seems breaking that good storyline. The ending. Somehow it feels like it has been chopped out. It doesn't have a strong conclusion for a solid ending nor a cliffhanger. It's like, it still have a little more things to tell before the game ends. It's not a bad ending, though. It's just seem not quite completed yet.
Well, overall the game is quite fun. I recommend Velvet Assassin because I like this game. It may not suitable for most gamer, but if you okay with the theme (really, It does have quite strong themes and there are srynges too, I warned you! XD) and doesn't expecting any fancy acrobatic or hi-tech stealth moves, then this game might worth your time.
PS: This is an old game. It may give some troubles with newer hardwares or operating system. You may need to look for some instructions on how to install this game on your PC before having it in your steam library. And I played this game offline, so 1 hour gameplay record on this review is not the actual time.

Overall writing quality and characters aside, KOTOR 2 is a much inferior game compared to its Bioware-developed predecessor. As the people behind the Content Restoration Patch and other mods could only do so much without full access to the game's engine, it remains a buggy mess even at the time of this review, sadly. Quests, dialogue and cutscenes keep bugging out regularly, more often than not stuff doesn't make any sense at all, and the level design is downright terrible. Locations are empty, ugly and repetetive, and are the prime example for how unfinished and rushed this game is.
If you're a huge Star Wars fan, KOTOR 2 might still be worth your time and (especially) patience. I can't really recommend this obviously flawed game to anyone else though.

Such promise for this game...
It may turn out to be really good once it is finished, and for a while a few months ago, it was really fun. But as of right now with recent changes, it is NOT worth the price.
This game used to have about two or three different maps you could play on where you could play as dinosaurs trying to survive. You could herd up in groups with herbivore players or gang up in packs as carnivores and over time the game had built up a community that functioned something like an actual ecosystem in the Sandbox mode.
However then they added the experimental progession system in Survival mod, while getting rid of Sandbox mode altogether. Which now meant that if you wanted to be a big dinosaur, you would have to start small and work your way up. Sounds alright. Here's the catch though: it only tallys points for time spent alive in the game...not for hunting or surviving or even giving extra points for doing so... but just sitting about for an hour until you get the points to progress to the next level. So most players are just idle until they get the points to upgrade their dino. And if you die, everything is set back to zero...
So this leads into the problem for those who actually try playing carnivores normally usually have no one active to hunt for food as they are hidden away farming points, meaning either starving, killing your friends for food, or by chance stumbling across someone AFK and simply offing them.
But what about the AI dinosaurs the game says it has? Can't they be hunted for food? Sure...if you can find them. Only one or two at a time spawn on a map, and that is if the server admins allow it. And even if you do find them, they just walk in circles around prelaid node paths and don't react at all to players. So the only reliable/interesting food scource to find for carnivores in Survival are the herbivore players...who are hidding away and farming their points...so by the time your tiny raptor has found someone to hunt, they've already gotten to stegosaurus levels and you're left to starve or die to them if you even get close.
However with the last big update they did bring back Sandbox mode...but they deleted all the previous maps and replaced it with one huge one that is that is almost always night. So now no one can find each other in the dark, empty map because it's three times the size of the past maps and because well...straining your eyes looking for anything in the dark enviroment sounds pleasent, doesn't it? Oh, also, the new map constently has trouble properly spawning you in without crashing or glitching...
Seriously, this game did have potential. A lot, and still may have some. However the developers keep making bizzare choices in developing their game, spending time making all these maps and skins for dinosaurs, but only to delete it all, basically having wasted the time put into them instead of using it to farther develop the actual game. This game was released WAY too early for its own good.
So for now, just follow the game's progress and wait to see if it manages to turn into something before actually getting it...but at this point my hopes are low. If you still want a dinosaur survival game, check out Dinosaur Battlegrounds or Saurian. They're looking much better right now and should be releasing soon...

I can't heap enough praise on this game. I used to play it when I was young, but I never understood the more philosophical concepts, and even the story until now. To me, the Star Wars Universe has always seemed somewhat childish, but this game takes the universe to a different level. Even though it came out in 2005, I think it has aged surprisingly well, but this is in part due to a relatively recent graphical update. Even though this is the second installment in the series, you don't have to play the first in order to understand the second game (this one). It takes roughly 50 hours to finish.
There are however a couple things wrong with the game in that there are some bugs and a good amount of cut content that starts to become apparent towards the end. The bugs were't game breaking though, they mostly involved the game skipping through multiple lines of dialogue or even whole conversations, after which I would revert to a previous save and try again. The cut content wasn't all that noticable until the last 5 hours of the game, and thats where some parts of the story didn't add up. I would highly recommend picking this game up, as it's basically a gaming classic.

This game is pretty sparse on the story but the atmospheric lighting and decent music score make for an immersive playthrough. The default controls with a gamepad are pretty horrible so I recommend altering them to make the game a little bit easier on the hands. Gameplay becomes a bit redundant and routine but if you're a fan of stealth games, give it a shot. This game has, by far, one of the greatest stories you will ever experience. And I would sex 227 more times.
The creators place you in a mediocre home. one large window in the front of the home, an average couch, family portrait, lamp. And it begins with your mother, gazing at you in discontent. She sports a rather dull purple blouse and a navy blue skirt. The real story hits you hard at this point. She seems to dissipate into thin air, appearing to drive away in a what looks to be an Audi or Mini Cooper. The young girl watches, waits, stares, looks, observes, sees, and any synonym thereof.
She then shyfully, makes her way to her dolls. One male, one female. This is where you, the player, take control of this delectable, ripe little girl. The choice is yours, you smash and rotate dolls in an increasingly curious rush to discover how you "do it." The blonde thinks of the sex scene in the Titanic and things her Mimi has told her.
So very fascinating.
Then, her mother returns, which makes you question where she went in the first place. You immediately throw down the dolls and turn around blushing. The game promptly ends and tells you how many times you have had sex.
This game has truly opened my eyes in terms of story writing. I implore you to play this game for a minimum of 24 hours to truly experience how great this game is. It baffles you how much you can learn.

Oh boy. Where to begin...
This is Supergiants third outing and their third triumphant success. Though it is a departure from their previous games, Bastion and Transistor, they have clearly become masters of their craft. This game is filled to the brim with stunning character design and excellent writing. How they can write such a rich world of engaging characters with so many branching paths is beyond my understanding. Make no mistake about it, this game will make you feel for the characters with which you must suffer in exile. However, perhaps the most impressive aspect of the writing is that, unlike any story-driven game I can think of, winning or losing doesn't help or hinder you directly. In fact, there is no failure state. At all. Ever. Either result will be reflected in-universe. This game will not forget five minutes later. That result will send ripples throughout the entirety of the game. Many times I considered conceding to my opponents, to offer them a chance at a better life. Though I only did this once, I've never felt so good throwing a game. I felt it's effects for the rest of my playthrough... And I loved it.

Of course, I have yet to touch on the music. This is because, just like the storytelling in Pyre, so, too, does the music deserve its own paragraph and praise. Like the story itself, the songs have branches and paths unlike any game before it. Each song is dynamic, providing a different focus on instrumentation depending on who is talking or what choices you are making. When your adversaries threaten you, you will feel it, as that sweet percussion kicks in. On top of this, there are multiple arrangements of each song. There's plenty more about this mind-blowing soundtrack I wish I could share but to do so would include too many spoilers. Trust me when I say this is Darren Korb's most complex work yet, to say nothing of it's amazing orchestration.

And so... on to Gameplay. The world and its story hide within it a surprisingly polished, balanced and engaging class-based sports game, which are referred to as "Rites." Learning to use your companions to their fullest feels great and incredibly fun. It's easy to understand but quite challenging to master. After a time, you are also offered modifiers to challenge you further, such as making your opponents stronger or respawn faster, which I recommend selecting if you haven't been having much trouble. Remember, win or lose, the story will go on. Outside of the Rites, you'll mostly be talking to other exiles, purchasing trinkets and choosing paths to your destination. Different events, bonuses and stat-changes will occur depending on where you decide to go.

Honestly, if you're in the market for a horror game, I don't know if there's a better one than SOMA. Sure, the horror elements aren't the jump scares that entice Youtubers, but the haunting locations, terrifying monsters, and the huge plot make for an even larger horror experience. The game is also incredibly well polished and feels like a AAA title that is well worth the standard 30 dollar price tag.
On the topic of the plot, not only is it absolutely horrifying, but it's just pretty dang good, which is one of my major gripes with this game since I'm not typically a horror guy: the horror element can potentially drive people away from the thought provoking narrative. I've heard people online say that the gameplay elements of running and hiding can be tedious in some sections, but removing them makes the game a "walking simulator" in a sense. Because I had the Wuss mod installed, I was able to pretty much tailor the experience to something I much prefer (since I don't do jump scares and the gameplay sounded frustrating) but it's something to think about before purchasing.
Even with the Wuss mod installed, the game is super spooky, mainly because of the ambience that permeates throughout the game, the rich narrative spread throughout small tidbits of collectibles and secrets, and just the world itself deep within the ocean. Tight corridors, creepy looking facilities, and darkness are commonplace along with... other things...
tldr: SOMA is the best game I'd never play again

The original Darkness is one of those games I’d label as a cult classic. It didn’t sell amazingly well, but it has a passionate fan base that has seem to have grown over the years. The gory combat and unique darkness powers alone were awesome, but it was the dark hopeless story of mafia hit man, Jackie Estacado, and the struggles he went through after obtaining the demonic powers of the Darkness that made it so interesting. With the original developer Starbreeze having moved on, there was a lot of skepticism when it was announced that Digital Extremes was doing a sequel so long after the first came out. Could they really capture what made the first game so great? In short, yes.
The game takes place two years after the end of the first and has our main hero Jackie Estacado living the good life as the don of his crime family. He’s been keeping the Darkness suppressed all this time, knowing if he lets it out it will consume him. That doesn’t last very long. When Jackie gets ambushed while at a restaurant, it forces him to release the darkness and tear though New York looking for revenge. Soon Jackie learns the hit was the work of the Brotherhood, a cult lead by the horribly disfigured Victor. They of course want to take the Darkness away from Jackie and keep it for themselves. The Brotherhood’s backstory and motivations are interesting enough, but they take a bit of a backseat during the second half to allow the game to focus more on Jackie.
The times when the action slowed down for the more character driven scenes were a highlight of the first game. It really added a lot of depth and made you feel for the characters, which made it all the more heart breaking when everything went to♥♥♥♥♥♥ The Darkness II still manages to pull these moments off pretty successfully. Jackie still hasn’t gotten over the death of his girlfriend Jenny and he suffers periodically from ghostly images and flashbacks of her. These moments let Jenny still play an important part in the story and allow for some scenes between her and Jackie, such as dancing in a dinner. In fact, the game spends a lot of time dealing with Jackie’s struggle of both the loss of Jenny and with the Darkness itself. This largely manifests with Jackie waking up from time to time in a mental asylum that’s bares a striking resemblance to the one in One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest. Here all the people in Jackie’s life are ether patients or staff members and the Darkness is simply a delusion that Jackie suffers from. Bringing in the idea that Jackie may simply be crazy and the majority of the game is an illusion, is a neat twist that is by far the most interesting part of the game.
This all works so well thanks to a great cast of characters and the voices behind them. Kirk Acevedo doesn’t return as Jackie but his replacement, Brian Bloom, does an excellent job replacing him. Mike Patton returns as the voice of the Darkness and continues to give a wonderfully creepy performance. I find something very enjoyable about hearing that disturbing voice that I can’t quite explain. Even the side characters are pretty good. Jackie’s crew of mobsters all sound their part, giving off that stereotypical Italian accent with plenty of character.
Jackie’s path of madness and revenge has plenty of enemies for you brutally mutilate and disfigure along the way and from the get go you’re given plenty of ways to kill. In addition to your guns, which you can duel wield, you get your two darkness tentacles. The right tentacle can be used to slash up enemies as well as obstacles that get in your way. The left tentacle is used to pick things up. It can pick up hearts off dead enemies and eats them to regain health. It picks up objects such as pipes that can be used to impale guys Commando style. And it even picks up stunned enemies so you can finish them off with a gruesome execution. It’s all just really satisfying.
It almost feels like you’re too powerful at the beginning of the game because the standard thugs and henchmen aren’t much of a challenge, spending most of their time freaking out as you murder their comrades. It’s once you start fighting the brotherhood that there is more enemy variation. There are guys with shields that you’ll have to loosen before you can rip them off of them. Some guys teleport around avoiding your attacks. The two more interesting enemy types include these weaker enemies that carry giant lights to try and disable Jackie’s darkness powers with them, and dudes with a whip that disarm Jackie of his weapons. The addition of these guys makes it much more necessary to use all your different powers rather than relying on a few.
Everything you do, whether it’s shooting a guy or eating his heart, gets you dark essence. You use the dark essence as currency and spend them on a skill tree to buff(?) current abilities or even gain new ones. Skills range from more ammo for guns, summoning deadly black holes, or unlocking even more horrifying executions. All of this does a great job at keeping the combat feeling fresh during the latter half of the game.
The structure of the levels is fairly linear and mostly consists of shooting your enemies, with the exception of an occasional sequence where you control your incredibly British darkling buddy. The only real non-linear parts are in between missions where you do get a chance to roam around Jackie’s penthouse. These act as good breathers from all the merciless killing and give you a chance to talk with all your mobster buddies.
The single player ran me about 5 and a half hours to beat which sounds short, but I can’t think of anything else they could have added without making it feel padded out. You could always pop back in with new game plus to finish upgrading your powers and collect any artifacts you missed, or you could head into vendettas. It’s a 4 player co-op mode featuring a cast of colorful characters all infused with some of the darkness’s powers. The game modes are fairly straight forward, with your group running through the area and basically killing everyone in your path. Every character has their own unique weapon such as an evil samurai blade or a voodoo staff but their powers are all lifted from the campaign so it doesn’t feel especially different. There is some interesting dialogue between the characters and while they’re not really necessary to the overall story, it does at make it more entertaining. Vendetta’s is a fun distraction, but it’s something that most people will probably play once or twice for the achievements and then be done with it.
It’s kind of amazing that a sequel to The Darkness was able to happen at all so long after its release. What’s even more amazing is how well Digital Extremes was able to recreate what made the first game so good, and then expand on it and make it their own, especially with the track record of their last couple of games. The Darkness II has succeeded in reinvigorating my excitement for more Darkness, and that’s certainly not a bad thing.

is a breathtaking World War II stealth game about the missions of Violette Summer, a British spy loosely based on the real-life British intelligence agent Violette Szabo. Summer lies badly wounded in a hospital in France and recalls her operations behind enemy lines from the streets of occupied Paris, over Hamburg, to the Warsaw Ghetto, taking out Nazi officers and sabotaging Germany’s war machine all the while handling more than limited resources to pursue her objective. At no point does Velvet Assassin shy away from pointing out the horrors of war and tries its best to stay true to historical accuracy, but even more amazing than its premise and the suspense created within the game is that this World War II-era title was developed by a relatively small, independent German studio.
Given that this title was created by such a small company that had to shut its doors mid-2009, the game does not have as high a production value as Konami’s
series or Square-Enix’s
franchise. Because of that, the enemy AI might not be as sophisticated as in other games of the genre, nor are the levels as big as one might know them from AAA titles. Despite these restrictions,
manages to very easily capture the player’s attention right from the get-go and keep it up until the very end of its roughly 16 to 20 hour long campaign. Fans of
will feel right at home here.
At any given point in time, Violette can only carry up to three weapons, one of which is always her trusty knife with which she stabs Nazis from behind or slits their throats. Bullets for the guns are extremely scarce (usually she will only have about seven of them with her) and prevent players from just running and gunning through the streets of Europe. With that said, if you are an inexperienced player or become antsy quickly,
is a definite pass, but if you are patient and mindful of enemy patterns, you'll have a blast of a time.
In addition to the difficulty level, this game autosaves at certain spots that aren’t far away from one another area-wise, but due to the need to sneak through the levels strategically while exing off enemy soldiers, can take quite some time to get to. One of the more infuriating parts of the game is dying at a section then lurking in the shadows, waiting for the guards’ conversation to be over for the n-teenth time so they start patrolling and Violette can finally kill them and move on. At least, it was infuriating until I remembered that she can whistle to attract their attention, which not only immediately cut their conversation short, but also got them in a spot where eliminating them was that much easier.
The game’s cohesiveness in enemy encounters is what I appreciated the most as there are no almost no infuriating action sequences that do not fit the gameplay style. The only problematic segment was a cover-based shooting segment against the 36th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS also known as the Dirlewanger Brigade where players will have to fend of an onslaught of SS soldiers. Unless you are either really good at shooter games or have leveled up Violette's life meter, you will get stuck there for quite some time.
The game starts off with Violette lying in a hospital in France in 1944 during the war. She is badly wounded from her latest mission and dreams about/remembers her assignments in Germany, Poland, and France. To alleviate her pain, the staff injects her with morphine that slows down the time within her dream. If killing a Nazi soldier should become too difficult for the player, the morphine can be activated as basically a freebie (By leveling up her stats, Violette will eventually be able to carry three syringes instead of one and can thus use the morphine up to three times per stage). During this morphined state, Violette runs around in a negligee for some reason, mist rises from the ground, and rose petals fall from the sky. She can then straight up run to one enemy and stab him to death. Players should be careful that whichever Nazi soldier they want to stab isn't accompanied by anyone else, as after he is killed, the game returns to normal, the other enemy soldier will be alerted, and will surely attempt to kill Violette in an instant.
The design is fabulous. The stages have everything from romantic promenades to eery sewers. The music then completes the scary atmosphere and the German soldiers speak German fluently, which came as a welcome surprise.
Regrettably, the game’s options menu is rather bareboned and might leave players with a couple of wishes. Although I do not mind, some players may not appreciate motion blur in their video games. In their cases, they can head to the 《Velvet Assassin》 folder in Windows, then go to the 《FX》 folder and then to 《PostFX》, where they can then erase the 《directional_blur.pfx》 file.
is a must get for stealth game fans. It is very engaging and brings with it a nice twist to both the stealth as well as the World War II game genre while maintaining to be historically accurate with just enough artistic license to make the game as thrilling as it is. The music, the graphic design, and the voiceover are superb, but the fight against the Dirlewanger Brigade can put a dent into things. Being a small studio’s game, the less sophisticated enemy AI is definitely forgivable and so is the fact that stages are not the same size as in Metal Gear. The options menu is not perfect, but everything that can be customized, is easily accessible in the game’s folders (provided one knows where to look and what to look for). With all that in mind,
is an outright gritty game that does not shy away from discussing the horrors of the Nazi regime. Stealth game fans will most certainly enjoy it and feel right at home.

Sniper Elite V2 is a good game, it's not great, but it knocks a few things out of the park.
Let's start with the things this game does right, sniping. There is no other game that offers sniping like this.
along with the animations that go along with hits. those are great fun. Let me give you an example of the amazing physics of this game. I shot at a sniper up in a window, it then showed the bullet animation, through that i learned that my hit was a little low and not direct. The bullet actually ricocheted off of the windowsill. Then the flattened bullet spinned upward into the snipers head.
Now the things it does wrong. The stealth in this game is mediocre, which is unfortunate because you are trying to sneak most of the game. The way in which enemies see you seems to be random. I will Randomly be spotted behind cover sometimes, and then right in front of an enemy without him seeing me other times. Or I can be away from an enemy 200 meters in prone position and be spotted like i was right in front of the guy. Taking cover behind objects is not smooth, compared to other games at least. Cover that should be linked together for a continous crawl isn't. And emerging from cover sometimes results in looking right into more cover. The last small complaint I have is the enemy snipers. Which at least in the sniper elite game mode (Hardest Difficulty,) they are dead accurate. By this I mean they will not miss ever, if I sneak to another peice of cover and emerge there, there is no readjustment time for the enemy sniper. They are the real elite snipers in this game, I don't think anyone can adjust in time to hit one before they hit you, which will never insta kill you, but is annoying none the less.
All in all I would give this game a solid 6.5 out of 10. I don't think it's worth picking up for 29.99, but if it's on sale I would recommend giving it a try, it is definitely fun, just annoying at times.
TL;DR game is great when it comes to sniping but has a lot of bugs concerning stealth. 6.5/10

You are not a true Star Wars fan until you've played KOTOR 2 with the Restored Content Mod. Few stories in all of Star Wars history can match the sheer quality of story and depth of character in this game. You get detailed, in-depth character development, an intriguing story, consistent moral quandries, ruminations on the nature of the Force and the Jedi and one of the most greatest Jedi characters you will ever see. No matter how you play him/her, the Jedi Exile's personal story is utterly exceptional, as s/he is forced to face the crimes of their past and the perils of their future.
If you're an action gamer who skips all the cutscenes, give this a miss. KOTOR 2 is very dialogue heavy, full of rich storytelling and complicated questions. If, however, that sounds right up your alley, then strap in.
This is one of the finest Star Wars stories ever written.
Eventually, you'll have to hit "Y" to exit to DOS. But you'll be back.

This is not Dead by Daylight, this is 100X better. Much more dynamic games with multiple objectives and much more intricate strategies. Teamwork is vital and communication is key, which means if you play with a good group the social rewards and fun are amazing.
A lot of people complain that Jason is OP, but that's the point! DbD has nerfed the killer so that randos, each playing their own non-strategy can win the game in Generator Repair Simulator. This is not that game. It's balanced so that Jason is a serious force to contend with, and only by working together can you defeat him.
I haven't had this much fun playing a game for a long time. There are so many epic moments. The only caveat I have for this game is that you need to find good people to play with who know how to be team players. Disorganized people playing solo will get slaughtered by Jason. Find friends who will talk to you using the awesome proximity chat, and you will find yourselves escaping plenty of times! There will be epic moments, funny moments, and soul-crushing "what happened?" moments.
I totally recommend this game. Give it a shot. I hope there are a lot more expansions and DLC in the future to continue the fun dynamics I've experienced so far. =)

So I bought this game thinking it would be something unique, I trust the developers of this game; they have yet to make a game I have not enjoyed immensly.
Pyre exceeded every expectations.
The game has 3 pillars which in my opinion make the game great.
1. The Story,
The narative immerses you in a world unlike any you have seen, which some loose inspirations for Alice in Wonderland & Dune, full of beautifuly designed creatures and lands to explore. The story itselves draws you in with its mysterious world it presents you with; only to captivate you with a breaktaking story that will keep you engaged untill you finish the game.
2. The Gameplay,
While most of the game takes the form off an RPG, the real gameplay meat lies in the "Rites" you must perform throughout the game. Essentially, its a magical sports game where your goal is to jump into the enemy teams bonfire. While as confusing as that may sound it is the biggest breath of fresh air I have played in a long time. There is really nothing else like it. Every character you meet behaves differently with unique abilities and atributes that make them stand out. Its definetly something I look forward to trying with my mates, as the game does support local multiplayer.
3. The Characters,
Usually I don't care much for charcters in video games, if throwing princess peach into a volcano meant I could unlock a bonus level you bet I would. This game caused me actual stress when I faced with decisions that would impact the fate of my new friends I made traveling the world, and there is nothing else like it. It says something about a game and the characters that preside in it when my personal favorite character is an orb.
I cannot reccomend this game enough for anyone intrest in games, excellent stories, or just a unique experience. This is easily one of my favorite games of all time.
